Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended _ v. , His Majesty in the House of Peers, where His Majesty Speech re- was pleased to make a moil Gracious Speech from the ported. Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr.

Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as fob loweth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Since 1 last met you in Parliament, the Disputes which appeared to threaten an Interruption to the Tranquillity of Europe have been brought to an amicable Conclusion; and I continue to receive from Foreign Powers the strongest Assurances of their friendly Disposition towards this Country.

At home. My Subjects experience the growing BlelT-ings of Peace, in the ExtensionofTrade, the Improvement of the Revenue, and the Increase of the public Credit of the Nation.

For the further Advancement of those important Objects, I rely on the Continuance of that Zeal and Industry which you manifested in the last SclUon of Parliament.

The Resolutions which you laid before Me, as the Basis of an Adjustment of the Commercial intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland, have been, by My Direction, communicated to the Parliament of that Kingdom; but no effectual Step has hitherto been taken thereupon which can enable you to make any further Progress in that salutary Work.

I have ordered the Estimates for the present Year to be laid before you: It is My earnest With to enforce

Oeconomy in every Department; and you will, I am persuaded, be equally ready to make such Provision as may be necessary for the Public Service, and particularly for maintaining our Naval Strength on tlje 109ft secure and reiftf&able Footing. — Above all, let recommend to you the Establishment of a fixed |*lan for the Reduction of the National Debt The flourishing State of the Revenue will, I trust, enable you to effect this important Measure with little Addition to the Public Burthens.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Vigour and Resources of the Country, so fully manifested in its present Situation, will encourage you in continuing to give your utmost Attention to every ObjeCfc of National Concern; particularly to the Consideration of such Measures as may be necessary in order to give further Security to the Revenue, and to promote and extend, as far as possible, the Trade and General Industry of My Subjects.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty our tnoft humble Tlianks for His Gracious Speech from the Throne:

To express our Satisfaction that the Disputes which appeared to threaten an Interruption to the Tranquillity of Europe have been brought to an amicable Conclusion; and, that His Majesty continues to receive from Foreign Powers the strongest Assurances of their friendly Disposition towards this Country:

To allure His Majesty, that we are deeply sensible of the Blefiings which we experience from the Enjoyment of Peace, in the Extension of Trade, the Improvement of the Revenue, and the Increase of the Public Credit of the Nation; and that His Majesty may rely on the utmost Exertion of our Zeal and Industry for the farther Advancement of these important Objects:

That, in order to promote, as far as in us lay, the common Interests of all His Majesty's Subjects, we humbly laid before His Majesty, in the last Session of Parliament, several Resolutions, as the Basis of an Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; but that, as uo effectual Step has been hitherto taken thereupon by the Parliament of that Kingdom, we do not find ourselves at present enabled to make any farther Progreis in that salutary Work:

To express our Gratitude for His Majesty’s gracious Assurances of His earnest Wilh to enforce Oeconomy in every Department; and our Readiuefs, at all Times, to make such Provision as may be necessary for every Branch of the Public Service, particularly for maintaining the Naval Strength of these Kingdoms on the most secure and respectable Footing: That, as we are fully imprefied with the Necessity of establishing a fixed Plan for the Reduction of the National Debt, we shall lose no Time in entering on that important Consideration; and that it will afford us the most solid Satisfaction to find that this most desirable Object may be attained with little Addition to the Public Burthens:

That the Vigour and RefourCes so happily manifested in our present Situation mud give Encouragement and Confidence to all His Majesty’s Subjects; and cannot fail to animate our Exertions in endeavouring, by a continued Attention to the Security of the Revenue, and the Extension of Trade, to confirm and improve the increasing Prosperity of the Empire;

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers resident in the Town of Halifax, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, burthened as they are with the Duty imposed on Retail Shops, beg Leave to seek that Redress from Parliament, which, they conceive, the Justice and Equity of their same require, and, as the Ground of their Application, to ltate to the House, that the Oppression of the said Tax is grievously felt by them; that the Equivalent promised and held out to the Shopkeepers of this Kingdom, at the Time the said Duty was imposed, by abolishing the Licences granted to Hawkers and Pedlars, made them at that Time chearfully acquiesce under what appeared to the Petitioners a necessary Imposition upon the Subject, yet, eventually, such promised Compensation has, in a great Measure, been denied to them; and that the Petitioners, sensible as they are, that the Legislature of this Kingdom meant not to tax any Set of Men without having an Eye to Equality in its Consequences, crave Permission to inform the Commons of Great Britain, that, from Experience and Observation, the said Tax operates immediately upon them as an additional House Duty, without a Possibility of reimbursing themselves by a Charge upon any of the Articles they vend: Under these Circumstances, the Petitioners presume to ask and hope, that the House will take their same into serious Confederation, and afford them the fought-for Redress, by a Repeal of that Law which bears fb partially hard upon a Description of Men whole Inclinations are forward to support the Exigencies of Government, in common with the rest of their Fellow Subjects, to the utmost of their Power.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Bailiffs, Burgesses, and Common- Tewkesbury alty, of the Borough of Tewkesbury, in the County of Pavin8* Gloucester, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Borough of Tewkesbury is a large and populous Market Town, situate in the great Road from Holyhead, Chester, Salop, and Worcester, to Gloucester, Bath, Bristol, and other Places in the Western Parts of the Kingdom; and that the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and Places, within the said Town, and the Precincts thereof, are irregularly paved, and not properly cleansed or lighted, and are annoyed by Incroachments and Nuisances, and have no regular Watch; and that it would be of great Utility to the Inhabitants of the said Town, if Power was given to regulate Carts and other Carriages, and to ascertain the Rates of Carriage therein; and, it would be a public Convenience, if Part of the Street called Church Street was widened: And therefore praying,

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's' most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty our humble Thanks for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We learn, with great Satisfaction, that the Disputes which appeared to threaten an Interruption to the Tranquillity of Europe have been brought to an amicable Conclusion, and that Your Majesty continues to receive from Foreign Powers the strongest Assurances of their friendly Disposition towards this Country.

We are deeply sensible of the Blessings which we experience from the Enjoyment of Peace, in the Extension of Trade, the Improvement of the Revenue, and the Increase of the Public Credit of the Nation: And Your Majesty may rely on the utmost Exertion of our Zeal and Industry for the further Advancement of these important Objects.

In order to promote, as far as in us lay, the common Interests of all Your Majesty’s Subjects, we humbly laid before Your Majesty, in the last Session of Parliament, several Resolutions, as the Basis of an Adjustment of the Commercial Intercourse between Great Britain and Ireland; but, as no effectual Step has been hitherto taken thereupon by the Parliament of that Kingdom, we do not find ourselves at present enabled to make any farther Progress in that salutary Work.

We cannot refrain from offering the warmest Expressions of our Gratitude, for Your Majesty’s gracious Assurances of Your earnest Wi(h to enforce Oeconomy in every Department: We shall be equally ready, at all Times, to make such Provision as may be necessary for every Branch of the Public Service, particularly for maintaining the Naval Strength of these Kingdoms on the most secure and rel'peftable Footing. Fully impressed with the Necessity of establishing a fixed Plan for the Reduction of the National Debt, we shall lose no Time in entering on that important Consideration; and it will afford us the most lolid Satisfaction to find that this most desirable Object may be attained with little Addition to the Public Burthens.

The Vigour and Resources so happily manifested in our present Situation mull give Encouragement and Confidence to all Your Majesty’s Subjects, and cannot fail to animate our Exertions in endeavouring, by a continued Attention to the Security of the Revenue, and the Extension of Trade, to confirm and improve the increasing Prosperity of the Empire.

The Sum of Two millions Eight hundred and Thirty-three thousand Nine hundred and Forty-two Pounds, Nine Shillings, and Eight Pence Three Farthings, the Net Produce, of the Customs in this Year, as stated in 4*‘ this Account, does not agree with the Sum of Two millions Seven hundred and Seventy-two thousand Three hundred and Forty-six Pounds, Six Shillings, and Four Pence Halfpenny, stated in the Account of the Auditor of the Imprest to have been paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer: Nor does the Sum of Two hundred and Eighty-one thousand Two hundred and Twenty-two Pounds. There are feme Articles, both in the Receipts and Payments, at the Out Ports, which were erroneous when transmitted from thence to the Board of Customs. These Errors could not be corrected Time enough to have the Articles inserted with Accuracy in the Account before the Auditor j but they are set right in this last Account, which is a correct State of the Ports in that Year. But, independent of such Errors, the Net Produce can hardly ever agree with the Sum paid into the Exchequer: — The component Parts of these Two Sums are not the same: The Sum paid into the Exchequer includes the Duties remitted to the Receiver General from Scotland and the Plantations; the Net Produce is the Produce of those Duties only which are collected in London and at the Out Ports: The Sum paid into the Exchequer does not contain such Part of the Duties collected at the Out Ports, as were not remitted to the Receiver General, or if remitted, were not turned into Cash during the Year; but the Net Produce comprehends all the Duties collected at the Out Ports during the Year, whether they became Cash in the Hands of the Receiver General or not: The Sum paid into the Exchequer consists of Cash only, arising either from Duties actually paid, or from the Discharge of Bonds given in preceding Years to secure the Duties; but the Net Produce includes not only the Duties paid to the Receiver General in Cash, but also those secured by Bonds, which, though remaining in his Hands in the Shape of Securities, are yet blended with the Duties he has received, and charged upon him in One compound Sum.

We should have proceeded to the Examination of the Articles, that composed this Sum of Charges for the Year 1781; but we found, upon Inquiry, that among so great a Number of Officers, feme being dead, others having resigned their Employments or changed their Situations, it would be hardly possible to procure a complete Account of the Emoluments of the Officers for a Year so distant from the present

Time; and therefore we turned our Attention to the Expences of the last Year, and required from the Office of the Customs Two Accounts; the one, of the Grofe Salaries, Fees, Allowances, and Gratuities received by the Commissioners and the Officers of the Customs in the Port of London, distinguishing by what Authority they are respectively appointed, with the Payments for Taxes, Deputies, Clerks, and other contingent Expences, all distinguished under their levered Heads, and the Net Produce received by each Officer for the Year 1784; the other, a similar Account of the Officers at the Out Ports.

The Return to the First of these Requisitions con- n° 6. tains the Officers belonging to the Customs in London.

They are ranged under Two general Divisions: First,

The Board, with the Officers attending them, and employed io conducting the general Business of this Revenue: Secondly, The Officers of the Port of London. — These Two comprehend several Subdivisions.

The First includes the Commissioners — the Secretary and Clerks — the Housekeeper — the Law Officers — the Officers of Receipt, Payment, Control, Examination, and Account The Second Class are distinguished either by the Business they transact, or the Place where they transact it. The Business arises from Imports or Exports, by Natives or Foreigners, or from Carriage Coastwise: It is carried on in the Long Room at the Customhouse — on Shipboard — at the Waterside — and, in Warehouses.

In this Return, the Salaries and Allowances paid to the Officers by the Crown, that is, out of this Revenue, . are distinguished from the Fees and Emoluments they receive from the Merchant, with a View of al’certaining how much the Revenue and Subject each contribute to the Support of these Offices; and the Salaries and Allowances paid to the Deputies and Clerks, by the Principal or other Officers, are placed in a separate Column from those paid to them by the Crown; because, being included in the Salaries and Allowances paid by the Crown to the Principal or other Officers, they would, unless so distinguished, be Twice charged to the Account of the Revenue.

The Deductions from the Profits of the Officers, by the Payment of Taxes, are distinguished from the other Deductions; because the Taxes returned into the Exchequer have the same Effect as a Payment back to the Public of so much of their Salaries and Allowances, and, consequently, are so far a Diminution of the Public Expence, excepting, what cannot easily be computed, the Diminution these Taxes suffer by the Charges of Collection, and the Lois sustained by the Public from the Delay of their Return into the Exchequer. One of the Taxes to which the Salaries and Payments to feme of these Officers are subject, is the Superannuation Fund, which has been long established in the Customs, as a Support for certain of the Officers, chiefly in the inferior Departments, who are worn out in the Service. As this Deduction from the Pay is not applied to the Use of the Public, we have separated it from those Taxes which are paid into the Exchequer.

The Circumstances to which we principally attended, in this Inquiry, are — the Authority that appoints — the Mode of Appointment — the Duration of the Interest — the Business transacted — and the Reward for the Execution. William Stiles, Esquire, Secretary to the N° 7. Commissioners of the Customs, gave us Information on these Subjects.

The Appointment of every Officer, is either by the King, the Board of Treasury, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Commissioners of the Customs, or the Superior Officers in the Departments. — The King appoints by his Letters Patent. The Board of Treasury either appoints by Constitution or names by Warrant. The Chancellor of the Exchequer appoints

46 Geo. III. 370 Januarii. 11

by Warrant. The Board of Customs, by Comvniffiori or Order.

A Constitution by the Board of Tre&fary, contains both the Nomination and Appointment of the Officer but the Warrant of that Board is only a Nomination of the Person, and a Requisition to the Commissioners of the Customs to appoint hhn: The Mode of Appointment is by Commission under the Hands of Four of them, and the Seal of Office; and from hence the Officer derives the Authority and Powers annexed to his Office. The Officers thus constituted by the King, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, or these Boards, comprehend all that are paid, either by Dormant Warrants, or upon the EstablHh-ment.

Where the Commissioners of the Customs aft without the Intervention of the Treasury, they appoint either by Commission or by Order of the Board: These are called Incidental Officers.

The Deputies are alt appointed by the Patentees, subject in some Instances to the Approbation of the Treasury. The Clerks are appointed, forne by the faperior Officers in the Department, tome by or with the Approbation of the Board of Customs, and others by the Treasury.

Upon every Nomination to an Office by Warrant of the Treasury, the Commissioners of the Customs direct an Inquiry whether the Person named has ever been dismissed the Service; if he has, they return the Warrant to the Treasury, stating this Objection, and the Person to be therefore madraitlible. Where the Office is that of a Collector, unless the Objection of Difoiiffion ariles, the Commissioners appoint him without farther Inquiry. If it be the Office of a Landing Surveyor, Landing Waiter, or Coast Waiter, and the Person named appears, upon Inquiry, to be ignorant of the Duty of the Office, he is put under Instructions for a certain Time, and not admitted to the Office but upon the Certificate of the proper Officer that he is duly qualified. Where it is an inferior Office, and there are Objections to his Age or Qualifications, the Commissioners return the Warrant, and state the Objections to the Treasury.

The Tenure of these Offices is either for Life, or during Pleasure. Some of the Letters Patent grant an Interest for Life; but most of them, and all the other Forms of Appointment, are during Pleasure only.

We procured from the Office of the Customs a List of the Offices holden by Letters Patent, with the Date of each Patent, the Names of the Officers in Possession, and their respective Interests therein; and from the Office of the Treasury, a List of those granted in Reversion, with the Dates of each Grant, the Names of the Grantees, and their respective Interests therein.

Many of the Offices are Sinecures; the Officer never attends, nor executes any Part of the Business; it is transacted entirely by Deputies and Clerks. We examined into the Duty and Business transefted in every Office, unless where the Description of that Duty is contained in the Examination of the same, or any other Officer, annexed to our last Report.

The Emoluments accruing from these Offices, are — Salaries — Allowances — Fees — Gratuities — and, Shares in the Produce of Seizures. The Salaries are some of them expressed in the Patents, Constitutions, and Warrants: In some of these Instruments they are not expressed, but ascertained by Reference to those Salaries inierted in former Instruments, or that have been usually annexed to the same Appointments. Other of the Salaries depend upon the Commission or Order of the Board of Customs; and the ferae Officer has frequently a Variety of Salaries given him by different Instruments.

The Allowances flow either from the Warrants Vo l.41.

of the Treasury or Orders of the Board of Customs. An Allowance is frequently not eafrly to be distinguished from a Salary: It is fotnetimes an Annual Payment, in Addition to, or in lieu of, a Salary; sometimes a Recompence for fomte special Service. One of these Allowances is for the Quarantine Service. The Execution of tire Orders of the Privy Council, relative to Ships performing Quarantine in all the Ports of England, is intrusted to the Officers of the Customs; but being properly no Part of the Business of the Customs, the Board of Treasury, by Warrant dated the 19th of December 172a, in Confe-

Juenee of a Memorial from the Commissioners of the lustoms, directed Two hundred Pounds a Year to be paid to each of the Commissioners for their extraordinary Service, Care, and Pains relating to the Quarantine, until it should, by the King’s Command, cease to be performed. This Allowance was extended, by subsequent Warrants, to the Secretary, the Western, Northern, and Copying Clerks, and to some other Officers. The Payments are all made by virtue of an Annual Warrant from the Treasury, directing the Receiver General to pay to the Officers named in a List transmitted to the Treasury from the Customs, and annexed to the Warrant, the Sums therein mentioned. The Allowances are different: That to each of the Commissioners is a fixed Sum; that to the other Officers is according to the Number of Ships — a certain Sum to each Officer, or Set of Officers, for every Ship put under Quarantine during the Year, except Men of War and Transports.

Four of these Allowances are Poundages: One upon the Coinage Duty; anotlter upon the Gross Produce arising from the Sale of Tea, Coffee, and Spirits, called the enumerated Goods, seized, condemned, and fold, pursuant to the Act of the Twelfth of George the First, Chapter the 28th; the Third upon the Coal Duty; and the Fourth upon the Produce of Seizures paid into the Exchequer.

The Poundage upon the Coinage Duty is grounded upon the Act of the 25th of Charles the Second, Chapter the 8th, which empowers the Board of Treasury to allow to the Officers employed in the Collection and Receipt of that Duty, out of the Money arising therefrom, Salaries and Allowances not exceeding in the Whole Twelve Pence in the Pound of the Money collected. By Warrant of the Treasury, dated the 13th of December' 1714, this Poundage is directed to be equally divided, in the Port of London, between the Receiver of the Duty, the Controller General, and the Receiver General; to each Four Pence in the Pound.

The Poundage upon the Gross Produce arising from the Sale of the enumerated Goods, is regulated by a Minute of the Board of Customs, dated the 9th of May 1728, and paid out of that Produce. This Minute directs what Poundage shall be paid to those, Officers, both in London and at the Out Ports, who are employed in the Conduct of this Business, as a Reward for their Service.

The Poundage upon the Coal Duty relates to the Out Ports only, and is grounded upon a Warrant of the Treasury, dated the 19th of September 1699, which directs Three per Cent, upon the First Thousand Pounds, and One per Cent, upon every Hundred Pounds afterwards, collected at the Out Ports, and so in Proportion, to be divided between the Collector and Controller, Two Thirds to the one, and One Third to the other, as a reasonable Compenfetion for their Service in this Branch of Duties.

The Poundage upon the Sum arising from the Produce of Seizures paid into the Exchequer, being the Emolument of a Angle Officer only, the Inspector of Prosecutions, will be aescribed hereafter, in the Account of that Office.

All the Salaries and Allowances, except the Poundages and the Incidental Expences of the Customs in London, are paid, unless otherwise directed by the Warrant or Order, out of the Duties placed under the Head of Customs; and in the Out Ports out of any Money in the Hands of the Collectors, to whatever Branch of Duty it may belong, unless it be one of the excepted Branches.

Regularly every Duty should defray the Expence it occasions: It ought to bear its Proportion of the General Charges of Management; but that is utterly impracticable, as the same Officer, or Class of Officers, with a Variety of different Stipends, collect and keep the Accounts of the numerous Branches, and the Amount of the Duties arising from the several Branches in the same Year, or from the same Branch in different Years, is very unequal; and as the same Incidental Expence relates to many or all of the Branches, it is near to an Impossibility to apportion the Salary, Allowance, or Expence among the several Branches, lb that each shall contribute its due Share to the common Charge.

N° 14. R appears by a Memorial of the Board of Customs to the Treasury, dated the 19th of May 1758, that before the Year 1709, the Charges of the Establishment, in every Port, were paid out of the Duties received under the Head of Customs: But by the Warrant of the Lord High Treasurer dated the 25th of

April 1710, the Collector of a Port, where the Receipt under that Head fell short to answer the Charges, was permitted to supply the Deficiency by borrowing from Five other Branches therein enumerated; which Five, together with the Customs, are called The United Branches. These too being frequently deficient, a Warrant of the Treasury, of the 31st of July 1761, issued in consequence of the Memorial of the 19th of May 1758, authorized the Board of Customs to direct the Application of all the Branches (except the Coinage Duty) to the Charges of Management This Warrant the Board carried into Execution by their Minutes of the 7th of August and 10th of October 1761.

The Fees received in the Customs are grounded, some upon Acts of Parliament, some upon Usage, and others are demanded and paid under the Name of Fees, but of which neither the Origin nor Authority appears. We required from the Office an Account of such Fees as the Officers are authorized to take by virtue of any Act of Parliament, and for what Business such Fees are payable.

Five Tables of Fees were returned to us pursuant ,5> to this Requisition. The First of them is the Copy of a Table hung up in the Long Room at the Customhouse in London.

The 24th Rule, at the End of the Book of Rates, annexed to the Act of Tonnage and Poundage, directs, " That no Officer belonging to the Customs shall receive any other or greater Fee, than such as are, or " shall be, established by the Commons in Parliament " assembled, on Pain of Forfeiture of his Office, and " Incapacity." By an Order of the House of Commons, dated the 17th of May 166a, and signed by Sir Edward Turner, then Speaker, mentioned and continued in force by the Act of the lit of Anne, Chapter the 13th, a Table of Fees for the Port of London was settled and confirmed, and a Copy directed to be set up in the Customhoulc.

At the End of a Collection of the Statutes, relative

to this Revenue, passed soon after the Restoration, printed by the King’s Printers, in the Year 1663 (produced to us by Mr. Richard Frewin, the Examiner of the Duties Inwards) this Order of the House of Commons is inserted, with the Table annexed; which appears, upon Comparison, to be the same with the Table returned to us firom the Long Room at the Customhouse.. Both the Order and Table are likewise to be found in some of the Books of Rates compiled and published for the Use of the Customs.

The other Four are Tables of Fees for the Ports of N* 16,17,18. Bristol, Great Yarmouth, Kingston upon Hull, and ,£>* Chester; and are copied from an old Book in the Customhouse.

It appears, from the Journals of the House of Commons, of the 17th of May 1662, that Tables for the Three First of those Ports were that Day reported to the House, and agreed to These Fees, established by the Legislature, are for Work done at legal Times and Places; but, for the Accommodation of Trade, the Act of the 6th and 7th of William and Mary, Chapter the 7th, authorizes the Officers to receive, for any Extraordinary Service, such a Recompence as the Commissioners in London, or any Two of the Collector, Customer, or Controller at an Out Port, shall determine.

By the Eighteenth Rule, annexed to the Book of Rates, the Attendance of the Officers who fit in the Customhouse in London, is from Nine to Twelve in the Forenoon; and one Officer, or able Clerk, is ordered to attend in the Afternoon, during the Time the Officers at the Waterside are in waiting. At the Out Ports, their Attendance is for the same Time in the Forenoon, and from Two to Four in the Afternoon.

By the Thirteenth Rule, the Merchant is permitted to lade or unlade his Goods, at the lawful Quays, from the 10th of September to the 10th of March, between Sunrifing and Sunletting; and in the other Half Year, from Six in the Morning to Six in the Evening; and the Officers appointed to attend the lading and unlading must, upon Notice, be in waiting. These not having been altered by the Legislature, still continue to be the legal Hours of Business, though departed from in Practice, changing with the Manners of the Times.

The Table for London, above-mentioned, contains the Fees payable to certain Officers, and for certain Business only: But, as the Business of the Customs and Number of Officers are greatly increased since the Restoration, and consequently many other Fees are paid at the Customhouse, and in the Port of London, than are to be found in this Table, we required from the Office an Account of all Fees usually taken by the several Officers of the Customs, including Patentees,

Deputies, and Clerks, and all others of every De-Icription whatever, in the Port of London, distinguishing for what Business or Documents such Fees are paid, exclusive of Stamps.

The Return to this Requisition contains a distinct Lift of all the Fees taken by each Officer and Clerk respectively, in every Department of the Customs in London; and consequently, it includes, though it does not distinguish them, the Fees established by the Legislature, as well as those grounded upon Usage, or the Discretion of the Officer. We have, in Obedience to the Injunctions of the Legislature, extracted from this Return, and annexed to our Examination into each Department, a List of foe Fees taken by the several Officers and Clerks in that Department. Such of them as derive their Authority from the Order of 1662 will, upon referring to it, be found in the Table established by that Order.

The Gratuities received 'by these Officers are, in general, as a Recompence for Business transa&ed either out of their proper Department, or out of Office Hours, or upon the Sufferance Quays, or for additional Trouble.

Among the Profits attending these Offices, we did not require what arose from the Produce of Seizures. This Species of Emolument is confined to Officers of certain Descriptions only: It is precarious in its Nature, very different in different Years, much diminished by late Regulations of the Legislature, and may, by similar Regulations hereafter, there is Reason to hope, be almost extinguished; and therefore the Knowledge of what each Officer received from it in the Year 1784 can be no Ground for the Regulation of his future Establishment: But although we did not require it, many of the Officers have included, among their Emoluments, the Allowances they receive out of the Produce of Seizures.

An Article of Commerce, liable to a Custo'm Duty upon Importation, must, to secure the Payment of the Duty, be watched from the Time the Ship enters the Port, until the Duty is paid; and being forfeited by evading the Duty, it may be pursued and seized. An Article liable to a Duty upon Exportation, rauft, to prevent its being changed or altered, be guarded from the Time the Duty is paid, until the Ship has quitted the Port: And an Article entitled to a Drawback or Bounty upon Exportation, must, to prevent the re-landing it, be guarded from the Time the Merchant delivers it to the Officer, until the Ship has quitted- the Port.

Hence arises the Necessity for different Classes of Officers, to attend upon and examine these Articles, at different Stages, in their Passage between the Ship and the Merchant; and to pursue them if they escape the Duty.

There are also Three Species of Commerce — Coals — East India Goods — and Tobacco, each of which is extensive enough to require and employ distinct Sets of Officers in the Management of those particular Branches only. Upon these Circumstances the Distinfiions of the following Classes are grounded.

The Landing Surveyors have all the same Salary from the Crown. Thirty-five Pounds is allowed them for every Sale of condemned Goods at the Custom-house. Their Fees arise only from the Business they transact oht of Office Hours, and at the Sufferance Quays; and are allowed them as a Compensation for such extraordinary Service, under the Act of King William. Both the Allowances for the Sales, and the Fees, are divided equally among the Nine Officers. The first Six received also a Present of Spices from the East India Company, valued at Five Pounds Four Shillings: But the Company having some Time ago resolved to discontinue this Prefect to all future Officers, the Three last, having been appointed since that Resolution, did not receive the Present; which occasions the Difference in the Amount of their Fees.

The Landing Waiters and Deputy King’s Waiters are all employed indiscriminately in the same Branch of Business; the superintending the Landing of all Foreign Goods imported. The Salaries of the Landing Waiters are equal, except that the Six last, called the Additional Landing Waiters, have a lei's Salary than the others. The Fees are customary Payments, by the Merchants, upon every Species of Merchandize, according to a certain Rate agreed upon by them. The Amount of them to each depends upon the Number and Value of the Ships to which he is appointed: But as these Officers are not appointed to Ships by Rotation, but at the Election of the Commissioner whole Turn it is to appoint during the Week under certain Regulations, there arises from thence a great Difference in the Amount of the Profits of these Officers, and of the Deputy King’s Waiters, in the same Year.

The Three Gaugers have each the same Salary. For Business on the Lawful Quays he has no Fees, but Gratuities from the Merchants: For Business on the Sufferance Quays, he has Fees grounded upon Usage.

The Patent King’s Waiters are paid each the same Salary upon the Establishment. Their Fees are only those inserted in the Legal Table: They are received by the Clerk of the Rates, and divided equally among them. The Deputies have no Salaries: The Profits of their Offices arile from Fees and Gratuities similar to those of the Landing Waiters, their Business being exactly the fame.

The Appointers, and Weighers in Fee, have each the same Salary upon the Establishment. The Fees and Gratuities received by the former are equally divided between them: Those to the Weighers in Fee depend entirely upon the Courtely of the Merchant.

The Preferable Weighers have each an incidental Salary, and Pay by the Day. Some Merchants give him a Gratuity, others nothing: He claims no Fee. The Payments and Gifts usually made by the Merchants to the Officers in this Class are all inserted in N® 98. the Appendix. The Amount of their Salaries is £.19,1*1.4.8. We have given the State of this Department, as returned to us by the Board of Customs, and have added One hundred and Eight Pounds, Twelve Shillings, to the Charges upon the Revenue, and Eighteen Shillings and Eight Pence to the Amount of the Taxes.

It appears from this Inquiry, that in the Year 1784, One thousand Six hundred and Six Officers, Clerks, and Assistants, with an indefinite Number of inferior Attendants, were employed in the Management of the Revenue of the Customs, at the Expence to the Public, in Salaries and Allowances, of One hundred and Ten thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-three Pounds, Nine Shillings, and Three Pence Three Farthings; and to the Subject, in Fees and Gratuities, of Sixty-four thousand and Seventy-nine Pounds, Eight Shillings, and One Halfpenny: That the Payment back to the Public, in Taxes, was Nine thousand Eight hundred and Seventy-four Pounds, Thirteen Shillings, and Ten Pence; which, being deducted from the Amount of the Salaries and Allowances, leaves a real Charge upon the Public of One Hundred thousand Eight hundred and Eighty-eight Pounds Fifteen Shillings, and Five Pence Three Farthings: This being added to the Amount of the Fees and Gratuities, gives One hundred and Sixty-four thousand Nine hundred and Sixty-eight Pounds, Three Shillings, and Six Pence Farthing, the total Expence incurred by the Public and Subjects on Account of the Officers of this Revenue, in the Office of the Customs and Port of London.

One of the Objefits proposed by the Act that directs our Conduct, is, " that a lese expensive Method of " collecting the Duties and Taxes may from henceforth " be established and, to that End, we are enjoined " to report what Defeats we have observed, during the " Course of our Examinations and Proceedings, in the " present Mode of collecting the Public Monies; and " to report such Regulations as, in our Judgment, " shall appear fit ana expedient to be established, in " order that the Duties raised for the Public Service " may hereafter be received in the Manner the most " advantageous to the Public."

In an Office that embraces so many Objects; that employs such a Number of Officers, in Districts so many and so remote from each other; that has undergone no Revision, that we can discover, fmce its Institotion; it may reasonably be expeCbed that such an Office will afford much Matter for Regulation.

What has occurred to us in the Course of this Inquiry is grounded upon Principles tew and simple, and has for its Object, that which the Act points out to us, Frugality in the Collection and Management of the Revenue; an Object it is the Part of Wisdom at all times to attend to; but, in the present Condition of the Finances of this Country, it is so intimately connected with the Justice, Honour, and Well-being of the State, that to neglect it is to draw into Peril the Public Character and Safety.

The Regulations in the Management of the Revenue of the Customs, which it is our Duty to suggest to the Wisdom of the Legislature, rest upon these Principles First, No Office should be holden but by legal Tenure; — Secondly, Every Office should have an ufefol Duty annexed to it; — Thirdly, Every Officer should execute, himself, the Duty of his Office; — Fourthly, Office's where the Duty is of the same Kind, should be consolidated.

Some of the Offices of the Customs have been the Subjecfc of many ACks of Parliament.

By the Act of the 14th of Richard the Second, Chapter the 10th, for the Relief of the coaonxm Profit of the Realm, it is ordained, " that, so Cuf-

" tomer, Controller, Searcher, Weigher, or Finder,

" have any such Office for Term of Life or of Years,

" but only so long as shall please the King, notwithstanding any Patent or Grant made to any to the " contrary." — The 17th of the same King, Chapter the 5th, ordains, " that (among other Officers) no " Searcher, Collector, or 'Controller of the Customs,

" shall have Estate in his Office for Term of Life or " Years; and if any Letters Patents be made to the " contrary, they shall be clearly amralled and void." —

The ill of Henry the Fourth, Chapter the 13th, enjoins, " that this last Statute be firmly bolden and " kept, and put in due Execution;" with this Addition, " that Customers and Controllers, in every Port of England, shall be resident upon their Offices in their proper Persons, without making any <e Deputy." — The 4th of Henry the Fourth, Chapter " the 20th, confirms the last Statute, and directs that the Customets and Controllers shall be sworn to observe the fame. — The 13th of Henry the Fourth, Chapter the 5th, confirms both the preceding Acts, and adds, " that all Customers, Controllers, Gaugers *( of Wine, and Searchers, shall he continually refi- dent and abiding upon their Offices, so that no " such Officer be absent from his Office by Three

Weeks at the most, upon Pain to lose his Office,

" unless he be in the Kings Service of Record." —

By the 31st of Henry the Sixth, Chapter the 5th, it is enacted, " that all Letters Patent made of the Officers of Searcher, Collector of Customs, or Controller,

" against the Effect of the preceding Statutes, shall be " void."

By the Lifts returned to us from the Office of the N* 8, Customs, and from the Treasury, it appears, that in the Port of Landon the Offices of Collector Inwards, Collector Outwards, Controller Inwards and Outwards, Controller of Cloth and Petty Customs Inwards and Outwards, and Controller General, are holden by Letters Patent for Term of Life or Lives, expressly contrary to the Acts above mentioned: And, from the Evidence before us, it appears, that -the same Offices (except that of the Controller General) together with the Offices of Controller of Great Customs on Wool and Leather, Chief Patent Searcher, Four of the Under Patent Searchers, and the Two Patent Searchers at Gravesend, are Sinecures; and that these Officers have not been resident upon their Offices, pursuant to the Injunctions of the same Statutes. How far these Letters Patent for Life are by feme of these Statutes liable to be vacated for Defect of Power to grant, or how far the Sinecure Offices are by others of them liable to Forfeiture for Non-residence, we are. not competent to decide: But, whatever may be the

Operation of the Statutes, there are Circumstances within our Cognizance, attending these and many other of the Offices of the Customs, on which we are warranted to ground an Opinion, that they ought many of them to be suppressed, and others to undergo material Alterations.

The Offices we allude to are either entire Departments, including Principals, Deputies, and Clerks; or, the Office of die Principal only. They may be distinguished under Three Classes: — First, where the Buli-nefe tran&Cted in the Office is useless; — Second, where the Business is useful, but the Officer becomes ufriels by converting his Office into a Sinecure; — Third, where the Business is useful, and executed by the Officer, but properly belongs to, and should be united with, the Duty of some other Office.

In the First Clafe, the whole Office should be abo-liftied, as a ufelcfe Expence to the Public. In the Second Clafe, the Office wmft remain, and the Sinecure only be suppressed, by vacating foe appointment of the Officer, he having rendered himself a ufelefe Member of that Department. In the Third Clafe, the Offices should be coafofeteted, or One of 8 them

The Office of Inspector of Prosecutions was insti-N° >45* tufted in the Year 1686, for the Purpose '"of taking " Care that Informations concerning uncuftoened " and prohibited Goods might be effectually prosecuted, " and that the Fines and Revenues be duly brought " to the King’s Account." At that Time common Informers might inftkuite and carry on Prosecutions for Breaches of the Laws of the Customs, without the Intervention or Knowledge of the Board of Customs, and therefore such an Officer might then be of some Use: but fine© the Act Of the 12th of George the First, Chapter the 28th, confined this Power t» His Majesty’s Attorney General and the Officers of this Revenue, the Board of Customs are privy to all legal Proceedings on these Statutes. An Account of the Shares of the Crown, arising from Seizures in the Hands of the Receivers for London and the Out Ports, is laid regularly before the Board; they order the Payments into the Exchequer, and the Tallies are produced to the Accountant of Petty Receipts. The Sums due to the Crown, recovered by the Solicitors, are paid by them into the Exchequer, either by Order of the Board, or of Course; their Accounts are laid before the Board, and they produce the Tallies to the Auditor of their Accounts. The Inspector of Prr/ecu-tions receives no Information relative to these Shares but from some Office in the Customs. He is indebted for all his Entries to the Register of Seizures, the Books of the Solicitors, the Certificate of the Accountant of Petty Receipts, or the Minutes of the Board. Since then the Board of Customs either have, or may have, full Knowledge, in every Cafe, both of the Shares of the Crown, and of the Sums paid under that Denomination into the Exchequer, any further Check upon these Payments seems to be utterly unnecessary; and heavy has been, and ftiil is, the Expence to- the Public for this useless Office. By a N* 146. Warrant of the Treasury, dated the 4th of August 1687, it appears that this was not intended at first to be an established Office. The Compensation allowed the Officer was a Poundage of Twelve Pence upon the Sum paid into the Exchequer. This Poundage has fuelled to a very considerable Magnitude; the Average Annual Amount for Ten Years, ending with the N* 147. Year 1781, appears, from, an Account of the Net Sums received Annually by the Inspector of Prode-£ 3/76- >3 3i- cutions, to have been Three thousand Six hundred and Seventy-six Pounds, Thirteen Shillings, and Three Pence Halfpenny. The Shares of the Crown being diverted by an Act of that Year, from the Exchequer to the Payment of the Charges of Management in the Office of the Customs, and the Profits of this Office being consequently diminished, this Officer obtained, K* 148. by his Memorial to the Treasury last Year, a Warrant

The Register of Seizures registers the Indenture of Appraisement; and, having compared this Entry with the Writ of Delivery, he annexes to the Writ a Certificate that the Goods inserted therein agree with those in the Indenture. A Copy of this Register it font every Year to the Board of Treasury, and Abstracts to the Barons of His Majesty’s Exchequer. As the Indenture of Appraisement is made out by the Ware-housekeeper, and the Writ of Delivery, which pursues the Indenture, and issuea out of the Court of Exchequer after Condemnation of the Goods, is executed by the same Officer, jointly with other Officers, there does not seem to be any necessity for the Intervention of a Third Officer, to see that those Two Iuftra-raents agree; and whatever Information may be requisite, for the Beard of Treasury or the Barons of the Exchequer, may be easily procured from the Office of the Warehousekeeper.

The Office of Inspector and Examiner of the Exchequer Books in the Out Ports, is merely nominal:

It has neither Deputy nor Clerk: No Duty is annexed to it: No BufmeTs whatever transufted, in it.

It is a Sinecure of Necessity j but die Officer has a Salary of Three hundred Pounds a Year. joo.

A Controul upon every Officer who receives and pays, is an essential Part of the Confutation of an Office of Revenue; but this has its Bounds: The Checks upon the same Sabjeft may be too numerous:

The Security is weakened w'bere the Number appointed to the same Duty is so great, that each being tempted to rely upon the Diligence of the rest, neglects his own Duty, or borrows from the Ihdustry of his Coadjutors.

The Duties Inwards are computed, and the Accounts of them kept, by Six different Officers. Four of them, the Controller, Surveyor General, Surveyor, and Examiner, are Checks upon the Collectof: The Clerk of the Rates is his Assistant. Three of them, the Controller, Surveyor General, and Surveyor, are also Checks upon, and keep the same Accounts of the Duties Outwards with, the Collector Outwards.

The Import into the Port of London is the most productive Source of the Revenue of the Custotos;

The Objects are numerous; the Computation is difficult and the Business continual: So that tire Controller, who is the proper Check upon the Collector, is alone not sufficient; but, with the Assistance of the Two efficient Officers, the Clerk of the Rates and the Examiner, the Collector may rest secure in the Accuracy of his Computation end Receipt, if he finds, upon comparing them, the Accounts of those Three Officers agree with his own.

The Duties Outwards are lb inconsiderable, that a Angle Check upon the Collection, that of the Controller only, seems folly sufficient: Should another be thought requisite, the Copying Clerk, who attends the Checks to compare the Description of the Goods upon his BHi with the like Description upon the Warrant, may be directed to compote and font up the Duties likewise. Should this, though reduced in Number, be deemed a sufficient Guard upon the Collection of these Two Branches of the Revenue, the Offices of Surveyor General, and Surveyor (the Principals of which are Sinecures) with their Deputies and Clerks, will become useless, and may be foppressed; no other Bofmefs being transacted in either of these Offices, than what is transacted in the Offices of the remaining Checks: And, should the Legislature judge it

The Reader of Warrants enters in a Book Copies of all the Entries Inwards in the Port of London, and fends it to the Exchequer. The Collector Inwards, and all the other Patent Officers concerned in that Collection, are equally obliged to send to the Exchequer their Port Books, which contain the very same Entries. If there is any Necessity, therefore, for this Service, it is sufficiently performed without the AQiftance of the Register of Warrants.

To Five of these Offices feme Duty appears to be annexed; but it is a Duty, from the Performance of which the Public receive no Benefit The Revenue will be conduced with equal Accuracy and Security if they do not exist; and, on the contrary, by the Suppression of them, and of that of the Inspector and Examiner of the Exchequer Books in the Out Ports, to which no Duty is annexed, the Expence of supporting Six Sinecure Offices, Five of them held by Patent, and One by Constitution, will be saved to the Public; and to the Merchant, the Fees he now pays to the Deputies and Clerks of feme of them.

The Transmission of Port Books to the Exchequer being mentioned in several of the Examinations, as the Duty of many Officers of the Customs, both in London and the Out Ports, we were led to enquire into the Origin, Ground, and PraCfcice of this Duty.

By the Rules and' Orders issued under the Great Seal, in the 7th Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, the Court of Exchequer is directed to fend, every Hilary and Trinity Term, to the Patent Officers therein named, in the Port of London and the Out Ports, Parchment Books under the Exchequer Seal, into which were to be entered all Goods and Merchandize imported, exported, and carried Coastwise. These Books are to be returned, in Michaelmas and Easter Terms every Year, into the Exchequer, under the Signature and upon the Oath of the Officer; and the Ground of this Order is expressed to be, " that the " Truth of all Entries might appear, and remain of " Record."

Mr. Edward Taylor, One of the Sworn Clerks in the Office of the Remembrancer in the Court of Ex-N° 150. chequer, and Clerk of the Coast Bonds, informed us, that these blank Books continue to be issued from that Office, Once in every Year to the Officers in the Port of London, and Twice a Year to Officers at the

Out Ports: And, by Lifts transmitted to us from that Office, containing the Officers to whom these Books were sent, and the Number sent to each, it appears, that at Christmas 1784, Forty-four of these Books, containing together Nine thousand Two hundred and Twenty-two Leaves, were sent to the Officers in the Port of London; and Two hundred and Eighty-one, containing Four thousand Eight hundred and Sixty-four Leaves, to the Officers at the Out Ports; and at Midsummer 1784, Seventy more, containing Eight hundred and Sixty-two Leaves, to Officers at the Out Ports; together, Three hundred and Ninety-five Books, of Fourteen thousand Nine hundred and Forty-eight Leaves.

Though the Court of Exchequer continue to yield Obedience to these ancient Orders, as far as relates to themselves, yet the Officers of the Ports do not fulfil their Part of this Service. The Returns' of these

Books into the Court of Exchequer are very irregular.

During the last Twenty-five Years some of the Ports have made no Returns at all; none of them have made all their Returns. In some of the Years no Return has been made from any Port: Few have been-the Returns in any Year: And of those Books which have been returned, no Use whatever has been made, that we can discover.

In an Account, procured by us from the Office of n* 15.. the Kings Remembrancer, it appears, that during Ten Years, ending with the Year 1784, Two hundred and Seventy-three only of these Books were returned into the Exchequer; a much smaller Number than is sent out from thence every Year. Of Seventy-four Ports to which Books were issued, Nine only made any Returns; and of these Nine, Seven made but One Return; and in Two of the Years no Return was made by any of them.

If these Port Books are of Use, the Orders of Queen Elizabeth ought to be enforced, and the Officers compelled to do their Duty. If they are ufelefe (as they seem to be) a Stop should be put to this expensive and unprofitable issue from the Exchequer.

Whatever Reason there might be for these Orders in the Year 1565, we are at a Lois to discover the Utility of them under the present System of the Customs.-The Entries in them are Copies of the Bills, Warrants, or other Instruments; all of which are entered in similar Books at the several Ports. Many of them contain exactly the same Entries: Their only Difference is, they are returned by different Officers. None of them contain an Article that is not to be found in feme one or more of the Official Books of the Customs. The Account they give of the Duties is trifling: Of the Sixty-eight Branches, One only, that of Customs, is inserted in them. When Information is wanted, Recourse is not had to the Port Books in the Exchequer, but to the Official Books in the proper Offices in the Customs, which fumi(h all that can be required relative to every Branch and Article of this Revenue.

By Two Accounts transmitted to us, one from the N° 15a. Seven hundred and Fifty-one Pounds, Eleven Shil- 751. n. lings, and Two Pence, is too considerable a Sum of Public Money to be wasted every Year, without any Advantage whatever to the Public arising from it.

The Offices of the Second Class, which are converted into Sinecures, are — the Supervisor of the Receiver General’s Receipts and Payments; the Register General of all Trading Ships belonging to Great Britain; the Inspector General of Imports and Exports; the Controller Inwards and Outwards; the Collector Inwards; the Collector Outwards; the Usher in the Long Room; Nineteen King’s Waiters; the Chief Patent Searcher; Five Under Patent Searchers; and Two Patent Searchers at Gravesend;One of which r, Offices is granted to Two Persons jointly.

Every one of these Thirty-four Offices (except the Supervisor of the Receiver General’s Receipts and Payments, and the Inspector General of Imports and Exports, which are holden by Constitution) are granted by Letters Patent; and there is but One of the Officers who does any Duty; that is, One of the

under

<2,6 Geo. III. 27° Januarii. 21

Under Patent Searchers; he executes the Office himself, but not as Patentee; for he holds the Patent in Trust for another; he acts as Deputy, and is allowed for the Execution the Salary and Profits of a Deputy only.

In these Offices the Emoluments are separated from the Execution. One Person receives a large Portion of the Profits without doing any Duty at all. Another does all the Duty, with but a scanty Share of the Profits. It is manifest, One Officer is fully sufficient for the Employment; for One only executes it. The Appointment, therefore, upon whatever Authority it may be grounded, should be made void, as being rendered of no Uses and the regulated Profits annexed to the Execution.

The Third Class of Offices are those where the Similitude of the Duty requires either their Consolidation, or the Suppression of one of them, and the Transfer of the Duty to the other.

The Rules of Simplicity and Uniformity require, that in every Office the Business should be so arranged, that all the Branches of that Business, which are of the same or a limilar Kind, should, as far as is practicable, be transa&ed in One Department only of that Office.

It may be, and frequently is, necessary that Accounts of the different Branches of the same Kind of Business should be kept distinct; and this may be easily effected, without creating Confusion, by allotting such particular Branches to distinfit Divisions in the same Department.

In every Office of Revenue there should be but One Treasury; in which the whole Produce should be deposited, and from whence every Payment to which that Revenue is subject should issue. In Proportion to the Multiplicity of Treasuries, the Accounts become complicate, the Passage into the Exchequer the more liable to Delay, the Danger of Loss encreased, and a Knowledge of the complete State of the Revenue the more difficult to be obtained.

There are in the Customs, besides the principal Treasury, which is the Office of the Receiver General, several inferior Treasuries, all independant of each other. Three of the Solicitors, and the Two Receivers of Fines and Forfeitures for London and the Out Ports, receive Sums arising from Penalties, Fines, Forfeitures, and the Produce of Seizures, out of which they make Variety of Payments; and such Portions of the Shares of the Crown as are intended for the Exchequer, they pay in, without the Intervention of the Receiver General, either of Course, or pursuant to their Instructions or the Orders of the Board of Customs.

We are of Opinion, that all these inferior Treasuries should be abolished; — that the Solicitors should pay all the Sums they recover of Penalties, Fines, and Forfeitures, and the Warehousekeeper in London all Sums he receives arising from the Produce of Sales, with all convenient Speed, into the Office of the Receiver General; and that all Remittances from the Out Ports, of Sums arising from the same Sources, be made to him; — that all Divisions of these Sums, whether to be paid into the Exchequer as Shares of the Crown, or applicable to any other Services, be paid by him in like Manner as he makes his other Payments.

By thus transferring the Business of these inferior Treasuries to that great and principal Department of Receipt, the Office of the Receiver General, the great Branches of Receipt and Payment in this Revenue will be uniformly transa&ed in One Department only, and the Two Offices of the Receivers of Fines and Forfeitures, for London and the Out Ports, will become unnecessary; the Controul upon the Remittances of the Sums produced by the same Branches of Vol. 41.

Revenue from the Out Ports, will be transferred to the Office of the Controller General; and the Office of Controller of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports will become useless: And these Three Offices may be suppressed. The Receiver General will pass his Accounts of these Branches in the same Office in which he pafies the rest of his Accounts; and, consequently, the principal Employment of the Accountant of Petty Receipts, that of passing the Accounts of the Two Receivers for London and the Out Ports, will be at an End, and that Office, at the Head of which presides an Officer with large Emolument, and with little Business, may be reduced. The Revenue has been in Danger of Losses, in Two recent Instances, from Receivers of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports. From the State of the Demands of the Public upon those Two Officers, procured by us from the Office of the Customs, it appears, that a considerable Part of the Public Money remitted to them, and converted to their own Use, had not been recovered to the Use of the Public.

The Quarterly Accounts from the Out Ports are of Two Kinds: First, the Quarter Books, which contain the Receipts of the Duties and the Payments upon Debentures, Certificates, and Portage Bills: Second, The Accounts of the Payments for Salaries and Incidents.

The Collector and Controller, and fomelimes the Customer, each fends up to the Board of Customs a similar Quarter Book: That of the Collector is examined with the Vouchers by the Examiner, it) compared with that of the Controller by the Surveyor of the Out Port Accounts, and delivered to the Controller General. The Vouchers are sent to the Inspector of the Out Port Collectors Accounts and Vouchers, and, after being entered in the Office, are delivered by him to the Controller General. The other Two Quarter Books are deposited with the Surveyor.

The Account of Payments of Salaries and Incidents, sworn to by the Collector before the Controller, and signed by both, is sent with the Vouchers to the Inspector, who, after Examination and Entry of the Vouchers, delivers them, with the Accounts, to the Controller General.

Thus there are Six Officers, the Surveyor, Inspec-for, and Four Examiners, whose Business it is to examine Accounts which are to be sworn to and passed by another Officer, the Controller General. It should seem as if the Examination of Accounts properly belonged to the Officer who passes them; and the Probability is, that where he swears to the Truth of them, his Examination will be sufficiently accurate, especially if, neither receiving nor paying one Article of the Account, he can have no Interest in any Error: And, therefore, we are of Opinion, that the Offices of Surveyor and InspeCfor, both Sinecures, and of the Four Examiners, should be suppressed; — that the Quarter Books, and Accounts of Payments of the Collectors and Controllers, should be transmitted, with the Vouchers, to the Office of the Controller General; — and that the Companion of these Books, and the Examination of the Accounts, be transferred to, and transa&ed in, feme Branch of that Department. It is not our Intention to increase the Business of any Office to an unreasonable Degree, or to subject the Officer to a Responsibility incompatible with the Nature of his Office. The Business of the Controller General is at present very laborious and extensive; and, relying upon the Accuracy of the Examiner, he is not now answerable for the Truth of the Computation of the Duties in the Quarter Books.

The Addition, therefore, here suggested, may, under. the present Circumstances, throw too great a Load upon him; but such will be the Relief to this

The Officers employed in the Collection of the Duties should not be multiplied uunecessarily, and every Duty of the same Kind should be collected by the same Officer. There are Three obvious Distinctions in the Duties — the Import — the Export — and, the Coastwise Duty; and accordingly each has a dif-tintt Collector. As these Three Divisions comprehend all the Duties, they should all be collected by these Three Officers, each receiving what belongs to his Division: But this Rule is not adhered to There are Three more Customers or Collectors, separate and independant of the others — the Customer of Cloth and Petty Customs Outwards — the Collector of Petty Customs Inwards — and, the Collector of the Great Customs on Wool and Leather exported, or, as he is also stiled, the Customer of the Great Customs Outwards.

The only Business of the Customer of Cloth and Petty Customs Outwards, is to collect the Duties on white Woollen Cloths exported, which amount to a Trifle (as appears from an Account of the Net Produce of those Duties for the last Ten Years) and to receive a Fee from an Alien Exporter (though the Alien Duty is abolished) to be divided between himself, the Controller, the Surveyor General, and Surveyor. The Collection of this Duty properly belongs, and should be transferred, to the Collector Outwards; and this Office, though inconsiderable, should be discontinued.

The Office of Petty Customer Inwards exists for the Purpose, not of collecting the Alien Duty Inwards, as the Title imports (for that is done by the Collector Inwards) but of ligning the Warrant and Bill of Sight, where the Entry is on an Alien Account, entering a Copy of the Warrant in a Book, and returning that Book to the Exchequer.

As the Duty is paid to the Collector Inwards, the Warrant, and Bill of Sight, undergo all the Formalities, Checks, and Signatures, with the like Warrants and Bills in that Office; and the Signature of this Officer is utterly useless, unless for the Alien’s Fee attending it: And should the Return of the Port Books into the Exchequer be considered, contrary to our Opinion, to be of Use, the Returns of all the other Patent Officers Inwards, of the same Books, will render the Return of this Officer superfluous.

The Business of the Collector of the Great Customs on Wool and Leather exported, consists of Two Articles — the Collection of the Duty on Leather exported — and, the Carriage of Wool and Leather Coastwise. Both these belong clearly to the Collector Outwards: The Duty on Leather, to that Branch called the Cocket Office; and the Carriage of Wool and Leather, to the other Branch, the Coast Office: And therefore the Management of these Two Articles should form a Part of the Duty of that Collector, and the Office of Collector of the Great Customs Outwards bp abolished.

In consequence of these Regulatiops in the Collection, the Controul upon every Article will pass to the Office of the Controller Inwards and Outwards; and the Offices of the Three Collectors or Customers, and Two Controllers, the one of Cloth and Petty Customs Inwards and Outwards, the other of the Great Customs Outwards, all holden by Letters Patent, and Four of them Sinecures, with, Four Deputies, may be suppressed.

We do not mean, that, by the Abolition apd Con-solidation of these Offices, the Whole of the Expence attending them will be save^ to the Nation. Such of them as remain, whether as separate Offices, or united to others, must be supported; and the Expence of that Support will be a Deduction from the Charge above stated. What that Expence may amount to capnot be ascertained; but it will occasion no very considerable Deduction, should a more liberal Measure of Payment be adopted, than that which, from the Allowances stated to have been made to Deputies and Clerks, for the Execution of the Duty, appears to have been pursued ip these Sinecure Offices.

It is probable, that, among such a Number as are returned to us existing in the Customs, there are many of the inferior Offices to which these Regulations may, with equal Propriety, be extended. Had we dqfcended to an Inquiry minute and particular enough to have enabled us to form a Judgment upon them, if would have engaged too much of our Time: Enough has already been consumed in the Labour of Inyeftiga-tion, to the Extent we have proceeded, though confined to the Office of the Customs, and Port or London only.

In feme of these inferior Offices the Duty does not seem to be of Consequence enough to warrant, the Continuance of them. For Instance, there are Sixteen Land Carriage Officers, at a Salary of Thirty-five Pounds a Year each, and a Surveyor, at a Salary of Sixty Pounds. Their Business is to attend at Inns in London and Westminster, in search of Goods, either prohibited or without Permit or Certificate.

They can hardly aft, with Safety to themselves, unless upon good Information; and upon such a

Ground any other Officer of the Customs may proceed equally with the Land Carriage Officer. Their Number is certainly greater than is wanted; for Three of them are otherwise employed, and execute no Part of this Duty. The Board of Customs know the Business transeaed by theft, and other Officers of the like Deftription; and are the belt Judges whether the Revenue derives from their Services a Benefit equal to the Expence of supporting the m. Where the Office is in their own Appointment, they can regulate or suppress it: where it is in the Appointment of the Treasury, they can represent

We have rested our Opinion for the Suppression of these Offices in the Cestoms, as well as of those in other Departments of the Revenue which have been before under our Confederation, upon the firm Ground of their Inutility, and the urgent Necessity of applying every unnecessary and luperfluous Expence to that most important of National Objects, the Accumulation of a Fund for the Reduction of the Public Debt.

We are aware of the Consequence some of theft Officers derive from the Power by which they are granted, and the Extent of the Interest. A Freehold, held under the Grant of the Crown, is a solemn Right, to be treated with Respefit, Delicacy, and Caution; but if the Subject of that Grant be a Public Office, and a Stipend be annexed to it, payable out of the Revenue of the Public; if rendering a Service useful to the State, as the Consideration for the Stipend, be of the Essence of such an Office (a Principle we have endeavoured to establish in our Eleventh Report, and from which we fee no Reason to depart) where the Utility of the Service is either wanting at the Time of the Grant, or in Process of Time ceases to exist, the Grant either had not at first, or has loft, the Quality essential to its Support; and no Power of the Grantor, no Condition of the Grantee, or Duration of the Interest, can supply the Defect: It cannot be supported in the Shape of an Office; for it has not the Character that distinguishes an Office from an Annuity or a Pension.

The Wisdom of our Ancestors declared the Freehold to be void in its Creation; and the Office, turned into a Sinecure, to be forfeited. The present Age has the strong Pleas of Necessity and Justice, to demand, that such Portions of their Revenue as have been applied to the Support of such Offices, lltould be hereafter dedicated to the Service of the Public.

We are sensible that the Persons in Possession of the Offices we have represented as deleft, may be entitled from Merit, either of their own, or derived from

their Ancestors, to a Recompence from the Public, equal both in Value end Duration to the full Emoluments of their Offices.

We do not call in Question the Amplitude of the Reward, nor impeach their Title to it: We can judge of neither. But we are of Opinion, that the Mode of Reward, by either creating or continuing, for that Purpose, a ufeleft Office, is calculated to mislead the Public; who conceive, that by a continual Exertion of the Labour and Abilities of the Officer in their Service, they are receiving back an Equivalent for the Emoluments they allow him. It tends to entail a perpetual Incumbrance upon the Revenue;^ for a Subject will be for ever found to fill the Office, though no' one should be found to deservek: And should the Suppression of these Offices be deemed a Measure expedient to be adopted, the Substitution of a Payment or Allowance, as a Cornpen-fation for the Claim of each meritorious Officer, may easily be provided.

It is no Mark of Wisdom, even in an opulent Nation, to laviffi the Public Treasure in Expences unprofitable to the State: But where the Subject is grievously oppressed by the Burthen of an enormous Debt, the Reduction of which is essential to the Justice, the Credit, and Security of the State, and that Reduction cannot without Difficulty be accomplished, even by the united Exertions of Wisdom and Oeconomy; in a Nation under such Circumstances, a Duty presses, both upon the Government and Subject, of no common Obligation. The one is bound, in the Administration of the Revenue, to cut off every unnecessary and redundant Expence; to iuppreft every ufeleft and superfluous Office; to correct every Abuse in the Publick Receipt and Expenditure; and religiously to apply to the Service of the State the Produce of every Branch of the Revenue. The Subject is bound, chearfully and liberally, every one in Proportion to the Extent of his Abilities, to contribute, without Evasion, his Share to the Support, Defence, and Security of the State, and to the Relief of the Necessities of his Country.
