The Examination of William Stiles, Esquire; taken upon Oath, April 18 th and 2 2d, May 25 th, June 2 2d and 27th, July 4th and 18th, August 5th, 8th, and 29th, and September ift, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That the Authorities by which the Officers of the Customs hold their Offices are, a Patent under the Great Seal; a Constitution under the Authority of the Board of Treasury, which is both a Nomination and an Appointment to the Office; the-Warrant of the Board of Treasury; and the Commission or Appointment of the Board of Customs pursuant to that Warrant, in which same the Officer derives his Authority from the Commission; these comprehend all the Officers paid upon the Establishment, and by Dormant Warrants. Others, called Incidental Officers, are appointed, some by the Commission of the Board of Customs only, under the Hands of Four of the Commissioners and the Seal of the Board, others by Order of the Board.

All the Deputies are appointed by the Patentees; but some of them must be approved by the Lords of the Treasury. An Appointment by Constitution, or by Warrant and Commission, or by Order of the Board, is, as he apprehends, an Appointment during Pleasure. The Salary received by the Officer is either that inserted in his Patent, Constitution, or Warrant, or referred to in those Instruments, or directed by the Order of the Board of Customs.

The Allowances are, some of them, Annual Additions to Salaries, others casual Payments for special Services; and are grounded either upon the Warrant of the Treasury, or the Order of the Board of Customs. The Fees received by many of the Officers are grounded either upon Acts of Parliament or Usage: There are other Officers who demand and receive under the Name of Fees, certain Sums for particular Branches of Business. Each Office has, or is directed to have, a Table of Fees hung up in it. Salaries, Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities, include all the Emoluments of the Officers of thp Costnms. pvclnfivp. of their Shares of Seizures, Penalties, Fines, and Forfeitures.

The Commissioners of the Customs, upon receiving the Precepts of this Board for Accounts of the Profits of the Officers of the Customs, issued their Orders to the proper Officers in every Department, both in London and at the Out Ports, to make a Return to them conformable to those Precepts.

The Establishment of the Officers is made out every Quarter, for every Department- in the Port of London, and for every Out Port. The Salary appointed to be paid to each* Officer upon the Establishment consists of his original Salary, and any Allowance by Warrant that may have been made to him subsequent to his Appointment.

All the Officers not upon the Establishment, except those paid by Dormant Warrants, are entered upon the Quarterly Incidental Lift, with the Salaries or Allowances payable to each; those who receive their Salaries by Dormant Warrants are chiefly Patent Officers, and are paid by the Receiver General, pursuant to those Warrants, without the Interference of the Board of Customs. Some of the inferior Officers, who are upon Day Pay, are paid Monthly, or oftener.

One of the Allowances to certain of the Officers, both in London and at the Out Ports, is for the Quarantine Service. The Privy Council transmit to the Board of Customs the Intelligence they receive concerning the Plague, and the Orders they make relative to the Quarantine Service, grounded upon the Act of Parliament; the Board of Customs communicate that Intelligence, and issue Copies of the Orders to the principal Officers, both in London and at the Out Ports, enjoining them to carry those Orders into drift Vol. 41.

Execution; these Officers superintend the Execution by Fourteenth the Officers of the Water Guard, and transmit to the RePort]. Board from Time to Time an Account of their Proceedings, with their own Observations; the Board transmit to the Privy Council such of them as are necessary, and with such Observations as occur to them i This Service not being a Part of the general Business of the Customs; Allowances are made to those Officers employed in the Execution, by Warrants of the Treasury issued at different Times, of which the Warrant of the i 9th of December 1722 was, as he apprehends, the first. Every Year the Board of Customs send to the Treasury a Memorial, inclosing a List of the Officers entitled to this Allowance, and the Sum to be paid to each, with the N umber of Ships put under Quarantine in the Course of the Year, and the Service performed by the Officers, and craving the Payment of those Sums: The Treasury, by their Warrant, direct the Receiver General to pay the Sums to the Persons inserted in that Lift.

Another of the Allowances to certain Officers, both in London and at the Out Ports, is a Poundage upon the Gross Produce arising from the Sale of Tea, Coffee, and Spirits, seized, condemned, and fold, which are called the Enumerated Goods; this Allowance is grounded upon an Order of the Board of Customs, dated the 9th of May 1728, and is intended as a Compensation to some of those Officers who are concerned in the Custody, Sale, and keeping the Accounts of the Seizures; This Poundage is paid out of the Gross Produce of Seizures, which uled to be a productire Branch of the Revenue. But an Act of the last Session9 directs all Spirits seized to be destroyed; and the Poundage upon Tea and Coffee will probably be done away by the Commutation Tax, and by the Reduction of the Duties upon Coffee.

The Office of Secretary of the Customs consists of the Secretary, the Western and Northern Clerks, the Plantation Clerk, the Clerk in the Bond Office, Thirteen other Clerks, and One Supernumerary.

The Secretary of the Customs is appointed by Constitution; his Annual Salary is Six hundred and Fifty Pounds, composed of Four hundred Pounds by his Constitution, One hundred and Ninety Pounds by Warrant, and Sixty Pounds by Order of the Board.

He receives by Warrant from the Treasury, for the Quarantine Service, Twelve Shillings for every Ship put under Quarantine^ except Men of War and Transports; this Allowance amounted, in the last Year, to One hundred and Sixty-three Pounds Sixteen Shillings.

He is allowed, by Minute of the Board, dated the 9th of May 1728, a Poundage upon the Grols Produce of the Enumerated Goods. This Poundage is Two Fifths of One Penny in the Pound on the Sum arising from the Sale; and in the last Year produced Two hundred and Thirty-one Pounds One Shilling and Eight Pence.

The Secretary receives likewise Five Eighths of the Fees which are inserted in a Table hung up in his Office, and

frounded upon Usage; and an Annual Gratuity of Ten founds from the East India Company, for the Trouble they give to the Office: This contains all the Emoluments received by the Secretary; they amounted in the last Year to One thousand Five hundred and Eighty Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Eleven Pence Three Farthings, which Sum was reduced, by the Payment of One hundred and Sixty-five Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence for various Taxes, to the Net Sum of One thousand Four hundred and Fourteen Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings.

The Duty of the Secretary is constantly to attend the Board, to read to them the Minutes of the preceding Day, and all the Reports of the General Surveyors upon the Charges referred to them against the London Officers; to read and state to them Variety of References, Petitions, and Letters; to take their Orders and Directions relative to those Applications; to draw up many of their Reports; to see that the Petitions are

O referred

K*

Fourteenth Report on Public Accounts*

5 o cl*]* jaA. 17 86.

referred to the proper Officers, and that the Minutes are correctly drawn up pursuant to the Orders of the Board; and to iuperintend the Business of all the Clerks in his Department. Besides the Correspondence with the Public Offices, the Board receive and answer Annually, upon an Average, near Ten thousand Petitions for the Port of London only, containing frequently difficult Points of Law or Practice, and from the Out Ports, near Nine thousand letters, upon many of which the Directions given by the Board are conveyed by the Secretary; he alone is like wife intruded by the Board to convey from them to the Officers all secret and confidential Intelligence, Orders, and Resolutions. He receives and answers continual Applications from Persons attending upon Business at the Custom House. His own Attendance there is daily, Holidays frequently not excepted, and generally for Nine or Ten Hours in a Day.

Upon every Nomination to an Office by Warrant of the Treasury, Search is made, by Order of the Board of Customs, whether the Person named, whatever the Office may be, has ever been in the Service, and dismissed; if he has, the Warrant is returned to the Treasury, dating the Objection, and the Person as inadmissible: Upon the like Nomination of a Collector, the Board of Cudoms make no Objection to appointing him, unless for having been dismissed the Service: Upon the like Nomination of a Landing Surveyor, Landing Waiter, and Coad Waiter, the Board direct an Enquiry, whether they have been instructed in the Duty of those Offices, if not, the Two fird are put under Indructions for Six Months, and the lad for Two Months; and upon producing, after the Expiration of that Time, a Certificate from the proper Officers, that they are duly qualified, and not until then, they receive their Appointment: Upon the like Nomination to inferior Offices, the Board direct an Enquiry into their Age and Qualifications; and if Objections arise, they return the Warrant to the Treasury, and date the Objections. Persons have been frequently appointed to the Offices of Collector, Deputy Controller, Deputy Cudomer, and feme other Offices requiring a Knowledge in the Cudoms, without having had any previous Indructions, and being utter Strangers to the Duties of their Office. The Hours which are at this Time considered as the legal Office Hours for transacting Business, are the same as were settled by the Rules and Orders annexed to the Act of Tonnage and Poundage.

The Office of Inspector of Prosecutions was originally instituted for the Purpose of taking Care that the King’s Share of Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures, was duly paid into the Exchequer, when cqpimon Informers had the Power of proceeding in the Court of Exchequer for the Recovery of them. The Act of the Twelfth of George the Fird, Chapter the Twenty-eighth, took away this Power from common Informers, and confined it solely to his Majesty’s Attorney General and Officers of the Revenue.

There used to be Seven Local Surveyors General, whole Duty it was to inspect the Conduct of the Officers in particular Didricts. The Board being of Opinion that these Officers did not answer the Purposes of their Indifution, in the Year 1771 represented the same to the Treasury by Memorial, and proposed the Abolition of these Offices as they should become vacant, and that in lieu of them there should be Four General Surveyors resident in London, who should be sent out occasionally, by Order of the Board, to inspect the Conduct of the

Officers at the Out Ports, and to examine all Complaints referred to them against Officers, as well in London as at the Out Ports. The Board of Treasury made an Order accordingly; since which Four of the Local Surveyors General are, as he believes, dead, and their Offices abolished.

The Superannuation Fund has been long established in the Office of the Cudoms, in Consequence of Memorials from Time to Time by the Board of Cudoms to the Treasury, and of their Warrants pursuant to those Memorials.

It is composed of Deductions from the Pay of certain Officers, chiefly, those oK the inferior Clatfes, both in London and at the Out Ports, and of all Mulcts impeded upon Officers: If the Officer is upon the Eltablrshment,-it is a Poundage of Six Pence in the Pound upon his Gross Salary, and deducted from it of Course at the Time of Payment: If the Officer is upon the Incidental Lid, it is, as he apprehends, optional, whether he will contribute or not to this Fund; if he consents, the same Poundage is deducted out of his Pay.

The Emolument the Officer derives from his Contribution to this Fund, is an Annual Payment during his Life, in Proportion to his Salary or Pay, upon his being deemed unfit to be continued in the Service, from Age or Infirmities; but to entitle him to this Annuity he mud be upwards of Sixty Years of Age, and have contributed for Ten Years to the Fund (unless disabled sooner by feme extraordinary Accident in the Execution of his Duty); he mud have behaved well, and have no other Means of Subsidence. The highed of these Annuities is Thirty Guineas, the lowed Ten Pounds. One of the Tables of Fees established by Act of Parliament in the Customs, returned to this Board, is signed by the Bench Officers in the Long Room, and was transmitted to the Secretary as a Copy of the Table hung up in that Room; the other Four are Tables for the Ports of Hull, Chester, Bristol, and Great Yarmouth; these are copied from an ancient Book at the Custom House, and appear to have been transmitted thither from those Ports many Years ago. He does not find, upon Inquiry, that there are any other Tables of Fees established by Act of Parliament to be found in the Custom House. Complaints are frequently made to the Board, by the Merchants and others, relative to Fees demanded of them by Officers of different Descriptions, and Complaints by feme Officers against other Officers, for receiving and withholding their Fees; these Complaints are referred to the General Surveyors for Examination, and upon their Report the Board decide. The Compensation for Extra Duty, under the Act of King William, is generally settled between the Officer and the Merchant; but there have been Complaints to the Board against the Demands of the Officers for this Kind of Service.

W. Stiles.

T. Anguish,

Memorial, 17th September 1722.

We have received your Lordships Warrant of the 17th of August last, for defraying the Expences relating to the Quarantine, which shall be duly obeyed; but we take Leave humbly to represent to your Lordships, that the Commissioners of the Customs being, by His Majesty’s Commands, intruded with the Care of the Quarantine in al! the Ports of England, and directed by the Council to examine the Particulars of every Ship’s Cargo, and the Growth, Product, and Manufacture of every Parcel of Goods on board Ships under Quarantine, and to make Reports thereof to your Lordships, or to tl»e Council, when required, and likewise obliged to give the necessary Orders to the Officers concerning the same; all which being a very great Addition of Business, and, as we humbly conceive, no Way relating to our Duty as Managers of the Customs; do therefore hope we may be in your Lordships favourable Consideration for such Allowance as youi Lordships think we may deserve for this extraordinary Service.

T.W. R.R J.S.

After our hearty Commendations.

Whereas, by our Warrant, to you directed, bearing Date the 17th August 1722, wre did authorize and iro-power you to cause all Charges and Expences whatsoever which had arisen or should arise, by Means of the Quarantine to be paid and defrayed out of the Old Customs under the Head of Incidents; and whereas, by your Memorial, bearing Date the 17th September last past, you have represented unto us, that the Care of the Quarantine in all the Ports of England was, by His Majesty’s Commands, intruded to you, and that you were directed by the Council to examine the Particulars of every Ship’s Cargo, and the Growth, Fro-duct, and Manufacture of every Parcel of Goods on board Ships under Quarantine, and to make Reports thereof to us, or to the Council, w hen required, and likewise obliged to give the necessary Orders to the Officers concerning the same; which being a very great Addition of Business, and as you conceive no Way relating to your Duty as Managers of the Customs, you have denred such Allowance as we shall think you may deserve for this extraordinary Service: Now we, having taken the Premises into our Consideration, do think it reasonable and fitting, that an Allowance, after the Rate of 200 L per Annum, be made to each of you, the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs, for such your extraordinary Service, Care and Pains; and that the said Allowance to each of you be made to commence from the 25th Day of August 1720, being the Day of the Date of His Majesty's Royal Proclamation for Performance of Quarantine, and.be continued to each of you until such Time as Quarantine shall, by His Majesty’s Command, cease to be performed: These are therefore to authorize and direct you to give Warrants to the Receiver General and Cashier of His Majesty's Customs, for paying to yourselves not only lb much as has incurred on the said Allowance of 200 per Annum each, from the said 2.5th Augmt vyio to the 25th Day of November last past, 1722, but also of such further Sum and Sums of Money as shall become due and payable from Time to lime on the said Allowance, alter the Rate of 2001, per Annum each, from the said 25th Day of November last past, until the Vol. 41.

Performance of Quarantine be ceased as aforesaid. That there be allowed, for Goods fold in the Out Ports, to each respective Collector, Four Pence, and

The Commissioners having had under Consideration the settling the Allowances for Payment of the Officers in the Out Ports employed in the receiving and collecting the present Duty on Coals, upon looking into the Produce of the said Duty in the several Ports for a Year, from the Commencement thereof, which was the 15th May 1698, to the 15th May last, are humbly of Opinion, That there be allowed, for the receiving and accompting for the said Duty, arising in the Out Ports for the said Time, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent, for the first One thousand Pounds, and One per Cent, for every Hundred Pounds afterwards; that is to say, where there has been received the Sum of One thousand Pounds, there be allowed the Sum of Thirty Pounds, Twenty Pounds whereof to be to the Collector, who has the Charge of receiving and accompting for the Money, and Ten Pounds to the Comptroller; and where the Sum of Two thousand Pounds has been received, there be allowed the Sum of Forty Pounds, Two Thirds whereof to be to the Collector, and One Third to the Comptroller, and so in Proportion; — which the Commissioners conceive will prove a reasonable Allowance for the Service afore-mentioned, and be considerably less than was allowed for collecting the former Duty on Coals: And there having been Occasion, in feme particular Ports, to employ feme of the Officers to inspect the Meters in Places where the Coals are delivered, being at distance from the ordinary Residence of the Officers, the Commissioners think it necessary to make them feme Allowance for their Care out of the same Duty, which they humbly hope their Lordships will approve.

And for Payment of the Meters, the Commissioners are of Opinion to pursue the former Method, and allow generally after the Rate of One Penny per Chalder, where the Meters are Corporation Meters, and where § otherwise

a6 Geo. III. 27° Januarii. 57

otherwise after the Rate of Two Pence per Chalder, except in some few Places, where the Coals being delivered at a considerable Distance from the Ports and common Place of Residence, it will be necessary to allow something towards the extraordinary Charge, which however will be no considerable increase thereof.

B. O. IVY.

After our hearty Commendations. — Whereas, in your Memorial of the 21st of August last, you have repre-fented unto us, that you have had under Consideration the settling the Allowances for Payment of the Officers in the Out Ports, employed in the receiving and collecting the present Duty on Coals; and upon looking into the Produce of the said Duty in the several Ports for a Year, from the Commencement thereof, which was from the 15th May 1698 to the 15th May 1699, you are of Opinion, That there be allowed for the receiving and accompting for the said Duty, arising in the Out Ports for the said Time, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent, for the first Thousand Pounds, and One Pound per Cent, for every Hundred Pounds afterwards; that is to say, where there has been received the Sum of One thousand Pounds, there be allowed the Sum of Thirty Pounds, Twenty Pounds whereof to be to the Collector, who has tlje Charge of receiving and accounting for the Money, and Ten Pounds to the Comptroller; and where the Sum of Two thousand Pounds has been received, there be allowed the Sum of Forty Pounds, Two Thirds whereof to -be to the Collector, and One Third to the Comptroller, and so in Proportion; which you conceive will prove a reasonable Allowance for the Service before mentioned, and be considerably less than was allowed for collecting the former Duty. And you having likewise represented to us, that there has been Occasion, in some particular Ports, to employ some of the Officers to inspect the Meters in Places where the Coals are delivered, being at Distance from the ordinary Residence of the Officers; and that you think it necessary to make them some Allowance for their Care out of the said Duty.

And for the Payment of the Meters, you are of Opinion to pursue the former Method, and allow generally after the Rate of One Penny per Chalder, where the Meters are Corporation Meters, and where otherwise after the Rate of Two Pence per Chalder, except in some few Places, where the Coals being delivered at a considerable Distance from the Ports and common Place of Residence, it will be necessary to allow something towards the extraordinary Charge, which, however, will be no considerable Increase thereof: — We, approving hereof, do hereby direct you to cause (be said several Allowances to be made, as you have above proposed; and for so doing this shall be, to you and all others herein concerned, a sufficient Warrant

Cha.

Memorial, 19 May 1758.

We beg Leave to represent to your Lordships, That by a Memorial of this Board, dated the 24th November 1709, to the Earl of Godolphin, then Lord High Treasurer, the Commissioners proposed (for the Reasons therein contained) that when the Receipt in any Port, under the Head of Customs, happened to fall short of answering the Charges of the Establishment in such Port, the Collector might be permitted to borrow from Money in his Hands, out of the Branches — Irnpost on Wine and Vinegar — Irnpost on Tobacco — Irnpost on East India and other Poundage Goods, from Christmas 1690 — New additional Impositions, from the ill March 1692-3 — and, the Duty on Whale Fins: And his Lordship, by his Warrant of the 25th April 1710, was pleased to agree thereto; and this Practice has been ever since pursued.

We further beg Leave to represent. That, as it frequently happens, that the Collectors of the Out Ports have not in their Hands, at the End of a Quarter, Money sufficient, arising by the Six above-mentioned Branches (called The united Branches) to pay the Salaries and incidental Charges of their Port, though the whole Receipt of the Port, upon all the Branches, may be more than sufficient for that Purpose: And this Practice having produced great Inconveniences and Confusion, the Board found it expedient to consult the Attorney General, whether they can or cannot by Law direct the whole Charges of Management to be paid out of the whole Receipt of the Thirty-seven Branches of which the Customs now conlift, or whether they are confined to pay the whole Charges of Management out of the Six Branches before mentioned; and he having given his Opinion in the following Words; vis.

" I conceive that the Charges of Management ought, " in Point of Law, to ifi'ue proportionably out of the " several Branches to which they are incident, all of " which, except only the Coinage Duty (which is otherwise provided for) are either expressly, or by Reference, or from the Nature of the Thing, burthened " with their own proper Charges, which Deduction is " incidental, and a primary Lien upon each Fund, to be " satisfied in the First Place, even if the Laws had been " silent in this Particular; but as the same Officers " are employed in all the Branches, it would be inconvenient and difficult to apportion the Management " of each upon that Branch, and make such a Piecemeal Payment; the Practice of Payment out of the " Branches, N* 1, has been followed for Convenience, " the Salaries having been first fixed upon them; but " I do not conceive that Practice is binding, but that " it would be just as legal to call the other Funds " in Aid to contribute their Quotas, if there should be " Occasion."

We therefore propose to carry the same into Execution, by applying all the Brandies (the Coinage Duty excepted) to the Charges of Management: And if your Lordships approve thereof, we humbly pray your Warrant accordingly.

C.A. B.H. E.H.

After our hearty Commendations. — Having perused the Memorial aforegoing, we approve thereof, and do hereby authorize and require you to give the necessary Directions to the several Officers of the Customs, to follow the Method therein proposed, for answering the Charge of Management in their respective Ports; for

Minute, 7th August 1761.

The Lords of the Treasury having, by their Warrant of the 31st Ultimo, upon the Memorial of this Board of the 19th May 1758, approved of the Payment of the Charges of Management in the Out Ports out of all the Branches of the Customs (except Coinage Duty) Copy of the said Memorial and Warrant is to be delivered to the Comptroller General, who is to consider and report to the Board in what Manner he thinks the same may be best carried into Execution.

Minute, 10th October 1761.

The Lords of the Treasury having been pleased to direct the Board to give the necessary Orders to their several Collectors in their respective Ports, hereafter to apply all the Branches of the Customs (except the Coal and Coinage Duties, and Six Pence per Pound to the Civil List) to the Charges of Management, the Six United Branches which have been hitherto applied to

1785.

this Purpose being found inefficient to answer die End, a general Letter is to be wrote to the several Collectors and Comptrollers in the Out Ports, to authorize and direct them to observe this Regulation for the future, and to defray the whole Expence of their respective Ports put of the whole Receipt in their Hands, so far as the fame, at the End of every Quarter, shall prove to be adequate thereto; but in case such Receipt should fall short of the Sum necessary for the whole Charge, they are to acquaint the Board therewith at the Expiration of each Quarter, and to crave an Ira-prest accordingly, which will be granted them upon the Collector Inwards in the Port of London: And they are like wile to be acquainted, that as the Board have thought fit to discontinue the Allowance of One Pound per Cent, for this Service, they are not for the future to crave such Allowance in their Accounts; and they are to observe, that this Order relates also to the present expiring Quarter, as far as they may be able, from the Money in their Hands, to answer the Directions of it; and Notice hereof is to be given to the Collector Inwards, and other proper Officers in this Port. — And the Board having taken into Consideration the extraordinary Trouble that will attend the Office and Clerks of the Collector Inwards, by the many Im-prefts to be paid Quarterly by them to the Collectors of the Out Ports, in consequence of the before-mentioned Regulation, the Commissioners have agreed to allow Mr. Andrew Reid, One of the Clerks under the Collector Inwards, the Sum of 50/. per Annum, upon Incidents on that Account, and an Order is to be prepared for paying the same from Time, to Time accordingly.

RULES which may serve for the Ports in general.

Whereas some Societies and Companies of Merchants do trade in a joint Stock, and enter the whole Lading and Cargo of a Ship Inwards in One single Entry; when the Adventurers therein concerned are many, the Officers and Waiters may take and receive such Gratuity as the said Company shall hereafter voluntarily consent to pay unto them, any Thing in this Order, or Table of Fees, or any other Act or Provision, to the contrary notwithstanding.

All Goods under the Value of Five Pound, in the Book of Rates, paying Subsidy the Sum of Five Shillings or less, shall pass without Payment of any Fees.

No British Merchant, that shall have Goods of his own to be landed out of One Ship or Vessel at One Time (although the Receipt of the Subsidy be distributed into several Offices) shall be charged to pay any more or other Fees than for a single Entry.

Goods in Partnership to pass as if the Proprietors were One single Person. Fish, by British, in British Shipping or Vessel, Towards or Outwards, or along the Coast, to pay no Fees.

Foreign Coin and Bullion Inwards may be landed by any Person, without Warrant or Fee.

Diamonds, Precious Stones, Jewels, and Pearls of all Sorts, to pass Outwards without Warrant or Fee.

Poll Entries Inward to pass without Fee under Five Shillings; if above Five Shillings, and under Forty Shillings, then Six Pence; but if the Custom to be paid exceed Forty Shillings, then it shall pay the full Fees as was paid for the First Warrant.

The Merchant shall pay for all Goods opening that shall be short entered above Ten Shillings Custom.

The Merchant shall pay for the weighing of all Goods that shall be short entered above Twenty Shillings Custom.

The Merchant not to be at any Charge if duly entered.

N* 26.

The Examination of Edward Hooper, Esquire; taken upon Oath, April 19th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is the Senior Commissioner of the Customs. The Commissioners of the Custorus are Nine in Number; they hold their Offices under a Commission from the Crown, during Pleasure. Each Commissioner receives, by virtue of his Corn-million, a Salary of One thousand Pounds a Year, paid Quarterly, subject to the Land Tax, the One Shilling, and Civil Lilt Duties, which reduce it to Seven hundred and Seventy-four Pounds Seventeen Shillings, exclusive of the Taxes on the Receipts. He receives likewise an Allowance of Two hundred Pounds every Year, by Warrant from the Treasury, paid Annually, for the extraordinary Care and Pains taken by the Board in the Quarantine Service, ftrifitly pursuing the Orders of the Privy Council. The Commissioners receive no other Salary, Fees, or Emoluments whatever.

The Board of Customs have not, as he apprehends, any Power over the Patent Officers of the Customs, nor over their Deputies, except the Power of fuf-pending them, in order to prevent any Prejudice to the Revenue, and to give Time for representing their Conduct to their Principals; nor any Power of rejecting the Persons appointed by Warrant from the Treasury; they have a Power, by their Commission, of removing or otherwise punishing Officers so appointed for Misconduct.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Richd Neavc,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

IViW* Roe.

N* 2t.

The Examination of Mr. George Robinson; taken upon Oath, April 20th, 26th, and 29th,

1785-

This Examinant faith, That he is Western Clerk in the Office of the Secretary of the Customs, and appointed by Warrant from the Treasury: It is the Business of his Office to receive all Letters and Papers relative to the Western Ports, which are Forty-two in Number, to read them to the Board, and take their Directions thereupon, and to settle and revile the Letters and Orders to those Ports. He attends at his Office Six or Eight Hours every Day, except on Holidays. He is paid Two Salaries of One hundred and Fifty Pounds a Yeai1 each, the first by virtue of the Treasury Warrant, the other by Minute of the Board; the Salary by the Warrant is’ subject to the Land Tax, the One Shilling, and Civil List Duties — the Incidental Salary, to the Two latter only j the Taxes amount together to Forty-nine Pounds Nine Shillings. He receives likewise Annually by Warrant from the Treasury, a Sum for the Quarantine Service, Six Shillings for every Ship performing Quarantine; this amounted, in the last Year, to Eighty-one Pounds Eighteen Shillings. He receives also One Fifth Part of the Net Poundage, and One Eighth Part of the Fees received by the Secretary; which, with Five Pounds, an Annual Gratuity from the East India Company, for the Trouble they give to the Office, amounted in the last Year to One hundred and Ten Pounds Four Shillings, and One Halfpenny.

s

The Net Produce of his Employment last Year, as Western Clerk, was five hundred and Fifty-eight Pounds Three Shillings and Ten Pence One Halfpenny. He was appointed in the Year 1782, by a Minute of ffie Board, the Examiner of Stationary, for which he receives a Salary of Thirty Pounds a Year, and Ten Guineas a customary Gratuity, from the Stationer; the Salary is reduced by Taxes to Twenty-seven Pounds Fourteen Shillings. It was customary to allow each Office in London, and each Out Port, every Year, a stated Allowance of different Kinds of Stationary. In Nomember 1783 the Board came to a Resolution to allow Annually, to the principal Officers of the several Outports, a Quantity of Stationary, not exceeding in Value a certain Sum, proportionable to the Gross Receipt and Bafinels in their respefitive Distri&s, which Stationary they are to apply for to the Stationer who has the Patent for supplying the Customs. In December 1784 the Board, after a long Inquiry, came to the like Resolution relative to the Officers in the Port of London, with this Difference, that the Office Books were to be lbpplied as usual at the Expence of the Crown, upon the Application of the Officers, stating the Necessity and Uses to which they are intended; this Regulation was in March last extended to the Officers at the Out Ports, upon their Representation that they were unable to purchase Office Books out of their Allowance. The first Regulation relative to the Out Ports produced a Saving to the Public of about Seven hundred and Seventy-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings a Year. The Regulation relative to the Port of London will, upon Calculation, produce a Saving of about Eight hundred and Twenty-three Pounds Seven Shillings a Year; together, above One thousand Six hundred Pounds a Year. All the Quarterly Bills of the Stationer, and the Cravings for Books, are examined and checked by the Examiner of the Stationary, to see that the Bills do not exceed the Annual Allowance, and that the Books are actually necessary for the Public Service. If the Annual Bills are leis than the Annual Allowance, the Officer has Credit with the Stationer for the Surplus in his next Year’s Account.

Geo. Robinson.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neave,

Sami' Beachcroft,

Wm Roe.

N* 25.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas Shaw; taken upon Oath, July lft, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Clerk in the Bond Office, which is a Branch of the Secretary’s . Office —

The Appointment to this Office was in the Secretary, it is now in the Board — One Branch of the Business is to make out all Bonds for the due Exportation of certain particular Articles, principally East India, and for the due Return of damaged Goods taken out of the Warehouse for the Purpose of dying or glazing —

He makes out Certificates of the Securities having been given — He keeps a Register of all the Wool, Yarn, and other Articles, imported into England from Ireland, and of all the Ships qualified for that Importation —

He makes out the Annual Account of the prohibited East India Goods, and Naval Stores from Russia, presented to Parliament — He receives, examines, and makes out, Lists of the Out Port, Corn, and some other Debentures, and enters the Cockets for the Exportation of Foreign Bullion, and of Wrought Silver Plate, and Watches, and prepares Letters for fending down certain Cockets to the Out Ports for Goods sent by Land Carriage.

He is paid, by Minute of the Board, a Salary of Eighty Pounds a Year — He receives Two customary Fees, One Shilling and Six Pence on every Bond, and One Shilling on every Plate and Bullion Cocket, and an Annual Gratuity from the East India Company of Five Pounds Five Shillings — These amounted together last Year to Two hundred and Thirteen Pounds Three Shillings — He paid for Taxes Four Pounds, and to a Clerk Twenty Pounds, which reduced his Net Income to Two hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Three Shillings.

T. Shaw.

N* 26.

The Examination of Mrs. Bridget Kelly-, taken upon Oath, April 28th and 29th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That she is Housekeeper of the Custom House of London, and has been so about Fourteen Years — She was appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, requiring the Commissioners of the Customs to issue their Constitution appointing her to the Office of Housekeeper — The Duty of the Office is to provide proper Servants to take Care of the House; to inspefct and report, in Writing, upon the Bills of Tradesmen for Repairs and Alterations made within the House, in order to satisfy the Board that the Work

T charged

Fourteenth Report on public Account*.

70 27° januarti. A. 1786.

charged has been actually performed (the Charge being referred to the Surveyor of the House); Coals, Candles, and other Necessaries for the Use of the House, are from Time to Time, as they are wanted, craved by the House-keeper, and ordered by the Commissioners of the Customs; the Tradesmen who furnish those Articles are nominated by the Board, and it is the Duty of the Housekeeper to see that the Quantity charged is actually fumished, and to report accordingly upon the Bills which are for that Purpose referred to her. — The Housekeeper is not employed to pay any of the Bills — She keeps an Upper Servant, who constantly resides in the House, and in her Absence performs the Duties of Housekeeper, and she occasionally resides in the House herself, and at such Times fees the Duty performed herself. — She always signs the Bills herself, and when flie is not at the House relies on her Upper Servants Account, that the Work has been done, or the Articles brought in.

She receives a Salary appointed by the Warrant or Confutation, of Three hundred and Eighty-five Pounds a Year, paid upon the Establishment; and upon a considerable increaie of Offices, the Commissioners of the Customs made an Addition to it of Forty Pounds a Year, paid out of Incidents.

The Housekeeper formerly had divers small Perquisites, amounting in the Whole to about Two hundred Pounds a Year, whit^i were abolished by an Order of the Commissioners of the Customs, in 1783 j since when she has received no Perquisites whatever. By Warrant of the Treasury, of the 6th of January 1785, she received Two hundred and Eighty-six Pounds Eleven-Shillings and Eleven Pence One Half-penny, in lieu of those Perquisites, from the 30th of July 1783 to the 5th of January 1785, which is at the Rate of about Two hundred Pounds a Year; and for the Quarter from the 5th of January to the 5th April Instant, a Warrant is ordered for Fifty Pounds out of these Allowances, making together Six hundred and Twenty-five Pounds. — She pays for Taxes One hundred and Two Pounds Eighteen Shillings, and for the Wages and Maintenance of Servants, Two hundred and Thirty-three Pounds Two Shillings, together Three hundred h irty-six Pounds a Year; which leaves to her a Net Sum of Two hundred Eighty-nine Pounds a Year, which is the whole Emolument arising from her Office.

Bridget Kelly.

The Examination of Mr. William; taked

upon Oath, April 27th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, that he is Solicitor for the toorthern Ports; he holds this Office by the Constitution of the Board of Treasury, during Pleasure. It is his Province to transact all the Law Business arising in the Northern Ports, except Criminal Prosecutions, and Proceedings upon Bonds. He receives a Salary of Two hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year by his Constitution, Twenty Pounds a Year by Minute of the Board, and Two hundred Pounds a Year also by Minute of the Board, for the Payment of Two Clerks and a Messenger, which Sum he pays to them.

As a Solicitor, he receives his Professional Fees for the Business he transacts, the Whole of which is paid, either by the Defendants, or out of the Produce of Seizures, or out of the King’s Share. The Taxes paid by him in the last Year amounted to Sixty-nine Pounds and Eight Pence; and the incidental Expences of Chamber Rent. Coals, and Candles, to Twenty-six Pounds, which reduced the Net Produce of this Employment, exclusive of his Professional Fees, to One hundred and Seventy-four Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence.

He attends every Day of Business at the Board of Customs, to receive the References from the Board, and to make Reports thereupon, which he understands to be the Consideration for his Salaries.

The Examination of Mr. John Arden; taken upoti Oath, 29th April, and 3d May, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy Inspector of the Prosecutions carried on by the Solicitors of the Customs. He is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, at the Nomination of the Principal, and holds his Office during Pleasure. He has been Sixteen Years Deputy to William Poynlz, Esquire, who is the Inspector of Prosecutions, by Patent, during Pleasure. The whole Business of this Office is transaded by the Deputy and One Clerk, without the Interference of the Principal. The Duty of this Officer is to see that the King’s Share of the Produce of Seizures, and of Fines and Forfeitures, is truly paid into the Exchequer.

A Register of all Seizures, taken from the Office of the Register of Seizures, and an Entry of all Prosecutions for Fines and Forfeitures, taken from the Books of the Solicitors, are kept in this Office. When the King’s Share of the Produce of Seizures is ascertained, and Payment of it into the Exchequer ordered by the Board, the Accountant of Petty Receipts fends to this Office a Certificate, stating the Sum to be paid into the Exchequer, whether the Seizure was made in London or at an Out Port.

Where a Penalty or Forfeiture is compounded or- recovered, the Minute of the Board, stating the Sum to be paid into the Exchequer, is transmitted to, and entered in, this Office. Every Quarter he receives from the Exchequer an Account of the Sums paid in for the Produce of Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures, for the Use of the Crown, during the preceding Quarter; he compares this Account with the Certificates and Minutes in his Office.

Some short Time ago, an Order was issued from the Board of Customs, prohibiting the receiving Gratuities from the Officers, upon the Payment of their Salaries; which Carder has been carried into Execution.

At the Time the Salaries are paid at the Treasury, the Land Tax for those Salaries is either paid to the Cdfle€tors of the Land Tax at the Custom House, by the Officers; or, being deducted by the Pay Officer, is paid by him to the Collectors.

Government pays the Land Tax for those Officers whose Salaries do not exceed Sixty Pounds a Year. The Amount of this Tax is paid to the Collectors by an Annual Warrant of the Treasury. The One Shilling, and Six Penny Duties, are deducted by the Pay Officer at the Time of Payment, and paid to the respective Receivers.

J. Mills.

The Examination of Mr. John Mills', taken upon Oath, July 8th, and August 26th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That the Salaries of the Officers of the Customs, paid by the Receiver General, are, for the most Part, paid out of the Branch of the Customs: Both the Establishments and the Incidental Lift are always paid out of that Branch, if there is Money enough upon it to pay them; if not, the Deficiency is taken out of Come other Brand), as is most convenient. This has been the constant practice of the Office. All incidental Expences likewise are paid out of the same Branch, unless otherwise directed by the Order of the Board.

The Examination of Mr. Humphry Bache; taken upon Oath, May 10th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Chief Teller to the Receiver General of the Customs, who appoints all the Officers in his Office. He is paid by the Receiver General a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year, out of which he pays Sixty 'Pounds to his Assistant He received from' the Officers, upon the Payment of their Salaries, certain Gratuities, in Proportion to the Quantum of the Salaries; which Gratuities have been paid to the Chief Teller Time immemorial, without any Variation, that he knows of; and which, including some other minute Articles, amounted last Year to Two hundred and Fifty Pounds; which made the Net Income of his Office Two hundred and Ninety Pounds.

The Treasury Warrant for the One hundred Pounds a Year to the Receiver General, specifies the Service to be the Payment of the Tidesmen, and other inferior Officers, who are very numerous, and paid their Subsistence Weekly, and were formerly paid by the Pay-master of Incidents, an Office not under the Receiver General. This Salary is paid to the Chief Teller and Vot. 41.

his Assistant, for performing that Service. The Gratui- Fourteenth ties are the only Emoluments he receives for receiving l{e(?"r.\. the Duties, and making the other Payments. Thele ^ecoants. He applied for a Compensation to the Board of Customs, but without Succels.

N° 36.

The Examination of Mr. John taken

upon Oath, April 18th> 4th, and August, the 29th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That the Account of the Salaries, Fees, Allowances, and Gratuities, received by the Officers of the Customs in the Port of London, was made out by him, for the most Part, from Returns made by the several Officers therein mentioned to the Secretary of the Customs, pursuant to the Precept of this Board.

The Salaries of the Commissioners, and the Taxes to which they are subject, being fixed, he made out the Accounts of the Produce of their Employments from his own Knowledge of them, and with the Confirmation of the Secretary; the Columns of Salaries and Allowances from the Crown, as stated in the Returns, include the Sums allowed the principal Officers for their Deputies and Clerks.

The Taxes inserted in the Column of Taxes include the Land Tax, the One Shilling, and Six Penny Duties, and, in some Offices, the Receipt Tax, and the Payments to the Superannuation Fund. All Officers whole established Salaries exceed Sixty Pounds a Year pay the Land Tax for those Salaries, which Land Tax is deduced from the Salary at the Time of Payment. Where the established Salaries do not exceed Sixty Pounds a Year, the Land Tax on them is allowed to the Officer, by virtue of a Warrant from the Treasury.

This Examinant further faith, That he is Deputy to Henry Ellison, Esquire, Supervisor of the Receipts and Payments of the Receiver General. The Supervisor holds his Office by Constitution of the Treasury, during Pleasure; he executes no Part of the Business of the Office himself, it is all tranlafited by his Deputy, and Two Clerks. He receives, by his Constitution, a Salary of Five hundred and Eighty Pounds, and, by Minute of the Board, an incidental Salary of Eighty Pounds: Out of which he pays, for Taxes, One hundred and Five Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence, and to his Deputy and Clerks Two hundred and Twenty Pounds; which reduced his Net Income, last Year, to Three hundred and Thirty-four Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence. No Gratuities are taken in this Office; the only Fees are small Fees for registering Instruments, paid to the Deputy and Clerks.

J. Dally.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond,

N° 37. N* 38.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas

taken upon Oath, May 6th and 10th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Warehousekeeper for the Collector Inwards. The Business of the Receiver of Fines and Forfeitures for London being trans-acted in that Office, he acts as Deputy to Isaac Needham, Esquire, who holds that Office by Warrant of the Treasury, during Pleasure. The Receiver attends the Office occasionally, to sign some Accounts to be laid before the Board: He receives an Allowance of Three Guineas upon each Indenture of Appraisement, of the Value of One hundred Pounds or upwards, of all Goods returned into the Exchequer, not enumerated in the Act of the Twelfth of George the First, which Allowance is deducted from the Gross Produce of the Sales; it was formerly made by Warrant of the Treasury to the Warehousekeeper, when the Offices of Warehousekeeper and Receiver were held by the same Person; this Allowance, last Year, amounted to Two hundred and Seventy-three Pounds Ten Shillings and Two Pence, to which was added Nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Six Pence, being Allowances to him upon the Sale of Horses and Carriages.

It has been usual for the Purchaser to pay to the Receiver a Imall Fee on the Sale of each Lot — One Shilling, if fold for Exportation, and Six Pence, if fold for Home Consumption; these Fees amounted, last Year, to Eighty-three Pounds Fifteen Shillings. He paid Twenty Pounds for Land Tax, Seventy-seven Pounds Twelve Shillings to his Clerk, and for Contingencies Six Pounds Six Shillings; which reduced his Net Income to Two hundred and Sixty-three Pounds One Shilling and Eight Pence.

This Examinant further faith, That he holds the Office of Warehousekeeper by Deputation from Sir Banks Jenkinson, during Pleasure. He is paid by a Poundage and Fees; the Poundage is Two Pence in the Pound upon the Gross Produce of the Goods enumerated in the Act; of the Twelfth of George the First, grounded upon a Minute of the Board of Customs, and deducted out of that Gross Produce; it was given in lieu of a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year: This Poundage, last Year, amounted to Three hundred and Eighty Pounds Ten Shillings and Six Pence. The Fees are customary Payments on the Discharge of Goods out of the Warehouse, and other Bufinefe transacted in the Office; these Fees amounted to Two hundred and Twenty-seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Nine Pence. He paid, for the One Shilling, and Civil List Duties on the Poundage, Twenty-eight Pounds Ten Shillings and Six Pence; to his Clerks, who are appointed by the Collector Inwards, Sixty-five Pounds; and for contingent Expences, One Pound Five Shillings; which reduced his Net Income, for the last Year, to Five hundred and Thirteen Pounds Two Shillings and Nine Pence. This Poundage has been greatly reduced by the Acts of the last Sessions, relative to Tea and Spirituous Liquors; it produced, in the last Five Months, under Twenty Pounds: The Average Amount of the Poundage, for the last Ten Years, has been One hundred and Seventy-eight Pounds.

Tho’ Chaantrell.

This Examinant faith, That he is Clerk to Richard Thompson, Esquire, the Receiver of the Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports: The Receiver holds his Office by Constitution of the Treasury, during Pleasure; he attends occasionally to superintend the Business of the Office, and every Fortnight, to sign the Account of the Receipts and Payments laid before the Board of Customs.

He receives, by virtue of his Constitution, a Salary of Six hundred Pounds a Year; out of which he paid, last Year, for Taxes, Eighty-five Pounds Two Shillings; and to his Clerk, whom he appoints, One hundred and Ten Pounds; which reduced his Net Income to Four hundred and Four Pounds Eighteen Shillings.

N* 39-

The Examination of Richard Stanley, Esquire; taken upon Oath, May 13th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Controller of Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports in the Office of the Customs; he holds his Office by Warrant from the Treasury, as he apprehends during Pleasure. He is paid, by Order of the Board of Customs, Quarterly, a Salary of Three hundred and Thirty-five Pounds Ten Shillings a Year; out of which he pays, for Taxes, Seventy-six Pounds Five Shillings and Three Pence; and to a Clerk, Sixty Pounds; which makes his Net Income One hundred and Ninety-nine Pounds Four Shillings and Nine Pence.

Every Fortnight an Account is made out in the Office, containing the Sum, in Calli, received for the King’s Share of Fines and Forfeitures during the Fortnight, and the Sum remaining in the King’s Chest, distinguished under the Heads of — Application — and The Sum of Bills in the Chest not converted into Calli; this Account is signed by the Receiver and the Controller, certified as to the Truth of it by the Accountant of Petty Receipts, and laid before the Board: The Accounts lent up from the Officers at the Out Ports are entered in Books kept by both Officers, the Receiver and Controller; the Entries in these Books are frequently examined by both, and always before the Account of the Fortnight is signed.

He frequently examines the Money and Bills in the King’s Chest, and always when he makes up the Account It is an Office of Trust, and he gives Security for the due Execution of it.

Rich* Stanley.

T. Anguish,

Sant Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will" Roe.

The Examination of Mr. dement NevUl taken upon Oath, May 10th and 13th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Clerk to Richard Stanley, Esquire, the Controller of Fines and Forfeitures for the Oat Ports. He was appointed by the Controller, at the Recommendation of the Board of Treasury,

The Collector at an Out Port remits the Produce of the Seizures, Fines, and Forfeitures received by him, by Bills transmitted to the Receiver of the Fines and Forfeitures for the Out Ports; at or near the same Time an Account of them is lent to the Controller, this Account contains a Division of the Sum remitted, under the Heads of — The King’s Share — Secretary’s Poundage — Accountant’s Poundage — Law Charges — The Allowance to the Register of Seizures — and, The Civil List Duty; a like Account is sent to the Office of the Accountant of Petty Receipts.

After the Bills are accepted they are locked up in an Iron Cheli, under Two different Keys, one kept by the Receiver, the other by the Controller; the Bills, when due, are received by the Receiver, and the Money deposited in the same Chest, until issued for Services pursuant to Orders of the Board of Customs.

Clem* Neoill Zouch.

This Account includes all the Duties collected at the Out Ports; but the Account of the Payments by the Receiver General into the Exchequer, in the same Year, does not include such Part of the Duties collected at the Out Ports as were either not remitted, or, if remitted, not received by him during the Year; and this Sum is very different in different Years.

The Collectors at the Out Ports pay the Salaries and Incidents out of any Money in their Hands, upon whatever Branch it may be, unless upon the excepted Branches, pursuant, as he believes, to a Treasury Warrant of the Year 1761; if they make these Payments out of the excepted Branches, the Controller General corrects their Accounts, and transfers those Payments to such other Branches of their Receipt as appear to him most convenient, and to reduce the Total of the Payments to an even Sum. The Examination of Mr. William Saxby; taken upon Oath, May 11th, 1785.

The Examination of Mr. Charles taken

upon Oath, June 10th, 1785.

This Examinant iaithj, That he is Deputy to, and appointed by, Heneage Leg Esquire, Register of His Majesty’s Warrants in the Port of London. The Register holds his Office by Patent, during Pleasure. He executes no Part of the Business, it is all transacted by the Deputy.

It is the Bufinefe of this Office to enter in a Book. Copies of all the Entries Inwards in the Port of London: No Use is made of these Entries; the Books containing them are returned from Time to Time into the Exchequer: They are never called for; but the Tradition is, that when the Customs were farmed, these Books, with others of the like Kind, were sent to the Exchequer, for the Purpose of informing them of the Number of Entries, and the Amount of the Customs.

Most of the Patent Officers make the like Returns of their Books into the Exchequer.

The Register has no Salary; He is paid by Fees from the Merchant-Two Pence for Entries liable to Fees* by Natives, and Four Pence by Foreigners. These Fees amounted last Year to Two hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Five Pence; out of which he paid, for Taxes, Sixteen Pounds; to his Deputy, One hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Five Pence (which was all the Emolument he received from the Office); and to the Collector of his Fees, Ten Pounds Eight Shillings; which reduced his Net Income to Sixty-two Pounds Fourteen Shillings.

This Examinant further faith, That he is also Attorney to Mr. Legge, as Inspector and Examiner of Exchequer Books in the Out Ports. He holds this Office by Constitution, during Pleasure. No Business whatever has been done in this Office ever since ho knew it, which is about Eighteen Years. This Officer has a Salary, by the Constitution, of Three hundred Pounds a Year; out of which he pays, for Taxes, Seventy-eight Pounds Fourteen Shillings. His Net Income was Two hundred and Twenty-one Pounds Six Shillings.

N* 48.

The Examination of Thomas Esquire;

taken upon Oath, May 24th and 26th, 1785*

This Examinant faith. That he is Deputy to Lord Pelham, the Surveyor General of the Customs; he has been Deputy for about Twenty-two Years. The Surveyor General holds his Office by Patent, for Life. He executes no Part of the Business of the Office, the Whole is transacted by his Deputies and Clerks. This Office is a Check upon every Import and Export in the Port of London. Every Bill is entered in this Office, and every Duty computed, examined with the other Checks, and entered in the Caffi Book. The Surveyor General is paid by Salaries and Fees.

His Salaries are, Five hundred Pounds a Year, inserted in his Patent, and Twenty Pounds a Year by Treasury Warrant; his Fees arise from Entries of Instruments in the Office, and from every Cocket Coastwise: All thtfe Fees are established by the Book of Rates; they amounted. Hi the Year 1784, to One thousand Five hundred and Nineteen Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Ten Pence; he paid lor Taxes One hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Sixteen Shillings; to his Deputies, Two Vox. 41.

hundred and Ninety-nine Pounds Seven Shillings and Six Pence; to Clerks, Thirty-four Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence; and for Stationary, and other Expences, Forty-five Pounds Five Shillings and Eleven Pence; these Payments reduced his Net Income to One thousand Four hundred and Ninety-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Eleven Pence.

The Deputy to the Surveyor General is paid a Salary of Two hundred Pounds a Year by his Principal, and no Fees or other Emoluments: The other Deputies are paid finall Salaries by the Principal; and the Deputy Outwards, and his Clerk, receive finall customary Fees from the Merchants, for Business done in the Office. The Surveyor General appoints his Deputies and Clerks.

Thomas Fanshaw.

N* 49.

The Examination of Arthur Hammond, Esquire; taken upon Oath, May 26th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he i3 the Senior of the Four Surveyors General resident in London. These Surveyors General are each appointed by the Constitution of the Treasury to hold their Offices during the King's Pleasure: It is their Business to superintend, either jointly or separately, the ConduQ. of all the Officers of the Customs, both in London and at the Out Ports, pursuant to the Orders and Instructions, either of the Lords of the Treasury, or the Board of Customs. Where a Complaint arises in a Minute of the

Board, containing the Subject Matter of the Reference, is transmitted to the Office of the Surveyors General — a Charge is formed against the Officer complained of — he is summoned, and heard, and the Surveyors report to the Board the Evidence, and their Opinion. Where the Complaint arises at an Out Port, or the Board suspect Miscondu6t, the Surveyor General is lent down by the Board, with full Authority to examine into the Conduct and Ability of every Officer at that Port, and to make his Report to the Board. Disputes between the Officers of the Customs, or between them and the

Merchants, are likewise referred to these Officers, and they form the Instructions for the Conduct of the Officers, and the Management of the Revenue, wherever either the Board or the Surveyor finds it necessary: Two of them, at least, constantly attend the Board of Customs whenever they fit

Each Surveyor is paid by his Constitution a Salary of Four hundred Pounds a Year, subject to Taxes, amounting to One hundred and Two Pounds Two Shillings, which reduces his Net Income to Two hundred and Ninety-seven Pounds Eighteen Shillings a Year.

When upon an Out Port Inspection, he is allowed, for himself and a Clerk, One Pound Seven Shillings and Six Pence a Day, and One Shilling and Three Pence a Mile for Chaise Hire. He has no Fee, Perquisite, or other Emolument whatever, except that he has received from the Board occasional Gratuities, amounting, in the Course of Three Years, to Twenty-eight Pounds Five Shillings, for extraordinary Services.

Ar. Hammond.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond,

Wiir Roe.

This Examinant faith. That he is Chief Clerk to the Register General of all Trading Ships belonging to Great Britain; He is appointed tv Peter Shaio, Esquire, the Register General, who holds his Office by Patent, during Life. The Business of ths Office is tranla&ed by the Chief and Four other Clerks; the Principal executes no Part of it In this Office are entered the Registers of all Ships trading to the British Plantations, and all Ships and Vessels entered from or cleared out to Foreign Parts at the Port of London, specifying, among other Things, the Number of Tons, and the Number of Men, and difdnguishing the Foreign from the British Ships.

The Collectors and Comptrollers at the Out Ports transmit every Quarter to this Office Lists of the Ships, both British and Foreign, trading to or from each Port

You 41.

during the Quarter, with the like Distinctions, and speci* tying also the Quantities of certain Enumerated Goods t They fend also Two Annual Accounts — One of the Number of Ships belonging to the Port, with the Total Tonnage, and Number of Men — the other the Number of the British and Foreign Ships trading to or from that Port, with the Total Tonnage, and repeated Voyages. The Surveyor at each Out Port transmits a Quarterly Account of all Goods landed from and Gripped to Foreign Parts during the Quarter, and of the Quantity of Coals, Culm, and Cinders landed there.

N# 52.

The Examination of Mr. John taken

upon Oath, May 26th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Assistant to John Pelham, Esquire, the Inspector General of Imports and Exports in the Office of the Customs. The Business of this Office is transa&ed by the Assistant, and Six Clerks; the inspector General executes no Part of the Business. He holds the Office by Constitution from the Board of Treasury, during Pleasure; the Assistant is appointed in the same Manner: The Six Clerks are appointed and paid by the Inspector General.

Every Bill for an Import or an Export, at the Port of London, is brought to this Office, and the Quantity of every Article upon each of these Bills is entered in this Office, distinguishing the Country from and to which each Article is brought or sent Every Out Port fends to this Office a similar Quarterly Account of the Imports and Exports, of which Entries are made in this Office; from hence an Account may be obtained from this Office, of the Quantity of every Article exported or imported, and to and from what Country, at any Port in England, for any given Time.

The Inspector General is paid by his Constitution a Salary of Seven hundred and Eighty Pounds a Year; out of which he pays One hundred and Forty-one Pounds Ten Shillings for Taxes, Two hundred and Sixty Pounds to his Clerks, and Six Pounds to his Assistant, to defray contingent Expences; which reduces his Net Income to Three hundred and Seventy-two Pounds Ten Shillings a Year.

The Assistant is paid Two hundred Pounds a Year by his Constitution, and receives Six Pounds from his Principal; he pays Fifty-one Pounds for Taxes, and Two Pounds for contingent Expences, which makes his Net Income One hundred and Fifty-three Pounds a Year: No Fees, Perquisites, or Emoluments are received in this Office.

Jn. Tomkyns.

The Examination of James Hume, Esquire; taken upon Oath, May 27th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is Chief Deputy to the Duke of Newcastle, the Controller of the Customs in the Port of London. The Business of this Office is transacted by a Chief Deputy, a Deputy Inwards, a Deputy Outwards, a Deputy for the Coast Business, and Three Clerks, all appointed by the Controller, who. executes no Part of the Business himself.

The Bench Officers, in the Long Room at the Custom House consist of the Five Chief Deputies, of Five Patentees, the Collector Inwards, the Collector Outwards, the Controller, the Surveyor, and the Surveyor General: It is the Business of the Bench Officers to attend Daily

at the Custom House upon Working Days, to administer Oaths, each to superintend his own Office, and to answer such References as are font to them by the Board. The Controller holds his Office by Patent, during Life; he is paid by Salaries and Fees: The Salaries are. Two hundred and Fifty-five Pounds by his Patent, and One hundred and Twenty Pounds by Treasury Warrants; the Fees are Payment by the Merchants, of very small Sums, upon all Entries Inwards, and all Outwards where the Subsidy exceeds Five Shillings; upon Debentures, and all Coast Documents: These Fees are received by the Clerk of the Rates, and the Deputy Collectors Outwards, and paid Monthly to the Chief Deputy Controller: The Controller’s Fees amounted last Year to One thousand Three hundred and Forty-eight Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence; he paid, for Taxes, One hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Ten Shillings; to his Deputies, Two hundred and Forty four Pounds Ten Shillings; and to a Clerk, Fifty

N° 57.

The Examination of Perry Player, Esquire; taken upon Oath, June ill, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is Customer of Cloth and Petty Customs in the Port of London: He holds this Office by Patent, during Pleasure; he executes it himself, with the Assistance of One Clerk, whom he appoints: His Business is to collect the Duties upon White Woollen Cloths exported, and these are the only Duties he collects; the Petty Customs, or Aliens Duties Outwards, has been long since abolished, and the Aliens Duty Inwards is collected by the Collector Inwards. Where Goods are entered Outwards by an Alien, though he pays no Duty as Alien, yet a Fee is due; if a whole Fee, Three Shillings and Six Pence, of which one Shilling and Six Pence is paid to the Customer of Petty Customs, Eight Pence to his Controller, Eight Pence to the Surveyor, and Eight Pence to the Surveyor General, the Customer receives and divides it: This Fee is paid to the Customer, upon the Cocket being produced to him, which he signs: These Fees amount to very little in the Year, for few Entries are made in the Name of Aliens* He receives by his Patent a Salary of Five Pounds a Year, and the Fees upon Entries of Cloths Outwards, inserted in the Book of Rates; the Amount of these Fees last Year was Seventy-six Pounds Twelve Shillings and Nine Pence; his Net Income was Forty-eight rounds and Three Pence. The Duties produced by this Branch are inconsiderable; he pays every Quarter into the Treasury all the Duties then in his Hands.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy Controller of Cloth and Petty Customs Inwards and Outwards in the Port of London; he is appointed by Lancelot Harrison, Esquire, the Controller, who holds his Office by Patent, for Life. — All the Business of this Branch is transacted by the Deputy, the Principal executes no Part of it. Where Cloth is exported, the Controller is a Check upon the Customer, both as to the Quantity exported, and as to the Computation of the Duties upon those Exports of Cloth liable to Duties: He compares the Articles entered upon the Bill with the Articles entered upon the Cocket, and computes the Duties, signs the Cocket, and retains the Bill; he enters the Duties in a Calli Book, and the Quantities in a separate Book. Every Week the Customer makes out

an

an Account, whether he has received Duties or not; he enters the Total Sum, received, and signs the Account; it is lent to the Controller, who examines it with his own Entries, and signs it. Every Quarter the Customer, before he pays the Duties into the Treasury, applies to the Controller, to fee whether his Total Receipt agrees with the Total of the Controller.

No Duties have been received as he apprehends, for many Years by the Customer, under the Title of Petty Customs Inwards; but every Entry by an Alien, and of certain Goods imported in Foreign Ships, paying the Petty Customs to the Collector Inwards, is registered in the Controller’s Office.

The Controller is paid, by his Patent, a Salary of Two hundred Pounds a Year; he receives small Fees for Entries and Clearings, established by the Book of Rates, amounting last year to Forty-one Pounds Eighteen Shillings: he paid for Taxes Fifty-five Pounds, and Twelve Shillings to his Deputy; which made his clear Receipt One hundred and Seventy-four Pounds Six Shillings.

He is paid Two Salaries, Sixty Pounds a Year by "his Warrant, and Twenty Pounds by Minute of the Board of Customs: He receives custoroary Fees for making out Sufferances, and for entering where the Ship is Quayed; these amounted last Year, to One hundred and Seventy Pounds: He paid for Taxes Three Pounds, and to a Clerk Thirty Pounds; which made his Net Income Two hundred and Seventeen Pounds.

The Deputy receives a Salary from the Collector, of Two hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year, by a Treasury Warrant One hundred Pounds, arhd upon the Incidental Lift Fifty Pounds: His Fees consist of One Third of ffie Coinage Fee of One Shilling in the Pound on Spirits, collected in the Port of London’, this produced last Year One hundred and Fourteen Pounds Six Shillings and Two Pence; of a Part of the Sufferance Fee, and of customary Fees for Incidental Business, these amounted last Year to Two hundred and Seventy-eight Pounds Ten Shillings and Nine Pence: He paid for Taxes Thirty-four Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Ten Pence, and for Incidents Eleven Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence: His Net Income was Seyen hundred and Forty-six Poulnds Fourteen Shillings and Eleven Pence.

upon Oath, June7th, 1785.

This EXanrtittatit faith, That he 13 Clerk of the Ships Entries; he holds His Office by Deputation from the Collector Inwards in the Tort of London: The Business of this Office is transa&ed by himself and One Clerk, appointed by the Collector.

The Report of every Ship, whether British or Foreign, arriving in the Port of London from Foreign Parts, signedand sworn to by the Master, is deposited in this Office; the Name, the Master, the Tonage, the Number of Men, and the Port from whence she comes, are entered in a Book kept for that Purpose.

The Clerk of the Ships Entries has no Salary; he is paid by customary Fees from the Merchant or Ship’s Owner upon every Report, and other small Fees for Business transacted in the Office; they amounted last Year to Five hundred and Fifty-two Pounds Seven Shillings and Eight Pence: He paid for Taxes Twenty-six Pounds Ten Shillings, and to his Clerk Fifty Pounds,

N* 64.

The Examination of Mr. William; taken upon Oath, June 7th and 9th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That it has been usual for the Cleric of the Rates to oolle& upon every Entry, where Fees are due, the Fees payable for that Entry to the CollectOr Inwards, the Controller, the Surveyor, the Surveyor General, the Register of Warrants, and the Patent King’s Waiters, and to pay over these Fees to each Officer; he receives also the Fee upon a Debenture for a Drawback, payable to the Collector;- — all these Fees are grounded upon the Table annexed to the Book of Rates: The greatest Sum of Fees that can be paid upon a single Entry, collected by him, is Four Shillings and Two Pence, which is divided among the Five Principal Officers, and Nineteen Patent King’s Waiters; the smallest Sum io divided is One Shilling and Three Pence; the Debenture Fee is either Eight Pence or Four Pence.

The Business of the Office of Clerk of the Rates is transacted by himself and Three Clerks; he is allowed by the Collector a Portion of the Poundage upon the Fees of Entries, which he receives for the Collector, Controller, Surveyor, Surveyor General, and Register of Warrants; and also a Portion of the Collector’s Fees on Poll Entries, on Debentures, on Entries of Goods liable to the Aliens Duty because imported in Foreign Ships; and the Whole of the Collectors, Controllers, and Surveyor General’s Fees on Portage Bills; these, together with a Salary of Sixty Pounds, allowed him by the Collector, amounted last Year to about Two hundred and Twenty-three Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny. For receiving the Fees of the Patent Kings Waiters, he has from them 5 /. per Cent, on the Amount of the Fees, and which produced to him last Year about Sixty-five Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence. He is also allowed, as Computer of the Impost on Tobacco, the Sum of One hundred Pounds a Year, by Warrant from the Treasury.

He has also certain small customary Allowances from the Merchants, on the parting of Documents through his Office; which, with an Annual Gratuity of Ten Pounds from the East India Company, amounted last Year to about Two hundred and Fifty-five Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Seven Pence; the Total of these several Salaries and Allowances last Year was Six hundred and Forty-five Pounds; out of which he paid for T&xee Twenty-eight Pounds Eleven Shillings and Eight Pence, and to Clerks One hundred and Ten Pounds, which reduced his Net Income to Five hundred and Six Pounds Eight Shillings and Four Pence.

The Three Clerks under him have, besides the Salary of One hundred and Ten Pounds paid by him, certain customary Allowances from the Merchants, for Business done; which Allowances amounted last Year to about Two hundred and Forty-four Pounds, and with the Salary made the Net Income of the First Clerk about One hundred and Forty Pounds; of the Second Clerk about One hundred and Thirty-

N*65.

The Examination of Mr. James Deacon; taken upon Oath, June 8th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That the Business of the Office of Receiver of the Grand Receipt is executed by him-feIf and Two Clerks, all appointed by the Collector. The Receiver has a Salary of Seventy Pounds a Year paid to him by the Collector, he receives customary Allowances of the Merchant, from Sixpence to One Shilling and Six Pence each, on the Payment of Debentures for Drawbacks and Bounties, and Two Shillings on each Return of Bills of Sight; where the Total Sum of the Duties upon an Entry produces a Fraction under Six Pence, the Merchant pays him the Six Pence, and where between Six Pence and One Shilling, the Merchant pays him the Shilling; These Odd Pence and Allowances amounted last Year to Six hundred and Sixty-seven Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Three Pence: He paid for Taxes Five Pounds One Shilling, to a Clerk Ten Pounds Ten Shillings, and for contingent Expences Fifteen Pounds Seven Shillings; his Net Income was Seven hundred and Six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Three Pence.

Regularly the Duties upon an Entry ought to be brft computed by the Clerk of the Rates, then pals the Four Checks, before the Officer receives them; but the Necessity arising from the Multiplicity of the Business, and the Difficulty of the Computation, is such, that the Receiver, to avoid Delay, is obliged to receive the Duties upon the Computation of any known Officer in the Long Room, subject to the subsequent Computation of tie Checks: If the Duty is in the first Instance under calculated, the Receiver is charged with the Amount of the real Duty, and mull recover the Deficiency from the Merchant; these Mistakes are very frequent, they have amounted, in One Year, to above One thousand Five hundred Pounds.

Ja. Deacon.

T. Anguish,

A. PiggoU,

Richd Neave,

Wilt* Roe.

N* 69.

The Examination of Mr. Peregrine Sims; taken upon Oath, June loth and 14th, 1785*

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy to Thomas Meggs, Esquire, the Petty Customer Inwards, who holds his Office by Patent, during Life; the Principal does not transact the Business of the Office himself, it is executed solely by the Deputy. For a Long Period of Time no Duties have been received by the Petty Customer; they are paid to the Collector Inwards. Where an Entry is on Alien Account, the Merchant, o t his Agent, brings the Warrant to the Petty Customer, who signs that Warrant, takes a Copy of it,

A a and

Fourteenth Report on Public AccoUqtf.

oO 27° Januarii* A. 1786.

and enters that Copy in a Book-, which is returned to the Exchequer: Upon every Alien's Warrant, produced to the Petty Customer, he takes a Fee of One Shilling and Eight Pence, when the Customs shall amount to Twenty Shillings or upwards; and when the Customs shall amount to Five Shillings, and be under Twenty Shillings, a FeeofOue Shilling and One Penny: Upon certain Articles of Commerce, imported in Foreign Ships, and thence subjefit to the Petty Customs, when the Customs shall amount to Twenty Shillings, or upwards, a Fee of Two Shillings is paid to the petty Customer upon that Entry; and a Fee of One Shilling and Three Pence upon similar Entries, where the Customs shall amount to Five Shillings, and under Twenty.

Every Bill at Sight, obtained by an Alien, or for Goods imported on Foreign Bottoms, and subject to the Petty Customs, must be ligned by the Petty Customer, for which he receives a Fee of Two Shillings and Sixpence; but no Fee is afterwards taken upon the Warrant made out from that Bill at Sight: These Fees are partly grounded upon the Book of Rates, and partly upon Usage.

The Petty Customer receives a Salary of Sixty-two Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, which is inserted in his Patent Out: of the Fees received by the Petty Customer he pays certain Proportions to the Collector Inwards, the Comptroller of the Petty Customs, the Surveyor, and Surveyor General: The Amount of the Fees he received last Year was Two hundred and Ninety-three Pounds Ten Shillings and One Penny; out of which he paid to the above Officers, as their Shares of those Fees, Fifty-nine Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Nine Pence: He paid for Taxes Eighteen Pounds Seven Shillings and Eight Pence, and to his Deputy Seventy-seven Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence; which left a Net Emolument from his Office last Year of Two hundred Pounds.

This Examinant further faith, That as Deputy to the Petty Customer, he received from his Principal a Salary of Sixty-two Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, and was allowed by him a part of the Fees, which together amounted last Year to Seventy-seven Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence; and this was the whole Income of that Employment.

Peregrine
