N* 71*

The Examination of Mr. White", taken

upon Oath, June 14th and 15th, 1785.

This Examinent faith, That he is Computer of the Duties of 15 per Cent, on Mullins and White Callicoes; he is appointed by Warrant from the Treasury; the Office is executed by the Principal, and One Clerk, appointed and paid by him: The Duty of the Office is to attend the Sales of the East India Company, to take an Account of the Lots of Mullins and Callicoes, the Prices they are sold at, and to compute the Duties upon those Prices; he compares, from time to time, his Account with that of the Comptroller Inwards, and of the Officers of the India Company; and at the End of the Sale he casts up the Columns in his Account to Totals, and compares them in the like Manner; he then draws up a State of his Account, signs it, and tranlinits it to the Receiver of the Grand Receipt; he computes the Drawback, and signs the Debenture.

He is paid by his Warrant a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year; he receives from the East India Company, and the Exporters, small customary Fees upon the Entry, Certificate, and Debenture; they amounted last Year to One hundred and Eight Pounds Ten Shillings; out of which he paid Twenty-one Pounds Two-Shillings for Taxes, and Fifty Pounds to his Clerk: His Net Income was One hundred and Thirty-seven Pounds Eight Shillings.

P. White.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neave,

Geo. Drummond,

This Examinant faith, That he is Chief Deputy to the Duke of Manchester, the Collector of the Customs Outwards in the Port of London. The Collector holds his Pffice by Patent, for Life: He executes no Part of the Business. — This Office consists of Two Branches, the Cocket Office, and the Coast Office. The Business of the Cocket Office is transa&ed by the Chief Deputy to the Collefitor Outwards, the Deputy, the Assistant Deputy, the Receiver, Eight Cocket Writers (Two of whom are the AfiHtant Deputy, and the Receiver) and an extra Clerk. The bufioels of the Coast Office

is transacted by a Deputy and Three Clerks. All thele Officers are appointed by the Collector. The Collector is paid by a Salary, and Fees; his Salary is Two hundred and Seventy-six Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence a Year, infeited in his Patent; the Fees are received by the Deputy, and paid over to the Chief Deputy for the Use of the Collector; they amounted lait Year to about One thousand Eight hundred and Fifty-five Pounds; his Payment for Taxes was One hundred and Fifty-six Pounds Nineteen Shillings, and for contingent Expences Three Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Six Pence; his Net Income was One thousand Nine hundred and Seventy Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence.

This Examinant further faith, That as Chief Deputy he has no Salary; but is paid by the Deputy Outwards, out of the Fees he receives from the Merchants,

The Examination of Mr. William; taken upon Oath, June 17th, 17S5.

This Examinant faith, That, as Deputy Collector Outwards, he collects certain Fees for certain Officers. He collects all the Fees due to the Collector Outwards, arising in the Cocket Office Outwards: These Fees consist of small Payments by the Merchants for Variety of Business done in the Office, and are all grounded upon the Table of Fees annexed to the Book of Rates, except the Fee of One Shilling upon the Plantation Bond, which is grounded upon Usage: He pays these Fees Monthly to the Chief Deputy, for the Use of the Collector: This is the principal Branch of his Fees. Where the Amount of the Old Subsidy is Twenty Shillings Net Money and upwards, a Whole Fee is paid; where under Twenty Shillings, and above Five, a Half Fee; and where under Five, no Fee.

For certain Business, dated in his Account of Fees transmitted to this Board, he receives the Fees due to the Controller, the Surveyor, and the Surveyor General, which are annexed to the Book of Rates; and the Fees due to the Deputy Controller, a Clerk in the Secretary’s Office, Two Clerks in his own Office, and himself, which are grounded upon Custom: He pays to these several Officers their Fees. Out of his own Fees, he pays to the Chief Deputy Three hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year, as a customary Composition for what used to be his Share of them. The Remainder amounted last Year to One thousand Four hundred and Sixty Pounds Four Shillings; out of which he paid for Taxes, Twenty-seven Pounds; to Deputies, Fifty Pounds; to Clerks, I2ighty-one Pounds Ten Shillings; for Stationary, Three hundred and Twenty-four Pounds; and to the Messenger, Twenty-five Pounds Five Shillings: His Net Income was Nine hundred and Fifty-two Pounds Nine Shillings. He has no Salary.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas taken

upon Oath, June aoth, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That, as Assistant Deputy Outwards for Foreign Business to the Collector Outwards, and as First Cocket Writer, he receives a Salary and Fees. His Salary is Forty Pounds a Year, paid to him by the Deputy Outwards. His Fees are customary Vol. 41.

Payments by the Merchant upon the Delivery of the Cocket, or of a Duplicate of the Content of a Ship’s Cargo to Ireland: He is paid for perusing the Warrant and Four Bills, and adjusting them, and writing a Cocket for the lame, from Six Pence to Five Shillings, according to the length of the Cocket; but where the Cocket Writer draws out and arranges an Entry from a complicated Lift of Articles, he receives a Gratuity, at the Pleasure of the Merchant, as for extra Business. All the Cocket Writers are paid in the same Manner for writing Cockets. His Fee for making out a Duplicate is Two Shillings and Six Pence. He receives all the Fees upon a Cocket wrote by him, due to the Collector, Controller, Surveyor, and Surveyor General; and pays Monthly to each the Fees belonging to him: All the Cocket Writers receive the like Fees for these Officers. The Amount of the Fees received by him last Year, on his own Account, was about Four hundred and Twenty-nine Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence; out of which he paid to a Clerk Forty Pounds, and for Stationary about Nine Pounds. His Net Income was Four hundred and Twenty Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence.

The Examination of Mr. James Dodson; taken upon Oath, June 17th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That as Receiver of the Customs Outwards he is paid by the Deputy Outwards a Salary of Ten Pounds a Year. He receives from the Merchants, upon Payment of the Duties, the Odd Pence between One Penny and Six Pence, and between Seven Pence and One Shilling, on the Amount of the Duties, either on One or more Entries; this, upon an Average, produces about Fifteen Pounds a Year. He receives small Fees for entering Out Port and Com Debentures: As a Cocket Writer, for adjusting the Warrant, and writing the Cocket, he has a Fee from Six Pence to Five Shillings, according to the Length; all these are customary Fees, and amounted together last Year to about Two hundred and Eighty-nine Pounds Fifteen Shillings, out of which he paid for Stationary, both as Receiver and Cocket Writer, about Eleven Pounds Seven Shillings, which reduced his Net Income to Two hundred and Eighty-eight Pounds Eight Shillings.

The Examination of Mr. Robert Seymour; taken upon Oath, June 21ft, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy to Frederick Augusta Barnard. Esquire, the Cnftomer of the Great Customs Outwards, who holds his Office by Patent, but executes no Part of the Business; it is all trail fueled by the Deputy.

The only Duty collected by this Officer is that on Leather exported: The Computation and Col left ion of the Duty, and the Computation of the Drawback,

is checked and transacted in the like Manner with other Export Duties, except that the Drawback is checked by his Controller only, and payable at the Excise Office.

Where Wool is to be carried Coastwise, the Owner or his Agent, producing his Petition, granted by the Board, gives Notice to the Customer, describing very, minutely every Circumstance that relates to it; the Customer makes out a Bond, to be entered into by the Owner or Agent, to secure the shipping of the Wool, and a Licence to ship it, and gives Notice to the Officers of the Port to which the Wool is intended to be lent. Two Returns of the Wool being shipped are made to this Office by the Coast Waiters; the Customer endorses a Cocket upon One of them, and makes out a Coast Bond, which is a Security to be given by the Master of the Ship to land the Wool in some Port in Great Britain', upon Execution of this Bond he delivers to him the Cocket.

The Certiftcate of the Landing, signed by the Collector, Controller, and Three Landing Officers, at the Port where landed, is brought to this Office; in consequence of his Return he cancels both the Bonds, annexes the Certificate to the Coast Bond, and transmits them to the Exchequer.

Where Wool- is brought into the Port of the Customer has Notice from the Out Port, receives the Cocket, compares it with the Notice, grants the Sufferance, after Leave obtained from the Board; and after landing, certified by the Coast Waiter, the Customer makes out a Certificate, and delivers it to the Persons applying. /

Where Leather is -carried Coastwise, he makes out and takes the Coast Bond from the Master of the Ship, and cancels it, in like Manner, upon the Return of the Certificate. All the Documents, except the Notices, are registered in this Office.

The Customer has a Salary by his Patent of Fifty Pounds a Year; he receives finali Fees for Business transa&ed in his Office, grounded some of them upon the Book of Rates, others upon Usage; they amounted last Year to One hundred and Ninety-five Pounds Five Shillings and Nine Pence; he paid for Taxes Seventeen Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Four Pence, to his Deputy Forty Pounds, and for printing Instruments One Pound Nineteen Shillings and Nine Pence: His Net Income was One hundred and Eighty-five Pounds Nine Shillings and Eight Pence.

The Deputy receives from his Principal, a Salary of Forty Pounds a Year, and similar Fees, grounded upon Usage, to the Amount, last Year, of One hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Five Shillings and Two Pence; he paid for Stationary Three Pounds Fifteen Shillings, which reduced his Income to One hundred and Sixty Pounds Ten Shillings and Two Pence.

The Examination of Mr. Perry Player Blommarl; taken upon Oath, June 23d, and 27th, 1785.

It is the Business of this Controllor to check the Customer in every Circumstance which regards the Computation and Collection of the Duty and Drawback on Leather exported, in a manner similar to what is practised upon other Export Duties; with this Difference, that the Computation of the Drawback by the Customer does not pass any other Check than this Officer.

When Wool is to be carried Coast wile from,

the Licence and Bond are brought to the Controller, signed by the Customer; he examines those Two Instruments, to see that they agree in all material Circumstances — he registers, and signs them; he examines the Notice to the Out Ports, the Return from the Coast; Waiters, and signs the Cocket which is endorsed upon One of the Returns.

When the Return is made by the Out Port Officers, certifying the Wool to have been landed, he examines the Return with the Entry formerly made in the Licence Bond Book, and in the Coast Outward Book, to see that they agree iu every Particular, and puts his Initials to the Return.

Where Wool is brought to London from an Out Port, he compares the Cocket with the Notice sent fromr the Out Port to the Customer and Controller; and if they correspond, he signs the Return, which is made out by the Coast Waiters in London, and transmitted to the Out Port.

Lrpon the Carriage of Leather Coastwise, he signs the Cocket and Sufferance; he examines the Return mtde by the Officers at the Out Port with a Register of those Instruments which he had previously made, and if they agree, he signs the Return with his Initials. The Controller registers all Documents, except the Notices Outwards.

The Controller has, by his Patent, a Salary of Thirty Pounds a Year; he receives Four Fees from the Merchant or Captains of Vessels, of One Shilling each; Three of them upon the Entry of Cockets Coastwise, which, as he apprehends, are grounded upon the Book of Rates; and One upon the Examination and Computation of Debentures, grounded upon Usage: These amounted last Year, as he believes, having assisted in making up the Three last Quarters of it, to Seventy-six Pounds Seven Shillings and One Penny; out of which Ten Pounds Fifteen Shillings was paid (or Taxes, which, with Ten Shillings paid for contingent Expences, reduced the Net Income of the Controller to Sixty-five Pounds Two Shillings and One Penny.

This Examinant further faith, That the Deputy to the Controller has no Salary; he has Three customary Fees, One of Two Fifths' of Two Shillings, the Fee on a Licence; of Four Pence for an Entry of Calves Skins; and Eight Pence on a Leather Debenture; these amounted, last Year, to Thirty-two Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Two Pence, which was the whole Emolument of that Employment.

P. P. Blommart.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Bushby; taken upon Oath, June 28th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is Clerk of the Certificates, under the Collector Inwards for the Port of London. He is appointed by the Deputation of the Collector, and has been in the Certificate Office about

Thirty-

a6* Geo. III. 27

Thirty-seven Years: The Business of this Office is transa&ed by biniself, and Three Clerks.

Every Article imported is entered in this Office from *the Bills of the Clerk of the Rates, or some other of the Checks in the Subsidy Book Inwards. When any of these Articles are to be exported, a Bill containing a Description of them is brought to this Office, and the Entries upon the Bill are compared with the correspondent Entries in the Office Books, and wrote Off in the Margin; this Bill is entered in the Certificate Book Outwards; a Certificate is then made out, as the Ground of a Debenture for the Drawback; it contains the Titles of the Branches of the Duties to which the Articles are liable upon Importation, and enumerates the Articles to be exported: This Enumeration is frequently very long, especially on the Export of unrated East India Goods; a Certificate has taken up Twenty-eight Sheets: This Certificate is signed by the Clerk of the Certificates, and delivered to the Merchant; it is afterwards brought back to the Office, with the Debenture annexed; the Articles appearing upon the Debenture to be actually shipped are compared with the Entries in the Certificate Book Outwards; he signs the Debenture, and delivers it, with the Certificate, to the Merchant or his Agent

The usual Office Hours are from Ten until Two; it is frequently impossible, when Business presses, to transafik it in the Office Hours.

The Clerk of the Certificates receive no Salary; he is paid by Fees: He collects the Fees payable upon the Out Port Certificate to the Collector, Controller, Surveyor, Surveyor General, and himself; his own Fees are paid by the Merchant, and are, grounded chiefly upon Custom; ithey arise from theinstruments that pais the Office, and are in Proportion to their Length: They amounted last Year to Nine hundred and Seventeen Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Five Pence; out of which he paid, for Taxes, Twenty-one Pounds One Shilling and Eight Pence, to the Clerks One hundred and Two Pounds, and for Contingencies Three Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence; his Net Income was about Seven hundred and Ninety-one Pounds Eight Shillings and Three Pence.

The Clerks 1 in this Office are paid Salaries , by the Deputy, and Fees by the Merchants upon the Instruments, in, Proportion to the Length of them.

N* 83.

The Examination of Mr. James Bttme; taken upon Oath, June 29th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Southern Plantation Jerquer in the Office of the Customs; he has been One of the Jerquers near Twelve Years, but in this Vol. 41.

Office only since October last. There are Five Jerquers, all appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; their Bufinefe relates to Imports only. As Ships arrive from different Parts of the World, Four of the Jerquers have different Ports allotted to them, they are called the Southern Plantation, the Northern Plantation, the Southern European, and the Northern European Jerquers, the other is called the Wine Jerquer,

D d whose

Fourteenth Report on Public

Accounts.

102

A. 1786.

2j° Januarii,

Fourteenth

Report

on Public Accounts*

whole Business it is to attend to all Ships, from whatever Port they come, having on Board Ten Tons of Wine or more; if the Ship has under Ten Tons, it goes to the Jerquer of the Division from whence the comes.

The principal Duty of the Jerquer is to examine the Books of the Land Waiter, as a Check upon that Office. It is the Duty of the Land Waiter to enter every Warrant in his Book, and upon the landing of the Goods to enter in the same Book, and in no other, under the Entry of the Warrant, every Article landed, describing minutely the Marks and Number, and the Weight of each Draught or Quantity weighed at One Time. Within Thirty Days after the Ship is cleared, Dr if an India Ship One Year, the Land Waiter ought to bring to the Jerquer’s Office all the Warrants belonging to that Ship, and his Books made up complete, and signed by himself and the Land Surveyor. The Jerquer having received the Ship’s Report from the Clerk of the Ships Entries (which Reports are sent to him Weekly) examines the Articles entered in the Report, Warrants, and Land Waiters Books, to see that they correspond; he examines the Computations and Callings in the Land Waiters Books, and fees that the Allowances for Draughts, Tares, and Damages, are just.

It is the Duty of the Tide Waiter to enter in his Book an Account of all the Goods delivered out of the Ship pursuant to die Orders of the Land Waiter, and to carry this Book to the Jerquer immediately after the Ship is cleared; the Jerquer compares the Entries in this Book with the corresponding Entries in that of the Land Waiter: There are always more than One Land Waiter appointed to each Ship, each keeps the same Account in his own Book.

All the Warrants, and the Books of all the Land Waiters, relative to the Same Ship, should be delivered to the Jerquer at the same Time, by One of the Land Waiters, who signs his Name to the Number, both of Warrants and Books, as put down in the Jerquer’s Ships Entry Book.

Upon a Reference from the Board, and the Jerquer’s Certificate that the Maftir is entitled to Portage, the Jerquer computes the Portage, and makes out and signs the Bill, and after it is ligned by the Commissioners registers it in a Book kept for that Purpose.

The Southern Plantation, and the Northern European Jerquers, have each Two Clerks, the rest but One: Each used to appoint his own Clerks, but the Board, by a Minute of the 9th of March last, declare, they will provide themselves for that Service for the future.

Each Jerquer has a Salary, by his Warrant, of One hundred Pounds a Year; the Fees paid to him are, on passing Portage Bills, in proportion to the Amount of the Portage; Two Shillings and Six Pence for each Letter of Attorney; and One Shilling for searching for a Warrant; all grounded upon Custom: These Fees, upon Computation, amounted last Year in this Office to Seventy-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence; there was paid for Taxes Twenty-three Pounds; which reduced the Net Income of this Office to One hundred and Fifty-three Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence.

By a Minute of the Board, of the 25th of November last, all the Fees anting from the Portage Bills are abo-lHhed; the remaining Fees have produced to him left than Forty Shillings since the 25th: of November last.

J' Burne.

The Examination of Mr. William Buddie-, taken upon Oath, July ill, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is First Clerk to Mr. James Burne, the Southern Plantation Jerquer; he receives upon the Incidental Lift a Salary of Forty Pounds a Year: Before the Year 1780, as he apprehends, this Salary used to be paid to the Principal, and by him to his Clerk; since that Time all the Clerks in these Offices have been put upon the Incidental Lift.

Where Goods are sent to the King’s Warehouse, the Warrants, Petitions, and Sufferances, accompany the Goods. Formerly, as he believes before the Year 1773 or 1774, the Land and Deputy King’s Waiters themselves took these Documents from the Warehouse, and brought them to the Office of the Jerquers; upon the Petition of the Land and Deputy King's Waiters, the Board of Customs directed that these Documents should be taken from the Warehouse by the Jerquers Clerks, for which Bufinest the Land and Deputy King’s Waiters agreed to satisfy them. These Documents are distributed in the Warehouse into Four Classes, for Four of the Jerquers Offices, omitting that of the Northern Plantation, that Office having been erected since the Order of the Board.

About Once a Month One Clerk of each of these Four Jerquers receives from the Officer at the Warehouse the Documents allotted to his Office, each delivers to the Fifth Jerquer those which lielong to him; for this Service each Land and Deputy King’s Waiter, being Fifty-six in Number, pays, by Agreement in Writing, to each Clerk One Guinea a Year: It was usual also for the Clerk to receive a Gratuity upon each Portage Bill, but this is now abolished by an Order of the Board in November last. The Produce of these Two Kinds of Profits amounted last Year to Eighty-five Pounds Twelve Shillings and Ten Pence. He paid for Taxes One Pound and Eight Pence, and a small incidental Expence of Four Shillings; which reduced his Net Income to One hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Eight Shillings and Two Pence.

Buddie.

N* 87.

The Examination of Mr. Ambrose Edwards; taken upon Oath, July 6th, 1785.

Where Cockets are made out for Goods entitled to Drawback, they are brought with a Bill to the Register of Certificates: The Cocket has certain Official Signatures upon it. The Cocket and Bill are compared, to see that they agree as to the material Circumstances; he then marks the Coeket with his Initials, retains the Bill, and enters it in a Certificate Book.

When the Debenture is made out in Consequence of the Certificate, after having gone through certain Official Checks and Formalities, it is brought to The~R5gifter, who compares it with the Entry formerly made in the Certificate Book, enters the Quantity certified by the Searchers to have been actually shipped, and signs the Debenture; it then goes to the various Checks, to have the Drawback computed, and is brought again to the Register, who, upon finding the proper Signatures to it, writes an Order for Payment upon the Debenture, signs it again, and delivers it to the Board; when the Commissioners have signed the Debenture, it is returned to the Register, who gives it, taking a Receipt, to the Person entitled.

The Register has a Salary of Two hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year upon the Establishment; he receives from the Merchant or his Agent certain customary Fees, in some Cafes of One Shilling, in others of Six Pence, on each Debenture; they amounted last Year to Two 'hundred and Seventy-three Pounds Fifteen Shillings; out of which he paid iQr Taxes Forty-six Pounds Fifteen Shillings, and to hia Three Clerks Sixty Pounds j this left him a Net. Income from his Office of Four hundred and Seventeen Pounds.

This Examinant further faith, That he is paid by his Principal a Salary of Ten Pounds a Year, and receives small Fees from the Merchants upon Debentures; they . amounted last Year to One hundred mid Forty-six Pounds Nineteen-Shillings, which made his whole Emolument One hundred and Fifty-six Pounds Nineteen Shillings. The next Clerk to him in the Office has a Salary from his Principal of Twenty Pounds a Year, and a small Fee from the Merchants upon Certificate Cockets: The Junior Clerk is paid by his Principal a Salary of Thirty Pounds a Year, and has no Fee, Of any other Advantage from the Office.

This Examinant faith, That he is Senior Clerk to Mr. fViUington Clark, the Register of Certificate Cockets, and Examiner of Debentures in the Port of London, and has been in the Office about Twenty-two Years.

The Register is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; he has himself the Nomination of all his Clerks. The Business of this Office is transafited by the Principal and Three Clerks.

A. Edwards.

N* 89.

'Pie Exaipination of Mr. Edmund j taken

uponOpfh, July 5th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is the Senior Landing Surveyor in the Port of London; he has been in thid Office about Sixteen Years. The Landing Surveyor superintends and controls those Officers who are. employed in landing all Goods imported, that is the Landing Waiters, and the Deputy King's Waiters.

It is the Duty of this Officer, upon the Inspection of all Packages landed, containing Goods the Duties on which are payable by Weight, to settle the Tare to be allowed to the Merchant, whether it be according to the Table of Tares, or by actually weighing the Package, or forming a Judgment of the Weight. Where the unpacking would be injurious to the Merchant, the Quantity allowed for Tare is entered in the Land Waiter’s Book, and ligned with the Initials of Two Landing Surveyors. ‘ At or soon after the Goods are landed or warehoused, and weighed, numbered, of gauged, and Entries made by the Land Waiters in their Books, of the Weight, Tale, or Quantity, the Landing Surveyor fees that the Denomination of the Goods landed agrees with the Denomination of the Goods expressed in the Warrant; he frequently directs an Article to be re-weighed, re-told, or re-gauged, to see that the Entry of the Weight, Tale, and Quppfity, be accurately inserted in the Land Waiters Books.

Upon a Reference from the Board of Customs to the Landing Surveyors, they survey the Goods that have received Damage, and settle the Quantum of the Damages to be allowed the Merchant. The Amount of these Damages is fpipetipaeg very coofiderablp, even to very near the Amount of the Duties} Sixty-three of Sixty-four Parts have been allowed.

There are Nine of these Officers in the Port of London: The lawful Quay of the Port of London is divided into Three Stations, Three Officers to each Station, except that One by Rotation superintends the Goods landed by Sufferance; and One Officer in each Station changes his Station every Week by Rotation.

This Officer is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury. He receives upon the Establishment an Annual Salary of Two hundred and Thirty Pounds. He receives,

for superintending the Sale of condemned Goods fold 4t the Custom House, One Ninth Part of Thirty-five Pounds allowed for every such Sale: His Share amounted last Year to Twenty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence. He receives no Fees or Gratuities whatever for the Business done upon the Quay at Custom House Hours; but for attending at Times and Places not required by Law, he receives Compensation from the Merchants, under the Authority of the Act of the Sixth and Seventh of King William: This amounted last Year to One hundred and Seventy-three Pounds Eleven Shillings. The Total Sum thus received from the Merchants, by all the Nine Officers, is equally divided among them. The First Six received from the East India Company an Annual present of Spices, valued at Five Pounds Four Shillings: The Company, by a Resolution feme time ago, have discontinued this Present, unless to those Officers appointed prior to that Resolution; whiqh makes the Difference of the Sum received by these Officers, as stated in the Return. The Payment for Taxes was Sixty-three Pounds Five Shillings, which reduced his Net Income to Three hundred and Fiffy? eight Pounds. Eight Shillings and Eight Pepce.

N* 91.

The Examination of Mr. James Dunphey; taken upon Oath, July. 8th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is One of the Landing Waiters in the Port of London; he has been so for Twenty-five Yean. There are in this Port Thirty-eight Landing. Waiters, and Eighteen Deputy King’s Waiters, all of winch are employed in the same Business, which is. to superintend the landing of all Foreign Goods iprpoEted.

The Commissioners of the Customsv upon a Ship’s being reported, appoint, at their Discretion, Three Landing Waiters to every Linen Ship, and Two to every other Ship. The. Landing Waiter, upon receiving the Warrant, fends to the Tidefman who has the Charge of the Ship an Order specHying the Marks uf those Packages or Calks described in the Warrant, which he is to deliver out; these Goods are in Consequence of that Order brought on Shore, in the Charge of some Tidefman. The Landing Waiter attends the Landing of the Goods, and enters In an Official Book, under the EnUy of the Warrant, the Marks, Number, Weight, or Measure of the Goods as they are landed.

After the Ship is cleared, he makes up from his Book an Account of all the Goods that have been landed on the Account of each Merchant; from the Amount of the Weight a certain Allowance is made for the Draft; that is, for any Error that may be occasioned from a Defett in the Weights or the Beam; the Allowance for Tare, where it is established, is entered opposite the Article; the Landing Surveyor examines this Entry, and signs it; a discretionary Tare is settled by both of them together. The Landing Waiter, after all the Goods are landed, compares the Quantity landed with. the Quantity entered upon the Warrant.; and, as. the former almost always exceeds the latter, he informs the Merchant of the Difference, and desires him to make his Post Entry, and enters in the Credit Book, kept in the Office of the Landing Surveyor the Quantity -for which the Merchant has not paid the Duty. The Post Entries- heing paid, he takes the Warrants for them from the Long Room, and ties up together all the Warrants, Prime- and Post, Petitions, and Sufferances belonging to that Ship; and carries his Book, with the Documents, to bn examined Vo l.41.

by the Landing Surveyor, who signs the Book; after which he deposits both in the Jerquer’s Office.

Until all these Duties are paid, the Landing Waiter stands charged with them, and cannot be discharged from the Ship; and the Landing Surveyors will not sign his Book.

The Landing Waiter is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; he has a Salary, by his Warrant, of Eighty Pounds a Year, subjefit to Twenty Pounds Two Shillings for Taxes. The Fees paid to the Landing Waiters are grounded principally upon Usage: There is a certain Rate of Fees upon every Species of Merchandize, paid by the Merchants, whether the Business is done upon a Working Day or a Holiday, upon the Free Quays or the Sufferance Wharfs; these Fees amounted, last Year, to Two hundred and Fifty-three Pounds Five Shillings and Six Pence; he paid, for contingent Expences, Seven Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Eight Pence; his Net Income was Three hundred and Five Pounds Eight Shillings and Ten Pence. The legal Hours of Attendance for all the Officers at the Water Side are from Six to Six in the Summer, and from Eight to Sunset in the Winter. The Difference in the Amount of the Fees, taken by the dist ferent Officers in this Department, arises from die different Value or Number of the Ships to which they are appointed.

James Dunphey.

The Examination of Mr. William Parke; taken upon Oath, July 12th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is King’s Gauger in the Office of the Customs in the Port of London; he has been in this Office Four Years, and is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury. It is his Duty to gauge, on the Part of the Crown, all Foreign Articles imported capable of liquid Measure, upon their being landed; upon gauging them he gives the Dimensions and Quantity to the landing Waiter, who enters them in his Book, and the Gauger signs the Initials of his Name, and the Day of the Month, to that Entry, and so makes himself responsible for the Accuracy of the Entry. There are regularly Three Gaugers; but ever since he ha* been in the Office there has been, except for about Ten Months, only Two acting Gaugers, the Third Office being either vacant, or the Officer under instructions. They are all appointed by the Treasury, and have a Salary, by their Warrants, of Eighty Pounds a Year.

The Gauger receives no Fees for Business done upon the lawful Quay; but the Merchant frequently, gives him a Gratuity of Three Pence a Calk: For Business done upon the Sufferance Quays, he receives certain Fees established by Usage: One of them is Seven Shillings and Six Pence for gauging every Hundred Barrels of Tar; this is now at an End, fiuce the Importation of Tar from America has ceased; the Tar from Russia, and all other Countries, is weighed, not gauged, the Form of the Calks not being adapted to gauging. His Fees and Gratuities, last Year, amounted to One hundred and Sixty Pounds Seven Shillings; he. paid for Taxes Sixteen Pounds Eight Shillings, and on receiving his Salary, and other contingent Expences, Thirteen Shillings. His Net Income was Two hundred and' Twenty-three Pounds Six Shillings. The lawful Quays reach from the Tower to London Bridge; they* are- divided into Three- Stations, and contain many

This Examinant faith, That he receives all the Fees for the Nineteen Patent King's Waiters, and divides the Total equally between them; they are all considered but as One Officer, and have no other Fees than those inserted in the Table established by the Order of

cers he chooses should attend the Delivery of that Ship; hence it arises that the Ships, both in Number and Value, are very unequally appointed among these Officers; frequently some have Six or Seven Ships, others only Two, upon the same Station; and the Profits of these Officers vary very much in their Annual Value, feme Officers get above Three Times as much as others. It is in the Option of the Merchant to what Quay be will carry his Ship, and no Officer can have Two Ships at the same Time in different Stations; but the Goods of a Ship quayed in One Station may be landed at a Quay in any other of the Stations, and the Officers appointed to that Ship muff follow them, except such Goods as are landed by Sufferance, over which other Officers are appointed. No Officer can change his Station until all the Ships he has upon his Station are cleared, unless by special Orders of the Board, too many Officers appearing to be upon one . Station, and too few upon another. By Minute of the Board, no Officer should be appointed to the same Station after all his Ships are out.

When the Merchant has made his Poll Entry, the Landing Waiter enters in the Credit Book the Date of the Post Entry opposite the Credit; he is chargeable with the Duties not paid immediately upon his Entry of the Credit, but the Board usually give about Ten Days or a Fortnight for the Payment of the Duties, before they surcharge the Landing Waiter with them, unless they deem it an improper Credit, in which same they demand immediate Payment from the Officers, or for them to shew Cause why they shall not be mulfit for their Neglect.

The Credit given to the Merchant is in many Cafes unavoidable. Where the Goods are Subjects of Weight, or of Liquid Measure, the Merchant cannot make a perfect Entry; the weighable Goods being subjefit to Waste, and the liquid Goods to Leakage, he cannot from his Invoice tell the exaQ: Quantities: If he makes an Over-entry, he muff recover the Duties over-paid by a Certificate of Over-entry, which it is not in his Power to procure without Trouble, Delay, and Expence.

Where the Goods pay Duty by. Tale, no ffiort Entry is permitted, and consequently no Credit allowed.

The Deputy King’s Waiter has no Salary or Allowance from Government, he is paid by Fees grounded either upon Act of Parliament or Custom.

N* 95.

The Examination of Mr. Cornelius taken

upon Oath, July 13th and 15th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is One of the Appointors of the Weighing Porters, and has been about Eight Years in that Office; there are Three of these Officers, One to each Station.

In the Weighing Department of the Customs in the Port of London, there are Twenty-five Weighers,

called Weighers in Fee, who are appointed by Warrants of the Treasury; Two hundred and Three Preferable Weighers, who are appointed by the Board of Customs; and Two hundred and Thirty Persons, including the Noon Tenders, attending upon the Quays to be employed when wanted, called Glut or Extra Weighers.

Out of the Weighers in Fee the Board of Customs felefifc Three Persons, who are called the Appointors, whose Duty it is to superintend all the Weighers. The Weighers in Fee, and the Preferable W eighers, are almost always in Employment; when more are wanted they are taken from among the Extra Weighers. There are Eighteen Noon Tenders, whole Business it is to attend from One to Three, to receive the Lighter and Boat Bills that come up at that Time, and to take Care of the Goods in Charge on Shore, whilst the Weighers are at Dinner; these Officers are likewise employed as Extra Weighers. The Appointors change their Stations every Week, and each takes a Number of the Weighers in Fee, and Preferable Weighers, to his own Station, and every Morning appoints them to the particular Business each is to execute during the Day; enters their Names, with the Ships they are appointed to, in a List; and delivers it to the Landing Waiter appointed to that Ship.

Where Goods are landed by Sufferance, the Appointor directs what Weighers shall attend them, and each stays a Month at the Sufferance Wharf, or until the Ship is cleared.

The Business of the Weigher is to weigh all Goods subjefit to Weight, in the Pretence of the Landing Waiter, who enters the Weight in his Book: He opens likewise all the Packages for the Inspection of the Landing Waiter, and makes them up again.

In every Lighter or Boat that brings Goods on Shore, the Officer who has the Charge of the Goods brings with him a Bill from the Officer on board the Ship, containing a List of the Goods to be landed from that Lighter or Boat: If it comes up in the Night, the Watchman of the Quay receives this Bill, ana delivers it the next Morning to the Appointor, or his Assistant; if it comes up in the Day, it is delivered to the Appointor himself, or his Assistant; and upon the Receipt of it, the Appointor directs what Weighers shall work the Ship. He enters every Day in the Station Book the Names of all the Weighers employed during the Day, and their respefitive Business; this Entry is signed by the Landing Surveyor for the Station, and at the End of the Week it is signed both by him and by the Appointor.

Every Month the Appointor tries by the Exchequer Standard the Weights upon his Station, and is continually examining the Beams, to lee whether they want Repair; and Once a Year he tries the Weights, and examines the Tackle, upon the Sufferance Quays.

Each Appointor and Fee Weigher has a Salary of Thirty-five Pounds a Year upon the Establishment. The Appointor weighs himself all the Silk, for which he receives from moll of the Merchants a customary Fee of Six Pence per Bale; he receives for stamping Morocco Leather One Shilling per Cafe, from every Hudsons Bay Ship One Pound One Shilling, every Vot. 41.

East India Ship One Pound, and a Gratuity from the Fourteenth Wharfingers upon the Sufferance Quays, amounting last Report Year to Three Pounds Nineteen Shillings; all these Fees and Gratuities are divided equally between the Accoun Three Appointors; they amounted last Year to Thirty-seven Pounds Six Shillings and Four Pence each; they paid for Taxes Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence — the Net Income of each was Seventy-one Pounds Seven Shillings.

Com' Floyd.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggotty Rich*Neave,

Sami Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will!* Roe.

The Examination of Mr. Stephen Thornton; taken upon Oath, July 15th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Weighers in Fee, called also the established Weighers, in the Port of London, and has been so about Fourteen Years: He was appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, and is paid upon the Establishment a Salary of Thirty-five Pounds a Year, subjefft to the Payment of Nineteen Shillings Yearly to the Superannuation Fund.

The Weigher in Fee has no established Fee, that he knows of; but it is customary for some of the Merchants or their Agents to give him such Perquisites or Gratuities as are inserted in a Schedule, signed by him with the rest of the Weighers in Fee, and sent to this Board.

Some of the Merchants refus'e to give any Perquisites or Gratuities whatever.

The Gratuities upon a Sufferance Quay are more advantageous than upon the Legal Quays. About Ten or Twelve Years ago the Russia Merchants agreed to pay the Weigher Two Shillings a Day, and One Penny per Ton, for weighing the Hemp, Tallow, and Flax, upon the Sufferance Quays: All the Gratuities amount to but a small Sum in the Year; the Sum -he received from them last Year was, to the belt of his Knowledge, about Three Pounds Ten Shillings.

" Thornton.

The Examination of Mr. George By; taken upon Oath, July 19th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That be is Deputy Chief Searcher to John Drously, Esquire, the Patent Chief Vol. 41.

Searcher in the Port of London; he has been in this Office above Ten Years.

The Office of the Searcher consists of Two Branches — the Patent Searcher’s Office — and, the Controlling Searcher’s Office. The Officers in the First Branch are, the Chief Patent Searcher, his Deputy, Five Under Patent Searchers, Ten Deputies (Two to each Under Searcher) and Six Clerks: The Second Branch consists

p g of

Fourteenth Report on Public Accounts.

I14 270 Jmuarii. J. 178

of Ten Controlling Searchers, the Surveyor of the Searchers, and Two Clerks; besides other Officers attending upon both Branches.

The Chief Patent Searcher transe&s no Part of the Bufiqeft of the Office, the Deputy executes the Whole. It is the Duty of this Officer to examine the Manifest, the Content, the Cockets, and the Victualling Bill, of every Ship clearing out from the Port of London for Foreign Parts; these Instruments are brought to him nearly at the same Time. The Manifest contains every Article of the Cargo put on board the Ship, except Stores allowed for the Ship, included in the Victualling Bill; this Manifest is made out by the Master, or his Broker, from the Ship’s Book, and when completed, is delivered to the Deputy Chief Searcher. All the Cockets belonging to the Ship being filed in the Searcher’s Office, the Deputy fees that they are signed by the proper Officers, and examines the Marks and Numbers of the Articles in the Manifest, with the like Description in the Cockets.

The Chief Clerk in the Searcher’s Office draws out from the Cockets a Content, that is, an Abstract of the Cargo of the Ship, which the Deputy examines by the Comets, signs the Manifest, the Content, and Victualling Bill; transmits the Content and Victualling Bill to the Controlling Searchers, and retains the Manifest; the Content, being sworn to by the Captain, is returned to the Deputy Searcher, who makes out a Copy, signs, and feuds it, with the Cockets and Victualling Bill, to the Searchers at Gravesend. The Cockets are entered in distinct Books in this Office; Copies of them, sworn to by the Deputy, are lent from Time to Time to the Exchequer. Three of these Books, the Certificate, Bounty, and Free Books, are very voluminous.

The Chief Searcher has, by his Patent, a Salary of One hundred and Twenty Pounds a Year; he has a Customary Fee upon the clearing of every Ship to Foreign Parts, pajd by the Master or his Broker, according to the Place to which she is bound. The Amount of these Fees (aft Year, was Five hundred and Sixty-seven Pounds Three Shillings; he paid for Taxes, Thirty-three Pounds Six Shillings; to his Deputy, Eighty Pounds; to a Waterman, Forty-five Pounds; for Stationary and other Contingencies, Twenty-five Pounds; his Net Income was Five hundred and Three Pounds Seventeen Shillings.

The Deputy, is appointed by the Patentee, with the Approbation of the Treasury; he receives from his Principal a Salary of Eighty Pounds a Year. He has no regular Fees annexed to his Office; but for examining the Manifest out of Office Hours, he receives a Compensation as for Extra Duty; the Ten Deputies receive a Variety of Fee? upon the same Ground: All these Fees form One Fuqd, and are equally divided between the Chief and the Ten other Deputies; the Share of the Chief Deputy amounted, last Year, to One hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, subject to no Deduction.

Geo. By, D. C. Sr.

T. Anguisfi,

Rich*Neaoe,

Geo. Drummond, liiU. Roe.

N* 100.

The Examination of Richard Devins, Esquire; taken upon Oath, July 20th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of die Under Patent Searchers; he was One of the Deputy Under Patent Searchers for about Fifteen Tears, and bas had

the Patent about Eighteen Months. There are Five Under Patent Searchers, each of them has regularly Two Deputies; Four of them do not execute any Part of the Business of the Office, it is transacted entirely by their Deputies; he is the only One of the Under Patent Searchers who executes his Office himself;,he has only One Deputy to assist him.

There are different Branches of the Searcher’s Business assigned to the different Deputies, and they take this Business by Rotation. The Under Patent Searchers take it by Turns to receive from the Merchants all the Cockets they produce during the Day, with the Number of Packages intended to be shipped that Day endorsed on each Cocket.

One of these Searchers attends each Station every Day; the Cocket is sent to that Searcher who attends the Station where the Goods lie; he compares the Endowments upon the Cocket with the Packages; he examines at his Discretion the Weight, the Number, and the Measure; permits the Merchant to ship diem, and returns the Cocket, if completed, to the same Searcher, who signs hfs Name to it; if it is not completed, it is returned to the Merchant, that he may endorse upon it such other Goods as he intends to ship afterwards. When the Cocket is completed, the Searcher examines the Endowments with the Entries, and the Cocket is entered at large in its proper Book in the Office, with the Quantity flipped; this Entry is examined by the Searcher, and signed with the Initials of his Name; the Cocket is filed until delivered, with all the Cockets belonging to the same Ship, to the Chief Searcher.

Some of die Searchers attend the like Examination upon the Water, and at the different Sufferance Quays; and the Examining Searcher is constantly attended by a Controlling Searcher, unless die Multiplicity of Business compels them to separate.

The Searcher who examines the Tobacco always weighs One Hogshead in Five without the Cafe.

The Under Searchers are appointed by Patent, with a Salary of Twelve Pounds a Year; they receive Fees from the Merchants, feme of which are inserted in the Table of Fees, others grounded upon Custora; these Fees are paid upon the Instruments that pass the Office; all of them are divided equally between the Five Searchers, except those arising from the Clearings, of which Half only belongs to them, the otiier Half belongs to the Chief Searcher.

The Share in these Fees of each Under Searcher amounted last Year to Nine hundred and Seventy Pounds Six Shillings. He paid for Taxes Fifty Pounds, for a Clerk Twenty-five Pounds, and for Stationary and other Contingencies Sixteen Pounds, Six Shillings; his Net Income was Eight hundred and Ninety-one Pounds. The other Four paid each to his Deputy One hundred and Sixty Pounds, which reduced the Net Income of each to Seven hundred and Thirty-one Pounds.

The Senior Deputies are appointed by the Under Patentee, subjectc to the Approbation of the Treasury, and are paid by their Principals One hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year; the Five additional Deputies are appointed by Warrant, or with the Approbation of the Treasury, and have the same Salary upon the Establishment: They have certain Fees grounded upon Usage, all of which are equally divided among the Ten Deputies, and the Deputy Chief Patent Searcher; the Share of each amounted last Year to One hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence. The Shares of the Senior Deputies being subject to no Deductions, the Net Income of each was Two hundred and Ninety-two Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, except his own Share, which amounted to One hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence only.

This Examinant further faith, lip doth not bold

this

26 Geo. III. 270 Jammu 115

this Office for his own Use and Benefit, but in Trust, and is paid for the Execution of it the usual Profits of a Deputy — a Salary of One hundred and Sixty Pounds, and ,his Share of the Fees.

It. Devins.

Sant Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

The Examination of Mr. Ednund ;taken

upon Oath, July 20th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Additional Deputies to the Under Patent Searchers; he has been in the Customs about Thirty-two Years, and Deputy Searcher about Nine Years.

He was One of the First of these Officers at the Time of their Creation; the Five acting Searchers were not enough to do the Duty. The Additional Deputy is appointed by the Principal, with the Approbation of the Treasury, and with a Salary of One hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year; his Business is exactly the same with that of the Senior Deputies, and he has an equal Share of the Fees: He paid last Year for Taxes Twelve Pounds One Shilling and Four Pence, but has Rea-fou to expect he shall be repaid the Twelve Pounds, that the Additional Deputy may be upon an Equality with the Senior Deputy.

E. Robbins.

N* 102.

The Examination of Mr. Robert Weston; taken upon Oath, July 21ft, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That be is One of the Controlling Searchers in the Port of London; he has been in the Customs near Thirty Years, and Controller about Nine Years. There are Ten of these Officers, who are' Checks upon the Ten Deputy Searchers, and attend them in Rotation through the several Branches of their Duty. At the same time that the Cocket is delivered to the Searcher, the Bill which corresponds with the Cocket is delivered to the Controlling Searcher, and goes to the Examining Controller, as the Cocket goes to the Examining Searcher; — these Two Officers join in the Examination of the Goods, and in comparing the Marks and Numbers of the Packages, with the like Endorsements upon the Cocket and Bill; they consult together what Packages they shall inspect. After the Examination, and no Objection arises, they permit the Merchant to ship the Goods. There are a Number of old Tidef-men, about Twenty-four, Part of the Water Guard, who have been long in the Service, appointed by the Board to attend the Goods from the Quays to the Ships; these Men are under the immediate Direction of the Controlling Searcher. If the Goods are Certificate, Bounty, prohibited, or out of Time, the Controller appoints One of these Men to attend the Goods in the Lighter, from the Quay to the Ship; this Man copies from the Bill the Marks and Numbers of those Packages he is particularly to attend to; this Copy is called his Ticket It is his Duty not to quit his Charge until he has delivered his Ticket and Goods to the Custody of the Officer on Board the Ship; he leaves his Ticket with

Vol. 41.

the Officer, unless it is a Tobacco Ticket, which he Fomrt««nth brings back to the Controller: Free Goods require no ReP£r‘ Guard. Books are kept in this Office similar to those kept in the Searcher’s Office; the Bills, when com- CC*M° pleated, are signed with the Initials of the Controllers Names, entered in these Books, and filed in the Office as the Evidence of the Goods shipped, and of the Difference between the Quantities entered and actually shipped.

The Content is brought to the Controller; be examines it with the Entries of the Bills, signs, and returns it.

The Ship is said to be cleared when the Mailer has sworn to the Content; (he is finally cleared by the Searcher at Gravesend.

This Office consists of the Ten Controllers, and One Clerk, appointed by Warrants of the Treasury, and One Clerk appointed by them. Each Controller has an established Salary of One hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year:

His Fees are grounded upon Usage only; the Quantum of the Fee depends upon the Species of Goods, or the,

Place to which the Ship is cleared; the Fees are divided equally among the Ten Controllers; the Share of each, last Year, amounted to Three hundred and Forty-one Pounds Thirteen Shillings. The Taxes were Thirty-two Pounds Two Shillings; the Contribution to the Clerk was Four Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Six Pence; the Contribution to the Surveyor of the Controlling Searcliers was Thirty-one Pounds Ten Shillings; and the contingent Expences Three Pounds Eight Shillings: The Net Income of each was Four hundred and Thirty Pounds Seven Shillings and Six Pence.

The Fees of the last Year far exceeded those of any for mer Year; the Average of Three Years, ending 1781, which was called for by the Board of Customs, was about Two hundred and Twenty-six Pounds only.

Rob' Weston.

T. Anguish,

Geo. Drummond,

Wilt. Roe.

N* 103.

The Examination of Mr. John Delane; taken upon Oath, August 3d, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Surveyor of the Searchers in the Port of London, and has been in that Office Seven Years. The ancient Duty of this Officer was to in(pect and superintend the Condu6t of the Controllers on the Patent Searchers or their Deputies, and to see that they attend their Duty according to their Instructious: By a Minute of the Board in January last this controlling Power was extended over both the senior and the additional Deputies to the Under Patent Searchers.

The superintending the Tidesmen carries him frequently on board the Ships, to see that the Goods endorsed on the Searcher’s Bills are actually on board. He fends Twice a Day to the Collector Outwards for the Bills or Copies of the Certificate Cockets, by which he fees what Goods are entered to be shipped; he inquires at the Controlling Searcher’s Office, whether the Goods specified in his Bills are cleared, and fees the Endorsements upon the Bills in that Office; he then directs Two Tidesmen next in Turn to go on board the Ship, in order to receive and guard the Goods. He enters on the Outside of a Book, called the Blue Book, the Day of the Month, the Names of the Ship and Master, whither bound, and the Names of the Tidef-men, and signs it: This Book he delivers to the Tidesmen, who enter in it all the Goods shipped; the Goods they are principally to attend to are prohibited Goods, and those entitled to a Drawback. It is not usual to place Tidesmen on board Ships on which Goods are

He makes out the Day Pay Bills of these Tidesmen, and signs them; he likewise every Month examines the Bills containing the Charges of the Outward bound Piazza Men, who attend the Goods to the Ship, and signs those Bills for Payment The Surveyor is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary of One hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year. The Fees received by the Ten Controlling Searchers are by Agreement equally divided between them and the Surveyor; the Amount of his Share of them lad Year was Three hundred and Ten Pounds Ten Shillings. N# 104.

The Examination of Mr. John Hankins’, taken upon Oath, August 3d, 1785. %

This Examinant faith, That he is Chief Clerk to the Patent Searchers, and has been in this Office Eighteen Years. After all the Cockets for putting Goods on board any Ship for Foreign Service are cleared (that is, after all the Goods endorsed are shipped) the Cockets are brought to the Searcher’s Office, from them the Chief Clerk makes out the Content, and delivers it to the Deputy Chief Searcher for his Examination and Signature, and then to One of the Controlling Searchers for the same Purpose, he then delivers it to the Broker; after it has passed the Offices, and is sworn to by the Malter, it is brought back to the Chief Clerk, who makes a Copy of it, and fends it by a Tidefinan, with the Cockets, to the Searcher’s Office at Gravesend, for which Cockets the Tidefman gives his Receipt. — The Original is retained in the Office: The Cockets are entered in a Book.

The Chief Clerk is appointed by the Five Under Patent Searchers, with- a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year, paid by them. His Fees are customary Payments for the Business transacted in the Office. If he does not pass the Content, he receives no Fee for it. His Fees amounted last Year to Five hundred and Twenty-seven Pounds; he paid for Taxes Six Pounds, and to his Assistant Forty Pounds; his Net Income was Five hundred and Thirty-one Pounds.

The Fees to his Assistant are paid to him by the Merchant, or his Broker, upon the Ship being cleared.

Jrt Hankins.

N* 105.

The Examination of Mr. Richard Price Jones; taken upon Oath, August 4th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is the Debenture Clerk in the Patent Searchers Office, and has been in this Office Ten Years.

It is his Business to receive from the Merchant all Debentures, whether for a Drawback or a Bounty; to enter them Alphabetically in Two separate Books, and pals them through the Searcher’s Office. He writes on the Front of the Debenture, in Words, the Goods actually shipped, according to their Quantity and Quality, which is taken from the Endorsements upon the Cockets in the Patent Searcher’s Office; after they are signed by the Patent and Controlling Searchers, he delivers them to the Merchant.

The Debenture Clerk is appointed by the Patent Searchers, at the Desire of the Board of Treasury, and is paid by them a Salary of Eighteen Pounds a Year: He receives from the Merchants small customary Fees upon Debentures and Cirtificates, which amounted last Year to Four hundred and Thirty-three Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence. He has Two Clerks under him, appointed by the Patent Searchers; and by their Direction he pays to One of them a Salary of Fifty Pounds, and to the other Twenty Pounds; they receive Gratuities at the Pleasure of the Merchant His Net Income last Year, which was a Year of extraordinary Business, was Three hundred and Eighty-one Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence: His usual Net Receipt is about Three hundred Pounds a Year.

„ Richard Price Jones.

.The Examination of Mr. Edward; taken

upon Oath, August4th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Four Officers for cutting off Stamps from Callicoes and other Linens, and Silks, exported. He receives Directions from the Commissioners Clerk in the Searcher’s Office to attend, Two of them together, at the Houses of the Merchants, to take off the Excise Stamps from the Goods they intend to export, to take an Account of the Goods, to fee them packed up, and to seal them with the Seal of Office; they deliver the Account of these Goods to the Commissioners Clerk.

He is appointed by the Commissioners, with a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year; he has no Fees but voluntary Gratuities from the Merchants, which are divided equally among these Four Officers; they produced last Year Sixty Pounds to each: Each paid One Pound Six Shillings to the Superannuation Fund, and to the Pay Clerks Eight Shillings: The Net Income of each was One hundred and Eight Pounds Six Shillings.

Edward Matthews.

N* 107.

The Examination of Mr. Nathaniel Bishop; taken upon Oath, August 5th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is one of the Six Coopers and Weighers in the Office of the Searchers: He has been in this Office above Nine Years. These Officers are appointed by the Board of Customs: It is their Duty to open such Packages as the Searchers choofu to examine, and to make them up again, and to weigh the Packages by the Direction of the Searchers. Two of these Officers attend each Station by a Weekly Rotation.

He is paid, by Order of the Board, a Salary of Five Pounds a Year for his Work on Holidays, and Half a Crown for every Day’s Attendance, paid Monthly; he is allowed by the Searchers a Gratuity for Porterage, and sometimes by the Merchant for working at extra Hours; these Gratuities are equally divided among the Six Officers; they amounted last Year to about One hundred and Eight Pounds: He paid to the Superannuation Fund, and for Stamps, One Pound Two Shillings.

N* 108.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Thames Rogers taken upon Oath, August 9th and 12th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Deputy Patent Searchers at Gravesend, and has been above Twenty Years in this Office. The Searchers Office at Gravesend consists of Two Patent Searchers, a Deputy to each, and a Controller; the Patentees execute no Part of the Business; it is all tranlacled by the Deputies.

The Patent to which he is Deputy is at present granted to Two Persons jointly: The Deputy is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury.

All the Cockets belonging to a Ship Outward-bound, with a Copy of the Content, and with the Victualling Bill, are lent from the Searcher’s Office in London, to the Searchers Office at Gravesend. Upon the Arrival of the Ship at Gravesend, the Searcher goes on board, and takes with him the Cockets; he compares the Entries of the Goods upon the Cockets with the Entries in the Blue Books in the possession of the Tide Waiters; he inquires «f them whether the Goods they have in Charge are all

on board, and examines himself, as far as he is able. If Fourteenth the Vessel has only Bounty or Free Goods on board, RePJ« no Tidesmen are put on board her, but the Searcher ^,cco^n,1^ inquires for the Ship’s Book, or of the Officers of the Ship after the Bounty Goods, and fees as many of them as he can without delaying the Ship too long, or disturbing the Cargo too much; there is not the same Reason to apprehend the re-landing of the Bounty or Free Goods, as of the Goods entitled to a Drawback.

The Searcher delivers to the principal Officer on board, the Cockets, and a Clearing Note, Signed by himself: He delivers to the Tide W'aiters a Certificate of the Time the Ship fails, Signed by the Watermen; and a Bill, Stating the Time they have been employed, signed by himself: He enters in a Book the Ships as they are cleared, and fends a Copy of it Thrice a Week to the Searcher’s Office in London.

The Patent Searchers have each a Salary of Twelve Pounds a Year, and Four Pounds allowed him for a Boat. The Fees they receive are, for clearing the Ship, and grounded upon Usage; they have likewise an Annual Gratuity of Twenty Guineas from the East India Company: These Fees and Gratuity are received by the Deputy, and the greatest Part of them divided between the Patentees, the Deputies, and the Controller; Two Thirds to the Patentees, the other Third is divided equally between the Two Deputies and the Controller:

There are feme few Fees in which the Patentees have no Share, but are divided equally between the Two Deputies and the Controller. The Share of the Fees and Gratuity to the Patentee last Year was Five hundred and Ninety-three Pounds Two Shillings and Two Pence.

The Patentee paid for Taxes about Twenty-two Pounds, to his Deputy Sixty Pounds, to the Watermen Sixty Pounds, and for Stationary and other contingent Expences Twenty-nine Pounds. His Net Receipt lait Year was Four hundred and Thirty-eight Pounds Two Shillings and Two Pence — that of the Deputy was Two hundred and Seventy-eight Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence.

The Duty of this Office is constant, Holidays, Sundays, and frequently after Dark; for this extra Service there appears to be an Allowance of a Recompence, by an ancient Minute of the Board of Customs.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Richf Neave,

Sunt Beachc,

Will. Roe.

Henry Thames Rogers.

Copy of the Board's Minute.

Dated the 24th April, 1695.

Sir Robert Southwell, - - Sir P. Ward.

Mr. Godolphin, - Mr. Clarke.

Memorandum,

That Mr. Williamson and Mr. Greatheedattended the Commissioners on Behalf of the Searchers, minding them that the Act is now pad for laying Duties upon Coffee, Tea, and Chocolate, and wherein there is a Vol. 41.

Clause that authorizes the Officers of the Customs to receive such Recompence from the Merchants, for their extraordinary Service and Attendance, as the Commissioners shall determine; acquainting them further, that there are at this time several Sufferances to be executed; praying that the Commissioners will make tome Determination therein, in pur-fuartce of the said Act, for the Officers Government. — The Commissioners determine, that they may receive such moderate Recompence for their extraordinary Service and Attendance, as the Merchants will willingly give, advising them to use such Moderation therein, that there be no Occasion of Complaint from the Merchants.

N* 111.

The Examination oft Mr. Joseph Netheringtoti; taken upon Oath, August 8th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Surveyor of the King’s Warehouse, and was appointed to that Office by Warrant of the Treasury, in November 1718.

The Officers employed in the King’s Warehouse are, the Surveyor, Two Assistants, and a Clerk j a Warehouse Keeper for the Crown, and his Deputy; a Warehouse Keeper for the Collector Inwards, and Two Clerks; Two Appraisers, Two Deputies, and their Controller; an' Examiner of Foreign Books, a Cooper, Eighteen Weighers, and a Locker at the Excise Warehouse.

The Species of Goods lent to the King’s Warehouse are, Goods seized, Goods deposited until the Duties are ascertained and paid, or until the Owners can be found, or where the Owners decline paying the Duties; the Effects of Public Ministers, and other Persons, either British or Foreign, coming from Abroad.

The particular Duty of the Surveyor is to superin-tend all the Officers in the King’s Warehouse, to see that they execute their several Employments; he attends and enters in a Book all the Sales in the long Room, and attends at his Office for several Hours every Working Day, and in the Afternoon during the Sales.

He has a Salary, , by his Warrant, of Two hundred Pounds a Year, and a Poundage of Two Pence upon the Gross- Produce arising from the Sales of the Enumerated Go6ds, which amounted last Year to Three hundred and Eighty Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Six Pence: He receives Fifteen Pounds for each Sale, and Ten Pounds for each of the Two Rummage Sales; which, with feme other small Allowances, amounted to One hundred and Thirty Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny.

It has been usual to receive customary Fees upon the Discharge of the Articles, from the Warehouse, and sometimes Gratuities from Foreign Ministers; these produced to him One hundred and Eighty-five Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence: He paid for Taxes Seventy-eight Pounds Ten Shillings and Six Pence, and to his Clerk Three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight-pence; his Net Receipt was Eight hundred and Fourteen Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Seven Pence: The Two Assistants are appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, the One with a Salary of Eighty Pounds, the other of Fifty; each receives a Poundage of One Penny upon the Sale of the Enumerated Goods, and Fees and Gratuities similar to those of the Surveyor.

Joh

T. Ahguish,

N° 115.

The. Examination of Mr. taken

upon Oath, August 1 oth, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is One of the Deputy Appraisers in the King’s Warehouse in the Port of London. He has been in this Office upwards of Twenty Years, and One of the Lockers upwards of Thirty Years.

There are Two Appraisers, holding their Offices under tire Appointment of the Chancellor of the Exchequer by Warrant; the only Bufinefe executed by them is swearing their Deputies to the Truth of the Appraisement, and signing their Names to it; each of them appoints a Deputy.

It is the Business of the Appraisers to set a Value upon all Goods seized; they are entered in a Book, and the appraised Value set against each Article. The Clerk to the King’s Warehouse Keeper takes a Copy, and engrosses it upon Parchment; which is called the Indenture of Appraisement; the Appraisers examine it with the Entries in their Book, sign and swear to the Truth of it; and it is delivered to the Solicitor.

The Appraiser has a Salary of Thirty Pounds a Year by his Warrant, he is allowed out of‘ the Produce of Seizures Two Guineas for every Indenture of Appraisement; out of the Two Guineas arc deduced the Taxes, and the contingent Expences of Parchment, Stamps, and Engrossing: The Residue is divided equally between the Two Principals and their Deputies; the Gross Amount of this Allowance to the Principal last Year was Two hundred and Fifty-seven Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eight Pence; his Payment for Taxes was Ten Pounds One Shilling, the Share to his Deputy was Ninety-two Pounds Six Shillings and Five Pence, and his contingent Expences Sixty-seven Pounds Four Shillings and Ten Pebce: His Net Receipt was One hundred and Eighteen Pounds Six Shillings and Five Pence.

The Locker is under the Direction of the Surveyor and Warehouse Keeper; it is his Bufinefe to assist in the Examination of the Goods seized, in the sorting and allotting them previous to the Sale, and to attend the Shewing, the Sale, and Delivery of them. The Emoluments of a Locker consist of a small Salary of Five Pounds a Year from the Board, and Two Shillings for every Working Day, and Gratuities

N* 114.

The Examination of Mr. Robert taken

oponi Oath, September ift and 2d, 1765.

This Examinant faith, That he is Warehouse Keeper for Victualling Stores. This Office was insti-' luted* by the Board of Customs, in the Year 1781, when he was appointed to it; it used to be executed by One of the Tide Waiters: It is his Duty to re-oeive all the Victualling Stores liable to Custom Duties, purchased for the Use of the Navy in the Port of London.

The Contracts are made by the Commissioners of the Victualling: The Stores purchased pursuant to those Contracts are, by Warrant of the Treasury, directed to be delivered into the Victualling Stores Duty-free, there to remain until wanted: The Board of Customs direct the Warehouse Keeper to receive them; and they continue in his Custody on the Part of the Customs, and of the Store Keeper on the Part of the Victualling Office: They are delivered out by Order of the Board, upon the Application to them of the Commissioners of the Victualling Office: The Warehouse Keeper keeps an Account both of the Receipt and Delivery.

A Surveyor of the Excise attends this Warehouse, and has a similar Custody, and keeps a similar Account of the Receipts and Deliveries of all Stores purchased, liable to the Excise Duties. Stores not wanted for the Service are frequently fold, liable to the Duties> after the Sale the Warehouse Keeper certifies to the Board the Quality and Quantity, and upon the Production of the Warrant on which the Duties appear to be paid, he delivers the Stores to the Purchaser.

Upon the Application of the Purchaser to the Board of Customs, the Stores fold are frequently removed to other Warehouses, still continuing in the Custody of the Warehopfe Keeper, until the Duties upon them are paid, which increases the Number of Warehouses under his Care. There are at present Sixteen Warehouses under his Care, of which he keeps the Keys; One by himself; Four of them jointly with the Victualling Office; Six jointly with the Excise Office; and Eve jointly with the Purchasers, in order to secure the Duties.

He has a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year by his Deputation, and he receives for the Delivery of every Calk fold, Six Pence, and a Fee of Four Shillings and Six Pence upon filling up a Bond for Exportation, and for Extra Attendance, at the Request of the Victualling Office, at the Rate of Five Shillings a Day, paid by them; these Fees amounted last Year to Fifty-four Pounds Five Shillings. He paid for Taxes One Pound Five Shillings and Eight Pence: His Net Receipt was One hundred and Two Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence.

Robert

N* 119.

The Examination of Mr. George taken

upon Oath, June 20th and 27th 1785.

This' Examinant faith, That he is Deputy for the Coast Bufinefe, under the Collector Outwards; he holds his Office by Deputation from the Collector, during Pleasure. This Collector, as far as relates to the Coast

Business, is Collector both Inwards and Outwards; but he receives no Duties.

The only Duties paid Coast wife are on Coals, Culm, and Cinders, which are received by the Collector of the Coal Duties; on Fifti and Salt from Scotland, received by the Collector of the Salt Duties; on Malt, from Scotland, received by the Collector of the Excise; and on Wine sent Coastwise to London, which is paid at the Out Port.

The Business of this Office is transa&ed by the Deputy

cd Geo. Ill,

27° Januarii.

Deputy and Three Clerks; the Principal executes no Part ot‘ it. The Business Inwards consists of receiving from the Master of the Ship his Sufferance and Cocket, entering the latter into the Exchequer Book, endorsing the Sufferance as a Permit to the Coast Waiter for landing the Goods, and after it is returned granting a Certificate for cancelling the Bond at the Out Port. The Business Outwards consists of granting the Sufferances for

D O

shipping the Goods, and after they are returned by the Coast Waiters, forming them into a Cocket, taking Securities from the Matters or Owners, and exonerating the Exchequer Book upon receiving back the Certificate. As Deputy for the Coast Business, he receives the Fees due to the Collectors, the Controllers, and their Deputies, the Surveyor and his Clerk, the Surveyor General and his Clerk, the Patent Searcher, the Patent Kings Waiter, and himself. The Collector has Four Fees — on a Certificate Inwards, One Shilling; on a Coast Cocket Outwards, One Shilling and Eight Pence; on a Transire Outwards, Six Pence; and by Land Carriage, Four Pence; these Fees amount, upon an Average, to about Seven hundred and Twenty Pounds a Year. He receives himself a Salary of Twenty Pounds a Year out of the Coal Duties, by Minute of the Board, for fending to the Inspector of the Coal Duties a Quarterly Lift of all the Coal Ships.

He has Three Fees; One Shilling for every Coast Bond, paid by the Master of the Vessel, out of which he pays Two Pence, being the Cost of the Bond; Four Pence or Six Pence for a Ticket to the Lord Mayor, as an Authority for a Meter j and One Penny for a Transire Outwards. These Fees are customary, and produced last Year Five hundred and Forty-one Pounds: Out of which he paid Eleven Pounds Five Shillings for Taxes; One hundred and Eight Pounds to the Three Clerks, all appointed by the Collector; and for Stationary, all of which he finds for the Office, about Fifty Pounds. His clear Income was about Three hundred and Seventy-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings.

JVelstead.

N* I2i.

The Examination of Mr. John Garbrand Hassard J taken upon Oath, August nth, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy Controller in the Coast Department, deputed by the Duke of Newcastle, as Controller of the Customs in the Port of London. After the Sufferances and Cocket are entered in the Office of the Collector Coastwise, they are brought to, and entered in, the Office of the Controller: The Certificate of Return being made out by the Collector, is signed by the Controller, and delivered by him to the Master.

In the Business Outwards the Controller signs the Sufferances, enters and signs the Cocket. Where the Goods are of that Kind that no Bond is given for the landing them, they are shipped by a Transire, which is, with the Sufferance, entered in the Controller’s Office, and signed by him.

The Certificate of Return, with the Bond annexed, is brought by the Collector to the Controller; he certifies on the Back of the Bond the Receipt of the Certificate: These Bonds and Certificates are sent by him every Year to the Exchequer, and a Schedule of uncertified Bonds, signed by the Collector and Controller, is sent every Year to the Solicitor of the Customs.

Where an Account of the Quantity of any Article carried Coastwise is required, that Account is made out in the Office either of the Collector or Controller, and examined in the other Office, and signed by both.

He receives from the Controller a Salary of Twenty Pounds a Year, and a certain Portion of the Sum paid by the Master of a Vessel, as the Amount of the Fees usually paid to the several Officers in this Department; these amounted last Year to Three hundred and Fifteen Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Six Pence. He paid for Assistance Fifteen Pounds Twelve Shillings: His Net Income was Three hundred and Twenty Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence.

J. G. Hassard.
