N° 122;

The Examination of Mr. Edward Whitehouse; taken upon Oath, August 11th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he has been Surveyor of the Coast Waiters for upwards of Thirty Years; he was appointed by Warrant of the Treasury. It is the Duty of his Office to superintend the Coudufit of the Coast Waiters; there, are Eighteen of them, all appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, their principal Attention is to the landing or shipping Coastwise Foreign Goods liable to Duties: Where the Goods are the Produce of this Country, and neither prohibited nor liable to Duties upon Exportation, the Revenue is in no Danger of being defrauded by the Carriage of such Goods Coastwise, and therefore the Officer is not under the same Necessity of attending to them. Where a Ship

LI arrives

i3°

2j° Jannarii. . 1786.

Fourtfcnth Report on Public Accounts.

arrives Coastwise, One of the Shipping Sufferances from the Port of Loading, endorsed by the Collector and Controller in the Port of London, with a Permission to land the Goods named in all the Sufferances belonging to the Ship, is delivered with all the Sufferances to one or more of the Coast Waiters. The Eighteen Coast Waiters are divided upon Nine Stations, to some of them Three, to others Two, to others One only; they are changed Monthly by regular Rotation. The Sufferances are delivered to the Coast Waiter on that Station where the Ship is designed to unload; he examines the Goods as they are landed, with the Sufferance, and after all are landed he signs the permitting Sufferance, and delivers it back to the Collector.

Where a Ship is to fail Coastwise, the Merchant, or his Agent, fills up an Instrument, which, when signed by the Collector and Controller, is called a Sufferance, and is a Permission to ship the Goods therein mentioned: The Sufferance is delivered to the Coast Waiter on the Station; his Duty is to examine the Goods as they are shipped, with the Entries in the Sufferance, and after they are Hupped he endorses on the Sufferance the Number of Packages shipped, and returns it to the Collector, who from thence makes out the Cocket. A Duplicate of the Sufferance remains with the Collector,

Where Foreign Goods liable to Duties are brought Coastwise, the Surveyor himself generally attends the Examination.

He receives a Salary by his Warrant of Sixty Pounds a Year; he has no established Fees, but receives from the Collector a Share of the Gratuities collected by him, for the Coast Waiters, for their Extra Service, and from the Merchant small Acknowledgments for his Attendance at Extra Hours, Days, and Places; these amounted together last Year to Fifty-nine Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence. He paid for Taxes Three Pounds: His Net Income was One hundred and Sixteen Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence: It has usually amounted to about One hundred and Forty Pounds.

Every Coast Waiter has by his Warrant a Salary of Forty Pounds a Year; he has Twenty Shillings a Week for his Attendance at Gravesend. He has no Fees, but Acknowledgments for Extra Attendance. The Coast Waiters upon every Station divide equally the Profits of the Month.

E. TVhitehouse.

N* 125.

The Examination of Mr. Thomas taken upon Oath, August 12th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is Assistant Surveyor of the East India Warehouses in the Office of the Customs; he has held this Office above Twelve Years. Both the Surveyor and his Assistant are appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; the Duty of each Office is the fame.

The East India Company have several Warehouses, about Ten in Number, allotted for the Reception of different Species of Goods; they have all separate Warehousekeepers on the Part of the Customs: The Two Tea Warehouses have Three each: During the unloading of their Ships each Warehousekeeper belonging to the Company delivers to the Surveyor a Pileing Bill for Piece Goods, containing an Account of all the Bales from each particular Ship deposited in his Warehouse. The Surveyor enters in his Book each Bale; he attends and examines them as they are opened, marks them off in his Book, and marks the Samples; he afterwards measures the Samples. Where the Goods are imported in Chests, Boxes, or Bags, the First Account of them given to the Surveyor is generally by the Landing Waiter's Abstract, which be makes out, after all the Cargo of the Ship is landed, and fends to the Surveyor;

Fourteenth Report on Public Accounts.

132 . 'I'f Januarii. A. 1786.

it includes all the Goods he has landed from that Ship, specifying the Number of Bales, Packages, and Weights; the Surveyor compares this Abstract with the Bills, and makes out an Account, which is an Abstract of the Cargo; be compares this Abstract with the similar Abstracts of the Inspector, Land Surveyor, and Landing Waiter; he then makes out a Warrant, which contains the whole Cargo of the Ship, sorted under Seven Heads, for the Information of the Officer who computes the Duties; this Warrant is signed by the Inspector and his Assistant, the Surveyor and his Assistaht, the Land Surveyor and Two Landing Waiters, and sent to the Office of the Collector Inwards: He enters his Abstract in a Book kept for that Purpose: He, together with the Surveyor, the Inspector, the Land Surveyor, and Waiter, and the Officers of the Company, examines and settles the Allowance for Tare and Damage of all Goods entitled to them, and enters it upon the Abstract.

The Assistant Surveyor has Two Salaries; Seventy Pounds a Year upon the Establi&ment, and Sixty Pounds upon the Incidental Lift, including Thirty Pounds for a Clerk. His other Emoluments are, customary Gratuities from the Company for making up the Accounts of the Ship, and for the Warrants, and from the Passengers upon their Baggage being discharged by Sufferance, and from the Officers for their Clearing Stores; the Amount of all these last Year was Three hundred and Thirty-six Pounds Three Shillings and Ten Pence: He paid for Taxes Twenty-three Pounds Nine Shillings: He had no Clerk last Year, but procured Assistance from his Friends, so as to reduce his contingent Expences to about One Pound Twelve Shillings. His Net Income became, from this Assistance, about Four hundred and Forty-one Pounds Two Shillings and Ten Pence.

Tho.

T. Anguish,

N* 126.

The Examination of Mr. David Maclean; taken upon Oath, August 16th, 1785.

' This Examinant faith, That he is Assistant to Frederick Augusta Barnard, Esquire, the Inspector of the Delivery of unrated East India Goods; he has been in this Office upwards of Twenty-four Years.

The Office of the Inspector is kept at the Custom House; it consists of the Inspector, an Assistant, and a Clerk. It is the Duty of the Inspector to superin-tend all the Officers on the Part of the Customs, in all the Warehouses belonging to the East India Company. Fie states to the Board the Weekly Attendance of the Officers, and occasionally such other Matters as are necessary for their Information. All Papers relative to the East India Business are referred to him by the Board, for his Report. His Signature is essential to the Warrants.

There are Fourteen established Warehousekeepers, Six Controllers, a Jerquer of the Warehousekeepers Accounts for prohibited East India Goods, and in every Warehouse a Number of Lockers, in proportion to the Business in that Warehouse.

The Duty of the Locker is to receive and guard the Goods, and in the Tea Warehouses he delivers them out; in the Warehouses for prohibited Goods he assists in examining the Goods, and packing them up, and attends them to the Water Side, and delivers them to the Searcher.

After Notice to the Inspector, given Weekly, or oftener, by the East India Company, of the Time and Place where the Goods are to be examined, the Inspec-for or his Assistant constantly attends: If the Cargo of the Ship consists of Piece Goods, he receives from the Company the Pileing Bill, which is a Copy of the Invoice: If the Cargo consists of other Goods, he receives from the Landing Waiter his Bill or Abstract: of the Goods he has landed, and from the East India Company the Sight, which is a Copy of the Entry; he Compares the Abstract with the Sight.

The Examination of the Goods by the Inspector is similar to that by the Surveyor: These Two Officers, in Conjunction with the Landing Surveyor and Waiter, ascertain the Tare and the Damage; each of these Four Officers makes up a similar' Account; they examine their Accounts together, and from thence form the Warrants. A11 Officer of the East India Company, called the Husband for Shipping, makes out a similar Account, and compares it with the Accounts of the Officers of the Customs.

Upon every Sale of Tea by the East India Company, the Controller of the Tea Warehouses makes out, upon One of the printed Sale Books, the Net Weight of every Lot, by deducting from the Gross Weight the Allowance for Tare, Draft, and Damage; lie delivers this Account to the Inspector, who compares it with a corresponding Account made out by the Company’s Husband, and transmits a Copy of it to the Bench Officers; he keeps the Original in the Office, and from thence checks the Number of Chests brought to Sale by the Company, by comparing the Number in these printed Sale Books with the Number in the AbstraCb of the Landing Waiters.

A similar Process is observed in the Sale of China, and other unrated East India Goods.

The Inspector is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary for himself and Clerks, of Two hundred and Ten Pounds a Year. He receives from the East India Company a certain Sum ]>er Ship, long since settled between them and the Board of Customs; and a Customary Gratuity of Six Pence for the Examination of every Parcel of private Trade, Sea Officers Clearing Stores, and Passengers Baggage: The Amount of them last Year was, as he believes, Four hundred and Sixty-four Pounds One Shilling and Nine Pence; out of which his Payment for Taxes was Thirty-six Pounds Eighteen Shillings, and to his Assistant and Clerk Ninety Pounds; which rendered his clear Income Five hundred and Forty-seven Pounds Three Shillings and Nine Pence.

David.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond,

WillmRoe.

N* 127.

The Examination of Mr. James Seddon; taken upon Oath, August 16th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Two Warehousekeepers for prohibited East India Goods; he was about Five Years a Controller, and has been about Eight Years a Warehousekeeper.

He receives from the Company a Pileing Bill; he enters the Bales in a Book, with a Number to each; upon the Bales being brought to the Warehouse, he puts the same Numbers upon them, as far as the Number of Bales brought agrees with the Number entered in his Book: He attends the Opening and Examination of the Bales, and enters in his Book the Number of Pieces in each Bale, with their- different

06 Descriptions;

26 Geo. III.

270 Januarii. 133

Descriptions; he retains them in his Possession until they are exported, or sent out to be dyed, glazed, or refrahed; after which they are returned to hiui for Exportation. The Merchant gives him an Account what Goods he intends to export; the Warehouse-keeper gives him a Certificate that those Goods are in his Possession, with the estimated Value. Upon a Certificate from the Board, that the Merchant has given Security to export, and a Coeket being produced to him, he permits the Merchant, attended by a Locker, to take his Goods to the Searcher at the Water Side; the Searcher and Locker sign the Certificate, which is deposited with the Warehousekeeper.

Every Half Year he makes out an Account of the Imports, Exports, and Remains, and transmits it on Oath to the Board; and the like Account Annually to Parliament

The Surveyor, jointly with the Warehousekeeper and Controller* take Half Yearly an Account of the Stock, as a Check upon the Account of the Warehousekeeper, and upon the Property of each Merchant. The Duty of the Controller is to keep the same Accounts, as a Check upon the Warehousekeeper: They, or One of them, attend at the Out Warehouses, for the Examination of private Trade, Baggage, and Piece Goods, in order to take an Account of the prohibited Goods, which are sent afterwards to his Warehouse, and treated in the like Manner as the prohibited Goods of the Company.

The Warehousekeeper is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year. The Fees of the Warehousekeeper and Controller are custoruary Payments for Business transacted in the Office, and for Extra Attendance. His Fees, last Year, were Forty-three Pounds and Three Pence; he paid for Taxes Twenty-three Pounds One Shilling and Four Pence; his Net Receipt was One hundred and Nineteen Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eleven Pence.

J. Seddon.

This Examinant faith, That he is Controller to the Warehousekeeper of prohibited East India Goods; he has beeu in this Office Twenty-four Years.

N* 130.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Halcomb; taken upon Oath, August 17th, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That he is Register General of Tobacco; he has been in the Office ever since the EstablKhment of it in the Year 1751, and Register General ever since the Year 1756.

This Office consists of the Register and Five Clerks; Two Clerks under the Collector Inwards, Two under the Controller, and several other inferior Officers. The Business of the Register is to keep an Account of all the Tobacco imported into Great Britain: After it is landed in the Port of London, the Landing Waiter delivers to the Register an Account of the Number of Hogsheads landed by him from every Ship, with the Weight of each Ilogfhcad; he enters this Account in his Official Book: He receives the like Account from the Collector and Controller at every Out Port. Upon Exportation, he receives from the Collector the Searcher's Bill endorsed with the Number and Weight of the Hogsheads to be exported; from thence he discharges his Account of those Hogsheads.

Upon Sale he receives from the Collector the Merchants Account, signed by him and the Purchaser, of the Number and Weight of the Hogsheads fold, and to whom delivered for Home Consumption, and discharges his Account accordingly. The like Account of the Disposal of the Tobacco is transmitted to him from the Out Ports, by the Collectors and Controllers. He raises an Account for every Purchaser, and charges him with all he purchases. Every Certificate for Removal is registered in his Office, and the Account of the Purchaser thereby discharged.

He receives* from the Locker an Account of the Hogsheads received into and issued from the Ware-house, and enters them in a Book kept for that Purpose.

He has a Deputy in Scotland, from whom he receives every Year an Account similar to that kept by him in London.

The Register General is appointed by a Constitution of the Board, of Treasury, with a Salary of Three hun-

Vol. 41.

dred Pounds a Year. He receives upon the Incidental Lift Eighty Pounds a Year. He paid for Taxes Seventy-six Pounds Ten Shillings, and to his Chief Clerk Twenty-four Pounds Twelve Shillings. His Net Income was Two hundred and Seventy-eight Pounds Eighteen Shillings.

All his Clerks are appointed and paid Salaries by Warrants of the Treasury. Neither himself nor his Clerks have any other Emoluments whatever.

H. Halcomb.

T. Anguish,

The Examination of Mr. Charles Thredder; taken upon Oath, August 19th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is First Clerk for the Inland Tobacco Business, under the Collector Inwards, and has been in this Office about Thirty-one Years. He was appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; and has a Deputation from the Collector Inwards. He enters, from the Bills in the Office of the Collector, the Quantities of Tobacco imported, and from the Landing Waiter’s Book he enters the stamped Number marked upon each Hogshead, and the Weight of the Tobacco it' contains. Upon the Exportation, a Bill, containing the Quantity to be exported, is marked by him with the Initials of his Name, and sent to the Certificate Office. The Searcher’s Bill is brought to him, and from thence he discharges his Account of the Quantity endorsed on the Bill. Where it is fold for Home Consumption the Importer delivers to him an Account, signed by himself and the Purchaser, of the Number and Weight of each Hogshead fold; from whence he discharges his own Account, and charges each Manufacturer with the Quantity he buys.

The Examination of Mr. John Sherlock; taken upon Oath, August 23d, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is Surveyor of the Laud Carriage Officers; he is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury. There are on the Establishment Fifteen Land Carriage Officers, all appointed by Warrant of the Treasury; and there is One Extra Land Carriage Officer appointed by the Commissioners of the Customs, betides an Assistant, who being a Tide Waiter, has no Salary as a Land Carriage Officer; they are all under his Superintendance and Direction, and he does himself the same Duty

as they do. London. Westminster, and Southwark ere divided into Four Stations, called the Eastern, Westeru, Northern, and Southern Stations; and on the First Tuesday in every Month Four of the Land Carriage Officers are by him appointed by Rotation to eaob of these Stations, except the Western, which has Five allotted to it

Xt is their Duty to attend at the Inns in London, Westminster, and Southwark, and to inspect all Carriages of every Kind, in order to see that there are no uncustomed Goods, or Goods without Permit or Certificate; they also inspect, in the belt Manner they are able, the Warehouses at the different Inns, for the same Purposes; when they find such Goods they seize them, and take them to the Custom House, where they are deposited in the Warehouse. When they receive Information of Goods liable to Seizure, they proceed to search for them according to the Information received, whether they are on the Land or on the Water. There are three of these Officers who do no Duty, being in other Services.

He is paid upon the Establishment a Salary of Sixty Pounds a Year. He paid to the Civil List, Superannuation Fund, and for Stamps, Three Pounds and Fight Pence, and Gratuities upon receiving his Salary Ten Shillings; which made his Net Receipt Fifty-six Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence.

The Land Carriage Officers are paid upon the Establishment a Salary of Thirty-five Pounds a Year each: They paid, as he believes, to the Superannuation Fund, Eighteen Shillings, and for Stamps Eight Pence, and upon the Receipts of their Salary Four Shillings.

He does not, neither, as he believes, do any of thp Land Carriage Officers, receive any Fees, Allowances, or Gratuities.

John Sherlock.

N* 136.

The Examination of Mr. Robert; taken

upon Oath, August 24th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he has been for Twenty Years One of the Inspe&ors of the River. There are Tour of these Officers, all appointed by Warrants of the Treasury.

The general Duty of the Inspector is to superintend the Officers that consticute the Water Guard, who are the Tide Surveyors, the Tide Waiters, the Watermen, and the Watchmen, and the Coast Waiters at Gravesend; "being altogether, as he believes, in Number about Six hundred.

The Four Inspectors take it by Turns to attend Weekly, One at Gt'ax'esend, One at the Office, ami Two upon

the River Duty. Another Branch of the Inspectors Duty is to report upon the numerous References made to them by the Board, ami to represent to them, by Memorials, such Observations and Regulations as occur to them relative to the Officers and Business under their Inspection: They examine and certify the Bills for the Payment of the Tide Waiters and Watermen, and the Incidental Pay of the Tide Surveyors. There are Ten Stationary Tide Surveyors constantly residing at particular Places, with each a Boat and Two Watermen. There are eight regular Established Tide Surveyors, and Nine additional Surveyors, who are Established Tide Waiter; these Seventeen all succeed, of course, by regular Rotation, to the Stations, which are divided into Six, some having Two, others Three Surveyors: The Stations are, the Gravesend, the Boarding Station at London, the Homeward-bound, the Clearing the Outward-bound, and the Quays and Office Station.

The Inspectors on the River visit the Ships, to see that the Tide Surveyors and Tide Waiters are upon their Duty, and that the Tide Surveyors, have duly signed the Blue Books of the Tide Waiters.

Upon Notice of the Arrival of an East Indiaman in the Downs, the Inspectors appoint a Guard to that Ship, consisting of a Tide Surveyor taken by Rotation, who is the Superintendant of the whole Guard, and an Assistant who is an Established Tide Waiter, Three Boats, Five Tide Waiters, and Ten Watermen. Eight Tide Waiters more are put on board her at Gravesend, One of whom the Inspectors appoint to be the Book-keeper: When flie comes to the Moorings, the Inspectors increase the Guard, by the Addition of a Day Galley and Four Watermen. The Inspeflor frequently visits this Ship, sometimes assists in the Rummage, and is always present at the Clearing.

The Inspectors examine into the Circumstances of those Ships which are liable to he put under Quarantine in the River, and make their Report to the Board, annexing the Examinations taken upon Oath; and upon their Certificate the Ship is discharged, and admitted to report. Tine Inspector at Gravesend fends by Express to the Tide Surveyors on the Quay Station, for a Supply of Tide Waiters, and furniilies them with Money for their Support, and every WeeJk delivers in his Account to the Receiver General.

The Inspector has a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year by virtue of his Warrant, and Nineteen Pounds Ten Shillings, payable out of Incidents, for his Service at Gravesend. He receives no Fees, but Ibme small Gratuities for Extra Business and Attendance, which are generally equally divided between the Four; they amounted last Year to about Twenty Pounds each. He paid for Taxes Twenty-three Pounds. His Net Income was One hundred and Sixteen Pounds Ten Shillings.

Rt. Weskett.

T. Anguish,

A Piggott,

Geo. Dnimmond,

Wilt" Roe.

The Examination of Mr. Matthew Poppleuell; taken upon Oath, August 26th, 1785*

This Examinant faith. That he is the Senior Tide Surveyor; he was Twelve Years in the Jerquer’s Office, and has been Twenty-three Years a Tide Surveyor.

The Duty of this Officer, upon the Gravesend and Boarding Stations, is to board every Ship from Foreign Parts, to take an Account of them, and to put on board the regular Number of Tide Waiters. Upon the Homeward and Outward bound Stations, he visits the Ships, fees that the Tidesmen are on board, and gives One at a Time Leave to go on Shore for Four Hours. On the Clearing Station, he attends the Office every Day, to receive the Orders of the Board relative to the Ships that are to be cleared; he visits the Ship, fends to the Ware-house the remaining Parcels, and when all the Goods are landed discharges the Tide Waiters, and enters their Names in the Tide Surveyor’s Office, that they may be again employed.

Upon the Quay Station, the Surveyor visits the Ships where the Tidesmen are on board, clears them, superintends the Watchmen, and detaches the Tide Waiters to Gravesend.

Upon every Station, the Surveyor rummages where-ever he finds Occasion.

The Eight established Tide Surveyors are appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary of Sixty Pounds a Year, and by Order of the Board Twenty Shillings a Week for their Attendance upon the Gravesend Station, and One Guinea a Week for their Duty on board East Indiamen; these Two Allowances amounted last Year to Twenty Pounds Seventeen Shillings. He receives customary Gratuities, amounting last Year to Fifty Pounds. He paid to the Civil List One Pound Ten Shillings, the Superannuation Fund One Pound Ten Shillings, for Stamps Eight Pence, and for his extraordinary Support on his Duty at Gravesend, and on board the Indiamen, and other contingent Expences, Thirty-four Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence. His Net Income w;as Ninety-two Pounds Seventeen Shillings. Formerly it was usual for the Tide Surveyor to dine on board with the Officers of the Ship, but that is now, by the particular Order of the Board, discontinued.

Matthew Popplewell.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Sam. Beachcroft,

The Examination of Mr. Benjamin Otbie; taken upon Oath, August26th, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That he is One of the Established Tide Waiters on the Superior Lift: The

Difference between the Superior and Inferior Lifts con-fists in the Salary only: There is also a Preferable Lift, confuting of Three hundred and Fifty-six, who are paid only when upon Duty; Three Shillings a Day when on Ship Duty, and Half a Guinea a Week when attending at Gravesend.

The Duty of the Tide Waiter is on board the Ship; he is put on board by the Tide Surveyor on the Station, and is to guard the Cargo of the Ship from being -landed withouf an Order, until Ihe is cleared. He receives Orders for the Delivery of the Goods from the Land Waiter, signed by him, and describing the Marks, Quantities, and Quality of the Goods to be landed; he enters them in the Blue Book as they are delivered, and fends a Note of them, by the Tide Waiter who has the Charge of them, to the Quay.

When the Cargo is all landed, the Tide Surveyor comes on board, rummages the Ship, and discharges the Tide Waiter. The Blue Book is signed by the Tide Waiter and Tide Surveyor, and delivered to the -Jerquer.

In moll Ships the Officer is maintained with the Ship’s Provisions; in some Ships he is refused Provisions, and is obliged, with the Leave of the Surveyor, to procure them from on Shore.

The Established Tide Waiters are appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary, the Superior Lift of Forty Pounds, and the Inferior of Thirty-five Pounds: Upon the India Duty he has an additional Allowance, when Assistant to the Surveyor, of One Guinea a Week, and when in the Boat, Two Shillings and Six Pence a Day. Each Officer pays to the Superannuation Fund. The Tide Waiters do not, that he knows of, receive any Fees whatever.

*The Examination of Mr. taken

upon Oath, August 17th> 1785*

This Examinant faith, That he is Clerk to Edmund Armstrong, Esquire, the Husband of the 4i Cens. Duty in the Office of the Customs. *

This Duty is collected in the Plantations in the Pro* duce of the several Islands, and that Produce is remitted by the Collectors to the Husband of this Duty in England, There are Six Islands subject to this Duty,

Antigua, St. Christophers, Nevis, and

Tortola.

The CoHedor in the Plantations fends to the Husband an Invoice and Bill of Lading of the Goods remitted for the Duty; they are landed pursuant to a Sight, which is a Direction to the Landing Waiter to land them, signed by the Husband, his Controller, and One Commissioner, and they are sent to the Ware-house; the Husband enters them, and pays the Duty. The Husband, the Controller, and the other Officers, fell, these Goods by Auction, at Itated Times. The Husband receives die Money produced by the Sales, and fends to the Board every Month a State of his Accounts, containing the Balance of the left Month, his Receipts and Payments during the Month, and the Balance remaining in his Chell, to abide the Order of the Board.

These Duties are liable to various Payments, feme by Warrants of the Treasury, others by Orders of the Board of Customs; others, beiq£ the incidental Expences attending the Management, are paid by the Husband or Controller. As loon as the Account of a Sale is made up, it is sent, with the Vouchers, to the Controller General, who is the Officer that pafles the Accounts of the Husband. He pays from Time to Time, into the Hands of the Receiver General, such a Sum as he can lpare, confident with the current Expences of the Office.

This Office consists of the Husband and his Clerk, an Examiner of his Accounts, a Controller, a Cooper, a Warehousekeeper, and Two Lockers.

The Husband is appointed by Warrant of the Treasury, with a Salary of One hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year; his Payment for Taxes was Twelve Pounds One Shilling and Four Pence; his Net Receipt was One hundred and Forty-seven Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Eight Pence.

The Examiner does no Business, nor ever attends; the Controller executes the Business of that Officer. All the Salaries, except Thirty-six Pounds Four Shillings to the Warehousekeeper, and the Allowances to the Lockers, are paid out of this Duty.

William Lawless.

T. Anguish

A. Piggott,

Richd Aeave,

N® 142.

The Examination of Mr. Bajlin; taken upon Oath, October 25th, and November lit, 1785.

This Examinant faith. That in the Account of the Produce of Seizures and Fines transmitted to this Board, the Charges inserted in the Column under the Title of Charges of Condemnation, §c. paid out of the Gross Produce, comprehend the Payments to all the Officers employed in the Condemnation and Sale, and the Poundages payable to the several Officers of Vol. 41,

the Customs, except that to the Inspector of Prosecutions; after these Charges are deducted out of the Grols Produce, the Remainder is divided into certain Shares between the King and the seizing Officers, according to the Directions of the Acts of Parliament relative to Seizures. The Shares of the fficers are paid at the Port; the Shares of the Crown are remitted by the Collectors to the Receiver for the Out Ports, but retaining in their Hands such Portions of those Shares as may be wanted for maintaining the Custom House Cruizers, and to defray such other incidental Expences at the Port as the Commissioners may think proper to order. Such Part of the King’s Share as is remitted to the Receiver for the Out Ports is applied to any of the incidental Charges of Management arising in London, pursuant to the Orders of the Board, and the Remainder paid into the Exchequer. The principal Heads of Expence defrayed out of the King’s Share, either arising in London, or remitted from the Out Ports, are, the Cutters, Trades-men’s Bills, Stationary, Rewards to the Soldiers who assist in making Seizures, to the Officers for seizing Snuff and Tobacco, and the Poundage to the Inspector of Prosecutions.

N* 143.

The Examination of Mr. James Stephenson; taken upon Oath, December 2d, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That the only Business transacted in the Inward Branch of the Office of Surveyor of the Port of London, is that of a Check upon the Three Divisions of the Receipt of the Collector Inwards. Neither the Debentures for Drawbacks or Bounties pals through this Department.

Every Year Three Books are sent from the Exchequer to the Office of the Surveyor — One for the Custom Duties on Wine, another for the Custom Duties by Merchant Strangers, the other few the Custom Dufies ob all other Goods: The Daily Bills are copied into these Books, as far as relate to that Branch of Duties called the Customs; but no other Brandies are entered there. Each Book contains the Account of a Year, and when completed is delivered to the Deputy Surveyor, and, as he believes, transmitted to the Exchequer. Duplicates of these Books are made out in like Manner from their own Bills, in the Offices of the Controller, Surveyor General, and Register of Warrants. He does not know that any Use is or can be made of these Books in the Exchequer.

Every Account contained in these Books may be obtained from the Offices of the Collector, Controller, Surveyor General, Surveyor, and Examiner.

The Outward Branch of this Office is a Check, in a similar Manner, upon the Collector Outwards; Debentures for Bounties are entered in that Office, and signed by the Deputy Surveyor. He receives and makes out, in like manner, Exchequer Books for his Department. This is the Whole of the Business transa&ed in that Office.

James Stephenson.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Richd Neave,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

N* 144.

The Examination of Mr. Peregrine Sims) taken upon Oath, December 2d, 1785.

This Examinant faith, That all the Bufinefe tranla&ed in the Inward Branch of the Office of Surveyor General is, the Check upon the Receipt of the Collectors Inwards, keeping a Sight Book, and making out the Exchequer Books; the like Check and Duplicates of these Books are kept, as he believes, in the Offices of the Collector, and all the other Patent Checks.

A Merchant Alien Warrant and Bill of Sight is signed by the Collector, the Controller, the Examiner, the Surveyor General or Surveyor, and by the Petty Customer Inwards: His Exchequer Book contains only the Custom Branch paid by Aliens, or upon Imports in Foreign Ships; the Alien Exchequer Book of the Surveyor General contains the same Entries. The Entry in the Exchequer Books of the Customer and Surveyor General is a Description of the Goods only; the like Account may be obtained, as he believes, from many of the Officers of the Customs.

Per. Sims.

After my hearty Commendations.

Whereas by your Report, of the 19th May last, vou have certified me, that you are of Opinion Mr. John Pearfe, of, London, Merchant, is fitly qualified to take Care that Informations concerning uncustomed and prohibited Goods be effectually prosecuted, and that the Fines and Recoveries be duly brought to the King’s Account; and have offered to me your Opinion, that I should make Trial of him for Twelve Months, with such Allowance as to me shall seem meet, upon Experience of his Service, with which Terms, you say, he is content; but that you conceive he ought to be obliged to leave off his Trade, wherein he is at present, or was lately, engaged, and give Security for his faithful Behaviour in the Said Employment. These are, therefore, to pray and require you to issue forth your Deputation to the said John Pearfe, for the Employment aforesaid, to continue for the Space of One Year from the Date hereof, and no longer; and you are to take Care that he leaves oft' his Said Trade, and give sufficient Security for his faithful Behaviour in the said Employment, as you have proposed. N* 148.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

The humble Memorial of William , In-

speftor of Prosecutions in His Majesty’s Court of Exchequer,

Sheweth,

That his late Majesty King George the I Id. was pleated to grant, by his Royal Patent, dated June 20th, 1741, to the Right honourable Stephen Poyntz, in Consideration of his long and approved Services in high and confidential Employments, the Office of Inspector of the Prosecutions in his Court of Exchequer, and to continue the same to your Memorialist, which laid Patent His present Majesty was most graciously pleased to reuew and confirm on his Accession to the Crown, which your Memorialist must ever remember with the greatest Gratitude; that by the Terms of his Patent he is entitled " to have, hold, exercise, and enjoy, the said Office and Place by himself, or sufficient Deputy or Deputies, with such Fees, Allowances, Profits, and Advantages to the said Place " belonging, in as full and ample a Manner as the " same were held and received by the said Stephen " Poyntz, or any former Inspector of Prosecutions did or might lawfully receive or enjoy in respect of that " Place."

The Emoluments derived to the Possessors of this Office, from its First Establishment, have been an Allowance of One Shilling in the Pound on the King’s Share of the Money paid into the Receipt of his Majesty’s Exchequer for prohibited and uncustomed Goods.

By an Act of Parliament passed in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign it is directed, " that " One Moiety of the Neat Produce arising by the Sale " of all Seizures (after the deducing the Charges *c of Condemnation and Sale from the Whole) shall " be paid into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, in lieu of His Majesty’s Share thereofAnother Act (which is hereunto annexed) passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty, to explain and amend the above-recited Act, directs, " that instead of One Moiety of the Neat Produce arising " by the Sale of all Seizures (after deducting the " Charges of Condemnation and Sale from the Whole) " being paid into the Exchequer, in lieu of His Majesty’s Share thereof, the Commissioners of His Vol. 41.

" Majesty’s Customs shall be authorized, where it Fourteenth " may be by them judged necessary, to order the " Charges arising by the Condemnation and Sale, Accounts. " an<T all Manner of Law Bills, and other Charges " of Management, to be paid out of His Majesty’s " Share of the Produce arising by the Sale of all " Goods which have been, or may be, seized and " condemned, in like Manner as may now be done out " of any other Branch of the Revenue of the Customs, which is by Law applicable to the Payment " of Incidents." Your Memorialist begs Leave to observe, that this Act, fb materially affecting his Interests, was passed without any Notice having been given to himself or his Deputy; that, from the Title of the said Act, it was not to be foreseen that such Clause would have been inserted in it, and that consequently he had not an Opportunity of defending his Rights, or submitting his Cause to the Justice of Parliament at the Time of the Act’s passing.

The Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs, by virtue of the discretionary Power conveyed to them by this Act, having judged it necessary to order all Manner of Law Bills, Purchase, Hire, Equipment of Cruizers in the Service of she Revenue, and various other Charges of Management, to a very considerable Amount (which were heretofore paid by Incidents) to be now defrayed out of the King’s Share of the Produce of Seizures, there has already been a great Decreaie of the Money paid into the Exchequer on this Account, and the King’s Share of the Produce of the Seizures may in Time be reduced to nothing, by being charged with a larger Proportion of the Expences of such Management: Your Memorialist therefore begs Leave to submit to your Lordships, that he has already fufJ fered a very great Diminution of his Income, in consequence of these Regulations (by which your Memorialist does not know that any greater Saving is made to the Public than the Poundage formerly received by the Inspector of Prosecutions) and has great Reason to apprehend that the Reduction will continually be increased, and that he may, in the End, be entirely deprived of his just Rights, conveyed to him by His Majesty’s Charter or Letters Patent.

Your Memorialist is ready to admit, that the Profits of his Place have been considerably greater than it ever was apprehended they would be at the Time it was granted; having, however, faithfully discharged the Duties of his Office, and conceiving his Title to the Profits of it to be sacred; having made all his Arrangements in the certain Hope and Expectation that he should have been permitted to enjoy these Profits in their full Extent for the Remainder of his Life, he cannot at this Period of it, and with a numerous Family, but severely feel so considerable and unexpected a Diminution of them; and thinks himself justified in submitting his same to your Lordships.

Your Memorialist, however, begs to be understood as not presuming to oppose the Interests of an Individual to any Regulations that may be thought beneficial to the Public, or in any Degree conducive to the better or more easy Management of the Revenue: He is far from wishing to obstruct any Regulation whatsoever# that may tend to such Improvement; and if the Commissioners of the Customs, upon a Reference of the Matter to them, to examine into and report the Fasts, should continue to be of the Opinion that it will be for the Benefit of the Public, that the Office of Inspector of Prosecutions should be abolished, your Memorialist is perfectly willing, with His Majesty’s gracious Permission, to surrender his Patent, trusting that your Lordships, in your Justice and Equity, will grant him such a Compensation as to your Lordships shall appear to be adequate and proper. He has subjoined an Account of the Produce of his Place for the last Twenty-five Years; begging Leave to observe, that the Receipt for the last Two Years has been consider-

After our hearty Commendations.

Whereas His Majesty, by Letters Patent, dated 4th March 1761, did grant unto William Poyntz, Esquire, the Office and Place of Inspector of the Prosecutions in the Court of Exchequer, concerning un-customed and prohibited Goods, with all such Fees, Allowances, Profits, and Advantages, to the said Office and Place belonging, in as full and ample Manner as the same were had and received by him and his Predecessors in that Office: And whereas, by an Act passed in the 3d of His present Majesty, it is directed that One Moiety of the Neat Produce arising from the Sale of all Seizures (after deducting the Charges of Condemnation and Sale from the Whole) should be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, in lieu of His Majesty’s Share thereof: And whereas, by a subsequent Act, passed in the 21st Year of His Majesty’s Reign, it is therein directed, that instead of such Moiety being paid into the Exchequer as aforesaid, in lieu of His Majesty’s Share, you the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs are thereby authorized, as often as you shall judge necessary, to order the Charges arising by the Condemnation and Sale, and all Manner of Law Bills, and other Charges of Management, to be paid out of His Majesty’s Share of the Produce arising by the Sale of all Goods which have been or may be seized and condemned, in like Manner as. may be done out of any other Branch of the Revenue of the Customs, which by Law is applicable to the Payment of Incidents; under the Authority of which Clause, a considerable Part of His Majesty’s said Moiety has been otherwise employed, by which Means the full Advantages, Profits, and Emoluments enjoyed by the said William Poyntz, and his Predecessors in the said Office, as granted to him by the said Letters Patent, have been already considerably diminished: And whereas, by such Clause aforesaid, the Fund applicable to the Incidents of His Majesty’s Customs has been greatly increased, and actually augmented, in Proportion to such Diminution of Profit or actual Lois as the said William Poyntz has thereby sustained; We, taking into our Consideration all the Circumstances attending the Cafe, and being desirous of afibrding some present Compensation to the said William Poyntz, until the Merits of his same shall been fully submitted to the Consideration of Parliament, do hereby authorize and require you to cause Payment to be made to the said William Poyntz, or to his Assigns, of the Sum of 558/. 104. Sid. without Account, which we have thought fit to allow him as a Compensation for the Loss he has already sustained in the Emoluments of his said Office in the Half Year ended at Midsummer last, in consequence of the said Act: and you are to cause the

Treasury Chambers,

19th Nov. 1785.

N* 150.

The Examination of Edward Taylor, Esquire;

Taken upon Oath, December 5th 1785.

This Examinant faith, that he is One of the Sworn Clerks in the Office of the King’s Remembrancer in the Court of Exchequer, and Clerk of the Coast Bonds in the same Office; he has been in both tilde Offices upwards of Twenty-five Years.

Every Year Blank Parchment Booooks are sent by the King’s Remembrancer, under the Seal of the Court, with proper Superscriptions on each Book to the Customer, Controller, and Searcher, at the Out Ports in England and Wales, with their Members, according to the Lift transmitted by him to this Board, marked N* 1; and every Midsummer One Book to the Customer and Controller at each Out Port, according to the Lift N* 2; and Annually the like Books to several Officers in the Port of London, according to a List of those Officers transmitted to this Board, marked N° 3. These Books are issued by the King’s Remembrancer, in pursuance of Orders under the Great Seal, in the 7 th Year of Queen Elizabeth, enrolled in the same Office; those Orders direct these Books to be returned Annually, upon the Oath of the Officer. Ever since he has been to the Office the Returns of these Book into the Court of Exchequer have been very irregular; in some Years no Books have been returned from any Port; some of the Ports have made no Returns at all, that he knows of; none of the Ports have made Returns of all their Books, and few have been the Returns to any Year.

Those Books that are returned are deposited in One of the Record Rooms of the Court at j

and he never knew any Use made of them.

Edward Taylor.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond,

Wilt* Roe.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petitions for private Bills after the 3d Day of March next.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Motion made Yesterday, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty;

Ordered, That His Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Tuesday Morning next.

Mr. Dempster presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for naturalizing Andreas Emmerich: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

The House being informed that One of the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition wa6 read; Setting forth, That an Act was made in the last Session of Parliament, granting to His Majesty certain Duties bn Shops within Great Britain, to be raised, levied, and paid, upon every House or other Building, then or thereafter to be erected, any Part of which should, for the Time being, be used as a Shop publickly kept open for carying on any Trade or for felling any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize by Retail, and, upon every Building, or Place, used for a Shop only for the before-mentioned Purposes, a Yearly Duty, according to the several Rates in the said Act mentioned; and, by the said Act, the several Duties therein charged are required to be paid over and above all the subsisting Duties on Houses and Windows imposed by former Acts of Parliament; and that, although the City of London and County of Middlesex already pay more than One Seventh Part of the Land Tax of Great Britain, yet the Weight of this Tax will fall so peculiarly heavy upon the extended Metropolis, as to levy thereon near a Moiety of the w hole Sum thereby proposed to be raised upon the Kingdom at large; and the Petitioners submit that the said Tax is not only burthenfomt and oppressive in its Operation, but partial and consequently unjust in its Principle, as throwing a most heavy and disproportioned Burthen on one Part of the Kingdom, and selecting a particular Oafs of Men as the Objects thereof, w ho already contribute more than their full Proportion to all the Supplies of Government: And therefore relying on the Wisdom and Justice of the House, to repeal the said Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers within the Town of Wakefield, in the County of York, was pre-

fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners most readily and chcarfolly contribute Voi. 41.

to the Exigencies of the State, whenever called upon in an equal and just Proportion with the rest of their Fellow Subjects; and that the Annual Pound Rate Tax upon Retail Shops, imposed by the late Act of the 25th Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, operates in Effect eastly like foe House Tax, and all other Pound Rate Taxes; but, inaftnuch as it affects only the Retail Dealer, and must be paid out of his Profits, the Petitioners, not having it in their Power, consistent with the common Course of Trade, to charge any Thing in Ease of the Tax on Sale of their Goods, consider it as a personal Burthen imposed upon a few only, beyond the Taxes payable by them equally with the rest of His Majesty’s Subjects: And therefore praying, That the said Act may be repealed, or that such other Relief may be granted the Petitioners as to the House fttall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Warden and Assistants incorporated for the Preservation of the Harbour of Dover, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the said Alliltants, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Harbour of Dover, from its Situation and Utility, hath long been accounted a Harbour of Importance, and thought worthy the Support and Assistance of the Legislaturc; and that, by an Act made in the 1 ith and 12th Years of the Reign of King William the Third, a Duty of Three Pence per Ton was laid upon certain Ships and Vessels, for a Term therein mentioned, for the Repair of the said Harbour, and the Term and Powers by the said Act granted have, by several subsequent Acts, been continued, and a Moiety of the said Duty has been appropriated to the making a Harbour at Rye; and that the Income arising to the said Harbour of Dover, from the Estates and other Articles which constitute what is called the old Revenues, is by no means adequate to carrying on, and keeping in Repair, the several considerable Works and Improvements which have been lately made, and are now making, to the said Harbour, or to supporting the Harbour in its present State; and that the Term for which the said Duty was granted, will expire on the lft of May 1786, Old Style, and the Trustees for the said Harbour of Rye have lately obtained an Enlargement of the said Term, lo far as respects their Moiety of the said Duty: And therefore praying, That the said Duty, so far as it respects the Harbour of , may be further continued.

Ordered \That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Sawbridge, the Lord North, &c.: And they are to meet upon Tuesday

Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of Robert Burton, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Somersham with the Soke, in the County of Huntingdon, and of the Right Reverend Father in God Richard Lord Bishop of Landaff, Rector of Somersham aforesaid, which includes the Towns of Fenton

and Colne, within the said Soke, and also of the Reverend John Jacob Oakes, Rector of Bluntisham with Eanth, also in the said Soke, and likewise of John Cole, Esquire, and several other Persons, being Owners of Common Right Houses within the Towns of Somersham, Pidley cum Fenton, Colne, Earith, and Bluntisham, within the Soke of Somersham aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there is, within the said County, a certain Tract of Open Land, called Somersham Heath, containing 2,600 Acres, or thereabouts, and, it is supposed, the greatest Part of the said Heath lies within the Soke of Somersham aforesaid, but the Metes and Bounds thereof not being precisely known, the same cannot be properly ascertained, so as to be divided and fenced off from the other Part of the said Heath, and thereby prevent frequent Trespasses; and that the Petitioners, and the several other Owners of Common Right Houses within the Towns aforesaid, are entitled to the foie and exclusive Right of Common upon such Part of the said Heath as lies within the said Soke, and it would be of great Advantage to them, if the extent and Boundary thereof were ascertained and fixed, and proper Fences erected and made for dividing and separating the same from the other Part of the said Heath, so as to prevent such Trespasses as aforesaid for the future: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and fencing off such Part of the said Heath as lies within the Soke of Somersham aforesaid, from the other Part of the said Heath, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And thflt Mr. Duncombe, and Mr. Wilberforce, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are there- Honiton unto subscribed, Electors of Members to serve in Parlia- Election, ment for the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon, was read; Setting forth, That, at the last General Election of-Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Honiton, Sir George Yonge, Baronet,

Sir George Collier, and John Baily, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Colder, by themselves and Agents, were guilty of grols Bribery and Corruption, by giving and promising the Voters of the said Borough, Money, and other Rewards, for their Votes, and thereby corrupted and influenced the said Voters; that the said Sir George Colder, previous to the Election, deposited Money in the Hands of his Agents, for the purpose of Procuring Votes, and which was applied for that Purpose, by which Means he corrupted and influenced the Voters; and that the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Colder, and their Agents, after the Teste of the Writ, and before the Close of the Poll, treated the Voters with Meat and Drink, and thereby influenced their Voices; and, by the undue Influence, the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Collier had over the Returning Officer, many unqualified Persons were brought to vote, and whole Votes were actually received, notwithstanding Remonstrances to the contrary; and that, by such and other Means of undue Influence, the said Sir George Yonge and Sir George Collier procured themselves to be returned Members for the said Borough, although the said Mr.

Baily had a Majority of legal Votes, in direct Opposition to the Rights of Election, and the Injury of the Petitioners Rights and Franchises: And therefore praying the House, to take the Prerniles into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall teem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday, the 14th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

A Petition of Sir Godfrey Webster, Baronet, and Seaford Thonuxs Alves, Esquire, was read; Setting forth, That Election. an Election of Two Barons, to serve in this present Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, came on there the 29th Day of March, last, at which Election the Petitioners, Sir Peter Parker,

Baronet, Sir John Henderson, Baronet, the Right Honourable Henry Flood, and Lawrence Parsons, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the Petitioners were elected by a Majority of legal Voters, but that Joseph -smith, Esquire, who acted as Bailiff and Returning Officer at the said Election, in taking the Poll, was guilty of the grossest Partiality and Injustice towards the Petitioners, by arbitrarily rejecting the legal Votes of several Persons who offered to vote for the Petitioners, and by admitting other Persons to vote for the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson who had no legal Right to vote; and in many other re-(pects the said Joseph Gouldsmith was guilty of unwarrantable Practices, as w’ell previous to, as during, the said Election j and that several Persons who voted for the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson had previously asked, received, and taken, Money and other Reward, and had agreed or contracted for Money,

Gift, and Reward, to give their Votes in the said Election, and had been guilty of other illegal and corrupt Practices, by Means whereof their Votes, so given, are, and ought to be declared to be, void; and that the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, by themselves or Come Person or Persons employed by them, or one of them, did, by Gift or Reward, and by Promise, Agreement, or Security for Gift or Reward, corrupt and procure several Persons to give their Votes in the said Election, and, by the said and other undue Means, the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson were returned to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford, in Prejudice of the Petitioners (who were duly elected and ought to have been returned) in Prejudice of the legal Electors of the said Town and Port, and in open Defiance of the Law and Freedom of Elections: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief therein as shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

A Petition of Henry Flood, Esquire, and Lawrence Parsons, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, was also read; Setting forth, That on Tuesday the 29th Day of March lall, 1785, the Election of Two Barons to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port was held, and proceeded upon, by Joseph Gouldsmith, Esquire, the Acting Bailiff and Returning Officer of the Place, and, at the said Election, the Candidates were, Sir Peter Parker, Baronet, Sir John Henderson, Baronet, Sir Godfrey Webster, Baronet, Thomas Alves, Esquire, Henry Flood, Esquire, and Lawrence Parsons, Esquire; and that the said Joseph Gould-smith, in proceeding upon the said Election, acted with great Partiality in Favour of the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, and against the Interest of the Petitioners, by illegally receiving the Votes of Persons who had no Right to vote, and by rejecting the lawful Votes of others tendered on Behalf of the Petitioners, and, by so unjustly conducting the Election, to the Prejudice of the Petitioners, as to give a colourable and fraudulent Majority on the Poll to all the other Candidates against them, in Consequence whereof, he has returned the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson as duly elected; and that a great Majority of Persons, duly qualified to vote, tendered their Votes for the Petitioners, by whom the Petitioners conceive themselves to have been duly elected, and ought to have been returned, although the said Acting Bailiff

arbitrarily and illegally refused to receive such Votes in their Favour; and that, at and before the said Election, various Acts of Bribery, and other corrupt Practices, were committed by the said Sir Peter Parker, Sir John Henderson, Sir Godfrey Webster, and Thomas Alves,

Esquire, in order to procure themselves to be returned; and, on the said Election, many Persons were admitted who had no Right to vote, and many were rejected who had a Right to vote, and undue Influence and Corruption of various Kinds were practised, whereby the Petitioners were prevented from being returned, a3 they ought to have been: And therefore praying such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of David Evans and John Burnett, of Coal Trade. Orders, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Retail Shopkeepers in Sheffield, in the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Tax laid on any specific Article comes, in the first Instance, to the Trader, and forms Part of the Prime Cost of such Article, which the Consumer pays for when he purchases the fame; and the Shop Tax, being assessed according to the Rent of the House, is the fame, in Effect, with the House Tax, and all other Taxes collected by Pound Rate, which have not, in any Instance, been laid on the Consumer; and that the present Shop Tax cannot be considered in any other Point of View than an additional House Tax, the whole Burthen whereof is sustained only by the Retail Traders, and, the Petitioners therefore hope and trust (as the said Tax must be paid out of the Profits of their Trade, and as they are at present heavily burthened, and have at all Times readily contributed their Quota towards the Exigencies of the State) that the House will not consider them in such a State of Opulence as to be marked out the only Objects of a Tax to which no other Persons (not even the Merchants or Wholesale Dealers) are liable to contribute: And therefore praying the House to take their Cafes into Consideration, and to give them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of Thirsk, in the County of York, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are truly sensible of the baneful Effects of the Tax imposed upon Retail Shops; that the same is a partial and Oppressive Tax, pregnant with the greatest Mischiefs, and in an eminent Degree dangerous to the Interests of every Species of Retail Traders, and that, had the said Tax been laid upon any specific Article, or more, which comes in the first Instance to the Trader, makes a Part of his Prime Cost, and is paid by the Consumer upon purchasing the Commodity, it would have been lese personal, and of course a more impartial and equal Tax, but, being assessed by the Rent of the House, it is precisely the same in Operation with the House Tax, and all other Taxes collected by the Pound Rate, which never has in any one Instance been laid on the Consumer, so that the said Tax can be considered in no other Point of View than as an additional House Tax, the heavy Burthen of which no Persons are called upon to sustain but the Retail Traders, as if an Annihilation of them had been thereby intended; and, as the said Tax must be paid out of the small Profits of the Retail Traders, the Petitioners hope and trust, that the House, when they consider how readily the Retail'Traders have at all Times contributed their Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, and how heavily they are at present burthened with various other Taxes, will certainly not think them in such a State of Opulence as to mark them out the Objects of a Tax to which no Men of

independent Fortune, nor even a Merchant or Wholesale Trader, contributes a Farthing: And therefore praying, That the said Obnoxious Tax may be repealed, and that another, more equal and impartial, may be substituted in its Stead.

A Petition of the Retail Dealers of the Town of Shop Tax. Liverpool, whose Names are thereto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are convinced that the Exigencies of the State must be provided for, and are ready, at all Times, with the utmost Alacrity, to bear their Proportion of the common Burthen, according to their Abilities; and that the Petitioners have seen, with Regret, that the increased Taxation of this Country, has been chiefly levelled at Trade, but they are more particularly alarmed and aggrieved by an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain, for by that oppressive Tax (while the Petitioners are contributing chearfully in common with their Fellow Subjects to the usual public Burthens) they find themselves selected from the common Mass of the Community, as Objects of a most unjust and enormous Tax, to which the extensive Manufacturer, the wholesale Warehouseman, the opulent Merchant, and People of Fortune of every Description, do not contribute a tingle Shilling; and that the Idea of the Tax in Question ultimately falling upon the Public, appears to the Petitioners futile and illusive, it being a known Fast, that there are, in every Town in the Kingdom, Men of bad Principles and desperate Fortunes (besides Itinerants) who, regardless of paying their Credit, undersell the fair Trader, and to these any Advance on the established Price of Goods would be an Advantage, and accelerate the Ruin of the honest Dealer; and that the Bulk of the Petitioners are obliged, from the Nature of their Employments, to crowd into public Situations, where the Rents are excessive, and their Habitations confined, inconvenient, and unhealthy, their Stocks in Trade chiefly upon Credit to pay at a certain Date, and mostly fold upon Credit, the Payment uncertain, and subject to innumerable Disappointments and Misfortunes, their Attention divided by humouring the public Taste, for a precarious Subsistence, by Provision for the stated Returns of Rent and Taxation, and the periodical Arrival of their untaxed wholesale Tradesmen; and that the Petitioners rely upon the Wisdom of Parliament, for a repeal of the said partial, oppressive, and impolitic Tax; partial, because laid upon a particular Description of People already over-burthened; oppressive, because Numbers must inevitably fink under its Weight; and impolitic, because it has an evident Tendency to crowd our Poor Houses, swell the Lists of Bankruptcies, and increase the Number of miserable Debtors, already too numerous in every Gaol throughout Great Britain:

And therefore the Petitioners hope, that the Premises may be considered, and such Relief granted as the House think belt.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers resident in the vTown of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, well knotting that the Exigencies of the State must and ought to be provided for, are ever ready most cheerfully to contribute their Proportions, with the Public at large, towards such Provision, but canfiot help feeling themselves greatly affected by an Act, passed last Session, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties oft Shops within Great Britain; and that the Petitioners, from the Nature of their Employments, are anxious to procure Houses and Shops in the most public Situations, consequently their Rents are heavy, and the House and other Taxes proportionably great and burthensome upon them; and, they submit to the House, that the Tax on Shops is partial and oppreffive, because no other Persons but the Retail Shopkeepers are called upon to bear any Part thereof, and because it is impossible that they can, in any Instanee whatever, with Justice, charge the same upon the Commodities which they fell in the Course of Trade, and such Tax, being assessed according to the Rents of Houses, must inevitably be considered as an additional House Tax Upon them, the Burthen of which will be felt by no other Description of People; and that, as the Petitioners are already heavily burthened with other Taxes, to which they have most willingly contributed their Proportion, and as the Shop Tax must be wholly paid out of the Profits accruing to the Retail Traders, the Petitioners trufr, with Confidence, that the House will not consider such Traders as Objects of a Tax to which no others, of whatever State or Degree, will at all contribute: And therefore praying, That the said Act may be repealed, or that they may be otherwise relieved in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of several Shopkeepers and other Inhabitants of the Tow n and County of Southampton, who are aftefted by the Operation of the present Shop Tax, and whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was also pre-lented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Generality of the Petitioners are under the Necessity of occupying large Houses, at heavy Rents, for the Purpose of carrying on their Trades; from which Circumstance, and the severe Pressure of the new Shop Tax, they are compelled to, contribute to the Public Revenue in a greater Proportion, and in a more Extraordinary Manner, than the rest of their Fellow Citizens; and that the Accumulation of the excessive high Duties which aftefted the Petitioners during the Continuance, and since the Conclufton, of the late War, in respect of their Houses and Household Offices, and the various Articles necessarily expended therein, together with the frequent Losses occasioned by the Multitude of Debts unavoidably contrafted in the Course of every Retail Trade, have produced such Effects as have unfortunately tended to the Distress ’of feme of the Petitioners, and to the Impoverishment of others; and, they conceive, that if railing the Amount of the Shop Tax upon the Consumer was a practicable Measure, it would be inconsistent with the Maxims of found Policy, and be productive of very injurious Consequences to the Public, as the Price of almost -every Necefl'ary of Life fold in a Retail Way would be increased thereby; and that, by the Industry of the Retail Shopkeepers, in the quick Disposal of their Goods, and the Application exerted by them in the Search and Discovery of new Channels for Consumption, the Commerce and Manufactories of this Kingdom are constantly encouraged and supported, and Navigation, so essential to its Welfare, promoted and assisted: In this Point of View the Petitioners flatter themselves, they will appear to the Legislature as very useful Members of the Community, and entitled to the same Privileges and Indulgences as

any other of His Majesty’s Subjects; and, when the Petitioners reflect, that, besides suffering the Grievances before stated, many of them pay a heavy Duty to the Crown for a Licence barely to exercise their Trades, and that they are called to new Hardships by the late Acts of Parliament transferring certain Taxes, which were under the Management of the Commissioners of the Ex-cife and Stamp Office, to the Commissioners of the Land Tax, whereby the Petitioners are subjected to the Execution of Offices of the most disagreeable Nature, filled only by Excisemen before that Period, and when they also reflect, that Five Eighth Parts of the Services created by those Officers are actually discharged by Retail Shopkeepers, and Persons comprized under that Description, to the great loss of their Time, and the Disquietude of themselves, their Friends and Neighbours, they trust their Situation with respect to the above-mentioned Tax, which is felt by the Petitioners as a double House Tax in its full Extent, will receive from the Legislature every Assistance and Alleviation that can possibly be afforded to it: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation, and to grant them such Relief as shall appear most effectual to redress the Grievances before let forth.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of Bristol was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the last Session of Parliament, an Act was passed, im poling a Tax on all Retail Shopkeepers in Aid of the Public Exigencies of the State, and, as Individuals, the Petitioners consider the said Tax as partial and oppressive, and consequently repugnant to that Justice to which, as Subjects in a free Country, they claim an undoubted Right; that our Ancestors, guided by the Wisdom and Spirit of our Laws, the true Palladium of our Liberties, have hitherto guarded us from Oppression, and, the Petitioners conceive, that no Tax ought to be imposed by the Legislature which is not founded in Justice, and shall not, in its Operation, be as equitab'e as the Nature of Circumstances will admit; and that the Advocates for the said Tax will recollect, that it operates precisely with the House and all other Taxes collected by Pound Rate, and the Petitioners believe it hath never been the Custom of any Tradesman in this Kingdom to lay an Advance on the Article he fells in Consequence of tiich an Impost; and that the Petitioners need not point out how far the Retail Traders have lately been subjected to more than a proportionable Share of* the Public Burthens, and are clearly and decidedly of Opinion, that the said Tax is, in its EiFefts, highly partial and oppressive, and therefore trull the House will grant them such Redress as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That Leave may be given to bring ia a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Memorandum. — By the Act passed in the Year 1781, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East " Indies, &c." the East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in Proportion to the Number of Troops sent, or to be sent, to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in The East Indies only; and, as it will be necessary to provide for the Subsistence of the Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present, for this Purpose, the Sum of Eight thousand Two hundred and Thirty Pounds Eight Shillings' Seven Pence and One Farthing, which it will be necessary to vote on Account for the above Estimate.

upon the Bill for confining, for a Time to be limited, the Trade between the Ports of the United States of America, and His Majesty’s Subjects in the Island of Newfoundland, to Bread, Flour, Indian Corn, and Live Stock, to be imported in none but British-built Ships, actually belonging to British Subjects, and navigated according to Law, clearing out from the Ports of His Majesty’s European Dominions, and furnished with a Licence according to the Form thereunto annexed;

Ordered, That the Account of the Number of Vessels which have cleared out from the several Ports of Great Britain, fornished with Licences to import Bread, Flour, or Live Stock, from any Place or Country belonging to the United States of,

into any Poit, Harbour, or Place, in the Island of Newfoundland, or the adjacent Islands to His Majesty belonging pursuant to the Provisions of the Act of the last Session of Parliament, Chapter iff, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of Bread, Flour, and Live Stock, imported into the several Ports of the Island of Newfoundland, between the 10th of October 1784 and the 10th of October 1785, distinguishing the said Ports, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Gilbert accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Shop<Tax. A Petition of the Retail Dealers of the Town of Preston, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are fully convinced the Exigency of the State mutt be provided for, and are ready at all Times, with the utmost Alacrity, to bear their Proportion of the common Burthen according to their Abilities, but feel themselves particularly alarmed and aggrieved by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain, for by that oppressive Tax (while the Petitioners are contributing chearfully, in common with their Fellow Subjects, to the usual Public Burthens) they find themselves selected from the common Mass of the Community, as ObjeCis of a most unjust and enormous Tax, to which the extensive Manufacturer, the Wholesale Warehouseman, the opulent Merchant, and People of Fortune of every Description, do not contribute a Angle Shilling; and that the Idea of the Tax in Question ultimately falling upon the Public, appears to the Petitioners vague and iliulive; and, they trust, it mult appear in the same Light to every candid Mind: That the Petitioners speak from Experience, but those who are Advocates for the Tax speak luperficially, and are Strangers to the Difficulties that the Retail Shopkeeper is exposed to; they consider not the Necessity he is under to fell his various Articles at as low a Rate as others in the same Line of Business, his very Subsistence depends upon this; they do not know, that the least Attempt to raise the Price of his Goods would drive his Cuf-tomers from his Shop: In every Branch of Business there are some whose Circumstances and Situations are better than others; those with such Advantages on their Side might take the Opportunity of keeping

their Goods at the same Price, till such Time as they saw those less opulent Traders reduced, distressed, and perhaps ruined for ever: And therefore relying upon the Wisdom of Parliament for a Repeal of the said partial and oppressive Tax.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Dunflabl* thereunto subscribed, Trustees of the Turnpike Road Roac1, leading from the The Black Bull Inn, in Dunstable, in the County of Bedford, to the Way turning out of the said Road up to Shafford House, in the County of Hertford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by Three Acts, passed in the Ninth Year of King George the First, the Tenth Year of King George the Second, and the Third Year of His present Majesty, certain Tolls and Powers are given to the Petitioners, for the Purpose of repairing and widening the said Road; and that the Petitioners have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money on the Credit of such Tolls, which is still due; and although the Whole of the Money borrowed, together with the Tolls, have been duly laid out, according to the Directions of the said Acts, yet some Parts of the said Roads still require widening, making, and repairing, and the same cannot be effectually completed, nor the Money due be repaid, unless the Terms and Powers granted by the said Acts are continued, altered, and enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to continue the Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers, of the above-mentioned Acts of Parliament; in such Manner, and under such Restrictions and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Grimston, Mr. Plume}', &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.
