Sir Joseph Mawbey reported from the Committee, Coal Trade, to whom the Petition of David Evans and John Burnett, of Lambeth, in the County of Surrey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Edward Stone being examined, laid, That he has been Principal Clerk in the Coal Meters Office for Westminster near 22 Years — That he is very certain, from the Experience he has had, that the Regulations provided by the different Acts of Parliament for establishing and regulating the Coal Meters Offices for London and Westminster, and the Parts adjacent, have been the Means of detecting and preventing numberless Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, to the great Advantage of the Con-fuiners.

That

26 Geo. III. 30 Februarii 17-3

That various Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, in the several Parishes of the County of Surrey, situate on the South Side of the River Thames, between the Parish of Putney inclusive, and Cuckold's Point, in the said County, have been frequently committed, to the great Injury of the Con-fumers thereof, several of which have been detested' by a Re-measurement, during the Course of the lad Year; one of which was of Coals delivered in Norfolk Street, for 39 Sacks, which really measured only 34, and another of which was a Quantity sent into Grosvenor Square, for 75 Sacks, and which really measured only 65!.

That he apprehends it would be of great Utility to the Inhabitants of the different Parishes aforesaid, and to the Consumers of Coals, and be a Means to detest and prevent the Frauds and Abuses which now exill in the Admeasurement of Coals therein, if proper Regulations and Orders were to be established by Law for the Admeasurement of Coals within the District aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals sold by Wharf Measur, within the several Parishes lying between Putney and Rotherhithe, both inclusive, in the County of Surrey: And that Sir Joseph

Mawbey and Mr. Norton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers in the Town of Shop Tax Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, whole Names are thereunto lubscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act, passed in the Twenty-fifth year of the Reign of His present' Majesty, a Tax was imposed upon all Retail Shops within Great Britain (except as therein mentioned) to be paid by the Inhabitants or Occupiers thereof, by a Pound Rate, according to the Rent of their Dwelling Houses; and that, owing to the Nature of Retail Trade, such Dwelling Houses and Shops are necessarily situated in the most public Situations, consequendy the Rents are considerably higher, in Proportion to their Size and Conveniencies, than those of others who are wholly exempt from the said Tax, and of Course the Retail Traders already contribute to the House Tax in a greater Degree than any other of His Majesty’s Subjects, and, the Petitioners conceive

Shop Tax.

176 6° Februarii: . 1786.

that the Shop Tax can be considered in no other Point of View than an additional IJoufe Tax, the Burthen of which no Persons are called upon to sustain but the Retail Traders, and mult therefore be deemed partial, and particularly oppressive upon the Petitioners, many of whom, are already charged with Payments for Annual Licences to carry on their several Trades; and that a Tax laid' upon any specific Article comes, in the first Instance, to the Trader, forms a Part of his Prime Cost, and the Conlumer pays it when he purchases the Commodity, but this partial and oppressive Tax being assessed according to the Rent of the House, is precisely the same in Operation with the House Tax, and all other Taxes collected by Pound Rate, which never has, in any one Instance, been laid on the Consumer; and that, as the Tax must be paid out of the Profits of the Retail Trader, the Petitioners hope and trust, the House, when it is considered how readily the Retail Traders have at all Times contributed their Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, and how heavily they are at present burthened, will not consider them in that State of Opulence as to be marked out the Objects of a Tax, to which no Men of independent Fortune, nor even a Merchant, Manufacturer, or Wholesale Trader, will contribute in the smallest Degree: And therefore praying, That the Act for granting a Duty on Retail Shops may be repealed.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the County of Middlesex, adjacent to the City of London, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, alarmed at the Burthens with which they are threatened by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain, are desirous of throwing themselves upon the Justice of the House, to deprecate the impending Mischiefs, and beg leave to impress upon the House, that the said Tax was justified on the Ground of its falling upon the Consumer, but the Petitioners, from the most candid Consideration, are fully authorized to declare, that neither the House Tax, nor any other Tax collected by the Pound Rate, ever has been, nor that this Tax never can be, laid on the Consumer; and, therefore being compelled to pay this Tax out of their Profits, beg the House to take into their Consideration the very great Hardships the Retail Traders have already to encounter; they are under the Necessity of seeking public Situations to carry on their Trade, where they arc obliged to pay enormous Rents, and though this is a Grievance of no ftnall Magnitude, yet *it is considerably increased by the High 'Faxes they have to pay upon those Rents; and the Petitioners request also to observe, that though they pay out of their Proportion to all Taxes heretofore calculated upon the Rent, yet they had the Satisfaction to feel they were not singled out, but that every Person bore some Part of the Burthen; and that the Petitioners feel themselves deeply concerned by this Tax, which cannot be considered in any other Light than a new House Tax, the Severity whereof Retail Traders are alone called upon to sustain, and beg Leave further to ltate, that there are many Persons keeping Retail Shops, by which they maintain Families with Decency and Credit, yet their Expences are so extremely heavy, it becomes necessary for the Parish Officers to excule them their Rates, but the Collectors of Parliamentary Taxes being actuated by different Motives from the Collectors of Parochial, will insist on being paid, therefore, should the Shop Tax be enforced, many industrious People will probably be ruined, and their Families become chargeable to the Parish; and that the Petitioners are at all Times ready to contribute their Proportion, when the Exigencies of the State require it, but they hope and trust the House will fee great Occasion to commife-

rate their present Burthens, and will take the same of the Retail Traders into Consideration, and grant them Redrels, by repealing an Act which threatens so much Oppression upon an industrious and useful Part of the Community, who strive hard to maintain their Families with Credit and Reputation.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the Bo- shop Tax. rough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Retail Shopkeepers are a necessary and industrious Class of People, promoting the several Manufactures of this Kingdom, and, by residing chiefly in Market Towns, and occupying Houses of large Rents, contribute more largely towards the Public Taxes than others of a like or even of superior Fortunes, and, by giving long Credit, they are more particularly liable to great Losses in Trade; and that from the General Decline of almost every Manufacture, and the Want of Employment for the lower Class of People, the Trade of many Retailers, very much dependent on that Clals, is so reduced as scarcely to afford, and in too many Instances do not afford, a competent Maintenance for their Families, and many Retailers have lately had Licences imposed on them, some paying for Three or Four Licences each, which, being of the Nature of a Personal Tax, must rest solely upon them.

Under these, and sundry other Disadvantages, the Petitioners feel themselves particularly aggrieved by a new Tax laid on them in the last Session of Parliament, whereby Retail Shopkeepers are selected, in a Angular and peculiar Manner, from the Community at large, as separate Objects of Taxation, w’hich could not arise, as the Petitioners conceive, from any Intention in the House of oppressing them, but from a Notion that the Tax would be eventually diffused and borne among their Customers; were that the Cafe, the Petitioners would be Gainers by the Tax, because a small Advance on their Goods would more than reimburse them; but they are convinced that this Notion is founded in Mistake, and ample Experience has shewn that no Personal Tax whatever (and the Shop Tax is of that Sort) has been found to affect any but those on w hom it has been laid. Sensible of the Necessity of Taxes, the Petitioners shall always most chearfully contribute, in Proportion to their Circumstances, but when more is required of them, they conceive it a Duty owing to themselves, to represent their Grievances to the Guardians of their Rights and Property as they now without the least intention of Fraud or Partiality, praying such Relief in the Premises as to the House may appear to be effectual and necessary.

A Petition of the Retail Dealers, Inhabitants of the Ditto. City and Liberty of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, that the Petitioners are dif-pol’ed chearfully to sustain their equal Share of the common Burthen, and to contribute their Proportion to the Maintenance of that Government by which they are protected, and they feel this Disposition the more ardently from the Know ledge that they have the Happiness to live under a Constitution, one of the original and declared Principles of which is, That no one Description of Citizens shall be taxed oppressively; and that, notwithstanding this explicit and glorious Maxim, the Petitioners have the Misfortune to find that, by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain, a very heavy, partial, and oppressive Burthen is laid exclusively upon the Retail Dealers of Great Britain, which, from its Inequality, they consider as a Grievance injurious to their known Rights as Englishmen, and which, in its Operation, must ultimately tend to the Ruin of Numbers, and more particularly of the Shopkeepers of the City and Liberty of Westminster; and that the Petitioners are

A PETITION of the Retail Dealers, Inhabitants of the City of Durham, and Suburbs thereof, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, ever disposed cheerfully to contribute their due Proportion to the Maintenance and Support of that Govern-ipent and Constitution under which they deem it an Happiness to be protested, cannot avoid representing with Concern their Disapprobation of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain, as partial, inequitable, and unjust; and that the Petitioners, having candidly and maturely considered the Operation and Tendency of the said Act, in every Point of View, conceive it to be, to all Intents and Purposes, imposing an additional House Tax on the Retail Traders of Great Britain, which will not be felt by the Merchant and Wholesale Dealer, or Opulent of any other Description, the supposed Idea, that the Load of this Tax will fall On the Consumer of Goods sold by Retail, being impracticable, from its not being laid on any specific Article, and, from the Inequality of its Operation, and a Variety of other Causes, the Petitioners represent it to the House as an oppressive and intolerable Burthen, and which will inevitably fall on the poor and industrious Shopkeepers, many of whom are bending under the Pressure of the numerous Imposts which have already been laid on them; and that, notwithstanding the Petitioners already contribute so large a Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, they beg Leave to re-assure the House, that they will, at all Times, to the utmost of their of Abilities, cheerfully pay every Duty laid on them in common with their Fellow Subjects, and, that their Resistance to the said Act arises entirely from a Conviction of its Partiality and Inequality: And therefore praying the House to take the said Act into Consideration, and, by a Repeal of the fame, or by such other Measure as to the House shall teem expedient, relieve the Petitioners from the ruinous Oppression I'uftained thereby.

A Petition of the Several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Retail Shopkeepers in the City of York, as well on Behalf of themselves as the other

Shopkeepers resident in that City and the Suburbs thereof, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and all the Retail Shopkeepers throughout the Kingdom, are by no Means in a State of Opulence to be marked out by the Legislature as the foie Objects of a Taxation, burthensome from its Amount, and in the highest Degree partial, from which the most wealthy and independent Part of the Community are wholly exempt; and that the Tax on Retail Shops, imposed in the last Session of Parliament, has in every Rel'pect the Effect of such a Taxation as the Man of Wealth, who lives without Business, and even the opulent Merchant and

Wholesale Dealer, are not in the least Degree chargeable, with; and that the Petitioners cannot transfer the Burthen of the Shop Tax on the Consumer of the Commodity, as alledged by its Advocates (w-hich may be the same when a Tax is laid on any Article of Trade) and by that Means render it general, but must bear the whole Burthen of it personally, as an additional House Tax:

Wherefore, as the Petitioners have at all Times cheerfully paid their Quota to the Exigencies of the State, and are ever willing to bear their proportional Part of any necessary Burthen which may be laid on the whole Community, to the Extent of their Abilities, they pray the House will take this Petition under their most serious Consideration, and repeal an Act so universally obnoxious and oppressive to every] Description of Retail Tradesmen.

A Petition of the Retail Traders of the Borough of Shop Tax. Chipping JVycomb, in the County of Bucks, was like-wife presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners understand, the only Ground upon which the Tax on Retail Shops is justified, is, that the Retailers will raise it on the Consumer; but the Petitioners cannot avoid considering that as an Impofiibility, for, if they thought otherwise, they should expect much Advantage, as it would in that same be unavoidably raised beyond Proportion to their Payment, and, they conceive, no Set of Men would petition to have a Source of Profit taken from them; and that the Petitioners feel the many Objections that lie against granting a Petition to repeal a Tax, and likewise know the Necessities of Government are great, and would with the utmost Cheerfulness contribute to One more general in its Operation: And therefore they hope that the House will relieve them from the said Tax, as they, cannot help copfidering it as personal, and of course partial and oppressive. s

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Borough of Yarmouth, in the Isle of Wight, in the County of Southampton, in Common Hall assembled;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners labour under a great Grievance, from an Act -passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, "An Act for " preventing Frauds and regulating Abuses " in His Majesty’s Customs," and other Laws now in force, by which no Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, can be thipped, or put on Board to be carried forth to the open Sea, from any Port, Creek, or Member in Great Britain, to be landed at any other Port or Place of this Realm, without a Sufferance or Warrant from the Officers of the Customs, a Cocket taken out for such Goods, and a Bond entered into to His Majesty for the due Delivery and Discharge of the same — an Act which not only operates as an excessive Restriction on the Trade of the said Island, but as a manifest Prejudice to the Petitioners, from the very great Expence they are subject to in performing the said Requisites; and that, by an Act passed so the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, a partial Relief was obtained by the County of Southampton, by a Repeal of so much of the said Act as to admit the Transportation of all Goods and Merchandize to the Isle of Wight which were not prohibited to be exported, or liable to Duties on Exportation, while the said Island remained under all the Restrictions of the former Act; and repre-fenting to the House, That the Petitioners are more particularly affected and oppressed by the Prohibition the said Act of the Fourteenth of Charles the Second imposes on their Trade from their insular Situation than other Parts of the Kingdom of Great Britain-, that they cannot export from the said Island to any other Yol. 41.

Part of the said County of Southampton any Goods (particularly Com and Cattle, the fta-ple Commodities thereof) without incurring a very considerable Expence, and, in frequent Instances, the mere Value of the Goods so exported bearing no Proportion to the Charges attending the fame: And therefore praying,

That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and afford them such Relief as the House shall deem fit

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

returned lor the said Borough: And therefore1 praying.

That he may be heard by Counsel, against the said Election and Return, and may be relieved in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Shop Tax. A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers resident in the City of Carlisle, in the County of Cumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, burthened as they are with the Duty imposed on Retail Shops, beg Leave to seek that Redress from Parliament which, they conceive, the Justice and Equity of their same require, and, as the Ground of their Application, to date to the House, that the Oppression of the (hid Tax is grievously felt by them, and that, from Experience and Observation, it operates immediately upon them as an additional House Duty, without a Possibility of reimbursing themselves by a Charge upon any of the Articles they vend: The Petitioners therefore, sensible as they are, that the Legislature meant not to tax any Sort of Men without having an Eye to Equality in its Consequences, presume to a(k and hope. That the House will take their same into serious Consideration, and afford them the fought-for Redreis, by a Repeal of that Law' which bears so partially hard upon a Description of Men whole Inclinations are forward to support the Exigencies of Government, in common with the rest of their Fellow Subjects, to the ntmost of their Power.

Ditto. A Petition of the Shopkeepers and Retail Traders of the Borough of Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Tax, laid in the last Session of Parliament, on Retail Shops, has been found in the highest Degree partial and oppressive, the whole Weight of it being borne by one distin£t and particular Clafe of Men, and the said Tax, being assessed according to the Rent of the House, does not fall, even upon the Persons who are the Objects of it, with Equality, and in Proportion to the Property, Income, and Advantages in Trade, of each Individual; and that the only Argument which has been adduced in Support Vol. 41.

of the said Tax, " That it must ultimately fall on the " Consumer," is ill founded and erroneous, as it can be considered in no other Point of View than an additional House Tax on Retail Traders, and must be, as all other Personal Taxes have been, paid by them alone: And the Petitioners, therefore, relying on the Justice of the House, hope that their same will be taken into Consideration, and such Relief granted, as to the House may seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers and Retail Traders of the City of Worcester, and the Environs thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That they feel themselves particularly aggrieved and burthened by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britain; and that the Petitioners have ever, with great Willingness, paid all Taxes impartially imposed on them

Vox,. 41.

in common with their Fellow Citizens, and, being conscious of the Necessity of heavy Taxes, for the Support of the Honour, and to supply the Exigencies of the State, they even now with Reluctance complain of the said Tax, to which they are chiefly impelled by the Duty they owe to themselves and their numerous Families, and will be ready most chearfully to contribute, with their Fellow Citizens, to any Tax which Parliament may devise as a Substitute for the said Tax upon Shops, and which shall be so formed as to diffuse itself more uni-verfally and indiscriminately amongst His Majesty’s Subjects in general; and that it is impossible for the Petitioners, by any Means whatever, to advance the Prices of their Goods, so that the Consumer may participate with them in the Burthen of the said Tax, and therefore the Petitioners, and the Shopkeepers and Retail Traders of this Kingdom, have thought themselves justified interming it a partial, unequal, and oppressive Tax, and consequently a Tax repugnant to the true Principles of the Constitution, and contrary to the wonted and known Wisdom and Justice of Parliament: And therefore beleeching the House to take their same most feriouly into Consideration, and to redress the Grievance complained of, by a Repeal of the said Act.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the Borough Shop Tax. of Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, was also presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have always manifested their ready Acquiescence with every Requisition which the Exigencies of the State have rendered necessary to be laid upon them in common with the rest of their Fellow Subjects, and are fully satisfied, that the particular Tax laid upon Retail Shopkeepers, in Distinction from all other Ranks and Classes of People in the British Empire, is partial and oppressive; and that they are also perfectly satisfied of the imprafticability of obtaining the least Relief from the particular Burthen of the said Tax any other Way than by a total Repeal thereof, without which it roust inevitably prove ruinous to many honest industrious Individuals: And therefore beseeching the House, That the said Tax may be repealed.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers and others, Inhabitants Ditt0-of the City of Coventry, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Tax on Retail Shopkeepers will operate, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, as a partial and additional House Tax, and prove extremely oppressive to a Class of Persons at present labouring under the Weight of the late Taxes on Houses and Windows, to which, as Shopkeepers, they contribute in greater Proportions than any other of His Majesty’s Subjects; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to assure the House, that the Tax on Retail Shops must be paid out of the Profits of the Retail Trader, and cannot be laid on the Consumer: And they therefore hope and trust, That, when the House considers how chearfully the Retail Traders have hitherto contributed to the Exigencies of the State, and how heavily those of the City of Coventry in particular are at present burthened (being actually chargeable with Parochial and other Taxes to the Amount of Seventeen Shillings and upwards in the Pound Rent) the House will not add to their Grievances, by marking out the Retail Shopkeepers as Objects of a Tax which must fall upon them only, but, taking the Premises into its serious Consideration, will either repeal the said Tax, or grant to the Petitioners such other Redreis as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers in the City of Chester, Ditto, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was likewise presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have hitherto contributed their Proportion to the Public Revenue, and still are willing so to do, in common with the rest of His Majesty’s Subjects,

Mr. North reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Warden and Assistants incorporated for the Preservation of the Harbour of Dover, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of thena-selves and the rest of the said Assistants, was referred; That the Committee bad examined the Matter of the said Petition; and bad directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Plane; and afterwards delivered it m at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Latham, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Harbour of Dover is, from its Situation, of great public Utility, and that the maintaining and supporting the said Harbour is an Object of great Importance to this Country.

And it appeared to Your Committee, by several Acts of Parliament, that certain Tonnage Duties have been from Time to Time granted towards defraying the Expence of maintaining and supporting the said Harbour, which Acts will expire on the 12th Day of May next; and the Witness said, there is no other Fund for maintaining and supporting the said Harbour, except certain Estates, called the Old Revenues, Part whereof, to the Amount of about 609/. per Annum, is applicable to repairing and supporting the said Harbour, which Sum is by no Means adequate to defray the necessary Expence thereof.

And the Witness added, That unless the said Duties are further continued, or some other Provision made for maintaining and supporting the said Harbour and Works, the same must very soon fall into total Decay.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term of several Acts of Parliament, for the Repair of Dover Harbour: And that Mr. North, Mr. Marsham, and Mr. Charles Robinson, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, a List of the Captaios on the Tea and Eight Shilling Lift of the Half Pay of the Navy.

Setting forth, That by an Act, made in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of King George the Second, intituled,

" An Act for annexing certain forfeited Estates in Scotland to the Crown unalienably, and for making Satisfaction to the lawful Creditors thereupon, and to " estabfifti a Method of managing the fame, and applying the Rents and Profits thereof for the better civilizing and improving the Highlands of Scotland, and " preventing Disorders there for the future,’’ all and every the Lands and Estates which were then in the Hands of his Majesty, by the Attainder of Simon late Lord Looat, and certain other Persons therein named, were declared to be unalienably annexed to the Imperial Crown of these Realms, and, it was declared lawful for his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, by Commission under the Privy Seal of Scotland, to authorize Commissioners and Trustees for managing the said Estates, and applying the Produce thereof; and that his said late Majesty and His present Majesty did, in pursuance of the said Act, from Time to Time, by Commissions under the Privy Seal of Scotland, authorize the Persons therein severally named as Commissioners and Trustees, to manage the said Estates, and apply the Produce thereof, and, the said Commissioners did, among other Things, in Execution of the Trust, estabhfti Schools in different Places in the remote Parts of the Highlands of Scotland, and grant Annual Salaries to the Persons appointed Teachers in the said Schools, payable (irom the Rents and Produce of the said forfeited Estates; and that by an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of His present Majesty 8 Reign, intituled, "An Act to enable His Majesty to grant unto Major General Simon Fraser, the " Lands and Estate of the late Simon Lord Looat,

that it appeared to the Society, that certain of the said Schools, the Salaries of the Teachers whereof amounted to the Yearly Sum of 113/. might be discontinued immediately; that certain other of the said Schools might be- discontinued after the Deaths of the present Teachers, whose Salaries amounted to the Annual Sum of 48/. and who would be reduced to Beggary, if deprived of their Salaries; Yearly, during the Lives of the present

Teachers, and to continue the Schools mentioned in the said Memorial, and above, as proper to be continued, and pay the Salaries of the Teachers thereof in Time coming, according to the Regulations of the Society; and that the Petitioners conceive the said Proposal to be reasonable and beneficial to the Public, and that they merit Encouragement for their Endeavours to promote Virtue, Loyalty, and Industry, in the Inhabitants of the Highlands: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for authorizing the Lord Chief Baron and Remanent Barons of the Court of Exchequer in Scotland, out of the unappropriated Money arising from the forfeited and lately annexed Estates in Scotland, to pay a certain Sum to the Society in Scotland for propagating Christian Knowledge, for the Purpose of enabling them to pay Salaries to the Teachers of the said Schools, according to the Distinctions above mentioned, and to continue such of the said Schools as are intended to be continued, under such Conditions as shall be thought necessary.

A PETITION of the Bailiffs and Burgesses of the Borough of Clithero, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, whole Common Seal is thereunto affixed, and of Thomas Lister, Esquire, Penn Assheton Esquire, and divers other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of divers Messuages, Burgages, Lands, and Tenements, situate within the Borough or Township of Clitheroe aforesaid, intitled to Right of Common upon the Commons and Waste Grounds within the same Borough or Township, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Borough or Township, divers Parcels of Commons and Waste Grounds, amounting by Estimation to 350 Acres, or thereabouts, which now lie waste and uncultivated, and are, in their prefect Situation, Vjoju.4L

incapable of Improvement, but, if the same were divided, inclosed, and held in Severalty, would be of great Advantage to that Part of the Country in general, and to the Petitioners in particular, as a great Part thereof may be converted into Plowing and Meadow Ground: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in, a Bill, to have the said Commons and Waste Grounds, in Clitheroaforesaid, divided, allotted, and inclosed, by Commissioners, in such Bill to be named, unto and amongst the Petitioners, and the rell of the Proprietors of Messuages, Burgages, Lands, and Tenements, in Clithero aforesaid, that have Right of Common thereon, in Proportion to their Estates, Rights, and Interests therein.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers of the Town of Alton, Sh°P T®* in the County of Southampton, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have always readily contributed their just Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, and are sorry to have Occasion to complain against aqy Tax which the Legislature has judged it expedient to impose on them; but they beg Leave to represent to the House, that the Tax on Retail Shops, passed during the last Session of Parliament, is most partial, oppressive, and discouraging to Trade — partial, as it does not afieft the Man of independent Fortune, the Merchant, or the Wholesale Trader, who are all more proper Objects of Taxation than the Retail Shopkeeper, whose Returns are small, and his Profits greatly diminHhed by frequent and unavoidable bad Debts — oppressive and discouraging, as most of the Petitioners already pay heavy Duties for Licences to exercise their Trades, and they can, from Experience, confidently affect, that it is impracticable for the Shopkeeper to lay this Tax on his Customers, upon which Ground alone the Advocates for the Tax have attempted to justify k; it can therefore be considered only as a very heavy additional House Tax, the Burthen of which falls on the Retail Trader alone, who is least able to sustain

aoo

13* Februarii. 178

it, being already sinking under the Weight of accumulated Irapofts, which he, however, chearfully labours to pay, when levied on him equally with the rest of his Fellow Subjects: And therefore praying the House to repeal the Tax on lletail Shops, and to substitute, in lieu thereof, one that is more equal and impartial, as they shall judge proper.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, Members to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require summoned, the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Twenty*four Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents for the Petitioners, and the Honiton Counsel and Agents for the said Sir George Yonge, Election. Baronet, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Sir George Collier, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Counsel for the said Sitting Members respedkivdy informed the House, that they were different Parties, and that their Canvas at the Election had been separate; that they had had no Communication in preparing their Defence; and that the said Sitting Members, with respect to this Cause, were perfect Strangers to each other; and that, upon the whole, the Interests of the Sitting Members being distinct and separate from each other, they therefore desired to separate in their Defence; to which no Objection being made by the Counsel for the Petitioners, the

Liverpool A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Streets &c. Common Council of the Town of Liverpool, in Com Vo l. 41.

mon Council assembled, and of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Traders, and others, residing in the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That several of the public Streets, Passages, and Places, within the said Town, are narrow and incommodious, and occasion great Inconvenience and Danger to the Owners and Inhabitants of Houses in and near those Streets, and to Persons and Carriages passing through the fame, and prove a great Prejudice and Hindrance to the Dispatch of Trade and Commerce carried on in the said Town; and that the said Inconveniences and Danger might be very much remedied, and the Ease, Safety, and Convenience of the Inhabitants of the said Town, and of all Persons resorting thereto, greatly secured, if Power was given to widen, enlarge, and alter the said narrow Streets,

Passages, and Places, and to open and lay out new Streets and Passages, and for those Purposes to purchase the several Houses, Buildings, Lands, and Premises, which may, from Time to Time, be deemed necessary; and that the present Mode of supplying the Inhabitants of the said Town with fresh W'ater, by Water Carts, is attended with considerable Inconvenience, which might be remedied if Power W'as given to dig for, and collect Springs within or near to the Liberties of the said Town, and to convey the Water by Pipes or Aque-dufts, into the several Streets and Passages of the Town, for the Use of the Inhabitants, and, such Mode of conveying Water into the said Town would alfe be particularly useful in the extinguishing of Fires which might happen to Buildings or Shipping in the Paid Town; and that it would also tend greatly to the Convenience and Accommodation of the Inhabitants of the said Towm, if Power was given to remove, and prevent in future, all Nuisances in or near the Streets, Passages, and other Places in the said Town, as also to aiter the Levels of several of such Streets, Passages, and Places, and to alter and amend the present and make new- Common Sewers, and to appropriate particular Places in the said Town to the Purpose of additional public Markets, and also if the several Clauses and Powers contained in an Act, passed in the Second Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, respecting the Hackney Coachmen,

Chairmen, Carters, Carmen, and Porters of the said Town, were extended to a reasonable Distance beyond the Liberties of the Town into the County of Lancaster: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the several Purposes above mentioned, with such Powers and Provisions, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Gascoyne, Junior, the Lord Penrhyn, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Inhabitants, and Occupiers of Houses, Lands, and Tenements, within the Town and Parish of Liverpool aforesaid, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That by an Act, made in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of King William the Third, for enabling the Town of Liverpool to build and endow a Church, and for making the said Town and Liberties thereof a Parish of itself, distinct from ffalton, it is enacted, that the Borough, Town, Township, and Lilierties of Liverpool, should for ever be a distinct Parish, and be divided from the said Parish of Walton,

Liverpool and from the Cure of the Rector and Vicar thereof, and Church, &c. ^eir Successors, and discharged of all Tythes, Oblations, Obventions, Mortuaries, Easter Books, and other Parochial Duties, and that the Inhabitants of Liverpool should build a new Church,. and provide and inclose a Church Yard about the fame, and also Ground, and build a House or Houses, and make a Garden or Gardens, for the Rector or Rectors of the said Church and Parochial Chapel there, and that the said Church and Church Yard should be the Parish Church and Church Yard of Liverpool, and that there should be Two Rectors of the said Town and Parish of Liverpool, with a perpetual Succession, the one for the said new Church, and the other for the said Parochial Chapel, who should be incorporated, and enjoy all Tythes, Offerings, Oblations, Obventions, and other Ecclesiastical Benefits and Advantages within the same Town and Liberties, as the Rector and Vicar of Walton had, or ought to have, enjoyed within the same, and also the said Messuage or Tenement, Messuages or Tenements, for their Habitation; and it was thereby further enacted, that, for erecting the said new Church, and House or Houses, and providing Grounds for the same respectively, and the Requisites in and about the fame, as therein mentioned, such Sums as shall be competent to accomplish the Premises, not exceeding 4,000l. should be raised in Manner therein mentioned, and that such a Yearly Rate, or Assessment, should be made and raised, within the same Town and Liberties, for the Use of the Rectors of Liverpool, as should, with the Tythes due to them, amount to 200/ Yearly, at the least; and that, ever since the passing of the said Act, the Sum of 200l. hath been Annually raised as aforesaid, for the Use of, and paid to, the Rectors of Liverpool, including the 'Tythes mentioned in the said Act to be due to them, but not any Satisfaction hath been made them for the Oblations, Obventions, Mortuaries, Easter Books, and other Parochial Duties by the said Act directed to be enjoyed by them, neither hath any House or Garden been built or made for their Use, but, in lieu thereof, they have received 10/. a Year each, the said,000l. having been expended in building the said Parish Church, so that the Petitioners have not Powfer to raise Money for building and making of any Houses or Gardens, or to make Satisfaction to the Rectors for the said Oblations, Obventions, Mortuaries, Easter Books, Offerings, and other Ecclesiastical Duties payable to them, without the Aid of Parliament; and that, in the Year 1718, the said Parochial Chapel was enlarged, by building a new Gallery, and erecting divers Seats therein, at the Expence of the Corporation of Liverpool, by virtue of a Faculty obtained from the Ordinary of the ttiocefe of Chester, and the Profits of the said Seats were direfited to be applied to the Use of the said Rectors, but, if they should thereafter infill upon Houses, in that same the Corporation were impowered to set and take the Profits of the said Seats, until they should be reimbursed the Charge of making the said Enlargement and building the said Gallery and Seats, and the Rectors of- Liverpool, from the Time of obtaining the said Faculty, have let and received the Profits of the said Seats, as the Petitioners, the present Rectors, now do; and that the said Town of Liverpool, since the making of the said Act, hath exceedingly' increased in Extent and Population, and all the Stipends, Salaries, and Provisions hitherto provided for the said Re6tors (including the Surplice Fees) are a very inadequate and insufficient Provision for the Rectors of so large a mercantile Town and populous Parish as Liverpool (where Provisions and all other Necessaries of Life are fb very dear) the whole Amount thereof to the present Re6tors not having ever exceeded the clear Annual Sum of 213 /. for each of them; and that, at the public Annual and General Vestry, held for the same Parish; 01

according to constant UTage, and agreeably to the Directions of the said Act, on Eas Tuesday last, the Parishioners of Liverpool, in Vestry assembled, declared it to be their Opinion, that the Income of the Petitioners, the Rectors, was inadequate, and ought to be increased, and resolved, that the Sum of 200l. a Year (that is to say, 100l. each) should be added to the Rectors Income, in lieu of all Claims of Tythes, Oblation.-, Obventions, Mortuaries, and all other Ecclesiastical Benefits which they claimed to be entitled to, but which they did not then enjoy, and that Parliament should be applied to for an Act more effectually to secure the same to them and their Successors, and that the said 100l. a Year each should be raised by a Tax upon the Inhabitants and Occupiers of Houses, except such as were under the Yearly Value of 5/.: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for carrying into Execution and confirming the said Order of Vestry, and veiling the Right of the said Seats, and also the Yearly additional Income of 100l. each, in the Petitioners, the Rectors, and their Successors, for ever, in lieu of all Tythes, Oblations, Obventions, Mortuaries, and all other Ecclesiastical Rights whatsoever (the usual Surplice Fees excepted) in such Manner, and under such Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

THE Earl of Courtown reported to the House, That their Addresses of Yesterday (that His Majesty would be graciously pleated to give Orders, that the several Papers therein mentioned might be laid before this House) had been presented to His Majesty; and that His Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that He will give Directions accordingly.

A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, Retail Shopkeepers in the City of Lincoln, as well on Behalf of themselves, as the other Shopkeepers resident in that City, and the Suburbs thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Tax on Retail Shops, imposed in the last Sessions of Parliament, has, in every Respect, the Effects of such a Taxation as the Man of Wealth, who lives without Business, and even the most opulent Merchant, and Wholesale Dealer, are not in the least Degree chargeable with; and that a Tax laid upon any specific Article comes in the first Instance to the Trader, forms Part of his Prime Colt, and the Consumer pays it when he purchases the Commodity; but this Tax being afleifed by the Rent of the House, is precisely the same in Operation with the House Tax, and all other Taxes collected by Pound Rate, which never has, in any One Instance, been laid on the Consumer; and that, as the Petitioners have, at all Times, cheerfully paid their Quota to the Exigencies of the State, and are ever willing to bear their proportional Part of any necessary Burthen which may be laid on the whole Community, to the Extent. of their Abilities, they therefore hope the House will take this Petition under their most

serious Consideration, and repeal an Act so universally abnoxious and opprdfive to every Description of Retail Traders.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Shop Tax. thereunto subscribed. Retail Shopkeepers in the Town of Beverley, in the County of York, was allb presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and all Retail Shopkeepers throughout the Kingdom, are by no Means in a State of Opulence to be marked out by the Legislature of their Country as the foie Objt fts of Taxation, burthensome from its Amount, and in the highest Degree partial, from which the most wealthy and independent Part of the Community are wholly exempt; and that the Tax on Retail Shops, imposed in the last Session of Parliament, has, in every Hefpcft, the Etft ft of such a

Taxation as the Man of Wealth, who lives without Business, and even the opulent Merchant and Wholesale Dealer are not in the least Degree chargeable with; and that the Petitioners cannot transfer the Burthen of the Shop Tax on the Consumer of the

Commodity, as alledged by its Advocates (which may be the same when a Tax is laid on any Article of Trade) and by that means render it general, but must bear the whole Burthen of it personally, as an additional House Tax; wherefore, as the Petitioners have, at all Times, cheerfully paid their Quota to the Exigencies of the State, and are ever willing to bear their proportional Part of any neccflury Burthen which may be laid on the whole Community, to the Extent of their Abilities, they pray the House will take this Petition under their most serious Consideration, and repeal an Act so universally obnoxious and oppressive to every Description of Retail Tradesmen.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers residing in the Ditto.

City of Gloucester, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners feel themselves greatly aggrieved by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, imposing a Tax upon Retail Shops, which is in its Consequence a partial Increase of the House Tax, upon a particular Class of the Community, who, from the Nature of their Business, are under the Necessity of having Shops in public Situations, where Rents, and consequently the House Tax thereon, are, exclusive of this additional Impost, very high; and that the Tax complained of not being a Tax upon any specific Articles, cannot be raised upon the Consumer, by Advance of the Price of any Articles in which the Petitioners deal, and consequently the Weight of this great and heavy Burthen must fall on the Petitioners only, in respect of their Dwellings, whilst their more opulent Neighbours are exempt from any proportional Burthen for the public Service, and it will therefore operate as a Tax upon the Industry of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Hardthip of their same into Consideration, and that the Act of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Retail Shops, within Great Britain, may be repealed.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be le erred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers in - Shop Tax.

ton, in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, a Motion is intended to be made for Leave to bring in a Bill to repeal an Act, pasted in the last Session of Parliament, inposing a Tax upon Retail Shops, and in Support of such Motion, beg Leave to state their same to the House: Although the Petitioners readily admit that Duties imposed on the specific Articles wherein the Retail Shopkeepers deal, ultimately fall upon the Consumer, yet they allure the House, That Duties or Taxes imposed upon Retail Shopkeepers, in any other Manner than upon the specific Articles vended, do not, in an adequate Degree, affect the Conlumers, but defalcate from, and dhninish, the Shopkeepers just Gains; the Tax therefore upon Retail Shops, as it at present stands, the Petitioners consider as a Tax upon Retail Shopkeepers, exclusively, for such they feel it to be in its Operation and Effects; and that the Petitioners conceive it to be a Principle, that for any particular Descrip-tiou of Men to become proper Objects of Taxation, their Opulence must be apparent, or their Gains exorbitant, but the Petitioners contend, that Retail Shopkeepers are not proper Objects of such particular Taxation, as they are far from being opulent, if taken collectively, and their Gains are very linall, especially when compared with those of Merchants, Wholesale Traders, and others; on the contrary, the Retail Shopkeepers labour under many Hardships peculiar to themselves; their Shops constitute a Part of their Dwelling Houses, which are, in general, very in.on-venient, and of little intrinsic Value, yet their House Rents, front the local Advantages of their Shops, are out of all Proportion higher than the large and elegant Houses of Merchants, and others, not requiring the like Situations, and those Rents operate as a heavy Tax upon the Shopkeepers Gains, which is rendered the more burthensome, as the House T^x, and all

other

26 Geo. III. 20° Februarii.

other Taxes, are proportioned according to the high and extravagant Rents they pay, and therefore the Petitioners infill, that, (exclusive of the Tax upon Retail Shops) they already pay and contribute more towards the Exigencies of the State than any other Description of Men, whose Trades or Employments bring in no greater Profits: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Hardships of their same into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall fcem meet.

Shop Tax. A Petition of the Retail Traders within the City and Suburbs of Oxford', was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners fee with Concern a Tax laid upon Retail Shops, by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, which is found to be partial and oppressive, and, if not repealed, the Petitioners fear will prove fatal to their Interest; that there are a great Number of Retail Shops, the Profits whereof are known to be barely sufficient to support the industrious Owners, and the said Tax will consequently reduce to Want a Description of Men, who have been long considered the Strength of this Nation; and that the Retail Traders have, on all Occasions, chearfully contributed to the Support of Government, but they now conceive the said Tax too partially affects them, as the Merchant, the Wholesale Dealer, and many other opulent Members of Society, who are better able to bear the Burthen, will support no Part thereof, and in the said City and Suburbs this Tax is peculiarly grievous, the Land Tax is enormous, and the Inhabitants obliged to support very expensive Poor, to which may be added, many local Expences which have brought on frequent Scenes of Distress: And therefore praying, That the House will substitute feme more general Taxation, equally productive, but lese partial.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Commonalty, of Damage by the Town of Faversham, in the County of Kent, being Powder Mills offered to be presented to the House; ^amaver~

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That, on the 17th Day of April 1781,

One of the Corning Houses, and the Dulling Mill, belonging to His Majesty’s Powder Mills at <*> sham, which are under the Direction of the Board of Ordnance, blew up, and by the Explosion thereof all the Powder Mills and Works adjoining were materially injured; several Houses and Buildings in the Town of Faoersham, and its Neighbourhood, setroyed, and many others, together with the Church of Davington, wholly, or in Part, unroofed* and otherwise greatly damaged, and in other Houses the Window Frames, and Door Cafes, were forced out, the Glafe of the Windows shivered in Pieces, and a considerable Quantity of Furniture and Effects demolished, or rendered useless; and that, in the same Month of April, a Petition from the Inhabitants of the said Town was presented to the Board of Ordnance, Hating the above Fa6ts, and praying, that the said Board, when the Damage could be estimated, would order the Expence thereof to be defrayed to the Sufferers, in such Manner as the Board should think expedient* and, in pursuance of the said Petition, Mr. John

A Petition of the Shopkeepers of the Borough of Lei- Shop Tax. cester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners feel themselves concerned at the Necessity they are under of laying before the House the Grievance they sustain by the Act lately passed for imposing a Duty on Retail Shops; an Act, in their Judgment, partial, because the Retail Traders cannot, in any Degree, be indemnified by adding to foe Prime Colt of their Goods, and thereby laying any Part of foe Duty upon the Consumera; without lofrng their Trade, consequently they alone muff sustain the Burthen of the Tax; and that, as Housekeepers, foe Petitioners are subject to many other heavy Taxes in respect to their Houses and Windows, and the Relief of the Poor (in the said Borough very numerous and expensive) and as Shopkeepers they are more particularly pppressed in those Respects, as they are under a Necessity of living in those Houses which are in the most convenient Parts of thq Town, and on that Account contribute more than the other Inhabitants towards the Payment of foafe Taxes:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Coplideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as the Circumstances of the same foall require.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers residing in the Ditto.

City of Nonoich, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed, in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Band the Retail Traders, on whom alone that Duty is to he levied, are Persons already labouring under heavy Burthens, and many of them scarcely able to support foemfelyes and Families with any Degree of Credit, and they consider foemselves therefore, with great Impropriety fiugfed out from foe general M&& of foeir Fellow Subjects, as foe Objects of severe Taxation; and that foe Petitioners have observed, that the Want of a practical Know ledge of Tt;ade has induced foe Advocates of the said Tax to state, that it would fall not on the Vender, hut on the Cqnfumer, ,of Articles in which they deal; and, was that Aifertfon well founded, he would have no Rculbn to complain, for could he reimburse himself in one Ioftance, he might, in many others to the great Detriment and Diladvaotage of the Public, but thf Fast is diametrically opposite, as every Tax laid upon a specific Article forms a Part of the Prime Cust of that Article, and goes to every Trader alike, and the said Tax varies not according to the Ability of foe Trader, or the Magnitude of his Concerns, but

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of Edinburgh, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the l ilt Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great , a very heavy

and burthensome Tax is imposed on the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Principle of all Taxations to be, that the Burthens necessary to be imposed for the Support of a State should be levied on the whole Members of that State, as equally as the Nature of Circumltunces will admit, and in Proportion to the Ability of those Members, and that it never can be the Intention of the Legislature to impose a Tax on any One Description of Men, who have already contributed their full Proportion to the Exigencies of the State, whilst others, far better enabled to bear such an Imposition, are totally exempted; and that the Petitioners have, from the Beginning, maintained that the Tax on Retail Shops is a personal One, and they have now the Sanction of Experience to confirm them in the Opinion they had formed of it; a Tax imposed on any sperific Article comes, in the first Instance, to the Trader, it forms Part of his Prime Cost, and he levies it from the . Consumer, by railing the Price of the Commodity, but the present Tax, being assessed by the Rent of the Shop, can never be raised from the Consumer, and its Operation is precisely the same with the House Tax, and others collected by the Rate of the Rent, which never has, nor never can be, laid on the Consumer; and that it has been asserted by the Advocates for the Tax on Retail Shops, that the Shopkeepers can lay it on the Consumer, but, when the Nature of a Retail Business is considered, this will appear impossible, for, were the Petitioners to endeavour to proportion the Tax among the great Variety of Articles in which, as Retailers, they must necessarily deal, it would be almost beyond the Power of Calculation to do so; and, however specious the Arguments of the Friends of the Tax may appear on a superficial View of them, the Petitioners declare, from Experience, that it is not possible for the present Tax ever to fall on the Consumer, and it can be considered in no other Light, than as a personal Tax, the Burthen of which must be defrayed by the Retailer out of his Profits; and that the Rent which a Person pays for his Shop (and which is the Rule by which the present Tax is

assessed) is in very many Cafes a fallacious Criterion of judging of his Ability to pay a Tax; Shopkeepers owe much of their Trade to Situation; hence the Desire which every one has for the most public Places in Towns, and hence the extravagant Rents which Shopkeepers are obliged to pay; they must content themselves with trifling Profits to enable them to defray those heavy Rents, and to defray the Expence of many taxed Commodities, of which they necessarily consume a much greater Quantity than any other Description of Men,-and when it is considered that out of these Profits they have now also an additional heavy Tax to pay, they hope the peculiar Hardship of their Situation will merit the Attention of the Legislature. Upon the Whole, the Petitioners apprehend it to be evident, that the Tax on Shops cannot be laid on the Consumer, but must be paid as a personal Tax by the Retail Traders: And, therefore, they hope and trust that the House, when they consider how readily the Retail Traders have at all Times contributed their Portion to the Exigencies of the State, and how heavily they are at present burthened, will not deem them in such a State of Opulence as to be marked out as the Objects of a Tax, to which no Men of independent Fortune, nor even a Merchant or Wholesale Trader, contribute any Thing; and the Petitioners therefore trust with Confidence in the Justice of the House for a Repeal of the said Tax, which they must consider as partial in its Principle, and which they have every Reason to fear will prove ruinous in its Consequences.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of London, is referred.

any Side Bar betwixt Handsworth and Attercliffe aforesaid, except such Side Bar as is therein mentioned and described, and atfo, to impower the Trustees of the said Road to erect ns many Gates or Turnpikes in, upon, or across the said Road, and also upon the Side or Sides thereof, and across any Lane or Way leading onto or lying near the fame, and to take the Tolls and Duties directed by the said former Act, as the said Trustees shall think proper to appoint; and that the said Proviso was agreed to, and established by the said Act, in favour of the Petitioners, before the making

178 6*

of the said Turnpike Road, and was intended to prevent any additional Charge on the Coal used in the Manufacture of Cutlery Wares at Sheffield, and it appears to the Petitioners, that a Repeal of the said Proviso, and the granting of such Powers to the Trustees of the said Road as before mentioned, will occasion an immediate and very considerable Advance on the Price of Coals in that Neighbourhood, and of consequence be highly detrimental to the Sheffield Manufactory, as well as to Individuals in general: And therefore praying, That the said Proviso in the said Act may be yet continued, that the Petitioners may have the full Benefit thereof, and that no Clause in the said Bill, which hath a Tendency to repeal the said Proviso, or to enable the Trustees to erect any Gate or Turnpike in, upon, or across the said Road, or any Side Bar (other than as in the said Act mentioned and described) or to take any Tolls or Duties whatsoever, nearer to Attercliffe than within Twenty Yards of the Blacksmith’s Smithy at The Three Lane Ends, near Handsworth aforesaid, may be allowed or suffered to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

That in the Year 1718 the said Parochial Chapel was enlarged, by building a new Gallery, and erecting Scats therein at the Expence of the Corporation of Liverpool, by virtue of a Faculty from the Ordinary of the Diocese of Chester, and the Profits of the said Seats were directed to be applied to the Use of the said Rectors, unless they should inlist upon having Houses, in which same the Corporation were empowered to let and take the Profits of the said Seats, until they should be reiuibursed the Charge of making the said Enlargement, and building the said Gallery and Seats; a'nd that the Rectors of Liverpool, from the Time of obtaining the said Faculty, have let and received the Profits of the said Seats.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of John L Esquire; and also, the Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Freemen of the Borough of Lancaster, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and having a Right to vote for Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Francis Reynolds and Abram Rawlinson, Esquires, for the said Borough, being

come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Two Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents for the Petitioners, and

Februariu 247

the Counsel and Agents for the said Prancis Reynolds,

Esquire, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Abram Rawlinson, Esquire, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The Counsel for the said Sitting Members respectively informed the House* That Mr. Reynolds was a Joint Candidate at the Election with Mr. Lowther against Mr. Rawlinson; that Mr. Reynolds and Mr. Rawlinson had no common Interest; that the said Sitting Memliers were complained of by the Petitions now taken into Consideration, upon the Ground of Bribery at the said Election, which Charge, in its Nature, would affect them separately, as their Canvas at the Election had been separate; that it appeared by the Poll, that Mr. Rawlinson s Voters voted for him solely, but many Voters polled for Mr. Reynolds and the Petitioner; and that upon the whole the Interests of the Sitting Members being diliinft and separate from each other, they therefore desired to separate in their Defence; to which no material Objection being made by the Counsel for the Petitioners, the House proceeded to the Appointment of the said Select Committee, as in the same of there being more than Two Parties on distinct Interests before the House.

Then the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Twenty-seven other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Six, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which the)' had before verified upon Oath; Two, on Account of their being Members against whole Returns Petitions were depending; One, on Account of his being a Petitioner to this House, complaining of an Undue Election and Return; Fifteen, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; One, on Account of his having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees; and Two, on Account of their having voted at the said Election.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, lb drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete, lifts of the said Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

Shop Tax. A Petition of the Shopkeepers in the Town of Stockport, in the County Palatine of , was presented

to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners conceive the true Principle of all Taxes ought to be Impartiality and Equality, but it is with extreme Concern that they observe this Principle departed from by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament granting certain Sums of Money to be

o4

raised from Retail Shopkeepers, by which the Petitioners are compelled to contribute to the public Revenue in greater Proportion than the rest of their Fellow Citizens; and that, as the said Tax cannot possibly fall on the Consumer, because it cannot be distributed among the Articles in which the Petitioners deal, and as it falls upon one particular Defoription of Men, whilst others, in far more opulent Situations, are not at all affected by it, and is a Tax to be collected by a Pound Rate, k operates as a Second House Tax upon Retail Shopkeepers only, and therefore the Petitioners consider it as a Tax partial and burthenlbme in the Extreme; and that the Petitioners have at all Times chearfully contributed towards the Exigencies of the State, and are still willing to bear a just Proportion of the public Burthens in common with the rest of their Fellow' Citizens, in any other Way that the House shall think tit to adopt: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall appear most effectual to redress the Grievance above fat forth.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers and Retail Dealers of Shop Tax. the Borough of Dei'by, in the County of Derby, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners conceive, that the late Act, imposing a Duty on all Retail Dealers, is extremely of-preflive and partial in its Consequences, and can, in no Point of View, be considered as being similar to ,a Tax which is laid on any specific Article of Trade, and which ultimately falls on the Consumer, but that, on the contrary, it operates strictly as a personal Tax on the Petitioners, who have no Means of relieving themselves from any Part of it; and Representing to the House, That, before the said Act passed into a law, the Petitioners contributed their Share to the public Taxes in common with their Fellow Citizens, and will at all Times chearfully bear their Proportion of such Taxes as the Exigencies of the State may require, but presume no substantial Reason can be assigned why they alone should be marked out as the Objects of the present Tax, which is fb apparently personal and burthensome: And therefore praying, That the House will grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem . meet and proper.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of London, is referred.

A Petition of the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars Hawkers in the Counties of Lancaster and York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are fully convinced of the Impofiibility of carrying on their Business, with Advantage to themselves, or Safety to their Creditors, under the Pressure of those severe Restrictions imposed upon them last Session of Parliament, and, unless the House will remove the unmerited Imputation of their Trade being unfair, by a Repeal of the Ninth and Eleventh Sections of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and " Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their Trade," the Petitioners will be obliged to decline the fame, for, as they value their Characters, they will not pursue a Business against which Government seem to entertain such a pointed (though ill-grounded) Suspicion; and that the Petitioners are willing and even desirous, of contributing to the Exigencies of the State, as far as their Abilities will admit, and the Legislature think necessary to require; and although the several Duties laid upon them are really heavy, yet they will pay the same without a Murmer, provided they participate of that Liberty which is the inherent Right of -

born Subjects; and that, if the Petitioners Trade mull depend upon the Will of a new Tribunal, which . in some Places has already shewn their hostile Intentions, even without any Crime being alleged or proved, the Petitioners conceive their Situation is such as no Clals of Subjects ever before experienced in this Kingdom, and earnellly entreat the House to consider their unhappy Situation, and not force then* to the fad Alternatives of submitting to Ruin and

Setting forth, That the Lands, Meadows, and Grounds, of the several Proprietors in the said Fields, lie greatly intermixed and dispersed, are subject to frequent Trespasses, and cannot, in their present Condition, be improved in the Manner they might be if inclosed; and that it would be an Advantage to the several Parties interested, if the said Common and Open Fields, and Common Grounds, were inclosed and divided, and specific Shares thereof allotted to each Proprietor, in Proportion to their Interests therein: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Common and Open Fields, and Common Grounds, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Robert Smith and Mr. Hungerford do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. John Lely, Treasurer to the Trust, being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act of the Sixth Year of His present Majesty, and of the Two Acts therein referred to, so far as the same relate to the Road from Spittlegate HiU to Foston Bridge, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money on the Credit of the Tolls, amounting to 3,300/; and that there is likewise owing to the Trea-forer the Sum of 563 /. for Money advanced by him for Payment of the Interest of the Money borrowed, and other Contingencies — That the Amount of the Tolls for 6 Years last past, to Midsummer 1785, have produced, upon an Average, the Annual Sum of 511/. or thereabouts; and that the Repair of the Roads during the same time has amounted Annually to the Sum of 433/. or thereabouts; so that there remains only the Annual Sum of 78 / or thereabouts, for Payment of Interest, Salary to Officers, and other Expences — That, unless the Term granted by the said Act is continued, and further provisions made for the Alteration and Amendment of the said Act, the said Road cannot be kept in Repair, nor the Money owing be repaid.

Mr. William Parker being examined, said. That the Materials which are at present made Ule of for the Road, being chiefly Stone, are exceedingly had; and that better Materials, which are intended to be fetched to put the Road in good Repair, lie at the Difiance of about Five Miles.

Mr. Beaufoy reported from the Committee, appointed

to inquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Encouragement and Extension, and to report the fame, from Time to Time, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had made a further Prozreft in the Matters -to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it i9 the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 5th Day of April 1786, no Lampreys or Wilks Ihoold, for a Time to be limited; be exported from Great Britain in any Ship or Veflek an left such Ship or Vessel shall be built, owned

by British Subjects, navigated according to Law, and fitted our for the Cod FiOnwy.

Resolved, That it the Opinion of tbie Committee, That, from and after the 5th Day of April 1786, no Lampreys should for a Time to be limited, be exported in any one Vessel whatever, at any one Time, in any Vol. 41.

greater Number than 2,000; and that, from and after the aforesaid Day, no Wilks should be exported in any one Vessel whatever, at any one Time, in any greater Quantity than 36 Bushels.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their Trade: And praying the House to take the particular Hardships of their same into Consideration, and permit them the free Use of their Labour and Calling, without Restraint, as other Subjects of this Realm, and without subjecting them to be suppressed, arbitrarily, by any Set of People, without being first legally convicted of any Crime to merit such Treatment; and that the House will afford the Petitioners such Relief and Protection as to the House shall seem meet. *

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
