A Petition of George Bishop, Proprietor of the Maid- BiA»of'» stone Geneva Manufactory, was presented to the House, Geneva* and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, having by long Residence in Holland, and great Attention to the Method of making Spirits there, which are known by the Name of Holland’s' Geneva, made himself Matter of the Art and Mystery of preparing the fame, erected, at a great Expence, a Manufactory for making Geneva at Maidstone, which he, for some Time, carried on to his own Advantage, and that of the Public, until he was prevented from Working by the Provisions of an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of His present Majestys Reign, intituled, "An Act " for repealing the Duties payable upon Chocolate " made in Great Britain, and for granting certain Inland Duties upon Cocoa Nuts in lieu thereof; for " the better and more effectual securing the Revenue " of Excise, and of the Inland Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, and for " preventing Frauds therein; for the more punctual " and ready Payment of the Allowances to be made " to Brewers out of the additional Duties imposed " on Malt; and for rectifying a Mistake in a Act,

" made in this present Session of Parliament, with ' " respect to the exempting of Candles from the additional Duty of Five Pounds per Centum upon, the " Duties of Excise imposed by the said Act;" and that the Provisions and Restrictions contained in the said Act, rendering it utterly impossible for the Petitioner to continue manufacturing the Spirits he had before made, and which had been in great llequest with the Public, both for Home Consumption and Exportation, he stated the Circumstances of his same to the House by Petition, and by a Clause in an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majestys Reign, intituled, "An Act to discontinue, for a limited Time, the Payment of the Duties upon Low " Wines and Spirits, for Home Consumption, and " for granting and securing the due Payment of other " Duties in lieu thereof, and for the better Regulatiop of the making and vending British Spirits, as " w'ell for Home Consumption as for Exportation,

" and for destroying all Home-made and Foreign " Spirits after the Condemnation thereof; and for " vesting in His Majesty the Duties of Excise within " the Lands of Ferentosh, in the County of Inverness,

" and for discontinuing, for a limited Time, certain " Imposts and Duties upon Rum and Spirits imported " from the West Indies," the Petitioner's said Manufactory was exempted from the Provisions and Restrictions of the said first-recited Act, for the Term of Two Years; and that, under the Sanction of the said Indulgence and Exemption, the Petitioner applied himself with unremitting Industry, to revive his Manufactory of Geneva, in which, after much Trouble and Expence, he has at length succeeded, and again brought the Spirits he makes into general Use and Esteem, whereby the illicit Importation of Holland's, Geneva hath been in a great Degree prevented, and the Revenue of Excise considerably benefited, the Petitioner having manufactured, -between the 1 ft of November 1784 and the ill of November 1785, Sixty-nine thousand Two hundred and Fifty-seven Gallons of Geneva, the Duty whereon amounted to 9,261/. 14& 8 id.;and that the Exemption granted to the Petitioner by the said last mentioned Act, being for a Term which is near expiring, he mull again

A Petition of divers of the Inhabitants of the Town Damages by of Faversham, in the County of Kent, and the Neigh-

bourhood thereof, on Behalf of themselves and others,

Sufferers by the Explolion of a, Part of the Royal Powder Works there, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty» having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up and read;

Setting forth, That, on the 17th Day of 1781,

One of the Corning Houses and the Dufting Mill belonging to His Majesty’s Powder Mills at Faversham, which are under the Direction of the Board of Ol d nance, blew up, and, by the Explolion thereof, all the Powder Mills and Works adjoining were materially injured, several Houses and Buildings in the Town of Faversham and its Neighbourhood destroyed, and many others, together with the Church of Davington, wholly. or in Part unroofed, and other*

wife greatly damaged, and in other Houses the Window Frames and Door Cafes were forced out, the Glass of the Windows shivered in Pieces, and a Considerable Quantity of Furniture and Effects demolished or rendered useless; and that, in the same Month of April, the Petitioners presented a Petition to the

Board of Ordnance, dating the above Fasts, and praying that the said Board, when the Damage could be estimated, would order the Expence thereof to be defrayed to the Sufferers, in such Manner as the Board should think expedient; and, in pursuance of the said Petition, Mr. John Groves, by Order of the said Board, and under the Direction of Sir Thomas Hyde Page, viewed the said Damages, and estimated the same at 1,422 A 185. 6d. and reported such Estimate to the said Board, together with a particular Account of the Lois of each Individual; and that no Recompence whatever having been made to any of the said Sufferers in consequence of such Report, the Mayor, Jurats, and Commonalty of the said Town, as Trustees of an Hospital for the Support of Six poor old Men in the said Town, in the Y’ear 1782, petitioned the Lords of His Majesty’s Treasury to be paid the Amount of the Damage sustained by the said Hospital in consequence of the said Explo-fion, which their Lordships ordered to be paid, and the same hath been since paid accordingly; and that the Petitioners again petitioned the Board of Ordnance, after such Estimate had been made by the said John Graces, praying to be permitted to make solemn Affidavits of their Lodes in consequence of the said Explosion, and to submit the Inspection thereof to any Persons whom the Board should appoint, and also imploring Relief, but they were afterwards informed, that the said Board could not grant any Relief in the Premises, and had laid the said Petition before the Lords of the Treasury, who

Bridge, and the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Peti-E^dhtowards ^on of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, of the Ireland. \ O L, 41.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Colonel Peacock being examined; said, That the Improvement of the Great Road leading through the Counties of Carnarvon and Anglesey, towards Irelandi is an Object of great public Importance — That the Passage of Porthaethwy Ferry, over an Arm of the Sea, between the Counties of Carnarvon and Anglesey, called The Streights of Menai, is frequently attended with very great Delay, Inconvenience, and Danger — That he has known People delayed; and has been himself delayed,- above Four Hours by the Negligence of the Boatmen. — Being asked, Whether that Delay arises from the Inattention or Delay of the Ferrymen, or from the Nature of the Ferry ? he said, It arises mostly from the Negligence of the Ferrymen; but that he has known it impossible to pass the Ferry, from the Wind being high — That the Ferrymen will frequently refuse to carry Persons across without an additional Fee — That he has several Times, in crossing the Streights, been in Danger of the Boat linking, from the Roughnels of the Water — That he has himself been detained Thirteen Hours by the Weather, which he believes is not a common Circumstance, although a Delay of Two or Three Hours for Wind or Tide is common.

Mr. Joseph Nickalls being then examined, said, That he is an Engineer, and lives in Gravel Lane, Southwark — That he has made a Plan and Face View of a Bridge with Three Draw Bridges, which is proposed to be built over the Streights of Menai, near Porthaethwy Ferry — That he thinks a safe and convenient Bridge may be built across the Streights at that Place — That he does not know a more eligible Place to build one — That he is conversant in making Bridges, but not over an Arm of the Sea — That he thinks the building a Bridge in that Place very practicable, as not being subject to Floods, as in Rivers — That the Tide there is by no Means so bad as the Floods in Rivers.

Being asked, If there are not Two Tides which meet at that Place? he said, Not in the Streights of Menai so forcibly as at the Isle of Man, that they have no visible Power in the Streights.

Being then asked, If there arc not many Tides more forcible than River Floods? he said, No: It is an extraordinary Tide which runs Four Knots and an Half an Hour in those Streights, and that many Bridges have been built in Currents that run from Eight to Ten Miles an Hour, particularly across the Colder and Air, and many others — That the Bridge intended to be built is proposed to be built with Timber.

Being asked, Whether a Timber Bridge at that Place is practicable, so as to refill the Tides ? he said, Yes; and while it exists it is equally safe — That it will last longer than a Timber Bridge over a River, as the Salt Water preserves the Timber — That Timber Bridges in general last, upon an Average, about Thirty Years. And the Witness added, That he has been informed, that there is no Worm which destroys the Timber in those Parts, and that the Bridge may be built in Two Years.

Being asked, Whether he has examined the Bottom of the Streights of Menai at that Place? he laid, He has; that he believes it is in general Rock at the Bottom of the Whole of the Streights, and that

Captain Thomas Totty, of the Royal Navy, being then examined, said. That he knows the Streights of Menai — That be has seen and examined the Plan of the intended Bridge, and thinks that the building a Bridge over that Part of the Streights, as proposed by the Plan, will not obstruct the Navigation of Ships. — Being aiked, Whether he had the Bridge in View when he passed over the Streights ? he laid, The Erection of a Bridge had been Matter of Conversation before he last passed the Streights, and at that time he saw no Reason to suppose, that if such a Bridge ever was erected, it would obstruct the Navigation of Vessels.

Being aiked, If he does not think it would obstruct them to a certain Degree, much more than at present? he laid, He thinks not at all, for these Reasons: According to the Plan which he has seen, there Js intended to be Two Draw Bridges in the Channel, and with a fair Wind there can be no Difficulty in passing through either of them; that he speaks as to Ships of 200 Tons — That if the Wind is foul they mull: have the Advantage of Tide, which will pulh the Vessel through — That there will be no Difficulty in passing the Bridge, the Pilots there being very skilful, and they always make use of them. And the Witness added, That if be owned Ten thousand Vessels upon the Streights, he would not object to the Bridge — That he does not apprehend that any Beds of Sand will collect from the Bridge, and that any Vessels that can navigate the can paf6 the Bridge with Safety.

A Petition of the Persons whole Names are thereunto fiibscribed, being Persons entitled to a Share of the Property captured at the Island of Saint Eustatius, on Behalf of themselves, and all others entitled to the said captured Property, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, in the Year 1781, serving in His Majesty’s Fleets and Armies, were present at the Capture of the Island of Saint and of the Property found in the said Island; and that His Majesty having, by Instructions, dated the 30th Day of March 1781, sent by Lord George Germain, (His Majesty’s then Secretary of State) to the Commanders in Chief, at the said Island, relinquished, in Favour of the Captors, his Right in the said Property, the Petitioners' became respectively entitled to a Share thereof ;- and, in consequence of such Instructions, Six Agents were appointed by the Navy and Army, to collect, dispose of,. and distribute the said Property, agreeable to His Majesty’s Intention, expressed in the said Instructions, and the several Agents, in virtue of such Appointment, became possessed of the said Property, and have dispersed great Part thereof, and held the Produce within their own Power; and that the Property so possessed is very great, and, as the Petitioners apprehend, ought, long since, to have been fully accounted for and distributed, so that the Petitioners might have received what they are justly entitled to; yet, notwithstanding Applications have been made to the Persons holding the said Property, to obtain such Account and Distribution, no effectual Account has been yet obtained, nor has any Part of the said Property been distributed, in consequence of which Delay the Petitioners are great Sufferers, and His Majesty’s gracious Intention has been hitherto prevented from taking Effect; and that the Petitioners have been informed, that an effectual Account and Distribution of the said Property cannot be obtained in the common Course of judicial Proceedings, without great Delay, Inconvenience, and Expence, inso much that the Costs of Proceeding would, in the same of a large Majority of those entitled to a Share thereof, exceed the Sum to be recovered, as separate Applications, in the regular Course of Proceeding, would be necessary for the Purpose: And therefore ’praying,' That Leave may be given to

bring in a Bill to vest in Commissioners, to be therein named, the Whole' of the Property captured at the said Island of Saint Eustatius, and that the said Commissioners, by such Bill, may be impowered to call all Persons, who shall appear to have, or to have had, any Part of the said Property in their Hands, to a speedy Account thereof, and if it shall appear that there are any Claims to Part of the said Property still undecided, that the several Sums of Money now in the Hands of Agents, and others, may be paid into the Bank, in the Name of the Commissioners, to be by them laid out on Government Securities, for the Benefit of the Captors, to the End, that a final Dividend may, in due Time, be made among the Persons entitled thereto, according to His Majesty’s most gracious Intention, or that the Petitioners may obtain such other Relief in the Premises as the House may think belt adapted to their Cafe.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House: ,

And it is referred to Sir George Howard, the Marquis of Graham, &c.: And they are to meet To-mor-

row Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, and Commonalty, Deal Small and principal Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of Debts. Deal, in the County of Kent, and also, of the principal Inhabitants of the several Parishes of Ripple, Sutton, Northbourne, Great Mongeham, Little Tdmanstone, Betshanger, Ham, Eastry, and in

the same County, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Town of Deal is large and populous, and is situated near to The Downs, by Means whereof a considerable Trade is carried on in the said Town, and also in the said several Parishes, on Account of their near Situation to the said Town; and that there are many Persons to whom the Traders of the said Town and Parishes are obliged to give Credit for small Sums of Money, who frequently refuse (although well able) to pay the lame, presuming on the Discouragements which their Creditors lie under from the great Expence they are unavoidably put to, and the Delays they meet with in filing for such Debts, and it would tend greatly to promote Industry, and support useful Credit, in the said Town and Parishes, if a more easy and speedy Method of recovering small Debts, within the same, could be obtained: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, with such Powers and Authorities, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Coal Owners, Fitters, and Ship Owners, of the Port and Haven of Sunderland, near the Sea, in the County of Durham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Port and Haven of Sunderland is the Second Port in the Kingdom, respecting its Consequence in the exporting of Coals, vending about 260,000 Nezccastk Chaldrons 03

Annually, in about 5,000 Sail or Ships Loadings, which Trade (from the Nature of the Place, being a dry Harbour) is attended with great Expence, Pains, and Danger, the Ships having generally to take in a considerable Part of their Loading in the Road or open Sea, which renders the Trade extremely dangerous, and is now made much more so by a Clause in a late Act of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for the better Regulation of " the Coal Trade," which enacts, " That from and after " the lft Day of August 1785 it shall not be lawful " for any Collector, Comptroller, or other Officer " or Officers of His Majesty s Customs, in any Port, " Harbour, or Creek, within the Kingdom of " Britain, to clear Coastwise, or for Parts beyond " the Seas, any Ship or Vessel whatsoever, laden, or " in Part laden, with Coals, Culm, or Cinders, nor " to sign, issue forth, or grant, any Cocquet, Letpals, Transire, or other Dispatch or Dispatches, " of any Nature or Kind whatsoever, for the clearing Outwards, either for a Coalting Voyage, or " a Voyage for Parts beyond the Seas, any such Ship " or Vessel, until the Master, Commander, or other " Person or Persons, taking Charge of such Ship or " Vessel, shall and do produce and deliver to the Collector, or other proper Officer of the Customs, at " such Port, Harbour, Haven, or Creek, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, where such Ship or " Vessel is lo laden, or in Part laden, as aforesaid, " Two Certificates from the Fitter or Fitters, or other " Person or Persons vending or delivering the Coals, " Culm, or Cinders, with which such Ship or Vessel " shall be laden, or in Part laden, as aforesaid, expressing the real Quantity so vended and delivered," whereby a very great Inconvenience and Hardship arises to a Number of the Owners of Ships belonging to the said Port, which Ships are obliged, for Want of Water upon the Bar, to eompleat their Loading in the Roads or open Sea, frequently from Twenty to Thirty, Forty or Fifty Sail at a Time, exposed to every Gale of Wind, the Commanders whereof, for Safety, are frequently obliged to flip or cut their Cables, get to Sea as fast as possible, and are frequently forced away without the Matter, or any Dispatches, which latter Dispatches are obliged to be sent to them, when informed by Post where they have arrived at, and the said Ships are detained at a great Expence, and their Cargoes cannot be delivered till the Dispatches arrive; and that the Expence of letting the Master or Commanders on Shore, and on Board, is very considerable, on Account of the great Danger that attends it, and there have been frequent Instances of Three Guineas having been paid for the Use of a Coble to set a Captain on Board, after he has been at the Custom House getting his Dispatches, and several Misfortunes have already happened by People being drowned in attempting to go off to their Ships; and that the Duties on Coals Coastwise are paid at the Delivering Port, by the Returns from which Port the Ships Burthens are ascertained by taking the Average of the Quantity they deliver for a Number of Voyages, and they are thereby rated, of consequence therefore can make no Difference to, or injure the Revenue in the least Degree; and that the Coals at the said Port are always east in the Day Time, which being the Time appointed by the Customs for clearing the Ships, viz. from Nine to Twelve of the Clock in the Forenoon, and from Two to Four in the Afternoon, the aforesaid Clause subjects the Owners to a considerable Expence, in paying the Officers Extra Fees for clearing the Ships out of Office Hours: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Petitioners Hardttiips into Consideration, and suffer their Ships, when properly rated, and clearing Coast-wile, to be cleared by that Rate, before they be fully

loaded,

and that a li-confed Theatre is much wanted in that Part of the Kingdom, and it will be also beneficial to the said Town, if His Majesty was enabled to grant Letters Patent for establishing a Theatre or Playhouse in the said Town, or the Liberties thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for better cleansing the Streets, Lanes, and public Ways, and Market Places, within the said Town, and the Liberties thereof, and for keeping the same free from all Nuisances and Annoyances, and for enabling the Petitioners, at the Expence of the said Corporation of Newcastle, to widen and enlarge the said Streets, Lanes, public Ways, and Market Places, and to make and open new Streets, Lanes, public Ways, and Market Places, and proper Communications therewith, where it shall be necessary or expedient, and also to enable the Petitioners (when in Common Council assembled) to make and ordain Orders, Rules, and Regulations, relating to the public Vol. 41.

A Petition of the Commissioners and Trustees, whole Names are thereunto fubl'cribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rell of the Commissioners and Trustees named, appointed, and elected, to put in Execution an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for laying out, making, and keeping " in Repair, a Road, proper for the Passage of Troops " and Carriages, from the City of Carlisle to the Town " of Newcastle upon Tyne," l'o far as the same relates to that Part of the said Road which doth lie in the County of Northumberland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Trustees, appointed to put the said Act into Execution in the County of Northumberland, several Years ago, caused the said Road to be made and completed, and have ever since applied the Money arising by the Tolls in carrying on the Repairs thereof, but the same is so very inadequate to keeping the said Road in Repair, that, not only a considerable Sum of Money is now due to Persons who did repair a Part of the said Road, but there is also a large Arrear of Wages due to several poor Labourers, who have, from Time to Time, been employed in repairing the said Road; and that the said Road is the great and common Road from Newcastle upon Tyne to Carlisle, and by Means of many heavy Carriages passing and re-passing thereon with narrow Wheels, a Vol. 41.

great Part of the said Road, which lies in the County of Northumberland, is in a ruinous Condition, having several steep Hills, large Watercourses, Drains, and Bridges, lying in and upon the fame, which cannot be effectually repaired and kept without a very great and extraordinary Expence, and the Materials used for the greatest Part of the said Road lying at a considerable Distance, it is im-

j o # m9

possible to complete and keep the said Road in Repair, unless greater and other Tolls are granted, and the Trustees enabled to borrow such Sums of Money upon the Credit of the New Tolls, as shall by them be deemed necessary to discharge the aforesaid Arrears, and to put the said Road into complete Repair; and that the completeing the Repairs of the said Road, so as to make it proper for the Passage of Troops and Carriages, will not. only be of National Benefit, but will tend greatly to the Improvement of the Landed Estates in the Neighbourhood, and the Increase of Trade and Commerce in the County of Northumberland, the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, the City of Carlisle, and Parts adjacent, and the Commercial interest of the Kingdom in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for repealing the said former Act, and for amending and enlarging the Powers thereby granted, and for more eflfeftually repairing, and keeping in Repair, the said Road, and for other the Purposes aforesaid, in fudi Manner, and by such Means, as to the House shall seem meet'.

Mr- Michael Angelo Taylor, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report, which, upon the 22d Day of February last, was made frorq the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Encouragement and Extension, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were readand are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Ten Shillings per Ton be laid upon every Ship or Vessel (not being British-buWt, owned by British Subjects, and navigated according to Law) importing Turbots or Lobsters into Great.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That upon all Turbots, measuring from the Eye to the Extent of the Tail Sixteen Inches, which shall be caught by the Crews of British Vessels of the Burthen of Fifty Ions or upwards, and imported into the Port of London, for the Term of Three Years, there shall be paid a Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Score; for all such Turbots, lo imported in the next succeeding Year, there 01

shall be paid a Bqunty of Twenty Shillings per Score; and for all such Turbots, so imported in the Year then next following, there shall be paid a Bounty of Ten Shillings per Score.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Bounty of Fifty Pounds be allowed for the greatest Number of Turbots, of the Dimensions aforesaid, caught and imported into the Port of London, in any One Year, by any British Vessel; that a Bounty of Forty Pounds be allowed for the next greatest Number of such Turbots so caught and imported within the same Period; and that a Bounty of Thirty Pounds be allow'ed for the next greatest Number of such Turbots so caught and imported within the same Period.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Lampreys, Lamperns, or Wilks, should, for a Time to be limited, be exported from. Great Britain, in any Ship or Vessel, unless such Ship or Vessel shall be -BrfrisA-built, owned by British Subjects, navigated according to Law, and fitted for the Cod Fishery.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Lampreys, or Lamperns, should, for a Time to be limited, be exported, in any One Vessel whatever, at any One Time, in any greater Number than Two thou-faqd; and that no Wilks should be exported, in any One Vessel whatever,' at any One Time, in any greater Quantity than Thirty-six Bushels.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Michael Angelo Taylor, Mr.

Beaufoy, and the Marquis of Graham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of Sir Thomas Dundas, Baronet, Sir Janies Bridges; Riddell, Baronet, Sir Hector Murvro, Knight of the Scotland. Bath, George Ross, Duncan Davidson, Kenneth Mackenzie, Alexander Gray, John Mackenzie, John Alexander Brodie, James Baillie, Simon Fraser, and Colin

Mackenzie, Esquires, for themselves, and on Behalf of the other Land Owners and Inhabitants of the Counties of Inverness, Ross, Caithness, and Die Orkney Islands, and Boroughs therein, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the large and rapid Rivers, catled Bewley and Conon, run across the Country immediately

to the Northward of Inverness, from the Mountains to the East Sea, and it is the singular Condition of both those Rivers to be absolutely without a Bridge from their Sources down to their respective Friths, from which uncommon Circumstance the large and populous Northern District above mentioned is sometimes utterly in-accdfible, and always reached, through dangerous Fords and Ferries, with great Inconveniency, and not un-frequently with the Lol's of Lives; and that the Funds and Abilities of the said District have been totally exhausted by making long Tracts of good Roads, and constructing numerous Bridges, feme on large, and others on smaller Streams, without the Assistance hitherto -of any public Aid to effect those laborious and expensive Undertakings, in the Counties to the Northward of the said Rivers, which Rivers run partly through, and partly contiguous to, Two of the most considerable of the late forfeited Estates, now restored to the Heirs of the former Proprietors; and that during the Time the said Estates were in the Hands of the Public, the Commissioners appointed for their Management entered at different Times upon various Proceedings for building Bridges on the said Rivers Conon and Bewley, and paying the Expences out of the Rents of the said Estates, but those Rents having been from Time to Time otherwise applied, neither were the said Bridges, nor any other public Work, carried on upon the said Northern Estates, nor in that Quarter of the Highlands where they lie, although their Rents were regularly levied for the Public, and were intended by Parliament for general Improvements in those Parts, as well as in other Quarters of Scotland; and that the late Grants of the forfeited Estates are charged with Payment into the Exchequer in Scotland of certain Sums, subject to the future Disposition of Parliament, and it being understood to be the Intention of Parliament to dispose of these Sums in useful and necessary public Improvements in Scotland, the Two Bridges above mentioned are conceived to be primary Objects of that Description, as nearly serving to complete the only Part that now remains unfinished of a Line of Communication from one End of the Island to the other, and the Expence of building the aforesaid Bridges is computed at about 10,000l.: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for appropriating the Sum of 10,000l. of the unexhausted Balance, which is subject to the Disposition of Parliament, directed by an Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign to be paid into the Court of Exchequer in Scotland, by the several Persons to whom the forfeited Estates in Scotland, are granted, towards building Bridges over the Rivers Bewley and Conon, in North Britain.

and St. John, bitants of the Parishes of Saint Margaret and estnuns r. j0f}n the Evangelist, in the City of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, an Act of Parliament was made for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Parishes, atld the Vestrymen of the said Pdrilhes are thereby authorized to make a Rate or Assessment upon the Inhabitants, not exceeding Six Pence in the Pound of the Yearly Rent or Value of their respective Houses, Tenements, and other Buildings, for defraying the Expence of maintaining and supporting the said Watch and Beadles; and, in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, another Act was made for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said City and Liberty, which directs, that the Number of Watchmen within the said Parishes Of Margaret and Saint John, having Beats, or Stands, shall be Forty or more, and the Number to patrol the Streets shall be Six at the least; and that, since the passing of the said Act of the Fourteenth of His present Majesty, it was judged neceflhry, for the Safety and Protection of the Persons and Properties of the Inhabitants, that a greater Number of Watchmen than is required by the said Act should be constantly employed within the said Parishes, thb Annual Expence whereof has amounted nearly to the whole Money received from the said Rate or Assessment; and that, nottwithstanding the great Number of Watchmen employed as aforesaid, several very daring Robberies and Burglaries were, in the Year 1782, committed within the said Parishes, whereupon it was found necessary to employ an additional Number of Men as a Patrol, but the Money arising from the Rate or Assessment authorized to be made as aforesaid not being sufficient to defray the Expence thereof, a Subscription was entered into by rtiany of the said Inhabitants, whereby a sufficient Sum hath been cOllefted for defraying such Explehce; and that the Petitioners are convinced, that the eftUbliffi-ing the said additional Patrol hath been the Means of . preventing matiy Bobberies and Burglaries within the said Parishes, and it is highly expedient the same should be continued, but as there is ild other Mode of railing Money to defray the Expence thereof, than by voluntary Subscription, which is not only partial and uncertain, but has of late greatly decreased, the Petitioners have reason to apprehend, that the Ibid additional Patrol canndt be continued, unless some certain PtOvision be established for raising Money to defray the Expence thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioners to raise a Ihiall additional Rate upon the Inhabitants, for decaying the Expence of supporting a proper and sufficient Patrol within the Ibid Parishes, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Shop Tax. A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the City of

Glasgow, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Tax laid upon the Petitioners, by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for. granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great Britai?t, is felt by them as a partial and unequal Burthen; and that the Petitioners consider the Principle of Taxation, like the Principle of Legilla-tion, as proceeding from the same Authority, to be Justice and Equity, and this Principle, when applied to Taxation, is Equality, or, io other Words, that

the whole Members of the State ought to be oblig-

O O

ed to contribute equally, according to their Circumstances, towards the Public Exigencies; and that. the Petitioners pay cheerfully the other Taxes. imposed by Law, along with their fellow Subjects, and, from the Nature of the Business, many of them are the Contributors or Collegers of a much greater Quantity of Taxes than any other Order of the State, the greater Part of Commodities, and Manufactures under Taxation necessarily passing through their Hands, and, in several Instances, the Advance for Taxes the Petitioners are obliged to make lqng be- fore Sale or Consumption, is a Species of additional.

Burthen; and that, considering these Circumstances, and upon Account of the; great Charges necessarily ‘ attending a Retail Shop Trade, there appeared to be Jess Reason for loading the Petitioners with an additional Personal Tax, than any other-Order of the-State; and that the Shop Tax is in Fa6t. a very heavy Personal additional Tax upon the Petitioners, more than-is paid by the other Subjects, and could not fail to be felt by them as an . unequal Burthen, for it is impossible to proportion it upon the Consumere, as may be done with Taxes on particular- Articles, as, in this Cafe, there are no particular Consumers to apply it to, it falls upon the Shopkeeper alone, and the Petitioners can tee no Reason why Retail Shopkeepers should be the only Members of the State tingled out to bear ah additional Personal Tax,: And therefore the Petitioners, relying upon the Justice of the House, have the most confident Hope and Expectation that they will repeal the Tax complained of.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Robert Taylor, all of London, Merchants and Owners of Ships, being a Committee appointed by the Merchants and Owners of Ships in London, and the other Ports of the Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; reciting an Act, made in the Seventh Year of King "George the Second, to settle how for Owners of Ships shall be answerable For the Acts of the Masters or Mariners; and Setting forth, That, on the Decifidn of a Cause which was lately tried in the Court of King’s Bench, the Judges of that Court declared the Caw to be, that Captains and Owners of Ships and Vessels are respectively answeraMe for the full Value and Amount of all Goods and Merchandize put on Board their Ships, in case the same are loft by Robbery, Fire, or any Accident, other than by Enemies, the Perils of the Seas, or the Act of Cod, or unless the Matter, or feme of the Ship's Company, are privy to such Robbery, in which same alone the Refyonfibility of the Owners is, by the above-mentioned Act of Parliament, limited to the Value of the Ship and Freight; and representing to the House, That the Petitioners and all other Merchants and Owners of Ships, in this Kingdom, are in a most disagreeable and dangerous Situation, on Account of die Responsibility to which they are ex-poled as the Law now stands, and the Alarm which nas spread itself through the City of London, and other Ports of the Kingdom, may tend to dil'courage Merchants and others from being interested in Shipping, and occasion the Decrease of Ships and VeflTds: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the said Act of Parnanaent, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled,

An Act to lettie how far Owners of Ships shall be M anfoerable for the Acts of the Matters or Mariners," and that the same Relief may be given to die Owners of Ships in Cafes of Robbery, in which the Matters or Mariners are not concerned, as they now have under the said Act of Parliament where they are concerned, and that they may be discharged from all Responsibility in Cafes of Lois or Damage occasioned from Accidents by Fire, or that they maybe relieved in such Manner as by the House shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Samuel Thotntonand Mr. Alderman Watson do prepare, and brbig in, the fame.

A Petition of Joseph Iodin Mauvoir, being of- Mauvou* fered to be presented to the House; Claim*.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner, in September 1775, fitted out a Ship called La Grue, from Nantes, for the Coast of Africa, where Ihe arrived in November following, end continued trading for Slaves till the 15th Day of July 1776, when, at a Time of profound Peace between Great Britain and France, lhe was violently seized at Portudal (a French Factory) by The Lord Dartmouth', armed Ship, which was feut . from Fort Lewis, in the River Senegal, for that Purpose, by Matthias Macnamara, Esquire, then Lieute--nant Governor and Commander in Chief of His Majesty’s Province of Senegambia; and that the Petitioner, on being informed of this Transaction, made Application to his Most Christian Majesty’s Ministers for Redrels, who transmitted an Account thereof to His Britannic Majesty’s Ministers, who protnifed to give immediate Orders to have the Matter investigated, and to satisfy the Petitioner, in case the Transaction proved to be as he had represented it; and that the Rupture, which loon after took place between Great Britain and France, prevented for a long Time any further Steps befog taken for the Relief of the Petitioner, and, in Consequence of the said Seizure, . the Petitioner has, for near Ten Years pali, futfered the greatest Distrefe, being wholly unable to answer the Debts contrafted in fitting out the said Ship: .

And therefore praying the House to take his same . into Consideration, and grant him such Relief as the Hardships and Losses he has undergone shall entitle him to.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Rose, the Marquis of Graham, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

A Petition of several Persons whole Names are End Florida, thereunto subscribed, befog Planters and Proprietors .'

of

‘ 1

26 Geo. III. 6 Martiu 297

of Lands in East Florida, in Behalf of themselves, and others, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the Houi'e, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read, Setting forth, That, after the Peace of 1763, by which the Province of East Florida became vested in the Crown, His Majesty in Council, or by delegated Authority to the Governor of East Florida, conferred upon the Petitioners Grants of Lands in the said Province, and several others have, at different Times, made Purchases therein; and that many of the Petitioners, relying on the Validity of the said Grants and Titles, as well as upon the Protection and Encouragement of Government, held out to them by repeated public Authorities, began and persevered in the Settlement and Improvement of the said Province, and many others of the Petitioners, who received limilar Grants, had prepared to cultivate, and would have cultivated, their Lands under such Grants, bad they not been prevented by the American War, and the Irruptions of the Americans into the Province, which not only put a Stop to all new Cultivation, but destroyed a great Part of the Improvements which had been already carried into Execution; and that many of the Petitioners expended large Sums of Money in Buildings, in clearing and cultivating-Lands, and in various other Means consonant to the Purpose of Advantage to themselves, and of increasing the Power of His Majesty’s Dominions, by rendering East Florida a populous and a flourishing Province, and the Lands bad already produced Sugar, Tobacco, Cotton, Corn, Rice, Indigo, Lumber, and Naval Stores, and were capable of producing other valuable Articles of Commerce, so that the Petitioners not only entertained the most reasonable Expectation of speedy Returns for their Rilque and Expenditures, but had before them the fair Prospect of establishing considerable growing Estates ' for themselves and their Posterity; and that, during the Rebellion in North America, the Province of East Florida continued inflexible in its Loyalty to the King, and Attachment to the Laws and Constitution of the Mother Country, chearfully submitting to may heavy Losses from Invasions, and from the Measures necessarily adopted for the Defence of the Province, and no Part of the Province was subdued either by the Americans, or by the natural Enemies of Great Britain, but the Whole thereof remained entire, and in full Possession of His Majesty at the Conclusion of the War; and that, by the Articles of the late Peace, East Florida was ceded to the King of Spam, in consequence of which Ceifion the Petitioners have been obliged to relinquish all their Lands, are in a great Degree deprived of the rest of their Property in the said Province, and many of them subject to the absolute Ruin of their Fortunes: And that the Petitioners, trusting in the Strength of their Claims, founded on that Regard which the Laws of all civilized States have paid to the sacred Rights of private Property, justified by the Analogy of every same where that Property has been taken for the Purpose of public Utility, and supported by the general Policy, Justice, and Good Faith of the British Government, therefore pray the House, to permit them to substantiate their Losses, and to grant them such Compenfetion as may be adequate thereto.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

That the Parish of Westbury is large and populous, and the Poor therein exceeding numerous, and although it confilts of many Tythings, and Two Hamlets, in each of which there is a Church or Chapel, yet, with refjiect to the Management of the Poor, it is considered as On Parish, and governed by Four Overseers only; and that the Overseers Annually chosen, being frequently People in a large Way of lluftness, generally execute the Office by interested Deputies, whereby the Money granted for the Relief of the Poor is often mifepplied, and carelessly given away to improper Objects, and the Poor Rates within the said Parish Annually increase, to the great Grievance of the Persons pacing to the Relief of the Poor, which, the Petitioners apprehend, might in a great Degree be prevented, if Power was given to appoint a fit and proper Person as an additional Overseer for the sole Purpose of looking after the Poor of the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for that Purpose, under such Regulations as may be thought proper and requisite.

A Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and several other principal Inhabitants of the Parish of i Barking, in the County of Essex, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Poor of the said Parish are, of late Years, greatly increased, and are supported at a very considerable Expence, and there is not any Workhouse belonging to the Parish for their Reception and Employment, and, if a proper Workhouse was provided within the said Parish, the Poor might be much better maintained, and at a less Expence, than they are at present; and that, many Years ago, a Free Grammar School was established within the said Parish, and Two large Buildings were erected, one for the School, and the other for a House for the Schoolmaster, and the Annual Sum of 20/. was made payable to the Schoolmaster, but no Provision being made for repairing the said Buildings, the same are become in a very ruinous Condition, and the School is of little Benefit to the Parish; and that, if Power was given to convert the Premisses whereon the said Buildings are erected, for extending the Workhouse intended to be built on other Premisses very conveniently situate and adjoining the said

School-house, which are now offered to the Petitioners ou very reasonable Terms, and also to appropriate the said Sum of 20/. per Annum towards educating the Children of those really Poor of the said Parish, whole Parents are as unwilling as nnable to give them such Education, but keep them at home in a State of Ignorance, as a Plea for receiving Relief from the Parochial Taxes, and train them in Vice, to the Destruction of their Morals, it would be of very great Advantage to the said Parish; and that there is within the Town of Barking a common Wharf, where divers heavy and bulky Commodities, such as Corn, Coals, Chalk, Lime, Timber,

Bricks, and Sand, are landed at, or embarked from, and are suffered to remain thereon for a considerable Time, to the great Injury of the said Wharf, and the Obflruftion and Annoyance of Persons making use of the fame, and it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Parish, if some Provision was made to oblige Persons to remove such heavy and bulky Commodities within a reasonable Time, and to regulate all *

Vessels lying at the said Wharf; and that One of the public Streets within the said Town leads to and communicates with the said Wharf, and great Numbers of Carriages heavy laden pass to and from the same along the said Street, to the great Injury thereof, and the said Wharf and Street are repaired and supported by the Inhabitants of the said Parish, at a very heavy Expence, and no Toll or Duty is authorized to be collected, either for the Use of the said Wharf, or for the Passage of Carriages along the said Street, and the Petitioners conceive, it is reasonable, that Carriages passing along the said Street, laden with Goods and Commodities which have been landed at, or are to be embarked from, the said Wharf, or at or from any Place near thereto, should for the future be subject to a finall Toll or Duty towards defraying the Expence of keeping the said Wharf and Street in Repair; and that the effecting the several Purposes aforesaid will be of great Benefit to the Petitioners and the other Inhabitants of the said Parish, and to all Persons making use of the said Wharf:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes before mentioned, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Gascoyne, Mr. Strutt, fee.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morn-

ing, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

gathorpe, Belton, SheCpshead, Garrertdon, Thorpe and Loughborough, and there to cross the Loughborough Canal Navigation which communicates with the Trent Navigation.

Mr. William Jessop being then examined, said. That from the Termination of the Canal above described, a Navigation may be continued by Means of widening, cleansing, and deepening the River Soar, and making necessary Cuts and other Works by the Sides thereof, to or near Lady’s Bridge, in the Parish of Saint Margaret, in or near the said Town of Leicester, or to or near West Bridge, in the Parish of Saint Mary, in the said Town of Leicester, both or either of those Places — by which Means a Communication may be made with the Loughborough Navigation, and through that into The Grand Trunk Canal, and through those Tra6is to the Ports of Hull and Liverpool.

Mr. Whitworth being further examined, said. That Railways for the Conveyance of Coal, Stone, Lime, and other Goods, to or near the several Coal Pits and Lime Works, opened or to be opened or worked in the several Parishes, Townships, or Places of Coleorton, Thringstone, Staunton Harold, Osgathorpe,

Breedon, and Grace Dieu, contiguous or near to Thringstone aforesaid, and the Line of the said intended Canal, may be made and completed from the said Canal Navigation.

And both the Witnesses laid, That the making the above Canal and Navigation will be very beneficial to the Town of Leicester, and the several Places through which it is intended to pass, and will also be of general public Utility.

Mr. Michael Angelo Taylor accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to he reported to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several Duties granted by an Act, made in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within Great " tain," (except the Duty thereby charged on any House, or other Building, or Place, the Yearly Rent or Value whereof shall be 30/. and upwards) shall cease, determine, and be no longer paid or payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu and instead thereof, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty, for and upon every House, or other Building, now or hereafter to be erected, any Part of which shall, for the Time being, be used, as a Shop publicly kept open for the Purpose of carrying on any Trade, or in which shall be fold any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, by Retail, or upon every Building, or Place, used as a Shop only for the Purposes before-mentioned, a Yearly Duty, according to the several and respective Rates following, over and above all other Duties now payable; that is to say, for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Five Pounos, and under Ten Pounds, the Annual Sum of Four Pence in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Ten Pounds, and under Fifteen Pounds, the Annual Sum of Fight Pence in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Fifteen Pounds, and under Twenty Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling in the Pound of such Rent; for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Twenty Pounds, and under Twenty-five Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling and Three Pence in the Pound of such Rent; and for every such House, or other Building, or Place, of the Yearly Rent or Value of Twenty-five Pounds, and under Thirty Pounds, the Annual Sum of One Shilling and Nine Pence in the Pound of such Rent.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of Dr. Cuthbert Gordon, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, from the natural Appearance of a Vegetable Substance, plentifully produced in the Grampian Hills, in Scotland, was led to think that a Dying, or Colouring Ware, might be thence obtained, and, after many Experiments, and much Application, he had the Satisfaction of producing a Dye Ware, which answered all the Purposes Vo l.41,

to which the Foreign Dye, called Archel, had been formerly applied; and, further Trials shewed that the new Material might be, in a certain Degree, substituted for Indigo and Cochineal; and that the Proportions were soon ascertained with Precilion, the new Article saved One Third of Indigo, in striking the various Shades of Blue and Purple on Silk and Woollen, and One Fourth of Cochineal in every same where that high-priced Article was necessary, Scarlets and high Pinks excepted, and to this new-invented Dye the Petitioner gave the Appellation of Cudbear: In such Cases

it is not enough to produce an Article of Commerce,’ the Inventor has to combat not only the Prejudices which a great Number of Mankind entertain against Novelty, but, what is still more difficult, the interested Views of the Traders in those Articles, the Consumption of which is proposed to be diminished or superseded by the new Discovery; the Petitioner accordingly maintained a long Struggle of this Kind, and only succeeded at last by submitting to the extraordinary Toil of personally instructing the Dyers and Manufacturers in the Use of the Cudbear, and this done, the Petitioner, and his late Brother established a Manufactory of the Cudbear at Leith, supported by a considerable Mercantile House

in the neighbouring City of Edinburgh, but the Failure of that House, in Consequence of other Connections, brought on a Dissolution of the Partnerlbip, and' all the bad Consequences attending a sudden and unexpected Stop in an Infant Manufacture; and that the Merit, however, of the Cudbear had been by this Time so far established, that a new Company was soon afterwards formed in Glasgow", the Prejudices of the practical Dyers gave way by degrees, the new Article came into more general Use and Estimation, in Consequence of which the Importation of Archel has decreased to a Trifle, and the Importation of the Articles of Indigo and Cochineal has like w ile decreased, and will continue to decrease in the Proportions before, mentioned; the Glasgow Company have been followed by several others, and, at this Moment, the Manufacture is carried on in London, Bristol,

Leeds, and Leith: The Petitioner, however, has not escaped the Misfortune usually attendant on Inventors in the Arts; the extraordinary Expences incurred in the Manufacture and Improvement of the Cudbear, as well as the Struggle for establishing it, ccc tlioned the Contraction of considerable Debts, to discharge which he was obliged to fell out his Share in the Glasgow Company, and the Peculiarity of the Petitioner’s Situation, in being excluded from the Advantages of a Manufacture established by himself, would have been distressing, had it not been alleviated by the Hopes of new and more important Discoveries in the Art of Dying; and that the Introduction of Cudbear had already established the Dyes of Blue, Purple, and Crimson, to be used on Wool, Silk, and other Animal Substances, and the Petitioner now directed his Attention to find out Materials that might answer on the Manufactures of Cotton and Linen: His Study and Application were at lust so far rewarded, by discovering that the Vegetable Filament, by a proper Treatment, might be impressed with all the Variety of Colours, equal in Lustre, and with the same Eale and Safety to the Subject, as Woo), Silk, or other Animal Substance, and this capital Fast being established in Two or Three Instances, reallmble Grounds were given to suppose that every Individual Plant was, by a suitable Process, capable of producing one or other of the Original Colours of Light, or a Variety or Shade of that Colour, peculiar to itself, and every successive Experiment afforded an additional Proof, and determined the Petitioner to dedicate his whole Time and the Wrecks of his linall Fortune to an Investigation of the Powers of our own indigenous Plants in the Production of Colours: He selected one

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Joseph Loxdale being examined, said, That His Majesty’s Gaols, and the Houses of Correction, for the said County of Salop, and the said several Juriltliciions, are very ancient Buildings, much out of Repair, and very inconvenient, and inadequate for the Purposes of Gaols and Houfts of Correction — That the same are very unsafe for the Custody of Prisoners, inibinuch that several Prisoners have lately broke out therefrom; and that the same are very unwholesome, particularly for Want of a proper l'upply of Water. — And the Witness further said, That if a new Gaol and House of Correction for the said County, and the said several Jurisdictions, was built upon a Garden, now in the Occupation of Mr. Edward Pritchard, or upon Ground near or adjacent thereto, situate within the Parish of Mary, in the said Town of Shrewsbury, and proper Avenues opened thereto, the same would be of great Convenience and Advantage to the Public, and contribute to the Safety and Health of the Prisoners confined therein; and that, to carry the said Purposes into Execution, it will be necessary to make a Purchase of the said Garden Land and Ground, together with some Houses and other Buildings situate near the said Garden; and that it will be necessary to raise a considerable Sum of Money for those Purposes.

Then an Act, passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for building a new Shire Hall and Guildhall for the " County of Salop, and the Town of Shrewsbury, in the " said County, and for the other Purposes therein mentioned," was read, whereby it appears, that Power was given by the said Act to raise and levy any Sum, not exceeding, in the Whole, the Sum of One Shilling and Four Pence in the Pound, in due Proportion to the Assessment of the Land Tax, upon every Town, Parish, o.r Place, within the said County, and also on the Town and Liberties of Ludlow, for executing the Purposes of the said Act.

And the Witness being further examined, said, That the Money so authorized to be raised by the said Act has been found inadequate for the Purpose of making the necessary Purchases, and for compleating the said Shire Hall and Guildhall, and that the said Act is in other Respects ineffectual to answer the Purposes thereby intended. — And the Witness added, That it will be necessary to raise a further Sum of Money for those Purposes.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. James Tappenden being examined, said, That in April 1781 One of the Corning Houses, and the Dufting Mill, belonging to His. Majesty's Powder Mills at Faversham, which are under the Direction of the Board of Ordnance, blew up, and by the Explosion thereof all the Powder Mills and Works adjoining were materially injured, several Houses and Buildings in and near Faversham were destroyed, others damaged, and considerable Quantities of Furniture, and other Etiects, demolished or spoiled.

That immediately after the above Accident a Petition of the Inhabitants of the said Town, stating the before-mentioned Facts, was presented to the Board of Ordnance, praying, amongst other Things, that the said Board, wheQ the Damage sustained could be estimated, would be pleased to order the Expence thereof to be defrayed to the Sufferers.

John Groves, Esquire, being then examined, said. That at the Time the above-mentioned Accident happened* he was Mailer Bricklayer to the Board of Ordnance; that the Chief Engineer sent to him to make an Estimate of the Damages; that he took Two Assistants with him, both belonging to the Boardr one Surveyor of the Works, and the other a Clerk; that he viewed the Situation of the Houses that had been destroyed of injured, took their several Dimensions, and made an Estimate of the Damage done.

And he delivered in to Your Committee a Copy of the said Estimate, which is hereunto annexed. And being further examined, he said, that if the several Sums expressed in that Estimate had been laid out, the Sufferers would, in- his Opinion, have been exactly remftated in their Property, as it was before the Ac* cident happened — That the Powder Mills have been greatly extended since they have been in the Hands of Govfefnment, and the Quantity of Gunpowder made there is, as he believes. Ten Times greatef than h was before.

Mr. William Bakombe being then examined, laid, That there were Powder Mills at Faversham before his Memory; thfet several of the Sufferers by the late Accident were labouring People, working at the Mills; that no new Houses have been built near the said Mills since the Works of the said Mills have been extehded; and that there are now near Four Times as many Buildings in the Manufectofy of Gunpowder at the said Mills, as when he first remembers them.

SIR Joseph Mawbey reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the ChurchwardenSj Overseers of the Poor, and several of the Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Sain the County of Surrey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed; vis.'

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Levy, Esquire, being examined, said, That the said Parish of Saint Saviour is divided into Two Districts, one called The Borough Liberty, and the other The Clink, or Bishop of Winchester's Liberty — That the said first-mentioned Liberty was new paved, lighted, watched, and cleansed, and cleared from Annoyances, under the Powers Of an Act, passed in the Sixth Year Of the Reign of His present Majesty, but the Streets, Lanes, Passages, and Places, within the last mentioned Liberty, are in general ill paved, and not sufficiently cleansed, lighted, or watched, and are altb greatly annoyed by Nuisances and Obstructions.

Mr. George Gwilt, a Surveyor, being then examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence of Mr. Levy; and added, That a certain Alley or Passage, called Frying Pan JUey, leading from the High Street of the said Borough of Southwark to the Parish Church of Saint Saviour, is very narrow and incommodious.

Mr. Levy being again examined, said. It would be a great Advantage and Accommodation to the Inhabitants of the said Clink Liberty to have the Streets, Lanes, Passages, and Places, therein properly paved, Cleansed, lighted, watched, and regulated, and the said Passage called Frying Pan Alley, made of a sufficent Width throughout, but that the same cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, Labes, and other public Passages and Places, within the Clink, or Bishop of Winchesters Liberty, in the Parish 01 Saint Saviour, Southwark, in the County of Surrey; for the Removal of present, and Prevention of future, Encroachments, Nuisances, and Annoyances therein, and for widening the Alley called Frying Pan Alley, leading from the Borough of Southwark to the Parish Church of Saint Saviour aforesaid; And that Sir Joseph Mawbey and Mr. Norton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants and Citizens of the City of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that Leave has been given to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Canal, from the Stourbridge Canal Navigation, in the County of Stafford, to the River Severn, at Diglis, near the City of Worcester, and for the Improvement of the said River between the Cites of Worcester and; and that the

Petitioners have often, in dry Sealbns, experienced a great Want of Coals, and sometimes the Price thereof has been nearly double, and great Delays have been occasioned in the Carriage of the Petitioners Goods and Merchandize between the said City of Worcester, the City of Bristol, and the Town of;

and that, if the said Bill pafies into a Law, the Petitioners are fully persuaded, they shall always have a regular and constant Supply of Coals, at a much cheaper Rate than at present, and that the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize will be facilitated: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pais into a Law.

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Borough of Tewkesbury, in the County of Gloucester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have been informed, that Application hath been made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, almost in a direct Line from the extensive Collieries at or near Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, to the River Severn, at or near the City of Worcester; and

that, from the Locality of the Borough of to the Severn, the Petitioners are well allured they shall be much benefited if the said Bill pafies into a Law, by the great Influx and more regular Supply of Coal into the Secern Markets, which will consequently reduce its Price, by connecting the Towns of Stourbridge and Bronis-grcrce, and their Manufacturing Neighbourhood, with that River, and, by a Participation of the general Extenfi'on of Commerce which will naturally arise throughout the Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

CAPTAIN Fanshawe reported from the Com- Plymouth mittee, to whom the Petition of the Guardians of Poor, the Poor of the Town of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition’; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared,’ by an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of Queen Anne, That the Petitioners were incorporated, and impowered to erect a Workhouse for the Use of the Poor; and, by a subsequent Act, of the Thirty-second of King George the Second, further Powers were granted for raising the Annual Sum of 1,000l. to be applied to the Purposes before mentioned: And,

Mr. Philip Longmead being examined, said, That the Money authorized to be raised by virtue of the said last mentioned Act hath been greatly deficient to answer the Purposes thereby intended; in Confirmation of which he produced an Account, from whence it appeared, that the necessary Expences for maintaining the Poor from Lady Day 1784 to Lady Day 1785 has exceeded the Income upwards of 290 /.

The Witness further said, That the Trustees under the said Act have been obliged to borrow and take up at Interest, and on Annuities, the Sum of 2,150/. which hath been expended for the Use of the said Poor, which are become very numerous, and are still increasing — That, notwithstanding the most prudent and frugal Management of the Corporation, they must inevitably go to Decay, unless some further Provision be made to enable them to discharge their present Debts, and to impower them to raise a larger Annual Sum, more effectually to support and maintain ,the said Poor for the future.

And he added. That it will be proper to extend the Provisions of the Act of the Twenty-second Year of the present King, which intlifts a Penalty on Parish Officers, passing Persons from One Parish to another, without any legal Order of Removal, to the Town of 4 M Plymouth,

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Stourbridge Bewdley, in the County of Worcester, and the Neigh- ^atwl-bour hood thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill will be brought into Parliament for making a Canal, from a Part of the Stourbridge Canal, within about Two Miles of the Staff ordshire and Worcestershire Canal, to the City of Worcester, and also, that a Bill will be brought in for improving the Navigation of the River Severn, from or near Coalbrooh Dale, in the County of Salop, to the said City of Worcester; and that the Petitioners apprehend, beyond a Doubt, that the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Severn, seeing the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal joins the same at Stourport, in the said County of Worcester, will be exceedingly beneficial to the Public, as a certain and easy Communication will be thereby made between the principal Sea Ports and Trading Towns of the Kingdom, and, amongst many other Advantages, the Freight of Goods will thereby necessarily be reduced; and that the Petitioners conceive, the Improvement of the Navigation of the Severn will afford every Advantage to the Public, and more than the said intended Canal, if made, can afford, wherefore the Petitioners cannot but consider the said intended Canal as unnecessary and useless: And therefore praying, that the Bill for making the said intended Canal may not pals into a Law’, and submitting the Improvement of the Navigation of the Severn to the Consideration of the House.

A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are Ditto, thereunto subscribed, being Owners or Occupiers of Mills, Forges, Iron and other Works and Manufactories, Lands, and Estates, lying between Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, and the City of Worcester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, Application is making to the House for a Bill to make a new Canal Navigation, from and out of the Stourbridge Canal, to communicate with the River Severn at Diglis, near the City of Worcester; and that, below the line of the said intended Canal, there are a great Number of Forges, Iron Works, Corn, Needle, Paper, Cotton, and other Mills and Works, at which are carried on very extensive Trades, and many large Sums of Money have been expended in planting and establishing such Works and Manufactories, and not only the greatest Part of the Property of many of the Petitioners has been risqued therein, but the very Support and Maintenance of a large Body of industrious Manufacturers and Labourers depend on such Works; and that there are also large Tracts of Landed Property, below the Line of such intended Canal, naturally sandy or barren Soil, but which, at much Labour and Expence, have been improved, and are now converted

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants of Wolverhampto in the County of Stafford, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have received great Advantages from the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, by a more easy and expeditious Conveyance of Merchandize ia general, to and from all the capital Sea Ports and inland Navigations in this Kingdom, and upon more reasonable Terms than before the making thereof; and that the Petitioners are informed a Bill is, or is intended to be, brought into Parliament, for making a Canal from the Stourbridge Canal (about Two Miles from th 0 Staff and Worcestershire Navigation) to a Place called Digits Meadow, below Worcester, and, that a Bill is also intended to be brought in for the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Severn; and that such Improvement of the Severn will so greatly enlarge the Advantages the Community now receive from the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Navigation, as to render the intended Worcester Canal totally unnecessary and useless: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making such intended Canal may not pass into a Law, and recommending the Improvement of the Severn Navigation to the Consideration of the House.

And the said Petitions were federally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Stourbridge Canal Navigation to the River Severn, near to the City of Worcester, be read a Second Tune; and the second-mentioned Petitioners are to be then heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said second-mentioned Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. William Philpott being examined, said, That the said

Town and Port of Sandwich is large and populous, and a Place of great Trade — that a considerable Trade is also carried on in the several Parishes and Places mentioned in the said Two Petitions, by Reason of their Contiguity to the said Town and Port of Sandwich.

That there are many Persons to whom the Traders within the said Town and Port, and the Parishes mentioned in the said Petitions, are obliged to give Credit for small Sums of Money, which they frequently refuse to pay, not from Inability, but presuming on the Discouragements which their Creditors lie under in suing for such Debts, on Account of the Delays and Expences attending such Suits — that it would therefore tend greatly to promote Industry and support ufefol Credit in the said Port and Town, Vill, and Parishes, if a more easy and speedy Method of recovering Small Debts within the same were established, under the San&ion and Authority of Parliament.

A Petition of the Attornies of the ancient Court of the Marshalsea, and of the Court of the King’s Palace of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the last Session of Parliament for granting to His Majel'ty certain Duties on Certificates to be taken out by Solicitors, Attornies, and others, practising in certain Courts of Justice in Great Britain, and certain other Duties with respect to Warrants, Mandates, and Authorities, to be entered and filed of Record as therein mentioned, imposing a Stamp Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence upon Warrants or Authorities to foe or defend in all 08

Actions indiscriminately, as well in all inferior as in the

superior Courts of Record in this Kingdom, where the Debt or Damages amount to Forty Shillings and upwards; and that in the Court of His Majesty’s Palace of Westminster the Duties at present imposed upon Writs by virtue of the several Acts of Parliament amount to Five Shillings, including the said Duty on Warrants or Authorities where the Debt and Damages amounts to 5/. only, and the Duties upon Writs in the superior Courts at Westminster, where the Debt or Damages may amount to 10,000l. or upwards, do not exceed the said Sum of Five Shillings, including the said Duty on the said Warrants or Authorities; and that it was the Intention of the Legislature to impofo the said Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence on the said Warrants or Authorities on the Profits of die Attorney prosecuting or defending such Suit, but the said Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence, contrary to the Intention of the Legifla-ture, is, of Necessity, paid by the Clients prosecuting or defending such Suits; and that the Profits arising to the Attornies of this inferior Court, where the Cause goes to Trial, and is finally concluded, are very trifling, and it is impra6ticable that the said Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence on the said Warrants or Authorities should be paid by the Attorney personally out of the Profits arising from suing out such Writs, because the Profit of suing out such Writ amounts to no more than One Shilling and Four Pence, whereas if the said Attornies were to pay the said Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence imposed on Warrants or Authorities as aforesaid, in such same the Attorney must inevitably be One Shilling and Two Pence out of Pocket upon every such Writ; and that no Proceedings are had on Nineteen out of Twenty Writs sued out in the said Court of the King’s Palace of Westminster, but are generally settled upon the mere issuing of the Procefe, and the said additional Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence on Warrants or Authorities falls particularly heavy upon the Suitors of inferior Courts, who are in general of the lower Class of People, and are, from their Circumstances, unable to apply for Relief to any of the superior Courts of Justice; and that if it was the Intention of the Legislature to impose the Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence on Warrants or Authorities in inferior Courts, under the Idea of increasing the Revenue, it is submitted, that the same was founded in Mistake, inasmuch as it would appear, were the Petitioners permitted to give Evidence at the Bar of the House, that the Imposition of the said Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence has considerably decreased the Revenue arising from the said Writs, and other Proceedings in the said Court; and therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and administer such Relief as to them shall seem meet, and that this Petition may be referred to the Committee to whom the other Petitions on the same Subject are referred.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.
