Shop Tax. An ingrafted Bill to explain and amend an Act of the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for " granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops " within Great Britain," for repealing several of the Duties granted by the said Act, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof, was read the Third Time.

An ingrafted Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, to declare, that the Tax shall not extend to Victuallers, as such.

And the said Clause was Twice read, and amended.

And the Question being proposed, That the said Clause be read the Third Time;

The laid Clause was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

The Amendment following was proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 3. 1. 12. After " this " to inlert " or of the " said recited."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act to explain and amend an Act of the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Duties on Shops within " Great Britain," for repealing several of the Duties granted by the said Act, and for granting other Duties in lieu thereof.

Hawkers and A Petition of the Manufacturers and Wholesale

Pedlars. Traders in Kendal, in the County of Westmorland, was presented to the House, and read; Recommending the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars to the Attention and Protection of the House, as a most frugal, industrious, and ufeiul Clafe of People, and not only greatly instrumental in promoting the Trade of the Petitioners, but also of the whole Body of Manufacturers of this Kingdom, whose Goods and Msmufactures they are enabled, from their Frugality and Mode of Living, to afford to their Customers on better Terms than they could otherwise be furnished, as well to the great Encouragement of such Manufactures, as to the Increase of the Revenue; V01. 41.

and Setting forth, That the Trade of the Hawkers and Pedlars being founded on the Faith of several Acts of Parliament, hath been long ago brought into, and continued in, a regular Channel, and extensive Credit given, as well by the Petitioners to them, as by them to their Customers; and that if the pth and 1 ith Clauses of an *

Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their Trade, be enforced, the necessary Consequences thereof must be the total Suppression of the fair Trade of the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars, by which a very considerable Part of the Debts due to them, and to the Petitioners from them, must be unavoidably loft, and, in such Case, their Places will be supplied by Smugglers, who will immediately Convey into the Countries, in which the Hawkers now travel, contraband Goods of every Denomination, to the Injury of the fair Trader, and the Decrease of the Public Revenue: And therefore praying the House to remove the Restrictions of the 9th and 11th Clauses of the said Act, and to give such Encouragement and Protection to the Trade of the licensed Hawkers and Pedlars as the Nature of their same may require, and to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House was moved, That the Entries in the East India Journal of the House, of the 28th Day of May 1782, Affairs, of the Six first Resolutions reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the several Reports which had been made from the Committees of Secrecy relating to the Affairs of the East India Company, and which were then agreed to by the House, might be read.

And the same were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as folio wet h; viz.

" Resolved, That the Orders of the Court of Directors of the East India Company, which have " conveyed to their Servants Abroad a prohibitory Condemnation of all Schemes of Conquest and Enlargement of Dominion, by prescribing certain Rules and " Boundaries for the Operation of their Military Force, ♦

" and enjoining a strict Adherence to a Syfiem of Defence upon the Principle of the Treaty of " were founded no less in Wisdom and Policy than in " Justice and Moderation.

" Resolved, That every Transgression of those Orders,

"without evident Necessity, by any of the several British " Governments in India, has been highly represensible,

and has tended, in a chief Degree, to weaken the " Force and Influence, and to diminish the Resources,

" of the Company in those Parts.

" Resolved, That every Interference, as a Party, in the Domestic or National Quarrels of the Country " Powers, and all new Engagements with them in oft'enfive Alliance, have been wifely and providently forbidden by the Company in their Commands to their " Administrations in India.

" Resolved, That every unnecessary or avoidable " Deviation from those well-advised Rules should be " followed with very leverc Represension and Punishment for it, as an Instance of wilful Disobedience of " Orders, and as tending to disturb and destroy that " State of Tranquillity and Peace with all their Neighhours, the Preservation of which has been recommended as the first Principle of Policy, to the British " Governments in India.

" Resolved, That the Maintenance of an inviolable " for Moderation, good Faith, and scrupulous " Regard to Treaty, ought to have been the timple " Grounds on which the British Government should " have endeavoured to establish an Influence liiperior to that of other Europeans over the Minds of the native

4 R " Powers

" Powers in India; and that the Danger and Discredit " anting from the Forfeiture of this Pre-eminence could " not be compensated by the temporary Succels of any li. Plan of Violence or Injustice.

" Resolved, That as any essential Failure in the exe-

" cutive Conduct of the Supreme Council or Presidencies " would make them justly liable to the most serious " Animadversions of their Superiors, so should any " Relaxation, without sufficient Cause, in these Principies of good Government, on the Part of the Directors " themselves, bring upon them, in an heavier Degree, " the Resentment of the Legislative Power of their " Country, which alone can interpose an effectual Correction to the general Misrule."

" Resolved, That it appears, that the Government

" General had been previously in Possession of a Letter " from the Duan of the Rajah of Berar, containing " Overtures for Mediation for Peace and Alliance with " the Pefliwa; and that this material Information was " wholly suppressed by them in their Dispatches to the " Court of Directors, but a Copy of it was sent, by the " same Conveyance, to the private Agent of Mr. Hast- ings; and that, in thus neglecting to make immediate

Communication to the Court of Directors of such " important Intelligence, the Government General appear " to have failed in an essential Part of their Duty."

Hawkers and A Petition of the Traders and Manufacturers in the Tedlars. city of Glasgow, and the Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Hawkers and Pedlars have been of very considerable Use in promoting, encouraging, and extending the Manufactures of this Country, by introducing them into Parts where they otherwise would not have been known; and that, under the Sanction of repeated Acts of Parliament, they have carried on their Trade, and engaged very considerable Sums, trusting that the Rights and Privileges granted by the Legislature would have been continued to them, but, by the 9th and 11 th Sections of an Act, passed in the lafit Session of Parliament, their Privileges are taken away, and unless repealed will reduce many Thousands of industrious People to Ruin and Beggary, not only without any Advantage to Government, but to the evident Prejudice of many of the Manufactures of this Country: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter under Consideration, and repeal those Clauses, or grant such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of James Ferguson, Esquire, of Pitfour, Aberdeen was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That the Election of a Member, to serve in Parliament for the County of Aberdeen, came on at Aberdeen, on Tuesday the 28th of February last, and George Skene, of Skene, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates at the said Election; and that at the said Election, One Freeholder, who afterwards tendered his Vote for the Petitioner, was unjustly expunged by a Majority of those standing on the Roll, and sundry Gentlemen, who produced unexceptionable Titles, and claimed to be inrolled, were illegally rejected by the same Majority, and these Gentlemen likewise tendered their Votes for the Petitioner; and that clear legal Objections were offered so many Freeholders in the Interest of Mr. Skene, w'hich were disregarded by the same pretended Majority of the Freeholders, although they ought to have been expunged from the Roll, or excluded from voting, and the Objections stated ought to have been fultaiued; and that Objections were likewise offered to sundry Claimants in the Interest of Mr. Skene, which were disregarded, though they were well founded in Law, and ought to have been sustained, nevertheless the said George Skene, Esquire, has been returned as duly elected; and that the Number of Freeholders, actually on the Roll, who voted for the Petitioner, or tendered their Votes for him, under Protest, after having been unduly expunged, or unjustly rejected, exceeds the Number of those who voted lor Mr. Skene, at least when those in his Interest are deducted who were continued on the Roll, but ought to have been expunged, or who were unduly admitted thereto, or lay under Disabilities which incapacitated them from voting; from all which it appears, that the Petitioner was duly elected, and the Return ought to be altered accordingly: And therrfore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and give such Redress therein as to them shall seem meet.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 9th Day of May next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " Tuesday, the 9th " Day of May," and inferring the Words " Thursday,

" the 27th Day of April," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Tuesday, the 9th Day of May" stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Thursday, the 27th Day of April," be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday, tire 27th Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of Sir Archibald Grant, of Baronet, Alexander Leith, of Freefield, Esquire, and John Taylor, Esquire, Purchaser of Part of the Estate of Belhelxie, Freeholders of the County of Aberdeen,

and having a Right to vote at the Elettion for a Knight of the' Shire to serve in Parliament for the said County, was also delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That at the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said County of Aberdeen, on the 28th Day of February last, George Skene, of Skene, and James Ferguson, of Esquire, offered

themselves Candidates to represent the said County in Parliament; and that at the said Election One Freeholder, who afterwards tendered his Vote for Mr. Ferguson, was unjustly expunged, by a Majority of those standing on the Roll, and sundry Gentlemen who produced unexceptionable 'Titles, and claimed to be inrolled, but were illegally rejetted by the same Majority, also tendered their Votes for him: and that clear legal Objections, offered to many Freeholders in the Interest of Mr. Skene, were disregarded by the same pretended Majority, although they ought to have been expunged from the Roll, or excluded from voting, and Objections were likewise offered to sundry Claimants in the Interest of Mr. Skene, which were disregarded, though they were well founded in Law, and ought to have been sustained, and thus the find George Skene, Esquire, has been returned as duly elected; and that the Number of Freeholders attually on the Roll, who voted for Mr. Ferguson, or tendered their Votes for him, under Protest, after having been unduly expunged, or unjustly rejetted, exceeds the Number of those who voted for Mr. at least when those in his Interest are dedutted who were continued on the Roll, but ought to have been expunged, or were unduly admittted thereto, or lay under Disabilities which incapacitated them from voting; from all which it appears, that the said James Ferguson, Esquire, was duly eletted, and the Petitioners therefore think themselves much aggrieved, and apprehend that the aforesaid Elettion and Return in Favour of Mr. Skene is an undue Election and Return, and they flatter themselves, that the same will be deemed by the House null and void, and hope that the said Janies Ferguson, Esquire, will be found entitled to fit in the House as Knight of the Shire for the said County of Aberdeen: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, and have such other Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the Gentlemen of the Grand Jury for > the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That it hath been represented to the Petitioners, that building a Bridge over the River Trent, at or near to the Ferry above Gainsborough, in the County of Lincoln, will be of gieat public Utility, by making a certain and safe Communication between the County of Lincoln and the Counties of Nottingham and York, which in its present State is ibmetunes impassable by Floods and Frost, and frequently very dangerous, the only Communication between those Counties from the Town of Newark to the River Humber, an Extent of Sixty Miles and upwards, being by Ferries acrose the River Trent; and that the Trade and Connections between the said Counties of Lincoln and York are very considerable, not only as to the Wool and Corn grown in the said County of Lincoln, but Cattle which are brought in large Numbers to the Fairs and Markets in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and for Want of a certain Communication such Trade and Intercourse are often interrupted: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given not only for bringing in a Bill for the building a Bridge over the said River Trent, but that the same may pals into a Law.

Sir George Howard reported from the Committee, Hand of to whom the Petition of the Persons whole Names are St. Eufotius. thereunto subscribed, being Persons entitled to a Share of the Property captured at the Itland of Saint Eustatius, on Behalf of themselves, and all others entitled to the said captured Property, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had direfiled him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Lieutenants Henry Martin and George Lewis being examined, said, That they, together with the Petitioners, served on board the Fleets as Marines, although in the Army, and w ere present at the Capture of the Island of Saint Eustatius, in the Year 1781, and of the Property found' therein.

And it appeared to Your Committee, by Instructions sent to the Commanders in Chief of the said Island, dated the 30th of March 1781, that His Majesty relinquished, in Favour of the Captors, His Right in the said Property, upon the Conditions therein specified.

[Copy of which Instructions are subjoined to this Report.]

Then,

Mr. Martin being further examined, said. That by general Reputation Colonel Cockbume, Colonel Fer-gusson, Mr. Forster, Mr. Acres, the Reverend Mr.

Paget, and Captain Young, afited as Agents for the Navy and Army, to collect and dispose of the said captured Property, and accordingly possessed themselves of the fame. — He further said, That the Commanders in Chief were upon the Island at the Time, and that the Nomination of these Agents by them was confirmed by the Assent of the Majority of the Officers.

And being asked w hether any Part of the Property has been dispersed ? he replied, Yes; feme has been sent to Saint Kitt's, and feme* to England, but he does not

5 B know

37° 21° Martii. - A. ij86*

know that the whole Produce of the Capture is within :ius. the Power of the Agents, as lie has heard Part of it has been paid to the Commanders in Chief, and the Remainder is in Possession of the said Agents.

And being asked. Whether he meant, by dispersed, that the Agents dispossess’ed them (elves of the Property ? he laid, He meant that they allowed the Produce of the Sales to get into hands, were it was certain the Captors never intended it should be. — And being further asked, Whether any Part of the Property was put out of the Power of the Agents ? he anl’wcred. He coukl not say it was.

And being asked. Whether he does not conceive that the Agents are (till answerable for the Property, notwithstanding it is out of their Hands? he replied, Yes.

Being further examined, the Witness said, He believed, that at the Time of the Conquest, Saint,

tins was a free Port, and that there were Goods and Merchandize as well as Shipping found there, the Property of various Nations, for some of which Articles he has hpard there have been Claims, as to the Number or the Amount he could not speak to; but he has heard some have been given in Favour of the Captors, and some in Favour of the Claimants, and Rel'titution awarded — That about Six Months ago he heard that the Claims that were*, then depending and unadjudged were reduced to Four.

And being asked, Supposing no Adjudication to have pa<Ted on these Claims, are not. the Agents bound to hold the Property in their Hands for the true Owners, till the Suits are determined? he said, He should think so, to the Amount of the Property claimed, not the whole Property — That he is of Opinion the Agents have a Power over all the Property -in their Hands, except what is sufficient to answer the Claims now fubfilting — That lie always understood the Amount of the Property captured at Saint Eustatius was very great; and from general Rumour, at the Time of the Capture, was l’upposed to amount to 1,000,000l. Sterling; and he is of Opinion, that so much of the Money as is not in Dispute ought long since to have been distributed — That he never heard the Amount of the Capture after the Island was retaken by the French, but he never understood that the re-captured Property was any Thing very considerable.

And being asked, From whence he deduced an Opinion, that after the Claims that are made have been satisfied, there will be any Surplus remaining ? he answered. From the Property itself being, as he conceived, so great originally, and from his never having understood that Half of the captured Property was claimed.

Mr. Richard Tromard, who’ is Agent to the Petitioners, being next examined, informed Your Committee, That he made Application by a Bill in Chancery, at the Request of the Committee of the Army, for an Account and Distribution, against the Commanders in Chief, and the Agents for the captured Property — To this Bill Answers were put in, ltating Accounts therein of Monies received and disposed of, and shewing that great Part of the Property had been sent to different Places to be disposed of; but it does not appear by the Answers that any Account was given of the Produce of the Property so fqnt, nor has any such Account been since given, nor as any Part of the Property, to his Knowledge, been distributed; therefore no effectual Information has been obtained. — The Bill was filed in Trinity Term 1783, by Charles Ruskj Robert Garstin, and on Behalf of themselves and others present at the Capture, against Lord Rodney, General Vaughan, Janies Cockburne, Joseph Fergusson, Forster,

Acres, and William Paget; and the Answers of the Defendants, as appeal s by the Witness’s Copy of the Plead-

ings, were put in at thq following Periods; Lord Rodneys, 10th November 1784 — General Vaughans, 21st July 1784 — Mr. Forsters, 29th 1783 — Mr.

Forster's further Answer, 16th 1784 — Mr.

burne's, 24th February 1784 — Mr. Paget's, 6th November 1784 — Mr. Fergussons, 9th 1783.

And being asked, Whether he never heard that there were regular Agents appointed in England to transact the Business of the Captors? he replied, Never to his Recollection, nor did lie ever esquire who had transacted their Business in the Admiralty Court for Condemnation of the captured Property; but Mr. Jackson told him he had a Sum of Money sent to him — That he does not recollect that Mr. Jackson told him he afited in the Capacity of an Agent,

nor did the Witness consider him as such.

And being asked, Whether Mr. Jackson communicated to him the Amount of the Money transmitted ? he answered, That upon perusing the Answers, and finding Mr. Jackson's Name mentioned as having received a large Sum of Money, he had it in Contemplation to amend the Bill, and make him a Party Defendant — That the Witness sent to Mr. Jackson upon the Subject, who called upon him at his Office, and acknowledged that he had a large Sum of Money in his Hands, which he did not wish to keep; and that if the Witness chole to make him a Defendant to that Bill, he would immediately put in his Answer, and dispose of the Money as the Court should direct- — That the Witness at this Time looked on Mr.:

as the Private Agent or Banker for those from whom he received the Money, and that he was accountable to those Persons, and they answerable to the Captors t and though he talked of making Mr. Jackson a Defendant in the Suit, he did not know he should be. able to charge him with the Sum in his Hands, as between the Plaintiffs and him — That he does not recolless't that Mr. Jackson told him he was Agent; for any Body j nor does he know from whom he said he received the Money — That he understood, from the Converlation he had with Mr. Jackson, be approved of being a Party; and if he had become a Party to the Bill, the Witness has not the least Doubt. but he would have submitted to the Jurisdiction, and have paid the Money in his Hands in the uiual Way. into Court, upon Application being made for that Purpose — But the Witness did not conceive it necef- ’ fary to do that to secure the Sum remitted him, as it was his Opinion that those who remitted it to him. were answerable for it, whole Security he supposed equally good; and he thinks it would not have been the best Way for the Benefit of the Captors, that that Sum, or any other Sum of Money, should get into the Court of Chancery, because, before a Decree could be obtained, the Proceedings leading to it would be extremely tedious; and the Proceedings in the Master’s Office after the Decree, to get the Money out again to the individual Captors, must be still more tedious, as every Man’s Claim must be ascertained, though ever so final], before the Court of Chancery could part with it; and the Expence attending the Application to obtain it, in the same of a Soldier or Sailor, would probably amount to more Money than his Share of the Prize.

And being asked, Whether at the Time of filing the Bill, he was aware of the Tediousnels of the Process? he said, He was; but to get. a Discovery of the Property he thought it necessary to file the Bill, as being the only Means of procuring a Discovery upon Oath ;. and as he knew that the filing a Bill for a Discovery, without praying something more, would be attended with the Inconvenience of throwing the whole Colts upon the Party complainant, it was a Matter of Course. to pray Distribution, though at the same Time he did not suppole a Distribution would ever be made upon a Master’a Report.

And being asked, Supposing the Discovery to be obtained, and the Plaintiffs afterwards had chosen to drop the Suit and not proceed in it, would they not have been liable to Costs? he replied, Certainly J tinless Terms could have been made with the Defendants.

Being further asked, When he found the Answers the several Defendants had put in did not contain a complete Discovery, no Account having been therein given of the Property that had been dispersed, did or did he not except to those Answers? he laid, With respect to Mr. Forster, he put in a Second Answer, but whether it was in consequence of Exceptions he can- not tell; the other Answers he believed were not excepted to.

And being asked, Whether he could not, by excepting to the Answers, have had a more complete Discovery of the dispersed Property? he replied, To the belt of his Recollection, such an Exception would not have held to the Answers, because the Answers say, that as to the Property dispersed they cantiot give an Account thereof.

And being asked. If he knew of Suits having been jnstituted in the Admiralty Courts ? he said, He has heard there are many, some disposed of, and some un-disposed of; but he never heard from the Petitioners how many Claimants had put in their Claims in those Courts.

Being further asked, If he knew of any feigned or improper Delays made use of by any of the Defendants, io as to procrastinate this Cause ? he said, Before the Answers were put in there were Delays, and the Process for Contempt was taken out for those Delays; since the Answers were put in (the last of which was in March 1785) there have been no Proceedings w hatever, to his Recollection, on the Part of the Pluintiffs or on the Part of the Defendants.

And being asked, -If he saw any Thing in this Cause, as it now stands, that stop the Proceedings of Replying, any more than in any other Cause that may be now before the Court of Chancery; and if there are such, Whether they arise from any Acts of the Defendants ? he answered, That the Objections to replying in every Cause muff depend upon its particular Circumstances — That in this Cause, before Replication can be filed, the Bill must be amended, other Persons made Parties, and a Variety of Matter ought to be investigated, that has come to the Knowledge of the Plaintiffs since filing the Bill; but the not replying does not arise from any Acts of the Defendants.

And being asked, Whether there was not a complete and satisfactory Explanation given by Colonel Fergusson why his Answers were not sooner put in? he replied. No, not to him or to his Knowledge; nor does he recoiled to have heard of any private Circumstances happening in Colonel Fergussons Family to have prevented him from so doing.

And being asked, Whether Colonel 9 An-

fwer, when put in, was not acknowledged by the Plaintiffs to be full and satisfactory? he said, He did not know that the Plaintiffs acknowledged it to be so; but he acknowledged it to be what is called a full Answer, but not satisfa&ory, because it did not render mi Account of the Produce of the dispersed Property, which he conceived ought to have been within the Knowledge of all the Agents, though he does not know that Colouel Fergusson could have given that Satisfaction.

Being further asked, Whether he does not know that there has been a general Condemnation in the 'Court of Admiralty of all the unclaimed Property taken at Saint Eustatius, so as to preclude all further Claims to be now given in? he replied, No; and this is the first Time he ever heard of it; nor does he Vox- 41.

know what Proportion the Amount of the Property Mnndof1 claimed bears to that in the Possession of the Agents S». liuAatias* from the Capture, never having heard the Amount of the Claims.

And beitig asked, Whether he can say frofn his own Knowledge, or from any and what Information, that after the Claims and Costs are fully satisfied there will beany Surplus? he said, Of his own Knowledge, he knows nothing of it; but the Expectations of h:s Employers are, that there will be a considerable Surplus.

And being asked his Opinion, Whether the Agents would be justified in distributing any Part of the Produce of the Capture, before all the Claims and Costs were fully adjudged and satisfied ? he said. He thinks they would be justified in distributing all the Property . in their Hands or Power, beyond the extent of the Claims; but his Employers never required, to his Know ledge, an immediate Distribution, they only desired the Money should be impounded.

And being asked. Whether he does not know that the chief Part of the Money arising from the Capture of Saint Eustatius is already vested in the Bank ? he answered, He never heard that any Part was lodged there; and his Idea always has been, that the chief Part has not been collected.

And being further asked, Whether the Answers mention the Number of the Suits? he replied, Yes — and states from Mr. Paget's Answer, which was put in in November 1784, that there are 64 Suits — that 23 only are heard; 9 only fully decided; and, from Sentences,

4 out of 9 have been appealed from — By the Answer of Mr. Forster, he claims to retain 4,950 /. Currency, for Commission; and by the Answer of Mr. he claims to retain 2,700l. Sterling — That he thinks other Sums are claimed by some of the other Agents, but he cannot recollect the Particulars.-

Being asked. If any Industry has been used by the Agents for procuring an Account of the dispersed Property? he replied. Not that he knows of; and if the Accounts had been obtained, he conceived it would, have come to his Knbwledge.

The Witness further states, That it appears by the Answers, that Six Agents were appointed by the Captors, besides Two Gentlemen; namely, Mr. Jackson and Mr. Lloyd, who were appointed by One or both of the Commanders in Chief.

And being asked, By whom were the Petitioners informed that an effectual Account and Distribution of the Property could not be obtained in the Common Course of Judicial Proceedings? he replied. By their Coupfel and Agent in the Chancery Cause.

And being further asked, Whether he does not know that the Court of Admiralty, or the Lords Commissioners of Appeals, would, upon Application and fufBcient Cause shewn, have ordered the Agents to bring into the Court all the Money that was in their Hands? he said. He was a total Stranger to Proceedings in that Court; nor did he endeavour to inform himself thereof previous to the filing of the Bill.

And being also asked, Whether he does not know or believe that the Court of Admiralty, and the Lords Court of Appeals, have Power to compel the Captors to give in Inventories of the Property captured which is come to their Hands or Knowledge; and whether the Lords of Appeals have not already ordered Inventories to be given in ? he replied, I le does not know that such is the Practice, but supposes it is; nor does he know that the Lords of Appeals have given such Orders.

INSTRUCTIONS for Our trustyand well* beloved Sir George Bridges Rodney, Baronet, Admiral and Commander in Chief of Our Naval Forces in the Leeward Inlands; and the Honourable GEORGE R. M ajor General rnghan, Commander in Chief ot Our Land Forces in the said Islands. Given at Our Court at James's, the Thirtieth Day of {L. S.) March 1781, in the Twenty-

first Year of Our Reign.

Whereas, by the Blessing of God upon your prompt and vigorous Execution of Our Orders, you have obtained Possession of the Dutch Blands of Saint Eustatius, Saint Martin, and Saba, and thereby, and in consequence

thereof, captured a large Number of Ships and Vessels, Merchandize, Naval and Military Stores, Provisions, and other Effects, the Property of the Enemy, which by Law appertaineth unto Us, in virtue of Our Prerogative Royal: But We, being graciously disposed to reward the Zeal and Bravery of you Our said Commanders in Chief, and of Our Land and Sea Forces under your respective Commands, employed upon thele Services, and to encourage all others Our Forces and their Commanders to pay the like ready and punctual Obedience to Our Orders, and to exert their utmost Vigilance, Alacrity, and Intrepidity in the Execution of them. Do relinquish, and have hereby relin-quished, all Our Right, Title, and Claim, to the said Ships and Vessels, Merchandize, Naval and Military Stores, and other Effects, of the Enemy, so captured by you Our said Commanders in Chief, and Our Land and Sea Forces under your respective Commands (except only the Whole of the Provisions, and the Ordnance, Arms, Ammunition, and other Military Stores, provided for the Defence of the said Islands, or which may be judged necessary by you and Our Engineer for that Purpose, which have been found therein) the same to be for your and their sole Use and Benefit, to be divided in such Manner as We shall hereafter direct and appoint; laving always to the settled Inhabitants of the said Islands, the Possession of their Lands, and Produce thereof, Houses, Slaves, Cattle, Furniture, Utensils, and Stock, that shall be found thereon, as also all such Effects as shall be proved to be the Property of British Subjects, lawfully exported thither, or which may lawfully be imported into Great Britain from thence.

G. R.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Kynaston reported from the Committee, to whom Severn the Petition of the Proprietors, Owners, and Occupiers Navigation of Lands, Mills, Iron Works, Founderies, Coal Mines,

Lime, and other Works, adjoining or lying near to the River Severn, in the Counties of Salop, Stafford, and Worcester, and also, of the Merchants, Manufacturers,

Barge Owners, Traders, and others, interested in the Navigation of the said River, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is ets followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

George Mathews being examined, said, That the Navigation of the River Severn is in several Places much obstructed by Shoals and other Impediments, by Means whereof great Delays are occasioned in the Carriage of Goods and Merchandize on the said River, to the Detriment of Trade and Commerce — That the Witness had, till within a Fortnight, large Iron Works and Founderies for Cannon upon the River, and has experienced the Inconvenience — That he is well acquainted with the Navigation between Meadow Wharf and Digits, and the Nature of the Trade upon the Secern — That there are very extensive Founderies, Iron Works, and Coal Mines, and the Commerce carried on between the Northern Counties and Bristol is very considerable — That on Account of the imperteft State of the Navigation, for want of a sufficient Depth in the Shallows, the Trade suffers frequent Delays, which is productive of great Inconvenience and Lois — That the Witness has sustained a Lois of 500 /. per Cent, by being obliged to fend Cannon for the life of Government by Land Carriage, at a Time when Vessels could not move for want of Water in the Severn, and Government have very often been put to great Inconvenience, by not having their Cannon iu lime — That Cannon call in that Neighbourhood have been proved at Woolwich superior to those cast at any other Foundery in the Kingdom, and are also sent in much larger Quantities — That iu dry Seasons Vessels cannot move on the Severn for 2 or 3 Months together; and the Witness has known more than Ten Instances when loaded Coal Barges, drawing between and 4§ Feet Water, could not proceed on their Voyage for Five Months at a Time, for Want of a sufficient Depth — That he has known when an empty Vessel could not swim in the River, which was the same for a Month or two last Summer — That the Average Depth of the Shallows below Coal-brook Dale, was from 16 to 12 Inches, for 2 or 3 Months last Summer — That he has known the River as shallow in other Summers, but not for so long a Period; and he said he meant those Shallows between Dale.

and Stourport.

That various other Goods are conveyed down the Severn; viz. Potteries, Manchester Goods, Coals, Lime,

Iron, Lead, and Navy Timber; and also great Quantities of Salt from the DroitwichCanal, both for Sale and for Government’s U fe — That the returned Carriage

from

t

26 Geo. Hi. 210 Martii.

Carriage from Bristol supplies the interior Parts of the Country, bordering upon the River, with Groceries, Wines, Glass, Cheese, Hops, Cyder, Wheat, Flour, and in general all Foreign Import Goods — That no Navigation ltands more in Need of Improvement than the Severn, which would then become a very important one, as it has Communication with the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, and from thence into The Grand Trunk, and to Birmingham — That those Navigations are in a very good State, and that nothing is wanting to make a complete Navigation between those Places, and Hull, Bristol, and Liverpool, but the Improvement of the Severn.

And being asked, What Obstructions he had known to the Navigation from Floods? he said, That he has several Times known when Vessels would not venture down the River to Gloucester with Coals, on Account of the Lowness of the Arch at Upton Bridge, as in Times of Flood they could not get through — That he has heard Barge Owners frequently complain of that Bridge; he does not mean that those Obstructions arose from too much 'Water in the River, but from the Bridge.

And being asked, Whether, supposing that Bridge was washed away, Barges could go at all Times? he said, He thought they could.

And being asked, Whether a great Part of the Business upon the Severn was not transacted between Coal-brook Dale and Stourport? he said, Yes, the Iron Manufactory.

And being asked, That being the Cafe, where was the Necetlity for Looks below Stourport ? he said, To convey the Goods to Gloucester, Bristol, and other Places; and that there is more Business, and of greater Value, done below Stourport, than above it.

And the Witness added, That he has known great Quantities of Cannon, for the Use of Woolwich Warren, sent down the Severn to the Stroud Canal, and from thence carried to Leachlade: Then

Mr. William Jessop, an Engineer, was examined, who said. That he had surveyed the River Severn, and is well satisfied that it is practicable to make it a good Navigation, by removing Impediments, and erecting Locks and Wears in proper and convenient Places in the said River, so as to maintain a sufficient Depth of Water to navigate Vessels in dry Seasons; and that it is proposed to erect 12 Locks and Wears lietween Meadow Wharf and Stourport, and from thence to Diglis.

And being asked, Whether he was certain that the Works could not be destroyed by the Rapidity of the Stream ? he said, He believed they are no more liable than similar Works in other Navigations.

And being asked. Whether the River Severn does not rife higher and quicker than any other River? he said. He did not knpw, but if it did lb, it was not, on that Account, more liable to do Damage than any other River.

And being asked. Whether the Locks will not occasion the Water to rife higher, to remain longer, and thereby flood the adjacent Lands, by flopping the Current of the Stream? he said, They will make it rife higher, but not remain longer, that he knows of, nor will they injure the Lands in the smallest Degree.

And being asked, What public Utility would arise by improving the Secern from Meadow Wharf to W r-cester, unless the Shoals below Worcester were to be also removed? be laid, No more than it would make all the River from Worcester upwards as good as that below — That Vessels will come from Coalbrook Dale to Worcester as easy as they now go from Wireester downwards; but that he thinks the Shoals below Worcester ought to be removed.

And being asked, Whether he apprehended that the Meadows below Worcester would be more liable to Vol. 41.

Floods, when Locks were erected, than they are at present ? he said, Certainly not; no more than the Meadows adjoining the River Thames.

And being asked, Whether he had taken so accurate a Survey of the Country below , on each Side

of the Severn, as to know what Number of Acres might be flooded, and of consequence lessened in Value, by a forced Rife of Water in the River, sufficient to carry Vessels up and down at all Times of the Year? he said, Though he had not taken a Survey, he could answer in the Negative, by saying, that no Land would be flooded.

And being asked, If any Obstruction be given to the Current of the Water in the River, whether ad the Lands on each Side of the Rivers same and Avon, which empty themselves into the S would not be more liable to Floods, by Means of such Obstruction? he laid, If ever lb great an Obstruction were to be made on the Severn, above the Places where the Streams fall in, it cannot affect the Meadows upon those Streams — If an Obstruction should be made below, it might or might not affect the Lands on the Sides of those Rivers, as that would depend on the Manner in which they were made, and the Degree of Obstrufction thereby occasioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of Five hundred Eighty-two thousand Four hundred and Eighty-eight Pounds, Fifteen Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings, remaining in the Exchequer on the 5th Day of January 1786, of the Surplus of the Sinking Fund, subject to the Disposition of Parliament.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was,

upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. William Wyndham Grenville reported from the Public Select Committee, to whom it was referred to examine {,nCon‘* an<l and state the several Accounts and other Papers presented *Pe,ldlluf*-to the House in this Session of Parliament, relating to the Public Income and Expenditure, and to report to the House what may be expected to be the Annual Amount of the said Income and Expenditure in future;

That the Committee had examined the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, ill at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followed); viz.

Your Committee having proceeded to the Considera* ation of die Matters referred to them by the House, have arranged the several Papers relating thereto under distinct Heads, containing the different Articles of the Public Income and Expenditure.

But before they enter on the First Part of their Report, they think it necessary to premise, that they have confined their Examination to the present State of the Revenue, as it appears either from the Amount actually received in the Periods contained in the Papers referred to them, or from the belt Estimates which they could form of the Produce of such Articles as had not been brought to Account in those Periods, but compose, nevertheless, a Part of the present Income of the Public.

The large Amount of Taxes imposed since the Commencement of the late War, in addition to the then subsisting Revenue; the Difficulties under which the different Branches of our Commerce laboured during the Continuance of that War; and the great and increasing Prevalence of Smuggling previous to the Measures recently adopted for its Suppression, appeared to Your Committee to render any Averages of the Amount of the Revenue in former Periods, in a great Degree inapplicable to the present Situation of the Country: On the other Hand, they did not think themselves competent to difculs the various Contingencies which may in future operate to the Increase or Diminution of the Public Income. A Revenue so complicated in its Nature, and depending so much on the various Branches of an extensive Commerce, must always be liable to temporary Fluftuations, even although no Circumstances should arise to occasion any permanent Alteration in its Produce. Your Committee have, therefore, judged it proper to submit to the Wisdom of the House this extensive Consideration, and to state in this Report the present Amount of the Public Income, as resulting from the Papers before them.

Estimates of this Kind being always subject to a Variety of c ontingent Alterations, it is impossible to make any Calculation that can be depended upon as accurate; but as far as we can judge, from the Experience of former Peace Establishrnents, compared with the present advanced State of the Fleet, and Improvements, in the Yards, we are hopeful, on a Suppofuiou that 18,000 Men are kept employed, that 1,800,000l. will be found adequate to the grcuteU Demands of the Fleet on a permanent Peace Establishment* and probably more.

If. B. But in the Interval, before she Fleet can be put compleatly on the Footing here described, the Grants for the Extra mud necessiirily exceed the Average here estimated; it cannot be dated

exactly to what Extent, but we conceive they may amount to a Sum from *2,000,000l. to 2,4.00,000l. for the whole of the Four Years.

Cha* Middleton, Edv/ Hunt, J. Henjlow, Geo. ilarsh, Geo. Rogers, W. Buhner, \Vm Campbell, E. Le Cras.

Should the same Number of Men here stated be kept compleat, the Four Pounds per Man per Menfein, granted for the Seamen of the Navy, will be generally found inadequate to the Expence, even in Time of Peace, not only from the increased Price of Provisions, j but from its being fuLjed to several Demands, not otherwise provided for by Parliament; no Reduction therefore can be expected Ion this Head.

f There is no Probability of this AtticJe.lessening, as the Increase of the Navy has naturally brought forward with it an Increase of \ Buildings, further Exteufion9 of the Yards and Instruments, which mud of course be continued for keeping Pace with the Business.

May be expected in the Course of a few Years to decrease to this Sum.

There js no Prospect of any Diminution on this Head, for the same Reasons as is given in the First Article of the Ordinary.

This Article is as low as can be expected.

These Two Articles are dependent on each other, and cannot, under the present Circumstances of the Fleet, be expected to diminiffi; we are hopeful, however, that when th£ Works of the Fleet are in greater Forwardness, 5,000l. per Annum may be laken from them, to reduce them to the Sum here stated.

The Increase of the Meet b*-s naturally brought an Increase of Expence on tins Article; but as the Moorings are in a better State of . Repair at present than they have been for many Years, it is to be hoped that, after some additional Moorings are laid down at Salfash for [the Ships at Plymouth, and at Oakhamness for those in the River Medway, this Article may be decreased to the Sum here elliniated. f As the Fleet may be supposed in a few Years to be in a very forwaid State of Repair, it is hoped the Expence on this Article will I confklerably decrease; which we have therefore ventured to put at this Sum.

) From the Experience of former Peace Establishments, the Expence on this Head has decreased so insensibly as not to be looked on as an ^Object of Reduction.

No Alteration, for the same Reasons as in the First Article.

f The preceding Calculations are grounded on what may probably be the State of the Fleet towards the F.nd of the Year 1790, and: which we have takeu as the bell Year for grounding a permanent Peace Establishment upon, taking it for granted the Improvements [in the Dock Yards will be forwarded as much as possible in the intermediate Time.

The present Peace Establishment being eoniidered as permanent, the probable Charge attending it must be considered as continuing the fame, excepting as to such Diminutions as may in Time take place on the Articles of Half Pay and Chelsea.

'l lie Extraordinary Expences of the Army may probably be expected to be reduced below the Expence of the present Year, according to the Paper annexed to this Report.

Towards defraying tiiefe Services, it is difficult to state with Precision what Sayings will accrue. — They must chiefly arile from the Sums voted upon Estimate for the Recruiting and Contingent Services, or from the Savings on Non-effectives; all of which must, from their Nature, be fluctuating. But it is probable, that supposing the Army to continue in tiiefe Ilefpe&s in its present State, there may arise Savings to the Amount of about 40,000l. per Annum, applicable to the defraying the Extraordinary Expences of the Army.

Expenditure. Navy Office, 21st March 1786.

An ACCOUNT Shewing the Amount of the outstanding Debt of the Navy on the 31st of December 1785, and whether any separate Provision will be necessary for discharging the fame, in Addition to the other Demands for Naval Services. Prepared pursuant to a Precept from the Committee appointed to examine and date the several Accounts and other'Papers presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, relating to the Public Expenditure and Income, dated 21st March 1786.

The Debt of the Navy on the 31st December 1785 ----- Money remaining in the Treasurer’s Hands, and to come in of the Grants of the last Year - 2,537,764 825,275 #. d. »7 5 3 — I

Which leaves the Nett Debt - - - 1,712,489 14 4?

But as a great Part of this Debt consists of Wages due to Seamen, the Claims for which must, from the Nature of them, be gradual, and Part probably never claimed at all, no separate Provision need be made for the Remainder, as a floating Arrear to nearly the Extent of it may always be supposed to exist.

AS. made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, to explain, amend and render more effectual, an Act, made in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the " more effectual Punishment of Persons who shall attain, " or attempt to attain, Possession of Goods, or Money, " by falle or untrue Pretences; for preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods; for the ealy Redemption of " Goods pawned; and for preventing Gaming in Public " Houses, by Journeytnen, Labourers, Servants, and Apprentices," so far as the same relates to the preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods; and for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned; and Setting forth, That Power has been given by the House, to make Provision in the said Bill to explain, amend, and enlarge some of the Powers and Provisions contained in the said Act, and the Petitioners conceive, it would be more convenient and beneficial to the Public, if the said Act of the Thirtieth Year of King George the Second, fb far as the same relates to the Trade and Business of Pawnbrokers, and the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty, were to be repealed, and the necessary Powers, Provisions, and Regulations contained therein, together with such Explanations, Amendments, and Additions, as that! be thought expedient to be adopted by the House, were to be contained and enacted in One Angle Act of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made for those Purposes, under such Rules and Restrictions as the House shall think proper, for the better regulating and carrying on the Business of a Pawnbroker.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Irrstruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

Mr. Aldridge presented to the House, pursuant to their Order,

A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported^ That the House; at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s

03. \

Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering his Royal Highness the Prince of [Vales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and the Lord Sydney, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act for the Regulation of His Majesty’s Marine Forces while on Shore.

An Act to enable the Persons therein named to provide proper Places on Shore for the Reception of the Crew of the Voorberg Dutch East forced by Strefe of Weather into the Port of Dartmouth.

An Act for enlarging the Term of Two Acts of the Fifth and Ninth Years of His present Majesty, so far as the fame"relate to the repairing of the Roads from Wats Cross to Cowden, and from Sevenoakes Common to Crockhurst Hatch Cprner, and from Penshurst Town to Southborough, in the County of Kent.

An Act to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from Cromf'ord Bridge, in the County of Derby, to the Turnpike Road at or near Langley Mill, in the said County.

An Act for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, for repairing and widening the Road from Worksop, in the County of Nottingham, through the Towns of Anston,

Aston, Handsworth, and Darnall, to the North East

End of AttercUffe, in the County of York, where the same joins the Turnpike Road from Batchy to Sheffield.

An Act for enlarging the Term of several Acts of Parliament, for the Repair of Dover Harbour.

That the Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending for making a Navigable Canal from the Stourbridge Navigation to Diglis, near Worcester, by which Bill the said intended Navigation is proposed to pals through great Part of the Parish of Bromsgrove, and near unto the said Town; and that such intended Navigation, in the present Line, will , intercept and cut through divers Springs and Streams of Water arising in the said Parish of Bromsgrove, which, with the Land Floods, are the Only, though barely sufficient, Supply and Support of divers very considerable Cotton, Needle, Paper, Corn, and other Mills and Works lying below the said intended Canal, and that a large and extensive Cotton Mill and Manufactory, as well as several Needle Mills and Works, have at a very considerable Expence, been lately established in the Course of the said Springs and Streams, which constantly employ a great Number of Persons at Bromsgrove, and notwithstanding the said Von. 41.

Mills and Works could, with Advantage, dispense with much more Water than the present Supply, yet certain Clauses are, or are intended to be, introduced into the said Bill, for taking the Whole of the said Land Floods, and Part of the aforesaid Streams of Water, and to cut through the said Springs, and for making Reservoirs below several of such Springs and Streams, for supplying such Navigation with Water; and that the Town of Bromsgrove is an ancient and large Market Town, and the chief Support of the Inhabitants is owing to the Trade and Market, which Market chiefly consists of Farmers bringing their Grain thereto for Sale, and Millers occupying the said Corn Mills, purchasing the fame, and( such Persons attending the said Market dealing with the Petitioners for Goods and Merchandize; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the aforesaid Mills, Works, and Manufactories will be very much injured, whereby a great Number of Persons employed thereat will become burthensome to the said Parish of Bromsgrove, and useless to Society, and the Market there will be very considerably injured, if not totally loft, to the great and immediate Detriment of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the House will not permit such Bill to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie ,upon the Table,

A Petition of Marmaduke Langdale, Esquire, was Stourbridge presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Canal. That, by a Paper annexed to the Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the Stourbridge Canal Navigation, at or near the Town of Stourbridge, to communicate with the River Severn at Diglis, near Worcester, it is stated, the Petitioner has assented to making such Canal, whereas the Petitioner never did signify his Assent thereto, but on the contrary, has always expressed his Disapprobation thereof, because he apprehended, and now believes, that such intended Canal will greatly injure his Estate, as it will cut through and interfe& the most valuable Part of the Petitioner’s Lands, and in a great Degree (if not wholly) deprive his said Estate of the Benefit it now receives from a certain Brook or Stream there, which is used for the Purposes of floating and watering his Meadows, and that the said intended Canal will not be of any real Utility to the Public: And therefore praying. To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And

Mr. William Roderick being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, with respect to the said District of Roads, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money for defraying the Expences of making and repairing the fame, which frill remains due, and cannot be repaid, unless the Term and Powers of the said Act be enlarged.

And the Witness further said, That the several Roads described in the Petition are for the moil Part in a ruinous Condition, narrow and incommodious for Travellers, and in some Places impassable for Carriages, and cannot be effectually amended and repaired by the ordinary Course of Law. — And he added, that it would be of great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the several Parishes lying adjacent to the said Roads, and to all other Persons having Occasion to pals thereon, if the same were amended, widened, and rendered safe and commodious for Travellers and Carriages; and that the same might be conveniently done under the Management of the Trustees for the said District of Roads.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, and the Neighbourhood thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is intended to be brought into Parliament, for making a Canal from the Stourbridge Canal to the City of Worcester, and that a Bill is liktwife intended to be brought in for improving the Navi-

Stion of the River Severn, from or near Coalbrook ale, in the County of Salop, to the said City of Worcester", and that the Petitioners apprehend the Improvement of the River Severn will be of the utmost public Utility, as by Means thereof, and the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal communicating with the same at Stourport, in the County of Worcester, a complete and easy Communication will be made between the Ports of Bristol, Liverpool, and Hull, and all the intermediate Manufacturing Towns, and, amongst many other Advantages, the Price of Coals, and the Freight of all Kinds of Goods navigated thereon, will be reduced; and that the Petitioners conceive, by the Improvement of the Navigation of the Severn, the Public will receive more and greater Advantages than by making the said intended Canal, wherefore the Petitioners consider the said intended Canal as unnecessary and ufelefe: And therefore praying, That the Bill for making the said intended Canal may not pass into a Law', and submitting the Improvement of the Navigation of the Severn to the Consideration of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Citizens, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of Worcester.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Application for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Canal from the Stourbridge Navigation, to communicate with the River Severn, at Diglis, near the City of Worcester;and Setting forth. That there has been already compleated, at a very large Expence, a much shorter and more expeditious Canal Conveyance from and out of the said Stourbridge Canal to the River Severn than that proposed by the said intended Bill, which has been found sufficient to answer all the Purposes of Water Carriage to the Severn, and the Petitioners and the Public in general have been greatly benefitted thereby; and that the Petitioners are informed, that Application is also intended to be made to the House, for a Bill for improving the Navigation of the River Severn, and, the Petitioners apprehend* the improving of the Navigation of the River Severn will be a Means of preventing a Monopoly in the Coal Trade, and will be of great public Advantage, and may be effected without destroying or injuring any Landed Property, and will lave the unne-celfary Expenditure of a very large Sum of Money in making the said intended Canal, which, if made, will run parallel with the present Navigation from its Commencement to its Termination, and much valuable Landed Property will be destroyed, and many Mills, Water Works, and Manufactories, materially injured by making such intended Canal, to the Detriment of Trade; and that the Petitioners apprehend no public Advantage can arise, from making Two parallel Navigations, adequate to the Waste of Property that will be occasioned thereby, and they also apprehend, that the said intended Canal is projected with a View to impede the Improvement of the Navigation of the said River, and to answer the private Views of interested Individuals, without regarding the public Good: And therefore praying, That the BiH for making the said intended Canal may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making and maintaining a navigable Canal from the Stourbridge Canal Navigation to the River Severn, near to the City of Worcester, be read a Second Time.

Ordered, That Mr. Scott, of Weobley, have Leave to go the Northern Circuit.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next,. Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the Right honourabJeJfairy Flood and Sir Godfrey Webster, Baronet, was delivered in at the Table, ana read; Setting forth. That, on Tuesday, the 21st Day of March Instant, an Election of Two Barons to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, came on there, at which Elefition the Petitioners, and Sir Peter Parker, Baronet, and Sir John Henderson, Baronet, were Candidates; and that the Petitioners were duly elected by a great Majority of legal Votes, but Lancelot Harison, Esquire, who afited as Bailiff and Returning Officer at tire said Election, in taking the Poll was guilty of grols Partiality and Injustice towards the Petitioners* by arbitrarily and illegally rejecting the Votes of several Persons who tendered to vote for the Petitioners, and by admitting other Persons to vote for the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson who had no legal Right to vote, and in many other Respefits the said Lancelot Harison was guilty of unwarrantable Practices, as well previous to as during the said Election, in favour of the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson; and that several Persons, who voted for the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, had previously asked, received, and taken Money, and other Reward, and had agreed or contracted for Money, Gift, and Reward, to give their Votes in tire said Election, and had been guilty of other illegal and corrupt Practices, by Means whereof their Votes so given are, and ought to be declared to be, void; and that the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson, by themselves, or Ibme Person or Persons employed by them, or one of them, did, by Gift or Reward, and by Promile, Agreement, or Security for Gift, or Reward, corrupt and procure several Persons to give their Votes in the said Election, and by these, and other undue Means, the said Sir Peter Parker and Sir John Henderson procured themselves to be returned to serve in Parliament for the said Town and Port of Seaford, in Prejudice of the Petitioners, who were duly elected, and ought to have been returned, in Prejudice of the legal Electors of the said Town and Port, and in Defiance of the Laws and Freedom of Elections: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday, the 25th Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two A fits, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cafes, were sent to the Parties, accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.*

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That Bounties be allowed to a certain Number of Vessels employed in the British Fishery on the Banks of the Island of Newfoundland, in Manner following; that is to say, to the firit One hundred Vessels which shall arrive, in each Year, in the Ports of the said Island, with a Cargo of Fish not leis than 10,000 by Tale, catched on the Banks thereof, and shall, after landing the fame, proceed for, and return with,' One Cargo of Fish more at least, catched upon the said Banks, if carrying not less than Twelve Men, Forty Pounds each, but, if such Men are carried upon Shares, Fifty Pounds each — if carrying leis than Twelve Men, and not less than Seven, Twenty-five Pounds each, but, if such Men are carried upon Shares, Thirty-five Pounds each — -and to the next One hundred Vessels that shall arrive in the said Ports with a like Cargo, and shall, after landing the fame, proceed again to the said Banks, and return from thence with One or more Cargoes of Fish, in Manner aforesaid, if carrying Twelve Men, Twenty-five Pounds each, but, if such men are carried upon Shares, Thirty-five Pounds each — if carrying leis than Twelve Men, and not less than Seven Men, Eighteen Pounds each, but, if such men are carried upon Shares, Twenty-one Pounds each.

GEORGE R.

It gives His Majesty great Concern, that it has not been found possible to confine the necessary Expences of His Civil Government within the Annual Sum of Eight hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds, now applicable thereto. A farther Debt has been necessarily incurred, an Account of which He has ordered to be laid before the House.

His Majesty relies on the Zeal and Affection of His faithful Commons, that they will take the same into their early Consideration, and make such Provision as the Circumstances may appear to them to require.

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Grounds adjoining and lying near to the River Severn, in the County of Worcester, and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that Application hath been made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill, under a Pretence of improving the Navi-

fation of the River Severn, by erecting Locks and f ears, and laying a Toll thereon, railing the Water, towering the Fed of the River, or otherwise; and that the Petitioners being almost the only Proprietors and Occupiers of Land on the Banks of the said River, running through the said County of Worcester (except such Proprietors as are Members of either House of Parliament) beg Leave to inform the House, that they are very apprthenlive great Injury will ensue to their Property, if an Act is passed agreeable to such Petition, as it will be laying a burthensome Toll on a free River, and that by a Set of Men totally unconnected with the said County of Worcester-, and that the Petitioners, as well from their own Knowledge, as from the Information of able and experienced Engineers and Surveyors, are fully allured that the intended Alterations, so far from answering the End proposed, will greatly injure the Navigation, much increase the Price of Coal and other Merchandize carried upon the said River, and be productive of many ill Consequences to the Property and Trade of the said County, all which the Petitioners are able and willing to prove to the House by very sufficient Evidence: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and that they may have Leave to be heard by their Counfei, agamic the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Barge Owners navigating on the River Severn, and other Inhabitants residing in and near Broseley, in the County of Salop, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petition; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are fully convinced* if such Bill should pass into a Law, it will operate widely- different to the avowed Intent thereof, and, instead of being a Benefit, will be a great Injury to the Trade and Navigation of the said River, for the Petitioners conceive that the Water cannot be raised without narrowing the River in particular Places, and consequently increasing the Velocity of the Stream, which will considerably ira-04

pede the Navigation, and render it much more dangerous than at present; and representing to the House, That, in the present State of, the River, the Petitioners, can pass the Vessels of each other by Night or by Day, whereas, if Wears, or any other Obstructions should be made in the River, it will not be safe or praftieable for the Petitioners to pass them in the Night, especially upwards, but they will be under the Necessity of laying by till the Morning, and which, by a Variation of Wind or Weather, may be attended with a long Hindrance in their Uufmefs, and a Loss and Inconvenience to the Public in general; and that a Number of the Petitioners Vessels frequently let Sail and proceed in their Voyages oh life said River together, without Hazard of ruuning foul of each other, but, if such Wears or other Obstructions should be made, there will be great Danger in a tempestuous Seal'on, even in the Day Time, of the Petitioners Vessels running against each other at such Wears, and of a Vessel passing through such Wears downwards running foul of a Vessel passing upwards; and that the principal Obstructions which, in the present State of the River, in dry Seasons, impede the Navigation, are Beds of Sand, and which the Projectors of the intended Improvement in the Navigation of the River propose to remove, but the Petitioners conceive that to be vain Labour, as Sands are a fluctuating Body, shifting with every Tide of Flood, and, if removed from one Place, will col left again in another; and that raising the Water in different Parts of the River will, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, increase the Height and Number of the Floods, which will not only impede the Navigation of the River, but greatly prejudice the Lands and Houses of several of the Petitioners, and others, adjoining the said River, and, if such Bill should pal's into a Law, it will tend to the Benefit only of the Projectors, who will receive at least an Interest of 201, per Cent, for the Money by them advanced, and it will also be a Prejudice to the County of Salop at large, and to the Trade and Commerce thereof, by laying a burthensome and unnecessary Toll on a Free River, and by dangerously obstructing, instead of improving, the Navigation of the fame; and that the Inhabitants of every Town, on or near adjoining the said River, will fuller greatly from the Number of Poor, which mull, in consequence of the said Bill passing into a Law, apply for Relief to the Parishes to which they belong, as not a Third Part of the Men, which at present maintain their Families by working on the said River, will meet with Employ, and, by reducing the Number of Men on the said River, the Navy of Great Britain must materially lliffcr, as on a moderate Calculation not less than i,',oo Seamen from the said - River w ere engaged in His Majesty’s Service the last War, owing to the Number of young Men who are Annually bound by Indenture to the Matters of Vessels trading thereon, whereby they are qualified to enter into the Service of their Country: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pals into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill for improving the Navigation of the River Severn, from or near a Place called Meadow in Coalbrook Dale, in the County of to

the Deep Water at or near a Place called DigUs, below the City of Worcester, be read a Second Time: And the first-mentioned petitioners are to be then heard by their Counfei against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counfei be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Coventr Coventry Canal Navigation was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the last Session of Parliament, a Petition was presented to the House, by the Petitioners, for a Bill to enable them to compleat the said Canal from Atherstone, in the county of,

to Fazeley, in the County of Stafford, and for other Purposes, arid afterwards, in the same Session, a Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, was also presented, for a Bill to make navigable the Rivers Trent,

Tame, and Anker, in the Counties of Stafford, , and Warwick, from the said River Trent, at or near Burton upon Trent, in the said County of Stafford, to the Borough of Tamworth, in the said Counties of Stafford and Warwick, and from thence to or near a Place called Field on Bridge, near Atherstone aforesaid, with several Cuts to communicate with the Coventry Canal at Atherstone aforesaid, with the Birmingham and Fazeley Canal at or near Fazeley, and with the Canal from the Trent to the Mersey at or near Wicknover, in the said County of Stafford, the compleating of which Navigation would have effected all the Purposes of the Extennon of the Coventry Canal, and consequently rendered such Extension totally unnecefiaiy; and that, in Expectation of such Navigation being made, no Proceedings were had upon the Petition so presented by the Petitioners, and neverthelefe no Proceedings were had upon the said . A Petition of the Barge Owners navigating on the Ditto. River Severn, and others residing in and near the Town of Bridgnorth, in the County of Salop, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, Application is intended to be made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for improving the Navigation of the said River, in raising the Water, by making Wears and Locks, or by lowering the Bed; and that the Petitioners have very maturely considered the Consequences of such pretended Improvements, and are fully convinced, if such Bill should pals into a Law, it will operate widely different to the avowed Intent thereof, and, instead of being a Benefit, will be a great Injury to the Trade and Navigation of the said River, for the Petitioners conceive, that the Water cannot be raised without narrowing the River in particular Places, and consequently increasing the Velocity of the Stream, which will considerably impede the Navigation, and render it much more dangerous than at present; and Representing to the House, That, in the present State of the River*the Petitioners can pass the Vessels of each other, uptill Parts of it, by Night or by Day, whereas, if Wears) or any other ObitrucHons, should be made in the River, it will not be safe or practicable for the Petitioners to pass them in the Night, especially upwards, but they will be under the Necessity of laying by till the Morning, and which, by a Variation of Wind or Weather, may be attended with a long Hindrance in their Business, and a Lois and Inconve-niency to the Public in generals and that a Number of the Petitioners Vessels frequently let Sail and proceed in their Voyage on the said River together, without Hazard of running foul of each other, but, if such Wears, or other Obltxuctions, should be made, there w ill be great Danger in a tempestuous Season, even in the Day Time, of the Petitioners Vessels running against each other at such Wears, and of Vessels passing through such Wears downwards running foul of a Vessel passing upwards; and that the principal Obstructions which, in the present State of the River in dry Seasons, impede the Navigation, are Ltds of Sand, and which the Projectors
