XXXIX. That the Revenue of the Country being anticipated, mortgaged, and dilapidated by the Counsel, Concurrence, Connivance, and Influence, and often by the direct Order of the said Warren Hastings, the whole Civil Government, Magistracy, and Administration of Justice, gradually declined, and at Length totally ceased, through the Whole of the vast Provinces which compose the Territory of Oude; and no Power was visible therein, but that of the Farmers of the Revenue, attended by Bodies of Troops to enforce the Collections; inso much that Robberies, Assassinations, and Acts of every Description of Outrage and Violence, were perpetrated with Impunity; and even in the capital City of Lucknow, the Seat of the Sovereign Power, there was no Court of Justice whatever to take Cognizance of such Offences.

XL. That the said Warren Hastings, when he did interfere in the Government of Oude, was obliged by his Duty to interfere for the good Purposes of Government, and not merely for the Purpose of extorting Money therefrom, and enriching his own Dependants, which latter Purpose alone he did effect in the Manner before-mentioned, but not One of the former. For the said Hastings having procured the extraordinary Powers given by and to himself by his Delegation of the 3d of July 1781, did declare the same to be for the Purpose, among many others, " ofaffifting the Nabob Vizier " in forming such Regulations as may be necessary for " the Peace and gpod Order of his Government, and " the Improvement of his Revenue." And in Consequence of the said Powers the said Warren Hastings did, in the Treaty of Chunar, obtain an Article from the Nabob, by which the said Nabob did promise to attend to his Advice in the Reformation of his Civil Administration; and be did give certain Instructions to the Resident Middleton, to which he did require him to yield the most implicit Obedience’, and did in One Article thereof direct him to urge the Nabob to endeavour gradually, if it could not be done at once, to establish Courts of Adewlet [Justice] and that the Darogas [Chief Criminal Magistrates] Moulabies [Consulting or Amstant Lawyers] and other Officers, should be Jelected by the Ministers, with his, the Resident’s, Concurrence: And afterwards, in his Instructions to the Resident Bristow, desiring him to pursue the fiune Object, he declared his Opinion, " that tl^e Want of such Courts, and the " extreme Licentiousness occasioned thereby, is One " of the most disreputable Pefects in his Highness the " Nabob’s Government And that while they do " not exist, every Man knows the Hazard which he " incurs in lending his Money." But he did give him the said Resident no positive Instruction concerning the lame, supposing the Establishment of such Courts a Matter of Difficulty; and did therefore leave him a Latitude in his Proceedings therein.

XLVI. That it appears by the said Letter, and the Papers therewith trani'mitted, as well as other Documents in the said Correspondence, that in Consequence of the Distress brought upon the Nabob’s Finances, certain of the Princes his Brethren, the Children of Sujah ul Dcrwla, the late Sovereign of the Country, were put

upon Pensions unsuitable to their Birth and Rank, and by the Mifinanagement of the Minister aforesaid (appointed by the said Warren Hastings) for Two Years together no considerable Part of the said inadequate Pension was paid; and not being able to maintain the Attendants necessary for their Protection in a City in which all Magistracy and Justice was abolished, they were not only liable to suffer the greatest Extremities of Penury, but their Lives were exposed to the Attempts of Afl'affins. The Condition of One of the said Princes, called the Nabob Bahadur, being by himself strongly expressed in Three Letters to the said Resident Bristow, the First dated the 28th of 1783; the

Second, the 7th of January 1784; and the Third, the 15th of January 1784; which Letters were duly transmitted in the Dispatch of the 29th of the same Month, to Warren Hastings, Esquire, and are as follow:

" Your own Servant carried you the Account of " what he himself was an Eye Witness to, after the

Affair of last Night. These arc the Particulars: — " About Midnight my Aunt received Twelve Wounds " from a Russian, of which she died. I also received " Six successive Stabs, which alarmed the People of the " House, who let up a Shouting; whereupon the Alfaffin " run off. Besides being zeith Food, or the Means of " providing any, this Misfortune has befallen me. I am xi desirous of sending the Coffin to your Door. You now stand in the Place of " his Excellency the Vizier. I request you will do me " Justice. What more can I say ?"

P. S. "I am also delirous to shew you my

Wounds."

The following Extracts are made from the Third Letter from the same Prince; dated January 15, 1784.

" The Particulars of the late and unforeseen Mis for-x‘ tune with which I have been overwhelmed, are not unknown unto you; that the innocent Blood of my " Aunt, the Prop and Ruler of my Family, was Ihed,

Formerly us Three " Brothers, Saadut Ally, Mirza Jungly, and I, the poor " and oppressed, were, in the Presence of our blessed " Father, whose Soul rests in Heaven, treated alike.

" Now the Ministers of this Government put me upon " a Footing with our younger Brothers, who have lately " left the 2!enana, and whose Expences are small. On " this Scale, which is in every Respect insufficient for " my Maintenance, they pay the pitiful Allowance only " zohen it is their Pleasure to do it. My Situation has

My Distresses are so great that I have not been able to pay " a Daum to the Surgeons for the Cure of my v and they too are discouraged from affording me their " Assistance, or furnishing me with Medicines. How " then is it possible for me to exist? Considering you as my Patron, participating in my Afflictions, I have " represented the Circumstances concerning my Situation; and I hope, from your Friendship, that you will " honour me with a favourable Answer."

L. But it appears, that to the Resident Bristow, who required to be informed whether the Reception of the fugitive Prince aforesaid in the Company’s Provinces would meet his Approbation, he gave no Answer whatsoever; by which criminal Neglect, or worse, with regard to a Brother of an Ally of the Company, who shewed a strong Attachment and Preference to the English Nation, and by suffering him, without any known Effort to prevent it, to attach himself to the Cause and Fortunes of the Marattas, who he, the said Hastings, well knew did keep up Claims upon several Parts of the Dominions of Oude, and had with Difficulty been persuaded to include the Nabob in the Treaty of Peace, and suffered him first to languish at Home in Poverty, and then to fly Abroad for Subsistence, and afterwards took no Step, and countenanced no Negotiations for his Return from his dangerous Place of Refuge, at the same Time that several of his the said Hasting's Creatures, had each of them Allowances much more considerable than would have sufficed for the Satisfaction and Comfort of him the said fugitive Prince — was guilty of a High Crime and Misdemeanor.

LXXXIII. And the said Warren Hastings did not only settle a Plan, of which the Agency and Interference aforesaid was a Part, and assert the beneficial Consequences thereof, but did also record, that the same " was " a great public Measure constituted on a large and established System, and destructive in its instant Effects of " the Interest and Fortune of many patronized Individualsand, in Consequence of the said Treaty, he the said Warren Hastings did authorize and positively require ajdSept. 1781. his Agent aforesaid to interfere in, and controul and re-A°Pp.J gulate, all the Nabob's Affairs whatsoever; and the said nu 1. <3. Warren Hastings having made for the Company, and its Name, an Acquisition of Power and Authority, even if it bad been abused by others, he ought to have remedied the Abuse, and brought the Guilty to condign Punishment, instead of making another Treaty, without their Approbation, Consent, or Knowledge, and to this Time not communicated to them; by which it appears he has annulled the former Treaty, and the Authority thereby acquired to the Company, as a Grievance and Usurpa-tion, to which, from the general Corruption of their Service, no other Remedy could be applied than a formal Renunciation of their Power and Influence; for which said Aftings and Doings the said Warren Hastings is guilty of an High Crime and Misdemeanor.

LXXXIV. That the Company’s Army in India is an Objfeft requiring the most vigilant and constant Inspection, both to the Happiness of the Natives, the Security of the British Power, and to its own Obedience and Discipline, does require that Inspection, in Proportion as it is removed from the principal Seat of Government; and the Number and Discipline of the Troops kept up by the Native Princes along with British Troops, is also of great Moment and Importance to the same Ends: That Warren Hastings, Esquire, pretending to pursue the fame, did, in virtue of an Authority acquired by the Treaty of Chunar aforesaid, give drift Orders, and to which he did demand a most implicit Obedience, that all Officers of the Nabob’s Army should be appointed " with " the Concurrence of the Resident;" and supposing the

LXXXV. That the old Brigade of British Troops, which by Treaty was to remain, had been directed, by the Instructions of the said Hastings to the Resident Middleton, and to the Resident Bristow, " not to be " employed at the Requisition of the Vizier, any " otherwise than through the Residentand the said Direction was properly given, it not being fit that British Troops should be under the lole Direction of Foreign independent Princes, or of any other than the British Government; yet, notwithstanding the proper and necessary Direction aforesaid, he the said Warren Hastings hath left the said Troops, by his new Treaty, without any local Controul, or even Inspection, notwithstanding his Powers under the Treaty of Chunar, and his own repeated Orders, and notwithstanding the Mischiefs and Dangers which the said Warren Hastings did foresee would result therefrom, if left under the foie Direction of the Nabob, and their own Discretion, the said Hastings having stipulated with the said Nabob not to exercise any Authority, or even Influence, secret or avowed, within his Dominions.

LXXXIX. That it appears, after the said Warren Hastings had, on Grounds so disgraceful to the British Nation and Government, agreed to remove for ever the British Influence and Interference from the Government of Oude, on Account of the Disorders in the said Government, solely produced by his own criminal Acts and criminal Connivances, that he did overturn his own Settlement as soon as he had made it; and did, after he had abolished the Company’s Residency as a Grievance, wholly violate his own solemn Agreement; for he did, for his private Purposes, continue therein his own private Agent, Major Palmer, with a N umber of Officers and Pensioners, at a Charge to the Revenues of the Country greatly exceeding that of the Establishment under Mr. Bristow, which he did represent as frightfully enormous, and which he pretended to remove; the former amounting to 112,950 /. the latter only to 64,2021.

XC. That his own secret Agent, Major Palmer, did receive a Salary or Allowance equal to 22,800 /. a Year, out of the distressed Province of Oude; and this the said Palmer did dec)are not to be more than he absolutely did really and bond side spend; and that he had retrenched considerably " in feme of the Articles, since " the Expence has been borne by the Vizier, and in " every Particular, he made as little Parade and " Appearance as his Station would admit," his Station being that of the said Warren Hastings's private Agent. But if the said large Salary must be conGdered as merely equal to the Expiences, large secret Emoluments must be presumed to attend it, in order to make it a Place advantageous to the Holder thereof. That the said Palmer did apply to the R°ard at Calcutta for a new Authority to continue the said Establishments, he conceiving their Continuance " after the Period of the tl Governor General’s Departure, depended upon the " Pleasure of the Board, and not upon the Authority of " the Governor General, under the Sanction of which " they were established or confi."

XCI. That the said Warren Hastings, in order to ruin the Resident Bristow, and to justify himself for his former Proceedings respefiting him, did bring before the Board a new Charge against him, for having paid a large Establishment of Offices and Pensions to the Company’s Servants, from the Revenues of Oude; and the said Bristcrw, in making his Defence against the Charge aforesaid, did plead, that he had found all the Allowances 00 his Bill established before his last Appointment to

the Residency; that they had grown to that Excess in the Interval between his first Removal by the said Warren Hastings, and his Re-appointment; and, having adduced many Reasons to make it highly improbable that the said Hastings was perfectly well acquainted with it, and did approve of the expensive Establishments which he the said simply had

paid, but not imposed, he did alledge, btlides the Official Assurances of his Predecefibr Middleton, certain Fads as amounting to a direfit Proof that the Governor General, Wurren Hastings, was not averse to the Vizier’s granting large Salaries to more than One European Gentleman; and the First Instance was to Mr. Thomas, a Surgeon, who, exclusive of his Pay from the Company, which was 1,440/. a Year, claimed from the Vizier, with Mr. Hastings's Knowledge, the Sum of 9,76.3 /. a Year, and upwards, making together 11,2031, per Annum. — The next was Mr. Trevor Wheler, who did receive upon the same Establishment, when he was Fourth Assistant at Oude, 6,000l. a Year; and which last Fad the said Hastings has admitted upon Record, " that the " Accusations of Mr. Bristozo and Mr. Cowper, did " oblige and compel him to acknowledge," denying at the same Time that the Allowance of the Residents Middleton and Bristozo, except in this single Instance, were ever authorized by him: Whereas his own Agent Palmer did, in his Letter of the 27th of March 178.5, represent that the said Salaries and Allowances (if not more and larger) were by him authorized or confirmed.

XCII. That the aforesaid Bristow did also produce the following Letter, in Proof that Mr. Hastings knew and approved of large Salaries to British Subjefiis upon the Revenues of Oude, and which he did declare that nothing but the Necessity of Self-defence could have induced him to produce.

" Dear Bristow,

XCIII. That Sir Eyre Coote aforesaid was, at the Time of the said Field Allowances, not serving in the Country of Oude, on which the said Allowances were charged, but in The Carnatic.

XCIV. That from the Declaration of the said Hastings himself, that it was the Convifition of Mr. Bristow and Mr. Cowper that could alone oblige and compel him to acknowledge certain of his aforesaid Practices, and that nothing but the Necessity of Self-defence could have induced «Mr. Bristow to make public another, and much stronger, Instance of the fame, it is to be violently presumed, that where these Two, or either or both, Necessities did- not exilt, many evil and oppressive Practices of the said Hastings do remain undiscovered. That if it had not been for the Contests between him the said Hastings and the Resident Bristow, not only the before-mentioned Particulars, but the Whole of the expensive Civil Establishments for English Servants at Oude, would have been for ever concealed from the Directors, and from Parliament; and

XCV. That in the said Deceits, Prevarications, Contradictions, malicious Accusations, fraudulent Concealments, and compelled Discoveries, as well as in the said secret, corrupt, and prodigal Dispofilion of the Revenues of Oude, as well as in his Breach of Faith to the Nabob, in continuing expensive Establishments under a private Agent of his own, after he had agreed to remove the Company’s Agent, the said Warren Hastings is guilty of an High Offence and Misdemeanor.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Articles be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Ordered, That the said Articles be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the several Articles of Charge of High Crimes and Mifelctneaners against the said Warren Hastings, Esquire, which were presented to the House by Mr. Burke upon the 4th Day of this Instant April, are referred.

The House being informed that One of the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew. *

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That by an Act, made in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, the Petitioners were impowered to build a Bridge cross the River t from Black-

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, palfed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second and the Fourteenth of His present Majesty, for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Parishes, were read; whereby it appeared that the Vestrymen of the said Parishes were authorized to make an Assessment upon the Inhabitants, of Six Pence in the Pound, for the Maintenance and Support of the said Watch and Beadles, and for other Purposes. And,

Mr. Thomas Drake being examined, said. That notwithstanding the Provisions of the above-mentioned Acts, several very daring Robberies were in the Year 1782 committed, whereupon it was found necessary to employ an additional Number of Men as a Patrol; but the Money arising from the Assessment authorized to be made by the said Acts not being sufficient, a further Sum of Money hath been raised by voluntary Subscriptions — That the establishing the said additional Patrol hath been the Means of preventing many Robt>eries within the said Parishes, and it is therefore highly expedient that the same should be continued Upon loine certain Fund, to be established for that Purpose.

Mr. Langston reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Capital Burgesses, and principal Inhabitants of the Borough of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Hodge, Town Clerk, produced to Your Committee the Charter of the said Borough, by which it appeared that the Corporation of Sudbury consists of a Mayor and Six Aldermen, and Twenty-four Capital Burgesses, but only Two can aft as justices; namely, the Mayor for the Time being, and also the Mayor for the preceding Year, who by the said Charter is like-wile His Majesty’s Coroner for the said Borough, for One Year.

That in the case of the Death of the Mayor, or of his Removal out of the said Borough, Power is given to elect a Mayor in his Room; but in case of the Death or Removal of the Justice and Coroner, no Power is given to elect a Justice and Coroner in bis‘Room, so Yol. 41.

that, in the last Event, the Borough may be reduced to One Magistrate ouly.

And Mr. Hodge said, That there are several Statutes now in force, which require Two Magistrates to be present, and to act in the Execution of those Laws, and that upon the Death or Removal of the Justice or Coroner as aforesaid those Laws cannot be executed, nor any Session holden within the said Borough, nor any Inquisition taken on the View of the Body of any Person who may happen to come to an untimely Death. — And the Witness added, That the appointing an additional Number of Magistrates for the said Borough would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants, and to the Public.

That by an Act of the Seventeenth Year of His present Majesty, all Persons employed in the Woollen and several other Manufactures, and who shall purloin or embezzle anj Materials used in the said Manufactures with which they are intrusted, must be tried before Two Justices of the Peace for the County, Town, or Place where the Offence is committed.

That an extensive Woollen Manufacture is carried on within the said Borough, and that the Magistrates of the said Borough of Sudbury usually employ a great Number of Workmen in the Woollen Manufacture, and are subject to great Losses, from the Materials used in the said Manufacture being purloined and embezzled by their Workmen or Persons with whom such Materials are intrusted, and that therefore if a Magistrate in the said Borough happens to have his Goods purloined or embezzled, the Offender cannot be proceeded against, unless such Magistrate was to act in the double Capacity of Accuser and Judge.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for increasing the Number of Magistrates for the Borough of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk, and for appointing a Coroner for the said Borough, in certain Cafe3: And that Mr. Langston and Mr. William Smith do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Alexander Mackenzie, Esquire, being examined, said. That the large and rapid Rivers of Reidey and Conon, run across the Country Northward of Inverness, from the Mountains to the East Seal — That it is the fingillar Condition of these Rivers to be without a Bridge, from their Sources down to their respective Friths, from which Circumstance, the large and populous Northern District above mentioned is sometimes inaccessible, and always reached through dangerous Fords and Ferries, with, great Inconveniency and not unfrequently without the Lois of Lives. — That the Funds and Abilities of the said District are insufficient for this Undertaking, the same having been exhaulted in making Roads and con-ftrttcting Bridges over various Streams in the Counties to the Northward of the said Rivers. — That* the Rivers Bewley and Conon bound the Eltattes of Locat and Cromarty, which have of late been restored to the former Proprietors — -That during the Time the said Estates were in the Hands of the Public, the Commissioners appointed for their Management, entered at different Times upon v&rious Proceedings for building Bridges on the said Rivers, and paying the Ertpences out of the Rents of the said Estates, but these Rents harving been otherwise applied, neither the find Bridges* nor any other public Work, were carried on upon the said Northern Estates, although their Rents were regularly levied for the Public, and were intended by Parliament for general Improvements in those Parts, as well as in other Quarters of Scotland. And the Witness added. That -the said Two Bridges are conceived to be of great Consequence, tending to complete the only Part that now remains unfinished, of a Line of Communication from one End of the Island to the other; and he produced to Your Committee, a certified Copy of Mr. John SnteatMs Estimate and Report, made to the Trustees of the forfeited annexed Estates in Scotland, of the Expeoce necessary for building the said Two Bridges, which is hereunto annexed by way of Appendix.

The REPORT of John Smeaton, Engineer, upon sundry Matters referred to him by a Minute of the Board of Trustees of annexed Estates, dated 29th January 1770; as also, by the Letter of Mr. Secretary Barclay, of the 17th July 1771: To which is added, his Opinion upon a Subject pointed out in the Course of his View, by Captain Forbes, who attended him.

The several Subjects are as follows:

Bridge over the River Bewlie -

Ditto - - - - Conan -

Ditto - - - - Altgran -

Harbour or Landing Place at Portleich -

Milns and Watercourse of Miltown, of New Tarbat

Stone Piers at the Ferry of Inverbreakie

-,) Board’s Minutes, 29th January 1770.

- Mr. Secretary Barclay's Letter.

Incroachments of the River Bewlie, upon the Lands at( on . ;n Bewlie ----- -J "

Having carefully viewed the above Subjects, in the Month of August 1771, I transmitted to the Honourable Board, Plans, Directions, and Estimates, for constructing the Three Bridges comprehended in the Three first-mentioned Articles, the 19th of February last; but being in the Course of this Business suddenly called away to London, upon Affairs relative to the Great Canal, as I then by Letter informed the Board, and having been, by a Succession of pressing Affairs, occupied ever since, it is only now that I am able fully to acquit myself of the above Articles.

What regards the Three First Articles, I have in a great Measure delivered myself upon as above mentioned, it only remains that I assign my Reasons for preferring the Situations for which these Plans are respectively drawn.

Respecting the River Bewlie; the River at the present Ferry is not only much wider and deeper than at the Place proposed at Dumballoch, but being much more in the Tide’s Way, would on that Account also be more expensive; and furthermore, as the River seems to threaten to break through the Neck of the Loop, at the extreme Bend of which is the Ferry, it might thereby happen, that the Bridge would become deserted (fee Sketch thereof, relative to the last Subject); and if the Bridge was originally built upon this Neck, the cutting

a4lir tJ

26 Geo. III. 130 Aprilis. 603

of the Neck, and forming of a Dam acrose the River at the present Ferry, with a Road upon it, of sufficient Bridges in Height to be out of the Water’s Mark, would be in itself a considerable extra Expence. At Dumballoch, Scotland, the River has a fair Run, is moderately wide and deep, and has a good Gravel Bottom; and, as I am informed, it will not carry the Road much about. I think, upon the Whole, that this Place is to be preferred to any that was pointed out to me, for the Situation of a Bridge over the River Bewlie.

The fitted Place for a Bridge over the River Conan, has been by the Country in general judged to be at a Place called The Rock. The Reason why 1 did not think this Place proper, I gave in my Letter of the 19th February last, which accompanied the Plans and Estimates; and which, to lave the Trouble of a Reference thereto, I here repeat: — " That I find the total Length of a Bridge there (at the Rock) will be greater, by almost 50 Feet, than " where I propose it, and that it will require One Arch to be built of 114 Feet Span; and as the Water is very " deep underneath, it will require so great an Expence to center and construct such an Arch, betides making " good the Passage over the Remainder of the River, which is almost 200 Feet more, that I apprehend it is far " more eligible to construct the Bridge in the Place 1 have fixed upon, where there is a fair and open Run of the " River.

" The Rock, as so called, being a Kind of concreted Gravel, which appears in a Degree to wear away, by " the Action of the Water, it is no ways certain that the River may not in Part undermine the Foundations of to " great and necessarily heavy an Arch, and which, from the Depth of the Water, it will be difficult to guard against " by artificial Means."

Besides the Place I have proposed; viz. at The Boat of Braan, there is also another Situation Westward, at The Turner’s Boat of Braan; this is so nearly equivalent with the former, that Die same Defigu would suit either Place. But by being further Westward, I apprehend it must take Travellers further round, the Passage at the Common Ferry over Conan being Eastward of all those Places.

Exchequer Chambers, Edinburgh, 9th February 1785.

Coals used in Mr. Parry reported from the Committee, to whom I-ofAnglefey. the Petition of John Dawes, Esquire, on Behalf of himself, and others, Owners, Proprietors, and Lessees of Copper and Lead Mines, in the Isle of Anglesey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Samuel More, Esquire, being examined, said, There are Two Mines of Copper in Anglesey, both of which he had seen, but had not any Interest in either — That the Ore is carried from those Mines to be smelted, the greater Part to Saint Helen’s, near Liverpool, and some to Swansea, in Glamorganshire, because there is not Fuel in the Island for linelting it — That no Duty is paid on Coals at the Places to which the Ore is lent. — Being asked. If the Copper Ore of Cornwall is carried to the Coal Mines to be smelted ? he said, He believed great Part of it is — That the Price of Coal in Lemcashire, where the Ore is sent to be smelted, is 5 s. or 5$. 6d. at the Delivery at the Works, and on Shipboard at Swansea 45. 3 d. per Ton — That the Freight of Coals from Liverpool to Anglesey is near 6 s. per Ton, and from Srvansea about 7 s.exclusive of Port Duties. — And being asked, Whether there is any Fire Engine yet erefited in Anglesey ? he laid, It is some Time since he was there — That there is not, nor any Work for smelting Copper — That when he was there the Mines were about Twenty Yards deep — That they are different from any Mines that be had ever seen, the Ore being all in one Mass, like Limestone and Gravel — That there are some Advantages in that, but which may hereafter turn out in some Degree to their Difedvantage, for as they have begun by opening a large Space, and will hereafter be obliged to fink Shafts, as is usual in Mining, the great Opening will serve as a Funnel to receive a large Quantity of Rain Water, and tend to fill up the Mine — That the Altitude of the Mountains from the Level of the Island may be about or under 200 Feet, and the Openings are very near the Summit of the Hill. — -And being asked. In what Degree the Discouragement the Mines are said to have suffered, has been hitherto felt? he said, The Company themselves are the heft Judges of that. — Being asked, Whether they are near the Bottom of the Ore? he said, That when he was there they were not near it. — And being asked, How soon his Observation led him to think a Fire Engine would be necessary? he said, He should imagine soon; that it depends much on Circumstances — That it may be necessary directly, and may not for a considerable Time. — And being asked, If he had tried the Ore? he said, He had, and all the Materials that come from the 01

Mountain where it is raised — That the Ore hi its Raw State is so poor, as not to produce on the Average One in Twenty. — And being asked, Whether he knew’, that, notwithstanding the Poorness of the Ore, the Work is exceedingly profitable ? he said. He was not competent to speak to that, but it is understood so to be — That he had always heard from the Parties themselves that it was. — And being asked, Whether the Miners have an ealy Method of increasing the Value of the Ore by burning it on the Grass when landed, without the Expence of Fuel I he said, The Nature of the Ore is such, that it is very easily let on Fire so as to be calcined in large Kilns, w’itbout much Expence of Fuel; but by being thus calcined in the open Air, a very great Proportion of the Metal itself is loft in the Operation, notwithstanding the Methods made use of to recover some of the Metal by Precipitation, by Means of Iron, Plates- — That after this Calcination, he should suppose the Produce of the Ore is on the Average about Two in Twenty. — And being asked, Whether the Water follow's in digging up the Ore from the Mate, as it does in other Mines? he said, Not near in the same Proportion as it does when the Veins are small. — And being asked. What is the Altitude of the Mountain from the Level of the Sea? he said, From 300 to 350 Feet, he believed, from that Part of the Mountain where they were at Work when he was there; and that Part of it next the Sea forms a bold Shore. — And being asked. What Stratum a Level from the High Water Mark to the Mine would go through? he said, He believed a hard Quartz, and not any Metals, for none appeared to him. — And being asked, If there are Adits from Mines in Cornwall of as great a Length as that which would be necessary from draining the Mines in Anglesey? he said. He believed there are. — And being asked. How the Water was got out of the Anglesey Mine when he was there? he laid, By a Horse Wheel, called A Whim. — And being asked. Whether, in case the Petitioners succeed, and the Drawback should be allowed, the Processes that w’ould then be used by the Proprietors in smelting the Ore, would be more injurious to the circumjacent Country than the Processes now used ? he said, Certainly not — That they cannot be more injurious; and, if they were, the Country is so ruined already, that it cannot be made worle. — And being asked, Whether the present Produce of the Ore will pay the Expence of an Act from the Mine as he had describedit? he said, It w’ould not. — And being asked. What will be the Expence of an Act ? he said. Nobody can tell — that he took the common Average Price of making Adits to be Twelve Guineas a Yard, but it may be more. — And being asked, What is the Annual Produce of the Mine? he said, He did not know. — And being asked, Why he thought the Mine would not bear the Expence of an Adit? he said, Because, if the Ore continues as poor as it is now, the increasing Charge of raising it will be such, that it will not bear both Expences. — And being asked, What is the Average Proportion of the Produce of the Cornish Mines? he said, Two and an Half in Twenty — That the Standard Price of Copper may be said to be 80 /. per Ton. — And being asked, What, at that Price, is the Anglesey Ore, which produces One in Twenty, worth to the Proprietors? he said, The general Rule for finding the Value of Ore is to multiply the Standard by the Product, which gives the Value in Shillings; from that Product to dedu6t 3 /. for Smelting Charges, which is universally allowed, and the Remainder will be the Value; which, in the Instance of the Anglesey Ore, is Twenty Shillings per Ton — That by the same Mode of Calculation, the Ore which produces Two and an Half in Twenty, is worth 7/. per Ton to the Proprietors; and that the great Increase of Value arises from the Smelting Charges being only 3 /. on each Kind of Ore. — And being asked, What Proportion

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, Woollen Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Bamest in the County of Decon, and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Exportation of British Wool, by secret and illicit Practices, from England into Foreign Countries, has lately increased to an alarming Degree, to the great Injury of this Kingdom in general, and the Woollen Manufactory in particular; and that the Petitioners apprehend large Quantities of live Sheep are Annually sent off from various Parts of the Kingdom, which adds greatly to the Injury com* plained of: And therefore praying the House to take these important Subjects into Consideration, and to take such Measures to remedy this Evil, as to them shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Woollen Manufacturers, and others, of the Borough of Ashburton, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the illicit Exportation of Wool from this Island, by secret Means, into Foreign Countries, has of late, the Petitioners have Reason to believe, increased to an alarming Degree, to the great Injury of this Kingdom in general, and of the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying the House to take the important Subject into Consideration, and enact such Laws as to the House shall seem meet, to supply the Defects of the present Statutes, so that the fulled and belt Use may be made of this native Commodity, on which the Value of Lands, the Trade of the Nation, and the Employment of its Inhabitants, do chiefly depend.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, em- Greenland ployed in the Whale Fishing from the Port of Dundee, ^shale was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, 1 ery‘ That the said Port, existing chiefly by its Trade and Shipping, to secure a Supply of Seamen for the Use of the Trading Vessels, the Whale Fishing was attempted in 1752, and was persevered in till 1781, when it was dropped, though then encouraged by a Bounty of Forty Shillings, and the Want of this valuable Nursery of Seamen has, since that Period, been very sensibly felt by the Trade of the said Place, in the Scarcity of Seamen,

and that the said George Ross, by himself, and his Agents in his Behalf, and others, by their Privity and Direction, previous to, during the Time of, or since the said Election, were guilty of Bribery and other corrupt and illegal Practices, entering into U nconftitu tional Agreements for that Purpose, keeping back the Writ, and forcibly excluding Persons entitled to be prefect at the Election, in order to procure the said Election in Favour of the said George Ross; and that the said George Ross was ineligible and incapable to serve in Parliament, having been an Army Agent, having Public Money in his Hands in that Capacity, and enjoying Emolument, Profit, and Advantages through the Medium of those by whom the Agencies of various Regiments in His Majesty’s Service were conducted; and that the Petitioner, having had the Votes of the Delegates of the Burghs of Wick and Dornwho were the only legal Electors at the said Election, ought to have been returned, notwithstanding which the said George , Esquire, was returned as the Burgefe duly elected to serve in Parliament for the aforesaid District of Burghs, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and give fu9h Redress therein as to them shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday, the 23d Day of May next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Mr. Burke presented to the House several other Articles of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal.

And the said Articles were delivered in at the Clerk’s Table, and read; and are as followeth; viz.

Further Articles of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Hastings, Esquire,

late Governor General of,

N° 17. Mahomed Reza Khan.

I. That it was the declared Policy of the Company, on the Acquisition of the Duannee of Bengal, to continue the Country Government, under the Inspection of the Resident at the Nabob’s Durbar in the First Instance, and that of the President and Council in the last; and for that Purpose they did stipulate to assign, for the Support of the Dignity of the Nabob, an Annual Allowance from the Revenues, equal to # Four hundred Pounds a Year.

II. That, during the Country Government, the principal active Person in the Administration of Affairs, for Rank, and for Reputation of Probity, and of Knowledge in the Revenues and the Laws, was Mahomed Reza Khan, who, besides large Landed Property, was possessed of Offices, whose Emoluments amounted nearly, if not altogether, to One hundred thousand Pounds a Year.

IV. That the Company’s Servants, in the Beginning, were not conversant in the Affairs of the Revenue, and stood in Need of Natives of Integrity and Experience to act in the Management thereof. On that Ground, as well as in regard to the Rank which Mahomed Reza Khan held in the Country, and the Confidence of the People in him, they, the President and Council, did inform the Court of Directors, in their Letter of the 30th of September 1765, that " as Mahomed Reza Khan's " short Administration was irreproachable, they determjned to continue him in a Share of the Authority;" and this Information was not given lightly, but was founded upon an Enquiry into his Conduct,

and a minute Examination of Charges made against him by his Rivals in the Nabob's Court; they having in-fmuated to the Nabob, that a Design was formed for deposing him, and placing Mahomed Reza on his Throne; but, on Examination, the President and Council declare, that " he had so openly and candidly accounted for " every Rupee disbursed from the Treasury, that they " could not, without Injury to his Character, and " Injustice to his Conduct, during his short Adminifixation, refuse continuing him in a Share of the " Government."

V. That the Company had Reason to be satisfied

with the Arrangement made, so far as it regarded him; the President and Council having informed them in the following Year, in their Letter of the 9th of December 1766, that " the large Increase of the Revenue must, " in a great Measure, be alcribed to Mr. s Affiduity, and to Mahomed Reza profound

" ledge in the Finances."

VI. That the then President and Council, finding

it necessary to make several Reforms in the Administration, were principally aided in the same by the Suggestion. Advice, and Assistance of the said Mahomed Reza KhAn-, and in their Letter to the Court of Di-

rectors of the 24th of June 1767, they state their Relo-lution of reducing the Emoluments of Otfice, which before had arisen from a Variety of Presents, and other Perquisites, to fixed Allowances; and they state the Merits of Mahomed Reza KhAn therein, as well as the Importance, Dignity, and Responsibility of his Station, in the following Manner:

" Mahomed Reza KhAn, has now, of himself with " great Delicacy of Honour, represented to us the evil " Consequences that must ensue from the Continuance " of this Practice; since by suffering the principal " Officers of the Government to depend for the Support of their Dignity on the precarious Fund of Perquisites, they in a Manner oblige them to pursue " oppressive and corrupt Measures, equally injurious to " the Country and the Company; and they accordingly " assigned Twelve Lack of Rupees for the Maintenance " and Support of the said Mahomed Reza KhAn, and " Two other principal Persons who held in their Hands " the most important Employments of that Government, " having Regard to their elevated Stations, and to the Expediency of supporting the n? in all the Shew and " Parade requisite to keep up the Authority and Influence of their respective Offices, as they are all Men of Weight and Consideration in the Country, who " held Places of great Trust and Profit under the former " Government. We further propose, by this Act of " Generality, to engage their cordial Services, and " confirm them steady in our Interests, since they cannot " hope, from the most fuccelsful Ambition, to rife to " greater Advantages by any Chance or Resolution of " Affairs. At the same Time it was reasonable we " should not lose Sight of Mahomed Reza Khan's past " Services; he has pursued the Company’s Interest " with Steadiness and Diligence; his Abilities qualify " him to perform the most important Services. The " unavoidable Charges of his particular Situation are " great; in Dignity he (lands Second to the Nabob " only; — and as he engages to increase the Revenues, " without Injustice or Oppression, to more than the " Amount of his Salary, and to relinquish those Advantages, to the Amount of Eight Lacks of Rupees per " Annum, which he heretofore enjoyed, we thought it " proper, in the Distribution of Salaries, to consider Mahomed Reza KhAn in a Light superior to the other Ministers. We have only to observe farther, that great " and enormous as the Sum must appear, which we have " allotted for the Support of the Ministers of the Government, we will not hesitate to pronounce that it is necessary and reasonable, and will appear so, on the

" Consideration

VII. T'bat the said Mahomed Reza continued, with the same Diligence, Spirit, and Fidelity, to execute the Trustreposed in him, which comprehended a large Proportion of the Weight of Government, and particularly of the Collections; and his Attachment to the Interest of the Company, and his extensive Knowledge, was again, in the Course of the Year 1767, fully acknowledged, and Hated to the Court of Directors; and it farther appears, that, by an irvceflant Application to Business, his Health was considerably impaired, which gave Occasion, in the Year following, that is, in February 1768, to a fresh Acknowledgment of his Services, in these Terms: "We must, in Justice to Mahomed " Reza Khdn, express the high Sense we entertain of 11 his Abilities, and of the Indefatigable Attention he has shewn in the Execution of the important Trust reposed in him; and we cannot but lament the Prospect of " losing his Services, from the present declining State of " his Health."

VIII. That as, in the Increase of the Revenue, the said Mahomed Reza Khdn was employed as a Person likely to improve the same without Detriment to the People, so, when the State of any Province seemed to require a Remission, he was employed as a Person disposed to the Relief of the People without Fraud to the Revenue; and this was expressed by the President and Council as follows, with relation to the Remissions granted in the Province of Bahar " That the general " Knowledge of Mahomed Reza Khdn, in all Matters " relative to the Duannee Revenues, induced us to " consent to such Deductions being made, from the " general State of that Province at the last Poonah, V as may be deemed irrecoverable, or such as may " procure an immediate Relief and Encouragement to the Ryots in the future Cultivation of their Lands."

IX. That the said Mahomed Reza Khdn, in the Execution of the said great and important Trusts and Powers, was not so much as suspected of an ambitious or encroaching Spirit, which might make him dangerous to the Company's, then recent. Authority, or which might render his Precedence injurious to the Consideration due to his Colleagues in Office; but, on the contrary, it appears that a Plan having been adopted for dividing the Administration, in order to remove the Nabob's Jealousies, the same was in Danger of being subverted by the Ambition "of Two of his Colleagues, " and the excessive Moderation of Mahomed Reza " Khdn." And for a Remedy of the Inconveniences, which might arise from the Excels of an accommodating Temper, though attended with irreproachable Integrity, the President and Council did fend One of their own Members, as their Deputy to the Nabob of Bengal, at at his Capital of Muxadavad; and this Measure appears to have been adopted for the Support of Mahomed Reza Khan, in consequence of an Enquiry made, and Advice given by Lord Clive, in his Letter of the 3d of July 1765; in which Letter he expresses himself of the said Mahomed Reza Khdn as follows: " It is with Pleasure " I can acquaint you, that the more I see of Mahomed " Reza Khan, the stronger is my Conviction of his " Honour and Moderation; but that, at the same Time, " I cannot help observing, that either from Timidity, " or an erroneous Principle, he is too ready to submit " to Encroachments upon that Proportion of Power that has been allotted him."

XII. That the said Warren Hastings, at the Time he gave his Orders as aforesaid, for arresting the said Mahomed Reza Khdn, did not take any Measures to compel the Appearance of any other Persons as Witnesses, declaring it as his Opinion " that there would be " little Need of Violence to obtain such Intelligence, as " they could give, against their former Master, when " his Authority is taken from him;" but he did afterwards, in Excuse for the long Detention and Imprisonment of the said Mahomed Reza Khdn, without any Proofs having been obtained of his Guilt, or Measures taken to bring him to a Trial, allure the Directors, itl direct Contradiction to his former Declaration, " that " the Influence of Mahomed Reza Khdn (till prevailed " generally throughout the Country, in the Nabob's " Household, and at the Capital, and was scarcely affected by his present Disgrace," — notwithstanding, as he, the said Hastings, doth confess, he had used his utmost Endeavours " to break that Influence, by removing his Dependants, and putting the Direction of " all the Affairs that had been committed to his Care " into the Hands of the most powerful or active of his " Enemies; that he depended on the Activity of their

" Hatred to Mahomed Reza Khdn, incited by the Ex-ix pectation of Rewards, for iuveltiguting the Conduct " of the latter; that with this the Institution of the new " Duannee coincided; and that the same Principle had " guided him in the Choice of Mrnny Begum and Rajah " Gourdass, the former for the Chief Administration;

The MOGUL delivered up to the Maratta*.

I. That Shd Allum, the Prince, commonly called The Great Mogul, or, by Eminence, The King, is, or lately was, in the Pofftffiou of the antient Capital of

tan; and though without any considerable Territory* and without a Revenue sufficient to maintain a moderate Slate, be is still much respected and considered; and the Custody of his Person is eagerly fought by many of the Princes in India, on Account of the Ule to be made of his Title and Authority; and it was for the Interest of the East India Company that while, on one

Hand, no Wars shall be entered into in Support of his Pretentions, on the other, no Steps should be taken which may tend to deliver him into the Hauds of any of the powerful States of that Country; but that he should be treated with Friendship, good Faith, and respectful Attention.

II. That Warren Hastings, in Contradiction to this safe, just, and honourable Policy, strongly prescribed and enforced by the Orders of the Court of Directors, did (at a Time when he was engaged in a Negotiation, the declared Purpose of which was to give Peace to India) Letter to cok* concur with the Captain General of the Maratta State, nelM" r, Sept. called Madajee Scindia, in hostile Designs against the tew AppeVto s0p. remaining Territories of that same Mogul Emperor, by plem"o *d R*" virtue of whose Grant the Company actually possess the p°rt’ Government, and enjoy the Revenues of great Pro-1

vinces, and also against the Possessions of a Chief called Nudjif Cawn, a Person of much Merit with the East India Company; in Acknowledgement of which they had granted him a Pension, included in the Tribute due to the King, and, together with that Tribute, taken from him by the said Warren,

though expressly guaranteed to him by the Company.

With both these Powers the Company had been in Friendship, and were actually at Peace at the Time of the said clandestine Concurrence in a Design against! them; and the said Hastings hath since declared, That the Right of One of them, namely, " the Right of the " Mogul Emperor to our Assistance, has been constantly " acknowledged."

III. That the said Warren Hastings, at the Time of his treacherous Concurrence in a Design against a Power, which he was himself of Opinion we were bound to assist, and against whom there was no Doubt he was bound neither to form nor to concur in any hostile Attempt, did give a Caution to Colonel Muir, to whom the Negotiation aforesaid was entrusted on the Part of the Company, against "inserting any Thing in the " Treaty which might expressly mark our Knowledge of his [the Maratta General’s] Views or Concurrence in " them." Which laid Transaction was full of Duplicity and Fraud; and the Crime of the said Hastings therein is aggravated, by his having some Years before withheld the Tribute, which by Treaty was solemnly agreed to be paid to the said King, on Pretence that he had thrown himself, for the Recovery of his City of on the Protection of the Marat las, whom the said Warren Hastings then called the natural Enemies of the Cora- oa»t pany, and the Growth of whole Power he then alledged *‘H-

to be highly dangerous to the Interests of this Kingdom in India.

IV. That after having concurred* in the Manner before mentioned, in a Design of the Marattas against the Mogul; and notwithstanding he the said Warren

by which Proposal, and Acceptance thereof, the East India Company was placed in a Situation of great and perplexing Difficulty, since either they were to engage, at an unlimited Expence, in new Wars, contrary to their Orders, contrary to their general declared Policy, and contrary to the published Resolutions of the House of Commons, and wholly incompatible with the State of their Finances; or, to preserve Peace, they mult risque the Imputation of a new Violation of Faith, by departing from an Agreement made on the voluntary Propofol of their own Government; the Agent of the fold Hastings having declared, in his Letter to the said Hastings, by him communicated to the Board, " That the Business of affifiting " the Shst [the Mogul Emperor] can and go on, if we with to be secure in India, or regarded as a Nation of Faith and Honour."

V. That the said Warren Hastings did, on the 20th Day of January 1784, fend in Circulation to the other Members of the Council, a Letter to him from his Agent, Major Browne, dated at Delhi, on the 30th of December 1783, viz. that Letter to which the foregoing References are made, in which the said Browne did directly prels, and indirectly (though sufficiently. and firongly) suggest several highly dangerous Measures, for realizing the general Offers and Engagements of the said Warren Hastings; proposing, that besides a Proportion of Field Artillery, and a Train of Battering Cannon for the Purpose of Sieges, Six Regiments of Sepoys in the Company’s Service should be transferred to that of the find King, and that certain other Corps should also be raised for the said Service in the English Provinces and Dependencies, to be immediately under the King’s [the Mogul’s] Orders, and to be maintained by Alignments of Territorial Revenue within the* Province of Oude, a dependent Member of the British Government, but with a Caution against having any British Officer with the fame; the said Major Browne expressing his Caution as followeth: — " If any European Officer be with this Corps, a very nice Judgment indeed mult direct the Choice; for scarce any are in the smallest Degree Jit " for such Employ, but much more likely to do Harm " than Good." And the Letter aforesaid, being without any Observation thereon, or any Disavowal of the Matters of Fact, or of the Councils so. firongly and

authoritatively delivered therein, by the said Warren Hastings's Agent, and without any Mark of Disappro-bation of any Part of his Plan, whether that of the Assignment of Territory belonging to the Company’s Allies for for the Maintenance of Troops, which were to be by that Plan put under the Orders of a Foreign independent Power, or that of employing the said Troops without any British Officer with them; or for his alarming Observation by him entered on the Company’s Records, which, if not an implied Censure on the Nature of the Service in which British Officers are supposed improper to be trailed, is a strong Reflection on the Character of the British Officers, which was to render them unfit to be employed in an honourable Service — -The said Warren Hastings did thereby give a Countenance to the said unwarrantable and dangerous Propofols and Reflections.

VI. That, a contiderable Time before the Production and Circulation of Major Browne’s Letter, the said Hastings did enter a Minute of Confutation, containing a Proposition similar in the general Intent to that in the said Letter contained, for assisting the Mogul with a Military Force; but the other Members of the Board did difegree thereto, and being alarmed at the Disposition so firongly shewn by the said Hastings, to engage in new Wars, and dangerous Foreign Connections, and possibly having Intelligence of the Proceedings of his Agent, did call upon him to produce his Infiruction6 to Major Browne; and he did on the 5th of October 1783, and not before, enter on the Consultations a certain Paper, purporting to be the Instructions which he had given to Major Browne the preceding March, the Time of his, the said Browne's, Appointment; in which pretended Instructions no Direction whatsoever was given to the Effect of his the said Hastings’s Minute of Confutation propounded; that is to foy, no Power was given in the said Instructions to make a direct Offer of Military Aid to the Mogul, or to form the Arrangements fiated by the said Browne, in his Letter to the said Hastings, as having been made by the exprefo Authority of the said Hastings himself. But the said Instructions contained nothing further on that Subject, but a Conditional Direction, that in case a Military Force should be required for the Mogul’s Aid or Protection, the Major is to know the Service on which it is to be employed, and the Re-fburces from whence it is to be paid; and the Instructions produced as his real Instructions by the said Hastings, are so guarded, as to caution the said Browne against taking any Part in the Intrigues of those who are about the King’s Person. By which Letters, Instructions, and Transactions, compared with each other, it appears that the said Warren Hastings, after Six Months Delay in entering of (contrary to the Company’s Order) any Instructions to the said Browne, did at last enter a false Paper as the true, or that he did give other secret Instructions, totally different from, and even of polite to, his public ostensible Instructions, thereby to deceive the-Council, and to carry on, with less Obstruction, dark and dangerous Intrigues, contrary to the Orders of the Court of Directors, to the true Policy of this Kingdom, and to the Safety of the British Poflessions in the East.

VII. That the said Letter from Major Browne was by the said Warren Hastings transmitted to the Court of Directors, without being accompanied by any Part of the previous Correspondence; by which wilful Concealment the said Wairen Hastings is guilty of an high and criminal Disrespect to the Court of Directors, and of a most flagrant Breach and Violation of their Orders, which he was bound by an Act of Parliament to obey.

X. That in a Letter dated from the same Place,

Lucknow, the 16th of the following June 1784, the said Warren Hastings informs the Court of Directors, that Major Browne, their Agent to the Mosul, bad arrived there in the Character also of Agent from the Mogul, with Two Sets of Instructions from Two of-polite Parties in his Ministry, which Instructions were directly contrary to each other; the First, which were the ostensible Instructions, being to engage the said Hastings, in the Mogul’s Name, to ehter into a Treaty of mutual Alliance with a Chief of the Country, then Minister to the said Mogul, called AJrasaib Khan; the Second were from another principal Person, called Mudjed ul Dowla, also a Minister of the said Mogul (but styled in the said Letter Confidential, for Distinction) which were directly destructive of the former; and the said latter Instructions, to which

it leems Credence was to be given, were sent " under " the most solemn Adjurations of Secrecy." The Purpose of these latter and secret Instructions were to require the Company's Aid in freeing the Mogul from the Op-pressions of his Servants, namely, from the Oppressions of the said AJrasaib, between whom and the Company Major Browne (at once Agent to that Company, and to Two opposite Fa&ions in the Mognl’s Court) accepted a Power to make a Treaty of mutual Alliance, under the Sanction of his Sovereign; and it does not appear that he, Warren Hastings, did discountenance the double Dealing and fradulent Agencies of his and the Company’s Minister at that Court; or did disavow any Particular in the Letter from him the said Browne, of the 30th of December 1783, stating the Offers ihade on his Part to the Mogul, so contradictor? to his late Declarations to the Heir Apparent of that Monarch, or did give any Reprimand to the said Browne, or did shew any Mark of Displeasure against him, as having acted without Orders, but did again fend him, with renewed Confidence, to the Court aforesaid.

XI. That the said Warren Hastings, still pursuing his laid evil Designs, did apply to the Council for Discretionary Powers relative to the Intrigues and Fa€Hons in the Mogul’s Court, giving Assurances of his Resolution not to proceed against their Scnfe; But the

XII. That in order to subvert the plain and natural Interpretation given by the Council to the Orders of the Court of Directors, and to justily his dangerous Intrigues, the said Warren Hastings, in his Letter of the 16th June 1784 to the said Court, did, in a most insolent and contemptuous Manner endeavour to persuade them of their Ignorance of the true Sense of their own Orders, and to limit their Prohibition of Interference with the Disputes of the Country Powers, to such Country Powers as are permanent; expressing himself as follows: " The Faction which now surrounds the Throne " [the Mogul’s Throne] is widely different from the " Idea which your Commands are intended to convey " by the Expressions to which you have generally applied " them of Country Powers, to which that of is a necessary Adjunct; and which may be more properly compared to a splendid Bubble, which the " slightest Breath of Opposition may dissipate, with every * Trace of its Existence." By which Construction the said Hastings did endeavour to persuade the Court of DireCkors, that they meant to confine their Prohibition of sinister Intrigues to those Powers only who could not be easily hurt by them, and whose Strength was such that their Resentment of such clandestine Interference was to be dreaded; but that where the Powers were weak and fragile, such Intrigues might be allowed.

XIII. That the said Hastings, further to persuade the Court of Directors to involve themselves in the Affairs of the Mogul, and to reconcile this Measure with his former Conduct, and declared Opinions, did write to them to the following Effect; that " at that former Period, to " which the ancient Policy with regard to the Mogul applied, the King’s Authority was sufficiently respected

[which he knew not to be true, having himself declared, " in his Minute of the 25th of October 1774, " That he " remained at Delhi, the ancient Capital of the Empire, " a. mere Cypher in the Administration of it."] to main-% " tain itself against common Vicissitudes. That he would

" not have advised Interference, if the King himself retained the Exercise of it, however feeble, in his own " Hands. That if it [the Mogul’s Authority] is suffered " to receive its final Extinction, it is impossible to foresee what Power may arise out of its Ruins, or what " Events may be linked in the same Chain of Resolution with it: But your Interests may suffer by it " — your Reputation certainly as his Right to

" our Assistance has been constantly acknowledged, and " by a Train of Consequences to which our Government has, not intentionally, given Birth; but " most especially by the Movements which Infuence, by too near an Approach, has excited, it has " unfortunately become the efficient Instrument of a " great Portion of the King’s present Distrefies and " Dangers;" intimating (as well as the studied Oblcurity of his Expressions will permit any thing to be discerned) that his own late Intrigues had been among the Causes of the Distrefies and Dangers, which by new Intrigues he did pretend to remove; And he did conclude this Part of his Letter with some loose general Expressions of lib Caution not

to affect the Company’s Interests or Revenues by any Measurrs he might at that Time take.

XIV. That the Principle, so far as the same hath been directly avowed, of the said Proceedings at the Mogul’s Court, was as altogether irrational, and the pretended Object as impracticable, as the Means takeu in Pursuit of it were fraudulent and dishonourable, namely, the Restoration of the Mogul in some Degree to the Dignity of his Situation, and to his Free Agency in the Conduct of his Affairs. For the said Hastings, at the very Time in which he did with the greatest apparent Earnestness urge the Purpose which he pretended to have in View with regard to the Dignity and Liberty of the Mogul Emperor, did represent him as a Person wholly diiqualified and even indisposed to take any active Part whatsoever in the Conduct of his ow n Affairs; and that any Attempt for that Purpose would be utterly impracticable: And this he hath ltated to the Court of Directors as a Matter of public Notoriety, in his said Letter of the 16th of June 1784, in the following emphatical and decisive Terms.

" You need not be told the Character of the King, whose " Inertness, and the Habit of long fullering, has debased " his Dignity and the Fortunes of his House beyond the " Power of retrieving either the one or the other. Whillt " his Personal Repole is undisturbed, he w ill prefer to

live in the meanest State of under the Rule " of Men whose Views are bounded by Avarice and " the Power which they derive from his Authority, thaa " commit any Share of it to his own Sons, though his Affection for them is boundless in every other Respect,

" from a natural Jealously, founded on the Experience " of a very different Combination of those Circumstances " which Once served as a Temptation and Example of " unlawful Ambition in the Princes of the Royal Line.

" His Ministers, from a Policy more reasonable, have " constantly employed every Means of Influence to " confirm this Disposition, and to prevent his Sons " from having any Share in the Distribution of Affairs,

so as to have established a complete Usurpation of " the Royal Prerogative under its own Sanction and " Patronage."

The Reality of the said Attachment was not improbable, but altogether useless; as the said Minister was the only one among the principal Persons about the King, who (besides the total YVant of all Military and Civil Ability) possessed no Territories, Troops, or other Means of serving and supporting him; but was himself solely upheld by his Influence over his Master; neither doth the said Hastings free' him any more than the Persons more efficient, who were to be destroyed, from a Disposition to alienate the King from an Attention to his Affairs, and from all Confidence in his own Family j but, on the contrary, he brings him forward as the very first among the Instances he adduces to exemplify the Practices of the Ministers against their Sovereign and his Children.

XXI. That in further Pursuit of the same pernicious Design, he the said Warren Hastings did enter into an Agreement to withdraw a very great Body of the British Troops out of the Nabob's Dominions; asserting, however truly, yet in direct Contradiction to his own Declarations, that " this Government [meaning the " British Government] has not any Right to force " Defence with its Maintenance upon him" [the Nabob]; and he did thus not only avowedly aggrandize the Maratta State, and weaken the Defence upon the Frontier, but did as avowedly detain their Captain General in Force on that very Frontier; notwithstanding be was well apprized, that they had Designs against those dependent Territories of Oude, which they had with great Difficulty been persuaded even in Appearance to include in the Treaty of Peace; and that they have never renounced their Claims upon certain large and valuable Portions of them, and have shewn evident Signs of their Intentions, on the First Opportunity, of averting and enforcing the m. And, finally, the said Warren Hastings, in Contradiction to sundry Declarations of his own, concerning the Necessity of curbing the Power of the Marattas, and to the Principle of sundry Measures undertaken by himself professedly for that Purpose, and to the Sense of the House of Commons, expressed in their Resolutiou of 28th 1782, against any Measures that tended to unite the dangerous Powers of the Maratta Empire under One active Command, has endeavoured to persuade the Company, that " while Scindia lives, every Accession of Territory

" obtained by him will be an Advantage to this [the " British] Government;" which, if it was true as

respecting the Personal Dispositions of Scindia, which there is no Reaibn to believe, yet it was highly Criminal to establish a Power in the Marattas, which must survive the Man, in Confidence of whose Personal Dispositions a Power more than Personal was given, and which may hereafter fall into Hands disposed to make a more hostile Use of it.

XXII. That in Consequence of all the before-recited Intrigues, the Mogul Emperor being in the Hands of the Marattas, he the said Mogul has been obliged to declare the Head of the Maratta State to be Vicegerent of the Mogul Empire, an Authority which supersedes that of Vizier, and has thereby consolidated in the Maratta State all the Powers acknowledged to be of legal Authority in India; in Consequence of which they have acquired, and have actually already attempted to use, the said Claims of general Superiority against the Company itself; the Marattas claiming a Right in themselves to a Fourth Part of the Revenues of all the Provinces in the Company’s Pofiession, and claiming in Right of the Mogul the Tribute due to him; by which Aftings and Doings the said Hastings has to the best of his Power brought the British Provinces in India into a Dependence on the Maratta State; and in order to add to the aforesaid enormous Claims a proportioned Force, he did never cease, during his Stay m India, to contrive the Means for its Increase: For it is of public Notoriety, that One great Object of the Maratta Policy is to unite under their Dominion

the Nution or Religious Sect of the Seiks, who being a People abounding with Soldiers, and possessing large Territories, would extend the Maratta Power over the Whole of the vast Countries to the North-West of India.

XXIII. That the said Warren Hastings, farther to augment the Power of the said Marattas, and to endanger the Safety of the British Possessions, having estab-liftied in Force the said Marattas on the Frontier, as afore recited, and finding the Council General averse in that Situation to the withdrawing the British Forces therefrom, and for disbanding them to the Extent required by the said Hastings, did in a Minute of the 4th December 1784, after stating a Supposition, that, contrary to his Opinion, the said Troops should not be reduced, propose to employ them under the Commaad of the Mogul’s Son, then under the Influence of the Marattas, in a War against the aforesaid People or Religious Sect called Seiks, defending the same on the following Principles: " I feel the Sense of an Obligation " imposed on me, by the Supposition I have made, to " state a Mode of rendering the Detachment of Use in " its prescribed Station, and of affording the appearance " of a Cause for its Retention."

XXIV. That the said Hastings did admit, that there was no present Danger to the Company’s Possessions from that Nation, which could justify him in such a War, as he had declared that the Marattas were the only Power that bordered on the Company’s Possessions and those of the Vizier; but he did assign as a Reason for going to War with them, their Military and Enthu-fiaftic Spirit; the Hardiness of their natural Confiitution; the Dangers which might arise from them in some future Time, if they should ever happen to be united under One Head, they existing at present in a State little different from Anarchy; and he did predict great Danger from them, and at no very remote Period, " if this " People be permitted to grow into Maturity without " Interruption." And though he doth pretend, that the Solicitations of the Heir Apparent of the Mogul, who he fays did repeatedly and earnestly solicit him to obtain the Permission to use the Company’s Troops for the Purpose aforesaid, had Weight with him; yet he doth declare, as he expresses himself in the Minute aforesaid, that " a " stronger Impulse, arising from the Hope of blasting " the Growth of a Generation whose Strength might " become fatal to our own, strongly pleaded in my Mind " for supporting his Wiihes."

XXV. That the said Warren Hastings, after forcibly recommending the Plan aforesaid, did state strong. 05-jeftions, that did, " in his Judgment, outweigh the " Advantages which might arise from a Compliance " with it." Yet the said Hastings, being determined to pursue his Scheme for aggrandising, at any Rate, the Maratta Power, in whose adult Growth, and the recent Effects of it, he could fee no Danger, did pursue the Design of War against a Nation or Sect of Religion in its Infancy, from whom he had received no Injury, and in whose present State of Government he did not apprehend any Mischief whatsoever: And finding the Council fixed and determined on not disbanding the Frontier Regiments, and thinking that therein he had found an Advantage, he did ground thereon the following Proposition.

" If the Expence [of the Frontier Troops] is to " be continued, it may be surely better continued " for some ufeftil Purpose, than to keep up the " Parade of a great Military Corps, designed merely " to lie inactive in its Quarters. XXVI. That the said Warren Hastings did, in the said Proposal, endeavour to circumvent and over-reach the Council General, by converting an apparent and literal Compliance with their Resolution into a real and substantial Opposition to and Disappointraent thereof. For his First Proposal was to withdraw the Company’s Troops from the Viziers Country, on the Pretence of relieving him from the Burthen of that Efrablishment, but in Reality with a View of facilitating the Maratta Pretentions on that Province, which would then be deprived of the Means of Defence. And when the Council rejected the said Proposal, on the express Ground of Danger to the Province, by withdrawing from the Ma-rattas the Restraint of our Troops, the said Hastings, finding his First Scheme in Favour of the Marattas, against the Provinces dependant on the Company, defeated by the Refusal of the Council to concur in the said Measure of withdrawing the Troops, did then endeavour to obtain the same Purpose in a different Way; and instead of leaving the Troops, according to the Intention and Policy of the Council, as a Check to the Ambition and Progress of the Marattas, he proposed to employ them in the actual Furtherance of those Schemes of Aggrandizement, of which his Colleagues were jealous, and which it was the Object of their Resolution to counteract.

XXVII. That in the whole of the Letters, Negotiations, Propofols, and Projects of the said Warren Hastings 1,relative to the Mogul, he did appear to pursue but One Object, namely, the Aggrandizement of the lately hostile and always dangerous Power of the Ma-' ratios; and did pursue the same by Means highly dif-honourable to the British Character for Honour, Justice, Candour, Plain Dealing, Moderation and Humanity.

A Petition of the Retail Shopkeepers of the Town of Hawkers &nd Falmouth, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to PeiUani’ the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and many other neighbouring Shopkeepers, will be greatly affected and injured by the Bill for repealing the 9th and 11 th Clauses of the Hawkers and Pedlars Act, palfed last Year, in case the same shall pals into a Law, and therefore they cannot fee, but with deep Concern, such a Meal’ure intended to be enacted, as will totally destroy the Force of the aforesaid Clauses (the only Alleviation to the Petitioners for the heavy Shop Tax lately imposed) and which, if repealed, will render the Burthen of the last mentioned Tax (already fuf-liciently grievous) much more heay,;- and that the aforesaid Clauses, as they now stand, are beneficial to the Community, being the Means of preventing those Itinerants from imposing their (otherwise) unialeable Wares on the unwary Public, and who pay a very small Portion to the Public Levies, compared to the heavy and grievous Taxes with which the Petitioners and other Retail Shopkeepers are burthened: And therefore requeuing, That the aforesaid restraining Clauses may not be repealed, and that the House. wftl grant to the Petitioners such other Relief as to’ the House shall seem meet,

A Petition of the resident Shopkeepers within the Ditto. Borough of Truro, in the County of Cornwall, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is now before the House, to repeal an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their Trade: And therefore praying, That the House will take into their serious Consideration the ill Consequences that must inevitably follow -the Repeal of that Act to the resident Traders, who have heretofore suffered so much by those itinerant Traders, and who, by an Act of the last Session, were burthened by an additional Tax, on-their Shops, and will not suffer the said Bill to be carried into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill to repeal so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating " their Trade," as restrains Hawkers and Pedlars from exposing to Sale Goods in Market Towns, and as enables Justices of the Peace, of any County, to prohibit such Hawkers and Pedlars from vending their Goods within the same, and for further regulating their Trade, be read a Second Time.
