A Petition of the Merchants of Edinburgh and Lath, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, all Owners, or Part Owners of Ships concerned in the Whale Fishing at tjhe Port of Leith, was prefeuted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Number of the Petitioners were concerned in the Old Edinburgh Whale Fishing Company, with a Capital Stock of 12,775/. Sterling, which was all funk in the Trade, even with the Bounty of 40$. Sterling per Ton, excepting 1,825/. Sterling, when the Company came to be dissolved in July last; and that the Petitioners have again fitted out Four Ships from the Port of Leith, at a great Expence, on the Faith of the Bounty continuing, which employ near Two hundred of as good Seamen as any in the Kingdom, a Number of which could not otherwise be employed at the Port of Leith, although born and bred in the Place, and served their Country in the late War; and that reducing the Greetdand Bounty will nearly operate to the Extinction of that Branch of Bufinefe in this Country, and will be a particular Hardship on the Owners of Ships returning without Success: And therefore praying the House to continue the Bounty of 40 Sterling per Ton, at lead to give that Bounty to the Owners of those Ships which return to their respective Ports without Success, according to Justice.

A Petition of the Directors of the East Lothian and Merse Whale Fishing Company carried on at Dunbar, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have carried on at Dunbar the Whale Fishing Trade for Thirty-four Years, that the Bounty has been 40 s.person lor Twenty-nine Years, and for Five Years, from the Year 1777 to 1781,inclusive, 30 s.per Ton, and, in the early Part of their Business, the Ships fitted out from Scotland amounted, at One Time, to Sixteen; and that all the Adventurers gave up Business, and, in most Cafes, loft nearly their Capitals, except the Petitioners, who had the only Ships in that Trade from Scotland for several Years, and the said Company, in the Year 1770, were so much in Debt, that it was in Agitation to dissolve the Company, which would have been nearly the Lois of their Capital of 9,950/. but, by Perseverance, they struggled through their Difficulties, paid their Debt, and are now a flourishing Company, having increased their Ships from Three to Five; and that the Petitioners have kept very regular Rooks, from which a full Statement of the Particulars of their Trade, from the Year 1752 to 1785, is made out, find, during that Period, they have fitted out Niqety-

Yoi.. M.

eight Ships, and never loft One, and have caught to the Value in Oil and Bone 91,099/.; and that the Circumstances and Direction of their Company, for Thirty-four Years, are the most singular, in Point of Example, that they suppose can be brought forward for the Information of the House, and, the Petitioners apprehend, that the House, on considering the Facts contained in these Statements, will fee good Reason to continue the Bounty at 40& per Ton for feme Years longer, otherwise the new Adventurers will probably share the unhappy Fate of their Predecessors in the Trade: And therefore praying the House to take these Statements into Consideration.

Mr. Alderman Neumham reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as foloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for building a Bridge cross the River Thames from in the City of

London, to the opposite Side, in the county of,

and to make Ways and Passages to and from the lame, on each Side of the said River; and also, an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for com pleating the said Bridge, and the Avenues thereto, on the London Side of the said River, were read; by which last mentioned Act it appeared, that the said Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons were impowered to embank a certain Part of the North Side of the said River, within the Limits therein described, and, for the Purpose of providing a Fund to defray the Expences of lighting, watching, cleansing, and repairing the said Bridge, when built, that they were also impowered to charge the Ground to be obtained by the said Embankment with certain Quit Rents to arise therefrom.

Mr. Robert Milne, Surveyor, being then examined, said, That the said Bridge and Embankment are corn-pleated, as directed and required by the said Acts — That the Produce of the Fund anting by virtue of the said Acts, and thereby made applicable to the Support and Maintenance of the said Bridge, and of the lighting, watching, and cleansing thereof, amounts to no more than 175/1 per Annum; but that there are feme other small Pieces of Ground, at present under Dispute, which if let by the City of London may form an Addition to the said Fund of about 10/. per Annum. And he produced to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of watching, lighting, cleansing, watering, and repairing the said Bridge, by which it appeared, that the Annual Charge thereof will be 599 /. and upwards. And being further examined, he laid. That all the Particulars of the said Estimate, except the watering, are exprefely directed to be done by the said Acts of Parliament, and that the Calculations are formed upon a Plan of performing the said Works in such a Manner as will be but barely sufficient for the Safety and Accommodation of the Public. And being further examined, he said, It is apprehended, that a Sunday Toll on Carriages and Horses passing over the said Bridge, would be the most eligible Way of obtaining an Income sufficient to make up the Deficiency of the present Fund, applicable to the above-mentioned very useful and necessary Purposes;

!f"? of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against r‘ In^s‘ Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of

Bengal.

And the said Article was delivered in at the Clerk's Table, and read; and is as followeth;

Further Article of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal,

N* 19.

Libel on the Court of Directors.

I. That Warren Hastings, Esquire, was, during the Whole of the Year 1783, a Servant of the East India Company, and was bound by the Duties of that Relation, not only to yield Obedience to the Orders of the Court of Directors, but to give to the Whole of their Service an Example of Subnnffion, Reverence, and Reined: to their Authority: And that if they should, in the Course of their Duty, call in Question any Part of his Conduct, he was bound to conduct his Defence with Temper and Decency; and while his Conduct was under their Consideration, it was not allowable to print and publish any of his Letters to them, without their Content first had and obtained; and he was bound by the same Principles of Duty, enforced by still more Cogent Reaions, to observe, in a Paper intended for Publication, great Modesty and Moderation, and to treat the said Court of Directors, his lawful Matters, with Respect.

II. That the said Warren Hastings did print and publish, or cause to be printed and published, at Calcutta in Bengal, the Narrative of his Transactions at Benares, in a Letter written at that Place, without Leave had of the Court of Directors, in order to preoccupy the Judgment of the Servants in that Settlement, and to gain from them a factious Countenance and Support, previous to -the Judgment and Opinion of the Court of Directors, his lawful Superiors.

III. That the Court of Directors, having come to certain Resolutions of Fad relative to the Engagements subsisting between them and the Rajah of Benares, and the Manner in which the same had been fulfilled on the Part of the Rajah, did, in the Fifth Resolution, which was partly a Resolution of Opinion, declare as follows: " That it appears to this Court, that the Conduct of the " Governor General towards the Rajah, whilst he was at " Benares, was improper; and that the imprisonment of " his Person, thereby disgracing him in the Eyes of his " Subjects, and others, was unwarrantable and highly " impolitic, and may tend to weaken the Confidence " which the Native Princes of India ought to have " in the Justice and Moderation of the Company’s " Government."

Vol. 41.

IV. That the said Resolutions being transmitted to the said Warren Hastings, be, the said Warren Hastings, did write, and cause to be printed and published, a certain false, inlolent, malicious, and seditious Libel, purporting to be a Letter from him; the said Warren Hastings, to the Court of Directors, dated Fort William, 2oth March 1783, "calculated [as the Directors truly " affirm] to bring Contempt, as well as an Odium, on " the Court of Directors, for their Conduct on that " Occasion and the said Libel had a direct Tendency to excite a Spirit of Disobedience to the lawful Government of this Nation in India, through all Ranks of their Service.

V. That he, the said Warren Hastings, among other

inlolent and contumacious Charges and Aspersions on the Court of Directors, did addrels them in the printed Letter aforesaid, as follows: — " I deny that Rajah Cheit Sing was a Native Prince of India. Cheit Sing is " the Son of a Collector of the Revenue of that Province, which his Arts, and the Misfortunes of his " Master, enabled him to convert to a permanent and " hereditary Possession. This Man, whom you have thus " ranked among the Princes of India, will be astonished " when be hears it, at an Elevation so unlooked for; " nor less at the independent Rights which your Commands have assigned him; Rights which are so foreign " to his Conceptions, that I doubt whether he will know " in what Language to assert them; unless the Example " which you have thought it consistent with,

" however opposite to Policy, to shew, of becoming his " Advocates against your own Interests, should inspire " any of your own Servants to be his Advisers and " Instructors."And he did further, to bring into Contempt the Authority of the Company, and to excite a Resistance to their lawful Orders, frame a Supposition that the Court of Directors had intended the Restoration of the Rajah of Benares; and on that Ground did presume, in the said label, to calumniate, in difrefpedful and contumelious Terms, the Policy of the Court of Directors, as well as the Person whom he did conceive to be the Object of their Protection, as followeth: — "Of " the Conferences of such a Policy I forbear to speak. " Most happily, the Wretch whose Hopes may be excited

" by the Appearances in his Favour, is ill qualified to " avail himself of them, and the Force which is stationed " in the Province of Benares is sufficient to suppress any

Symptoms of internal Sedition’, but it cannot fail to " create Distrust and Suspense in the Minds both of the " Rulers and of the People, and such a State is always " productive of Disorder. But it is not in this partial " Consideration that I dread the Effects of your Commands, it is in your proclaimed Indisposition against " the First Executive Member of your First Government in India. I almost lhudder at the Reflection of " what might have happened, had these Denunciations " against your own Minister, in Favour of a Man univertally considered, in this Part of the World, as justly " attainted for his Crimes, the Murderer of your Ser- vants and Soldiers, and the Rebel to your Authority, " arrived Two Months earlier.’’

VI. That the said Warren Hastings did also presume to censure and asperse the Court of Directors for the moderate Terms in which they had expressed their Dif-pleasure against him, as putting him under the Necessity of stating in his Defence a strong Accusation against himself; and as implying in the said Court a Conscious-qefs that he was not guilty of the Offences charged upon him, being, as he asserts, in the Resolutions of the Court of Directors, " arraigned and pre-judged of a " Violation of National Faith in Acts of such complicated Aggravation, that, if they were true, no Punishment SHORT OF DEATH could atone for the " Injury which the Interest and Credit of the Public

" had

Charge* " had sustained in them And he did therefore censure

against the said Court, for applying no stronger, or more crimi*-

Mr. Mailings. nating Epithets, than those of " improper, unwarrantable, and highly impolitic," to an Offence so by them charged, and by him described. And though it be true, that the Expressions aforesaid are much too reserved for the Purpose of duly chara&erifing the Offences of the said Hastings, yet was it in him most indecent, to libel the Court of Directors for the fame; and his Implication, from the Tenderness of the Epithets and De-feriptious aforesaid used towards him, was not only indecent, but ungrounded, malicious, and scandalous; he having himself highly, though truly, aggravated " the " Charge of the Injuries done by him to the Rajah of " Benares," in order to bring the said Directors into Contempt and Suspicion; the Paragraphs in the said Libel being as follow: " Here I must crave Leave to " say, that the Terms ‘improper, unwarrantable, and " highly impolitic,’ are much too gentle, as Deductions " from such Premises; and as every Reader of the Jt latter will obviously feel, as he reads, the Deductions " which inevitably belong to them, I will add that the " strict Performance of solemn Engagements on one " Part, followed by Acts directly subversive of them, " and by total Dispossession, on the other, stamps on " the Perpetrators of the latter the Guilt of the " greatest possible Violation of Faith and Justice." — " There is an Appearance of Tenderness in this " Deviation from plain Construction, of which, however meant, I have a Right to complain; because it " imposes on me the Necessity of framing the Terms " of the Accusation against myself, which you have " only not made, but have dated the leading Arguments to it so strongly, that no one who reads " these can avoid making it, or not know it to have " been intended."

VII. That the said Hastings, being well aware that his own Declarations did contain the cleared Condemnation of his own Conduct from his own Pen, did in the dud Libel, attempt to overturn, frustrate, and render of none Effect, all the Proofs to be given of Prevarication, Contradiction, and of Opposition of Action to Principle, which can be used against Men in public Trust, and did contend that the same could not be used against him; and as if false Assertions could be justified by factious Motives, he did endeavour to do away the Authority of his own deliberate, recorded Declarations, entered by him in Writing on the Council Books of the Presidency; for, after asserting, but not attempting to prove, that his Declarations were confident with his Conduct, he writes in the said Libel as follows: For " were it otherwise, they were not to be made the " Rules of my Conduct; and God forbid that every c‘ ExprefSon dictated by the Impulse of present Emergency, and unpremeditatedly uttered in the Heat of " Party Contention, should impose upon me the Obligation of a fixed Principle, and be applied to every " variable Occasion."

VIII. That the said Hastings, in order to draw the lawful Dependence of the Servants of the Company from the Court of Directors, to a factious Dependence on himself, did, in the Libel aforesaid, treat the Acts and Appointments of their undoubted Authority, when exercised in Opposition to his arbitrary Will, as ruinous to their Affairs, in the following Terms: " It is as well known to the Indian World, " as to the Court of English, Proprietors, that the " first declaratory Instruments of the Dissolution of " my Influence, in the Year 1774, were Mr. John " Bristow and Mr. Francis Fowke: By your ancient " and known Constitution, the Governor has been ever " held forth, and' understood to possess the ostensible x< Powers of Government; all the Correspondence 02

" with Foreign Princes is cohduCled in his Name; and " every Person resident with them for the Management

" of your Political Concerns, is understood to be mom " especially his Representative, and of his Choice — and " such ought to be the Rule; for how otherwise can " they trust an Agent, nominated against the Will of his Principal ? When the State of this Administration " was such as seemed to admit of the /Appointment of " Mr. Bristow to the Residency of Lucknow, without " much Diminution of my oxen Influence, I gladly " seized the Occasion to fiiew my Rcadincfs to submit " to your Commands: I proposed his Nomination; he was nominated, and declared to be the Agent of my " own Choice. Even this Effect of my Caution is " defeated by your absolute Command for his Re-appointment independent of me, and with the Supposition that " I should be adverse to it. — I am now wholly deprived " of my Official Powers, both in the Province of Oude,

" and in the Zemindary of Benares."

IX. That, further to emancipate others and himself from due Obedience to the Court of Directors, he did, in the Libel aforesaid, enhance his Services; which, without Specification or Proof, he did suppose in the said Libel to be important and valuable, by representing them as done under their Displeasure; and doth attribute his not having done more, to their Opposition, as followeth: — "It is now a complete Period of Eleven " Years since I first received the First nominal Charge,

" of your Affairs; in the Course of it I have invariably " had to contend, not with ordinary Difficulties, but " such as most unnaturally arose from the Opposition of " those very Powers from which I primarily derived my " Authority, and which were required for the Support (f " it.My Exertions, though applied to an unvaried

" and confident Line of Action, have been occasional " and desultory; yet I please myself with the Hope,

" that in the Annals of your Dominion, which shall be " written after the Extinction of recent Prejudices, this " Term of its Administration will appear not the least " conducive to the Interests of the Company, nor the " least reflective of the Honour of the British Name;. " and allow me to suggest the Instructive Reflection of " what Good might have been done, and what Evil prevented, had due Support been given to that " tion which has performed such eminent and substantial " Services without it."

And the said Hastings, farther to render the Authority of the said Court perfectly contemptible, doth, in a Strain of Exultation for his having escaped out of a Measure, in which by his Guilt he had involved the Company in a ruinous War, and out of which it had escaped by a Sacrifice of almost all the Territories before acquired (from that Enemy which he had made) either by War, or former Treaties, and by the abandoning the Company’s Allies to their Mercy; attribute the said sup-pol'ed Services to his acting in such a Manner as had on former Occasions excited their Displeasure, in the following Words:

" Pardon, Honourable Sirs, this digreflive Exultation;

" I cannot suppress the Pride'which I feel in this successful Atchievement of a Measure so fortunate for " your Interests, and the National Honour-; for that " Pride is the Source of my Zeal, so frequently exerted " in your Support, and never more happily than in those " Instances in which I have departed from the prescribed " and beaten Path of Action, and assumed a Responsibility " which has too frequently drawn on me the most poinied " Effects of your Displeasure. But however I may yield " to my private Feelings, in thus enlarging on the Subject, my Motive in introducing it was immediately " connected with its Context, and was to contract the " actual State of your Political Affairs, derived a u happier Influence, with that which might have attended

That the said Eight Distri6ts are situated without the Liberties of the City of Edinburgh, enjoy no Benefit or Privilege within the same, derive no Protection or Accommodation from the Police Establishments thereof, and are, to all Intents and Purposes, as much unconnected with the said City, excepting the Angle Circumstance of Vicinity, as any other Part of the County of Edinburgh, and the said tight Districts have, on no Occasion whatever, been subjected to any Burthen imposed upon the City of Edinburgh, whether for the Support of its internal Government and Police, or for defraying the Expence of public Works within the same; and that, in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, the Magistrates and Town Council of Edinburgh o!>-tained an Act of Parliament for building a Bridge over the Cougate, and impoling certain Assessments for defraying the Expence of the lame, and, in Consideration of this Communication, which was an Object of considerable Benefit to the Inhabitants of the Eight Districts, and in Consequence of the Magistrates having further prouiifed to supply the said Eight Districts with Water, to make a Communication from the East to the West Parts

St. Nicholas A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and Gloucetten principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Sa'int Nicholas, in the City of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, of late, from, Year to Year, t,he Inhabitants of the said Parish have been at great Charges in repairing the said Church, and in particular, from the Month of July 1783 to June following, they expended in such Repairs the Sum of 149/. 65. 11;

and that, not, withstanding such Expence, they observed their Church to get so much more out of Repair, as to excite the Alarm of falling, and, on the 27th of February last, an Order of Vestry was made for its being surveyed by Five of the ablest Architects; and that, on the 8th Day of March last, and not before, Four of the said Architects made their Report, that the Church was in lb ruinous a State as to be imprudent to attempt further repairing, and recommended building a new Church, and, to the Enquiries of the Parishioners, informed them they could not warrant its standing a Month, on which the Parishioners removed their Effects out of the Church, and no Service hath been attempted there since, nor could the Petitioners present any Petition to the House within the Time limited for receiving Petitions for private Bills: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to present a Petition for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to preleut a Petition, as desired by the said Minister, Churchwardens, and principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Nicholas, in the City of Gloucester.

Then a Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Nicholas, in the City of Gloucester, and of others the Inhabitants of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Church of the said Parish of Saint Nicholas is an ancient Building, projecting out of the Line into the Street, and, from the Failure of its Foundation, and the rife of the Ground, its Floor is Five Feet 06

and upwards below the Street; and that, on the Erection of Spouts and Gutters round the said Church, irt pursuance of the Act of the Twenty-first of His. present Majesty, for regulating the Streets of the City of Gloucester, it was neglected to make Drains from them into the Street Gutters, but the Waters thereby collected were led down and suffered to drain themselves into the Graves in the said Church, whereby its Foundation is become a Quagmire, and lets in such a Manner as to endanger its falling; and that there being a Necessity for rebuilding the Church, it is thought most eligible to erect it on a new Site within the Line of the Street:

And therefore praying for such Powers to effect so good and pious a Work as may be thought right by the House.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers resident in the Bo- Hawkers* rough of Helston, in the County of Cornwall, was pre- Pedlars, fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are heavily burthened with Taxes, particularly that imposed' on Retail Shops; and that the great.

Number of Hawkers and Pedlars who resort to the said Borough (and, under the Pretence of felling cheap, vend such damaged and bad Goods as it would be impossible for a resident Shopkeeper, who has his Credit at Stake, to fell) are very prejudicial to the Petitioners, by taking from it its ready Money, by which Means the Petitioners are obliged to give such long Credit as must ultimately end in the Ruin of themselves and Families; and that the Petitioners observe, that a Bill is brought into the House, praying a Repeal of the 9th and 11th Clauses of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for the further Regulation of Hawkers and Pedlars, a Repeal of which Clauses will put the Hawkers and Pedlars on the same Footing as before the passing of the said Act, by which Means they (having no Parochial or other Taxes, or House Rent to pay, except for their Licences) will have a great Advantage over the fair resident Tradesmen, and greatly injure them and their Families; and that the Justices of the Peace of the County of Cornwall were so fully fenftble of the Inutility of those Itinerants, and the Harm they did to the fair Trader, that, at the last Michaelmas Sessions, they prohibited them from vending their Wares in the said County, by virtue of the Power vested in them by the said 11th Clause; and that the Petitioners have not the least Doubt but the Revenue of this Kingdom is much injured by the great Quantities of smuggled Goods, such as Mullins, Cambricks, Ir sh Linens, French Laces, and India Goods, which find a ready Sale by means of these Itinerants, and, therefore, hope, That the House, taking into their serious Consideration the Subject of this Petition, and the great Difedvantages the Petitioners will labour under in case the said Clauses should be repealed, will continue the same in full Effect.

To prove the Allegations of the said last mentioned Petition, an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to prevent " Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals,

" sold by Wharf Measure, within the City of London,

" and the Liberties thereof, and between Dock

" and Limekouse Hole, in the County of

and also an Act, passed in the Seventeenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for continuing the before-mentioned Act, were read: And

Mr. John Edington, a Coal Merchant being examined, find, That the said tirft-mentioned Act is in several Re-spefts defective, by Reason whereof great Frauds and Abuses have arisen in the Admeasurement of Coals, which might be prevented, and the Public greatly benefited, if the said Act was amended, and the Powers thereof enlarged.

Mr. Gregory French, a Coal Merchant, confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to prevent Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, sold by Wharf Measure, within the City of London, and the Liberties thereof, and between Tower Dock and Limekouse Hole, in the County of Middlesex: And that Sir Watkin Lewes,

Mr. Alderman Watson, Mr. Alderman Sawbridge, and Mr. Alderman Newnham, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

The House was moved, That an Act, made in the last Duties ua Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for reducing S®11the Allowances for Waste on Salt and Rock Salt; for regulating the Exportation of Salt to Jersey,

" Alderney, and Sark; for repealing the Laws allowing " the Use of foul Salt for Manure only; for allowing " a Drawback on the Exportation of Glauber or Epsom " Salts; for restraining Fill) Curers from being Dealers in " Salt; for regulating the Exportation of Herrings from " the Isle of Man; for better securing the Duties on " Salt; and for indemnifying Persons who have been " guilty of Offences against the Laws relating to the " Duties on Salt," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain the said Act; and for repealing so much of an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for encouraging and regulating the Trade and Manufactures of the of Alan,

" and for the more easy supply of the Inhabitants there " with a certain Quantity of Wheat, Barley, Oats, Meal,

" and Flour, authorized by an Act, made in this Session,

" to be transported to the said Island." as relates to permitting any Person to import into the Isle of Man, Fish from any Place whatever, except from Great Britain, without Payment of any Custom or other Doty whatlo-ever: And that Mr. Rose and Mr. Steele do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Mom- Refined ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole Sugar-House, to considerof the Exportation of British refined Sugar to the Isle of Man.

Maratta War, and Peace.

I. That by an Act passed in 1773, it was expressly

ordered and provided, " that it should not be lawful for " any President and Council of , or

" Bencoolen, for the Time being, to make any Orders " for commencing Hostilities, or declaring or making " War, against any Indian Princes or Powers, or for " negociating or concluding any Treaty of Peace, or " other Treaty, with any such Indian Princes or Powers " without the Consent and Approbation of the Governor " General and Council first had and obtained, except " in such Cases of imminent Necessity as would render " it dangerous to pdftpone such Hostilities or Treaties " until the Orders from the Governor General and Council might arrive." — That nevertheless the President and Council of Bombay did, in December 1774, without the Consent and Approbation of the Governor General and Council of Fort William, and in the Midst of profound Peace, commence an unjust and unprovoked War against the Maratta Government; did conclude a Treaty with a certain Person, a Fugitive from that Government, and proscribed by it, named Ragonaut Row, or Ragoba-, and did, under various base and treacherous Pretences, invade and conquer the Island of

Salsette, belonging to the Maratta Government.

II. That Warren Hastings, oft the first Advices received in Bengal of the above Transactions, did condemn the same in the strongest Terms; declaring,

a May I7th5' that " the Measurrs adopted by the Presidency of Rep.com. of " Bombay had a Tendency to a very extensive and Secrecy, n»6». Indefinite Scene of Troubles; and that their CoilduCfc was unseasonable, impolitic, unjust, and unauthorized." — And the Governor General and Council, in order to put a Stop to the said unjust Hostilities, did appoint an Ambassador to the Peihwa, or Chief of the Maratta State, resident at Poonaand d° n° n6 Ambassador did, after a long Negociation,

javarcVi7;6. conclude a definitive Treaty of Peace with the said Pefhwa, on Terms highly honourable and beneficial to the East India Company, who, by the said Treaty, obtained from the Marattas a Cefiion of considerable Tracts of Country, the Maratta Share of the City of Broach, Twelve Lacks of Rupees for the Expences of the said unjust War, and particularly the Island of Salsette, of which the Presidency of Bombay had possessed themselves by Surprize and Treachery; that in Appendix» Return for thele extraordinary Concessions, the Arse Rep. Nost. tides principally infilled on by the Marattas, with a View to their own future Tranquillity and internal Quiet, were, that no Assistance should be given to any

Subject or Servant of the Ptshica that should cause Disturbances, or Rebellion, in the Maratta Dominions, and particularly, that the English should not assist Ragonaut Row, to whom the Marattas agreed to allow Five Lacks of Rupees a Year, or a Jaghire, to that Amount, and that he should reside.at Benares; that nevertheless, the Presidency of Botnbay did receive and keep Ragonaut Row at Bombay, did furnish him with a considerable Establishment, and continue to carry on secret Intrigues and Negotiations with him, thereby giving just Ground of Jealously and Distrust to the Maratta State: That the late Colonel John Upton, by whom the Treaty of Poorunder was negociated and concluded, did declare to the Governor General and Council, " That while Ra- d°, 31st jDiy " gonaut Razo reside6 at Bombay, in Expedition of *777-

That the said Warren Hastings, concurring with his Council, which then consisted of Sir John Clavering, Richard Barzoell, and Philip Francis, esquires, did, on the 18th of August 1777, declare to the Presidency of Bombay, d*. n*i*. that " he could fee no lteafon to doubt that the Presence of Ragoba at Bombay would continue to be " an insuperable Bar to the Completion of the Treaty " concluded with the Maratta Government, nor " could any sincere Cordiality and good Understanding be established with them, as long as he should " appear to derive Encouragement and Support from u the English." Presidency to the Court of Poona; which late and reluctant Content and Authority were extorted from him, the said Hastings, in consequence of the Acknowledgment of his Agent at the Court of Madajee Scindia (upon whom the said JVarren Hastings had depended for enforcing the Clauses of the Maratta Treaty) of the Precariousness of such Dependence, and of the Necessity of that direct and separate Treaty with Tippoo, so long and so lately reprobated by the said JVarren Hastings, notwithstanding the Information and Entreaties of the Presidency of Fort St. George, as well as the known Distresses and critical Situation of the Company’s Affairs.

— That though the said JVarren Hastings did at length* give Instructions for negociating and making Peace with Tippoo; exprefely adding, that those Instructions extended to all tha Points which occurred to him or them as capable of being agitated or gained upon the Occasion;

— though the said Instructions were font after the said Commissioners by the Presidency of St. George, with Directions to obey them; though not only the said Instructions were obeyed, but Advantages gained which did not occur to the said JVarren Hastings; — though the said Peace formed a Contrail with the Maratta Peace, in neither ceding any Territory possessed by the Company before the War, or delivering up any Dependant or Ally to the Vengeance of his Adverferies, but providing for the Restoration of all the Countries that had been taken from the Company and their Allies; — though the Supreme Council of Calcutta, forming the legal Government of Bengal in the Absence of the said Warren Hastings, ratified the said Treaty: Yet the said Warren Hastings, then absent from the Seat of Government and out of the Province of Bengal, and forming no legal or integral Part of the Government during such Absence, did, after such Ratification, usurp the Power of acting as a Part of such Government (as if actually fitting in Council with the other Members of the lame) in the Consideration and unqualified Censure of the Terms of the said Peace. That the Nabob of Arcot, with whom the said Hastings did keep up an unwarrantable, clandestine Correspondence, without any Communication with the Presidency of Madras, wrote a Letter of Complaint, dated the 27th of March 1784, against the Presidency of that Place, without any Communication thereof to the said Presidency, the said Complaint being addressed to the said JVarren Hastings, the

8 D Substance

A. 178

654 28

Substance of which Complaint was, that he (the Nabob) had not been made a Party to the late Treaty: And

although his Interest had been sufficiently provided for in the said Treaty, the said Hastings did lign a

Declaration on the 23d of May, at Lucknow, forming the Bafts of a new Article, and making a new Party to the Treaty, after it had been, by all Parties (the Supreme Council of Calcutta included) completed and ratified, and did transmit the said new Stipulation to the Presidency at Calcutta, solely for the Purposes, and at the Jnftigation, of the Nabob of Arcol; and the said Declaration was made without any previous Communication with the Preftdency aforesaid, and in conlbquence thereof Orders were sent by the Council at Calcutta to the Preftdency of Fort Saint George, under the severest Threats in case of Disobedience; which Orders, whatever were their Purport, would, as an undue Assumption of, and Participation in, the Government from which he was absent, become a high Misdemeanor; but, being to the Purport of opening the said Treaty, after its l'olenm Ratification, and proposing a new Clause and a new Party to the fame, was also an Aggravation of such Misdemeanor, as it tended to convey to the Indian Powers an Idea of the Unfteadinels of the Councils and Determinations of the British Government, and to take away all Reliance on its Engagements, and as, above all, it exposed the Affairs of the Nation and the Company to the Hazard of seeing renewed all the Calamities of War, from whence, by the Conclusion of the Treaty, they had emerged, and upon a Pretence so weak as that of proposing the Nabob of Arcot to be a Party to the same — though he had not been made a Party by the said Warren Hastings in the Maratta Treaty, which profell’ed to be for the Relief of the Carnatic; — though he was not a Party to the former Treaty with also relative to the Carnatic; — though it was not certain whether, if the Treaty were once opened, and that even Tippoofhould then content to that Nabob’s being a

Party, whether he (the said Nabob) would agree to the Clauses of the fame, and consequently whether the said Treaty, once opened, could afterwards be concluded — an Uncertainty, of which he, the said Hastings, should have learned to be aware, having already once been disappointed by the said Nabob’s refusing to accede to a Treaty which he the said Warren Hastings made for him with the Dutch about a Tear before.

That the said Warren Hastings having broken a solemn and honourable Treaty of Peace, by an unjust and unprovoked War; having neglected to conclude that War, when he might have done it without Lol's of Honour to the Nation; having plotted and contrived, as far as depended on him, to engage the India Company in another War, as loon as the former should be concluded; and having at last put an End to a moll unjust War against the Marattas by a most ignominious Peace with them, in which he fiicrificed Objects essential to the Interests, and submitted to Conditions utterly incompatible with the Honour, of this Nation, and with his own declared Sense of the dishonourable Nature of those Conditions; and having endeavoured to open anew the Treaty concluded with Tippoo Sultan, through the Means of the Preftdency of Fort St. George, upon Principles of Justice and Honour, and which established Peace in India; and thereby exposing the British Pof-sessions there to the Renewal of the Dangers and Calamities of War — has, by these several Acts, been guilty of sundry High Crimes and Misdemeanors.

CORRESPONDENCE.

That by an A£1 of the 13th Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for establishing certain " Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs " of the East India Company, as well in India as in " Europe," " The Governor General and Council are c»p. 6j.$ec.j. " required and directed to pay due Obedience to all " such Orders as they shall receive from the Court of " Directors of the said United Company, and to correspond from Time to Time, and couftantly and diligently " transmit to the said Court, an exact Particular of all " Advices or Intelligence, and of all Transadlions and " Matters whatsoever that shall come to their Knowledge,

" relative to the Government, Commerce, Revenues, or " Interest of the said United Company."

That in consequence of the above-recited Act, the Court of Directors, in their General Inllructions of the 29th March 1774, to the Governor General and Council, did direct, " That the Correspondence with the " Princes or Country Powers in India, should be carried " on through the Governor General only; but that all " Letters to be lent by him should be first approved in " Council, and that he should lay before the Council,

" at their next Meeting, all Letters received by him " in the Course of such Correspondence, for their " Information."

And the Governor General and Council were therein further ordered, " That, in tranladling the Business of Plr- »

" their Department, they should enter, with the utmoR " Perspicuity and Exactness, all their Proceedings whatsoever; and all Dissents, if such should at any Time " be made by any Member of their Board, together " with all Letters sent or received in the Course of their " Correspondence; and that broken Sets of such Proceedings, to the latest Period possible, be transmitted " to them (the Court of Directors) a complete Set at " the End of every Year, and a Duplicate by the next " Conveyance."

That in Defiance of the said Orders, and in Breach of the above-recited Act of Parliament, the said Warren Hastings has, in sundry Inllances, concealed from his Council the Correspondence carried on between him and the Princes or Country Powers in India, and neglected to communicate the Advices and Intelligence he from Time to Time received from the British Reli-dents at the different Courts in India to the other Members of the Government; and without their Knowledge,

Counsel, or Participation, has dispatched Orders on Matters of the utmost Consequence to the Interefb of the Company.

That moreover, the said Warren Hastings, for the Purpose of covering his own improper and dangerous Practices from his Employers, has withheld from the Court of Directors, upon sundry Occasions, Copies of die Proceedings had, and the Correspondence carried on by him in his Official Capacity, as Governor General, whereby the Court of Directors have been kept iu Ignorance of Matters which it highly imported them to know, and the Affairs of the Company have been exposed to much Inconvenience and Injury.

That in all such Concealments and Acts done or ordered without the Consent and Authority of the Supreme Council, the said Warren Hastings has been guilty of High Crimes and Misdemeanors.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Articles be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Robert Beggar, Junior, Esquire (a Linen Manufacturer) being examined, said, That the said *Act has had feme Eftect, but not sufficient to produce the Eud that the Legislature had in View-«-That the English Flax has proved of an exceeding good Quality, and in feme Years preferable to the Foreign, and they would have consumed more of it, if it could have been supplied —

That for Want of a sufficient Home Supply, and the increased Demand upon the Foreign Market, the Price of Foreign Flax has ril'en near 40/. per Cent, which has exposed the Manufacture to great Hardlliips, and threatens the total Loss of it to Great Britain.

And the Witness added, That, from the Knowledge he has of the State of the Trade, he is of Opinion that a Sum, not less than from 3 /. to 400,000 I. is Annually expended in the Purchase of Foreign Flax and Flax Seed. Then,

Mr. Henry Jowett, a Flax Drefier, at York, being examined, laid, That he had inquired of the Farmers what was the Cause of their not obtaining the Bounty granted by the said Act, and found, that after growing the Flax they had claimed the Bounty at the Quarter Sessions, and could only obtain it for the Year 1782, and that only in Part — That from the Want of Succels in their Application other Growers were discouraged from applying at all — That the Expectation of the Bounty induced Numbers to grow for the first Year, but finding the y did not succeed in getting the Bounty, they seemed to be discouraged — That the Answer they received to their Application at the Quarter Sessions was, that the Magistrates had not the Money, nor any Orders to pay it.

That the Witness attended One or Tw-o Sessions for the County of the City of York, where Claims were delivered in, but no Bounty has yet been paid in consequence; and that if the Farmers had received the Bounty they expected, they would have been encouraged to grow more Flax than they have done.

A Petition of his Grace Henry Duke of Newcastle, Auditor, Philip Earl of HaGeorge Nugent Marquis of Buckingham, the Honourable John Jeffreys Pratt, Tellers of the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, and of Edward Roberts, Esquire, late Deputy to the Right honourable Sir Edward late Clerk of the Pells, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That by an Act, passed in the Third Year of King William and Queen Mary, the Barons of the Exchequer were required to present a Table of the ancient and legal Fees by them allowed to be taken by the Officers of the Exchequer* on all Sums of Money issued and received at the Exchequer; and that, by the Table of Fees presented in pursuance of the above recited Act, the Officers of the Exchequer were allowed to take Fees on all Pensions to the Amount of nearly Five per Cent. and on all Monies issued for Secret Service, Two and a Half per Cent, the Barons alledging it for a Reason, that many Pensions were paid out of Money issued for Secret Service, which Pensions, had the Service been known, would have been subject to the larger Fees of nearly Five per Cent, and those Fees have been invariably taken at the Exchequer upon all Gross Sums issued for Secret Service, although the Pensions paid out of such Secret Service Money have been received at the Treasury, clear of all Deductions whatever; and that an Office was instituted at the Beginning of this Century, for the Purpose of paying private Pensions, and the Fees upon the Gross Sums issued to the Paymaster of these Pensions were reduced to 1 /. 3$. 9 per Cent, which were taken at the Exchequer, though the Pensions were never charged with such Fees, the Paymaster being re-imbursed for them in his Bill of Contingencies; and that those were deemed legal Fees received under the Authority of Parliament, anti were constantly taken without any Opposition, until, by an Act passed in the Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty, to enable His Majesty to discharge the Debt contrafted on his Civil List Revenues, it was enacted, that the Payment of all Pensions should be transferred to the Exchequer, and that those which are so transferred should be subject to no Fees, except such Fees to which they were subject before the said Act; and that the Petitioners conceive that the Legislature, not knowing that the Gross Sums issued for paying the aforesaid Pensions were subject to Fees at the Exchequer, passed the said Clause, rather to prevent the Officers of the Exchequer from taking new Fees, than with an Intent to take away their ancient and legal Fees allowed by the Barons of the Exchequer; and, the Petitioners conceive it never was intended by the Legislature, at the Time that they were imposing a new and troublefeme Business upon the Offices of the Exchequer, instead of granting a new Fee (which those Officers neither expect nor desire) to deprive them of their ancient and legal Fees, to which they were entitled when this Service was performed by others; and that the Petitioners, having been but lately informed that the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury could not afford them any Relief, were prevented from presenting a Vol. 41.

Petition to the House before the Time limited for receiving Petitions was elapsed, and crave the Indulgence of the House to present a Petition for such Relief as the House shall think fit to grant

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Duke of Newcastle, Earl of Hardwicke, Marquis of Buckingham, John Jeffreys Pratt, and Edward Roberts.

Then a Petition of his Grace Henry Duke of Newcastle, Auditor, Philip Earl of Hardwicke, George Nugent Marquis of Buckingham, the Honourable John Jeffreys Pratt, Tellers of the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, and of Edward Roberts, Esquire, late Deputy to Sir Edward Walpole, late Clerk of the Pells, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Third Year of King William and Queen Mary, the Barons of the Exchequer were required to present a Table of the ancient and legal Fees of the Officers of the Receipt of the Exchequer to the Lords and Commons in Parliament assembled, which was presented accordingly, by which Table the Barons allowed Fees to the Amount of nearly Five per Cent, to be taken upon all Pensions paid at the Exchequer, and Fees to the Amount of Two and a Half per Cent, to be taken upon all Money issued for Secret Service, assigning for a Reason, because many Pensions and Free Gifts were known to be paid out of Monies issued under that Head, which Pensions, had the Service been known, would have been subject to the larger Fees allowed by the Barons in the aforesaid Table; and these Pensions paid out of Monies issued for Secret Service have been constantly received without Fees at the Treasury, though the Grols Sums, out of which they were paid, were always charged with the Fees aforesaid, according to the Settlement of the Barons of the Exchequer under the Authority of Parliament; and that, at the Beginning of the present Century, an Office was instituted for the Payment of private Pensions, and the Fee3 upon such Pensions were reduced to 1/. 3 s.9 d.perCent. large Sums of Money were issued to this Office, and the Officers of the Exchequer always deducted from the Gross Sums, out of which such Pensions were paid, the aforesaid Fees, but the Pensions paid at that Office have not, of late Years, been charged with those Fees, the Paymaster being re-imbursed for them in his Bill of Contingencies delivered to the Treasury; and that those Fees were always deemed legal, and were invariably taken without any Objection, previously to the Act of the Twenty-second of George the Third, to enable His Majesty to discharge the Debt contrafted on the Civil List, by which it is enacted, that all Pensions should be transferred to the Exchequer, and that they should pay no Fees, except the Fees to which they were subject before that Act: Yet the Petitioners conceive, that it was not proposed by the Legislature to deprive the Officers of the Exchequer of their legal Fees, but that, on the contrary, they, in that Act, as well as by a subsequent Act, for the Regulation of the Offices in the Exchequer, refused to make any Alterations in the Fees or Emoluments to which the Officers of the Exchequer were legally entitled, during the Lives of the present Possessors; and that the Petitioners conceive, that it was supposed, when the Act of the Twenty-second of George the Third passed, that no Fees were ever received by the Officers of the Exchequer upon any of the aforesaid Pensions, and that under that Mistake the Clauses

A Petition of John Christian, Esquire, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of a Citizen to serve in Parliament for the City of Carlisle, in the County of Cumberland, John Lowther, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that at the Poll taken upon the said Election before Richard Jackson, Mayor of the said City, the Returning Officer, a’ great Majority of legal Electors voted in Favour of the Petitioner, and many other legal Electors appeared and tendered their Votes for the Petitioner; and that the said Returning Officer, before and during the Time of taking the said Poll, acted with great Partiality in Favour of the said John lowther, and rejected many legal Votes, which were duly tendered in Favour of the Petitioner, and received lb many illegal Votes for the said John Lowther, as to leave a Majority, upon the Face of the Poll, in Favour of the said John Lowther, under Colour whereof the said John Lowther was re* turned, although the Petitioner was duly elected by a great Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief as shall appear to be just.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the Eighteenth Day of this Instant May, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word " Eighteenth," and inferring the Word " Twenty-fifth" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Word " Eighteenth " stand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Thursday the 18th Day of this Instant May, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

and that the said Parishioners have lately cauled the Pillars and Roof to be supported by Buttresses and Props, to prevent the falling thereof, and, upon a partial Survey, in the Beginning of this present Year, it was thought practicable to take down Part of the said Pillars, Walls, and Roof, and to repair the fame, which prevented the Petitioners Application to the House in proper Time, but, upon a recent general Survey of the whole Fabrick of the said Church, by experienced Architects, it hath been found, that to repair the same would be wafting a large Sum of Money, without answering any effectual good Purpose, and therefore necessary to pull down the said Church, and either to re-build the same upon the Sciteof the present Church, or upon some other more commodious Place and Situation, in the said Parish or Parochial Chapelry; and that the said Parish or Parochial Chapelry is very large and extensive, and now become very populous, and it would tend greatly to the Comfort and pious Dispositions of the Inhabitants thereof, to have a new Church built as foot: as possible; and that the Church Yard of the said Church is too confined and finall for the Burial of the Dead, and to have the same enlarged would contribute much to the Health and Convenience of the said Parishioners: And therefore praying, That (considering the urgent Necessity of the Petitioners Application) Leave may be given to present a Petition to the House, for the Purpose of bringing in a Bill to enable the Owners of Land, and Parishioners of the fetid Parish or Parochial Chapelry, to take down the said present Church, and to build a new one upon the Scite of the fetid present Church, or upon some other Foundation, in a more commodious Place and Situation in the said Parish or Parochial Chapelry, and for that Purpose, and for the enlarging foe said Church Yard, and for making convenient Avenues and Passages to the said Church and Church Yard, to impower and enable foe said Owners of Land, and Parishioners, to purchase certain Houses and Lands for the Use and Convenience, and as Part and Parcel of the fetid intended new Church and Church Yard, the same to be vested in Trustees, in Trust for foe Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of foe particular Circumstances set forth in foe said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by foe said Minister, Churchwardens, and Parishioners of foe Parish or Parochial Chapelry of All Saints, in the Town and County of Newcastle upon Tyne.

Sir William Lemon reported from the Committee, pilchard to whom the Petition of the principal Persons concerned Fishery. in the Pilchard Fishery, on Behalf of themselves, and other Adventurers interested therein, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of foe laid Petition; and had directed him to report the same, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where foe same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

It appeared to your Committee, from the Testimony of Mr. Richard Lawrence. That the Distresses of those engaged in foe Pilchard Fishery, and alledged in the Petition, are real; that the Alleviation of those Dif-tresses is an Object of public Importance; and that the Relief deemed adequate to such Effect, is an additional Bounty on the Hogshead of Pilchards exported.

The House having referred to the Committee a Report of last Sessions, from a Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the Pilchard Fisheries, Mr. Lawrence was questioned touching foe lame; and his Evidence corroborating each Circumstance and Statement in the Report alluded to, the Committee forbear a Repetition of such Matter as tends to elucidate the general Importance, Conduct, and State of the Pilchard Fisheries, under Impressions of the Accuracy of Evidence and complete Information, which were before the Committee iaft Year; and which, according to foe Ideas of the present Testimony, that Committee carefully and correctly availed themselves of — Your Committee referring to that Report, will therefore merely adduce such Particulars as are more especially in Point as to foe Matter of the Petition, or are new, as to foe general View of foe Subject.

It appears to your Committee, that in consequence of the Report of the Committee of last Sessions, a Bill passed, granting an additional Bounty, for One Year, of Two Shillings per Hogshead on Pilchards exported; but, from the Evidence now before your Committee, it is obvious, that the Fishery did not, in the Course of last Year, avail itself of such public

Assistanceto an Amount proportionate even to the Charge of Attendance and Expence in obtaining the fame; partly from the Advancement of the Season, at the Period of passing the said Act, and partly from the Fishery not having been lo productive as usual. — The Fluctuation in this important Brauch of the British Fisheries is duly noticed in the Report referred to your Committee; but the present Evidence further testifies, to the Pilchard having never in his Time, that is for Twenty and more Years back, quitted, or rather been so rare on the Coast for so long a Time as the present; but that he has heard old People, now dead, assert, that the Filli had for some Years together, in a great Degree, forsaken their accustomed Roads, and then returned in such Quantities as might fully compensate the Fisherman for puft Disappointment — Mr. Laurence states the Average of the Filli caught, Ten Years back, at 30,000 Hogsheads Annually; and those caught and exported, for the last Ten Years, to be 20,000 Hogsheads; of which the Average of the last Five Years is only 9,000; and that the lait Season of 1785 produced only 4,500 Hogsheads. — Whether the Speculations or Hopes of the Fitliermen are well founded, your Committee pretend not to determine; but it seems that Fancy (perhaps the Creation of or fub-ordinate to Desire) traces the probable Extinction of the Times of Dearth, and looks to an approaching Season, as if in due periodical Vicissitude, a Season of returning Plenty and Success.

Whatever and however sanguine may be such Anticipation, the Spirit of Adventure seems utterly depressed by present Poverty and Debt. Under such Circumstances it may, at first Sight, appear extraordinary, that the Evidence should insist on the Competency of so small an additional Bounty as Two Shillings per Hogshead for the great Purposes of sustaining so great a Capital as embarked, of encouraging and of procuring Credit to the Adventurer, of inspiriting and of enabling those who were before poor and despondent, and in a Word, of reviving a decaying Fishery so important, and heretofore extensive, as that of the Pilchard.

It must be remembered, that Seven Shillings per Hogshead is the present Bounty given by Law, and that a Bounty which in and by itself is little, considered as an Addition, may be great — That Two Shillings alone would be a Bounty of no Consideration, but added to Seven Shillings, may render a Sum, heretofore inadequate, effective and complete. No Fisheries are generally and intrinsically productive to those engaged therein; the Fluctuations in Success may attach the sanguine and the enter prizing, through Views to the higher Years of the Average Returns; but those Returns have a general Level, and to that in Process of Experience the ordinary Trader resorts, and he therein anticipates the Calculation of how much he is to lose in how many Years, and how much is wanting, and how he is to be induced to a Continuance of Exertions in so unpromising and infructuous a Trade; his Inducements in the first Instance must be a Guarantee from Loss, and thereon is founded his Estimate of Bounties. As to Loss and Advantage, it may be stated that in this Branch of Commerce, more peculiarly than in any other, to save, is to gain — In Fisheries, often Commodities and Manufactures of far other Consideration than Fish are the great Objects, collateral in Fad, but primary in Importance: If the Bounty, for Instance, balances the Loss and Gain of a Vessel, as to the immediate Expences of catching Fish, and the Returns from those Fish, the Parties are in a certain Degree satisfied; the Sail Maker, the Ship Builder, the Ship's Husband, and a Variety of others, who are benefited in the Outfits, and engaged in the Concern, are satisfied if not Losers by that Concern,

A. 1786

because they arc Gainers in other Points of View. — a public Consideration, the Revenue has yet more thi a proportional Advantage, considering a Bounty of tl Legislature as analogous to the Merchants Advance, ai considering the Ship or Boat, and Outfits, as payii Duties, as supporting the Manufacturer, and as furnif ing the Seamen. Such seems to be the Foundation that Policy which has induced almost every Nation promote Fisheries at the Charge of Bounties. — Advertii to the Peculiarities which distinguish the Pilchard Trad from such Predilection for this Commodity in the Mar of the Mediterranean, as to draw with it a Demand f other British Staples, such as Tin and Leather, co ditionally on that of Fish forming a Proportion in tl Assortment of Cargo; it appears to your Committee, < Grounds of Reafouing above stated, that the Argumen in Favour of Bounties, perhaps apply more fully to tl Circumstances of the Pilchard Fishery, than of any othe

The Evidence are of Opinion, that an addition Bounty of Two Shillings, and granted for a Period 1 not less than Seven Years, would induce those wl are yet able so to do. to keep their Crafts and Seins 1 Sea; and further, would induce the Merchant and E: porter to foster the Hopes and Credit of the poorer Fill erman, by necessary Advances, so as to preclude the al solute Necessity he is at present under of declining tl Fishery, from not having wherewithal to repair his Stoc and to engage his Men, after so long and heavy Series 1 Loss.

On the fullest Consideration, your Committee recon mend to the House the Adoption of such Bounty; ar they think it more particularly their Duty so to do, froi Conviction that unless some immediate Encouragement given, the Fishery is on the Verge of irrecoverable D< cline; as, should the Defpondencv and Necessities so fi operate this one Year as to leave the Craft to decay, ar the Fishermen to emigrate (and to this Effect the prefei Evidence deposed) it is not the Shoal of Fish coming c the Coast, in this or in any future Season, which w again or suddenly make a Fishery. To keep up s Establishment, when so many new Rivals on the Sea and particularly in the Fisheries.. have started forth, mt be difficult, or at least maylrequire Attention; but aga to recover, or to form an Establishment, must not only I a Work of Difficulty, but of Time.

It may not be irrelevant to observe, that the Ev dence examined before your Committee not only appei equally respectable as to Character, and competent i to Experience, but that Mr. Laxvrence having son Time withdrawn his share of Capital from the Pilchai Fiftiery, that hidden Bias, that unconscious Partialit which may unwarily influence the Language and Op nions of the belt Men, respecting a Business in whi< they are deeply interested, cannot be said to apply 1 the Testimony on which your Committee found their pr sent Report.

Articles in Trade, by the Sale of which the Petitioners now find great Difficulty to maintain themselves and Families, and to pay those large and very enormous 'luxes with which the Petitioners have of late been very much burthened, and which they are afraid they shall not be able to discharge with Ease and Comfort to themselves, if the above Clauses are repealed, as it will eventually prevent the Petitioners from felling such extraordinary Quanties of Goods, as might in tome Degree compensate for the Burthens already laid upon them, and which cannot, according to the Mode and Manner of Retail Business, be laid upon the Consumer; and that the Petitioners were in Hopes that the restricting Clauses above-mentioned having passed into a Law so late as the last Session of Parliament, and the Legislature being at that Time thoroughly satisfied with their Propriety, no Attempt would have been made to repeal a Law so recently and solemnly made, a Law which the Petitioners trailed and believed would have put the Retail Trade of this Kingdom upon that fair and regular System that Consumers, instead of dealing with those Itinerant Traders, might have been supplied by the resident Shopkeepers of their Neighbourhood, the Succels of whose stationary Situation mull depend altogether upon the Faimeft of their Dealings, and the Preservation of their Characters, and who in fact bear by far the greater Burthen of the Taxes with which this Country is at present loaded: And therefore praying, That the House will not repeal the restricting Clauses named in the Hawkers and Pedlars Act, passed last Session of Parliament, for the Reasons above-mentioned.

Introduction.

Before I enter upon my General Defence, I humbly solicit the Indulgence of this Honourable House, to be permitted to preface it with a few necessary Observations relative to the Circumstances which have progressively conspired to make me an Object of the present Enquiry. In the First Place, I beg Leave to remark, that I am here by no Obtrulion of my own. I have too humble a Sense of my own Consequence, to consider either my Reputation, Honour, Fortune, or Life, or all these Interests cohesively, as having any Claim to the lmalleft Portion of the valuable Time of this House, on any Ground, however just in itself, which has these only for its ObjeS. I have been brought before the Notice of this Honourable House by the Acts of others, independant of my Will or Desire; and all the Participation which I have in it, is in the Request made by a Member of this House on my Behalf, and at my Suggestion, that since it was determined that my ConduS was to be arraigned before this Honourable House, my Arraignment might be speedy, and that I might have the Time and Means afforded me to provide the Materials for my Defence: For after having been,' during a Course of Five Years, the continued Subject of the same Criminations, and from the same Quarter, with the Name of the Almighty solemnly invoked to attest the Pledge given to this House that the most undoubted Proofs should be produced to authenticate them — I allude, Mr. Speaker, to no Declarations made in this House, but to Publications out of it — I may surely be allowed, even with a Conscious-ness of the purest Integrity, to wife for a speedy Accom-pliftiment of a Menace thus made, and for such professed Purposes; and that it might not hang the Denunciations of Parliamentary Vengeance over my Head for ever.

Of the first Effects of this Injury I have a Right to complain; for in these the Injury affected the Public alone, through their Interests committed to my Charge. During a long and desperate Struggle with an Accumulation of Difficulties, and a Hod of natural Enemies combined against our National Possessions in India, when I required all the Support and Confidence of my Superiors in the Parent State to give Effect to my Exertions,

all my Actions were reprobated at Home, and my N linked to the foulest Inve6tive, even in Places of highest Authority; and every Dispatch from Eng brought Orders opposing my Measures in their Co and the Sentences of my Disgrace and Dismission. these caused no Alteration in my Conduct, or Rel tion of my Zeal for a Service in which my Labours met so ill a Requital, except from my respect Constituents, in whose Applause alone I received a ( solation under all my Discouragements. I steal pursued that Line which my Sense of Duty had scribed; and sometimes availing myself of the transi Moments of Power which the Hand of God affoi me, at others using the Resistance which the Influi of Possession or Opinion enabled me to make, or Caution of Opposition permitted; or endeavouring temper its Violence by qualified Submission, where Means of Resistance failed me; never possessing Allowance of Authority, but always charged 1 Responsibility; I persisted in the Formation and ] fecution of every Measure, which the Emergency of Service rendered necessary in my Judgment, and the conscious Triumph of seeing them all invarij terminate in their designed Objects: Nor did I re my Charge, until I had fulfilled every Duty which quired my Continuation in it; and 1 resigned it i State of established Peace and Security, with all Sources of its Abundance unimpaired, and even proved, notwithstanding the vast Drains which m made of its Treasures, and the multiplied Diversions its Strength, in the Support of the dependant and reir Possessions of the Company, and in the Maintenano their Wars, and of Wars in which the Company w involved by the Policy of Great Britain. I pai from the Scene of my public Life with the expre Regrets of my Fellow Servants and Countrymen; wt were followed by a like Declaration frQm all the C cers of the Army w ho had served during my Adminif tion; and on my Return to my own Country, I received by the Court of Directors, my immed Masters, with their Thanks; and I gratefully remem the Chairman's emphatical Pause on the Epithet wf was joined to them, their Unanimous Thanks, for Services; with a Notification of those which had b feme Time before bestowed on me by the Votes of Proprietors, my honoured Employers, which were the less acceptable for their Consistency with the unift Tenor of their Sentiments and Condu6t respecting through the whole Course of my Administration. this Honourable House is desirous of knowing in w Estimation I stood with the Princes and Rulers of In and with the Subjects of our own Dominion, the C nions of both may be easily obtained, by Enquiry the Witnesses whom my Prosecutor has called to eft lish his Charges against me: And I will anticipate tl Evidence — It will tiate, that my Political Conduct 1 invariably regulated by Truth, Justice, and Good Fa that all Persuasions of Men were impressed with a fef ftitous Belief, that a fortunate Influence directed all Actions to their destined Ends; and that my Depart was scarcely less regretted by the Inhabitants of Provinces of my late Dependency, than it was by own Countrymen. I believe this Honourable Houli in Pofiession of One Testimony of the former, in Letters which Madajee Sindia wrote to His Most G cious Majesty, and to the Company. These w written many Months after my Departure, and cont much more of my Praise than his own Wants or Req fitions, unless the former is inserted as an Implication his Desire that others may be instructed to govern the selves by my Example: — And who will question feet Authority ?

internal Applause of my own Mind superseding all Evidence, what was my Surprize to find, on my Arrival in England, that my Character still continued to be

I am since told that no such Intention existed; and that my own Intemperance, -and the Zeal of my Friends, has forced my Accuser to verify his own Declaration.

I have no Right to credit such an Assertion, nor will I believe, new and unpractised as I am in the Modes of Life in which I am now become a Participator (and I have learnt by it to know more Things than were dreamt of in my Philosophy) that so daring an Imposition could be either practised upon this high and dignified Assembly, or permitted by it. Though I might have thought myself entitled by my Services to a different Reception, and my Body and Mind, worn down by the Labours of Thirty-five Years, to an Interval of Repose; and though I might erroneously imagine that no Power upon Earth had a Right to impeach me for the Exercise of a Trull which those for whom I held it had repeatedly declared, and in the moil authentic Terms, that I had discharged to their Benefit and entire Satisfaction; yet I was glad to fee some fub-flantial Ground on which I could build my Hopes of a speedy Trial and definite Termination. There too my Expectation failed me. The Prosecution began, not as is the universal Practice of every System of Jurisprudence established either in this or any other civilized Nation, by the Introduction of specific Charges, and the Examination of Witnesses to prove them: For the latter indeed there was little Need, since my Accuser had long before asserted, that he was in the actual Possession of Proofs, and of such Proofs as were to fill the Breasts of this Honourable Assembly with Horror. Why therefore aggravate them with new Proofs? But Witnesses were ordered to attend, and Reams of Official Documents demanded, produced, and printed; Additions were daily made to these during the Courl'e of many Weeks; and the Eyes of the World were fixed upon me as a Man blackened by the Imputation of feme unknown Guilt, which was the blacker for its Concealment. No Grounds were alledged for the Accumulation of such a Mass of Evidence against me; no specific Objects to which it was to be applied; nor was it known to this Honourable House, perhaps not even to that Member of the House who had required these Materials, what the Charges were to be, which he was to establish by them.

At Length I heard that a Day was fixed for the Production of the Charges; but here too I experienced a fresh Cause of Disappointment and Mortification. Three Weeks were assigned for the Term of their Appearance; and when that Term expired, this Honourable House knows (for £ may not perhaps affirm what I have heard) whether even then any of the Charges were presented, and whether, when they were presented, they were optionally given.

In all this long and painful Interval I myself, though the Object of the Enquiry, remained in total Inaction, a mere Spectator of the passing Scene; for I knew not, nor could I know, what Defence to prepare, not knowing what Charges were to require my Defence. And when tliev were produced, I was told that I could not be admitted to my Defence, because, by the Rules of the House, I could not know the Charges exhibited against me, nor that any had been exhibited; nor indeed were all exhibited at the same Time, but followed tardily, and the Three last (if indeed those are the last) not till last Wednesday. How much my Reputation mufl have suffered in the Opinion of all Mankind from this Publication; how severely my Feelings must have been wounded by so unfair and iniquitous an Appeal to their Judgment, while the Charge itself, loaded as it was with Crimination against me, yet waited its flow Term of Maturity for the Examination of it before its allotted Judges, I leave to the Decision of every Member of this Honourable House, who will bring the Question home to his own Judgment and his own Passions, by supposing that same to be his own which I have described as mine.

Nor is this the only Injury of the Kind that I have suffered. Every Daily Paper has teemed with Reflections upon me; and Pamphlets, filled with the most scandalous and libellous Abuse, have been written on various Subjects of the Charge, to influence the Prejudices of the Public against me; and it has been boasted that they have produced the Effect.

Pressed by the Load of Slander thus heaped upon me, I resolved to try the only Resource which afforded me a Chance of Red refs; and in Opposition to many and weighty Discouragements, I threw myself upon the Justice of this Honourable House, and petitioned to lie allowed to make my Defence in Person, — and I succeeded. Whether I owe this Indulgence to your Goodness, or your Justice, I accept it with equal Gratitude.

Of the Discouragements to which I allude, I shall mention but Two Points; and these it is incumbent on me to mention, because they relate to Effects, which the Justice of this Honourable House may, and I trust will, avert. The First is an Objection to my being at all Personally committed in my Defence, since in so wide a Field of Discussion it would be impossible not to admit feme Things of which an Advantage might be taken to turn them into Evidence against myself: Whereas another might as well use as I could, or better, the same Materials of my Defence, without involving me in the same Consequences. But I am sure that this Honourable House will yield me its Protection against the Cavils of unwarranted Inference; and if the Truth can tend to convict me, I am content to be myself' the Channel to convey it.

The other Objection lay in my own Breast. It was not till Monday last that 1 formed the Resolution; and I knew not then whether I might not in Consequence be laid under the Obligation of preparing and completing in Five Days, and in Effect so it as proved, the Refutation of Charges which it has been the Labour of my Accuser, armed with all the Powers of Parliament, and at One Time greater, to compile during as many Years of almost undisturbed Leisure.

But I knew myself equal to the Undertaking; and I now only revert to my Difficulties, that the Consideration of them may bespeak the candid Allowance of this Honourable House for any Inaccuracies, or for any Thing defective which may appear in my Defence; but I claim no other Indulgence on this Account.

It might perhaps be expected, that I should object to the Construction of the Articles of which the Charge is composed; for, in Truth, they are not Charges, but Histories and Comments. But they are yet more; they are made up of mutilated Quotations; — of Facts which have no mutual Relation, but are forced by false Arrangement into Connection; —
