The Remainder of this Charge is more a Defence of

Mr. Bristow than an Attack upon me. — I shall not trouble this Honourable House with a Detail upon this Subject — For the present, I shall merely observe, that in the Month of September 1782 Mr. was appointed Resident at Oude — That a very few Months after his Appointment, very great Heats and Animosities broke out between Mr. Bristow on the One Part, and the Nabob and his Minister on the other — I had no Enmity to Mr. Bristmo, nor had I any Personal Motives to gratify by his Removal. — These Disputes were referred to the Council in Calcutta — I took the Part of the Nabob and his Minister; my Council justified Mr. Bristow — But a Government so dilbrdered could not possibly exist — It became necessary, in the Month of December 1783, either to remove Mr. Bristow, or to authorize him to assume an absolute Authority in Oudeand this I stated to the Council, who were alarmed at the Prospect before them; and, though they were all the strenuous Defenders of Mr. Bristow, agreed to his Removal, and to delegiate to me the Power of settling every disputed Point with the Vizier, provided I would be responsible for his Payment of the Balance due to the Company, not with my Fortune, as my Accuser truly fays, but with my Character, which I prize infinitely higher. — I accepted the Trust, and it detained me One entire Season in India — I proceeded to Lucknow; I met the Nabob upon the most friendly Terms; I declare to this Honourable House, that 1 treated him with the Respect and the Attention which was due to his high Rank — that I never presumed to speak to him in an authoritative Tone; and that, by Argument and Persuasion, I carried all my Points both with the Nabob and his Minister — I never interchanged an unplealant Word with him, during the Five Months which I remained at his Court, and near Four of that Period lived, with Thirty English Gentlemen, and numerous Guards and Domestics, within the same Enclosure; nor in that Period did the flightcft Dispute ever arise between his People and mine.

From the Secret Committee of the Court of Directors to Mr. Hastings, dated the 28th August 1771.

" By our General Address you will be informed of the Reasons we have to be dissatisfied with the Administration of Mahomed Reza and will perceive

the Expediency of our divesting him of the Rank and Influence he holds, as Naib Dewan of Bengal. " Although the Proceedings of the Board very minutely recorded all the Measures which were taken for prosecuting the Enquiry into the Conduct of Mahomed Heza Cawn, and my own Sentiments, both in the Course and the Issue of it, yet as I was originally honoured with your separate Commands for conducing this intricate Business, I conceive it to be in feme Measur incumbent on me to address you on its Conclusion. 'You will be pleased to recollect that the Charge was general, without any Specification of Time, Places, or Persons; I had neither Witnesses, Vouchers, nor Materials to begin with; for these I relied chiefly on the Abilities, Observation, and afitive Malignity of Nund — comar. In the Course of the Enquiry I proceeded with*, the most rigid Impartiality; not suffering (I can iafely say) thefmalleft Bias to incline me. You will fee witls. what Materials I was fumished; I am sorry to say, that some were collected with so little Regard to Decency or Truth, as to make me apprehensive of the Effects which, they might have produced on my Character, from th^ Countenance which I afforded Nundcomar in the Prose — cution, had I not, in my own immediate Conduct, invariably adhered to the strictest Rules of Justice. Not — . withstanding the Consciousness which I possess of my own Integrity, and the Certainty that my Conduct: throughout this ungrateful Business will, on the most rigi«^| Scrutiny, do me Credit, yet I am not without my Fears. " I mult declare that I have another Motive for my Fears; the dark and deceitful Character of whole Gratitude no Kindness can bind, nor even his own Interest disengage him from those crooked Politics which have been the Study and Practice of his whole Life: Of this I have had many extraordinary Proofs.

Mahomed Reza Cawn was acquitted by me, and appointed iu 1775 to the Superintendance of the Nabob’s Household, during his Minority, and to the Administration of Criminal Justice throughout the Provinces. -From these Offices he was removed in 1778* by the Board, where I had a casting Voice, the Nabob being then 20 Years of Age. Of this Removal the Court of X)ireQors disapproved; and, against the most strenuous llemonftrances of the Nabob and all his Family, he was re-appointed in 1780, when the Nabob was 23 Years of Age. On repeated Petitions from the Nabob, I again removed Mahomed in 1781, from

being Guardian of the Minority of a Man who was then £24 Years of Age, but he was continued Chief Criminal Judge of the Provinces, and that Office he still retains. I have settled Jagheers on his Two Sons, which produce them a liberal Income. To my Justice and Impartiality Mahomed Reza Cozen has often declared he owes his Life and Honour, when the deepest Schemes iof Villainy were laid to deprive him of both. He has received many Offices of Kindness from me; and I am sure his Sentiments for me are those of Gratitude and Affection.

I hope I may be allowed to make an Observation on the Conduct of the Court of Directors, as it respefited Mahomed Reza Cawn, Nundcomar, and myself. The Gratitude which I owe to them, and the Respect which I feel for the Individual Members of that Court, is as great as can warm the Breast of any Man; yet I had substantial Cause of Complaint against them for the Return I met with for a rigid and literal Obedience to their Orders in the Instance I have quoted. I employed Nundcomar, and I prosecuted Mahomed Reza Caum. The Directors were well aware of the faithlels Character of the first, and assured me, that under no Change whatl'oever should the latter be restored to Power; yet both these Men, within Two Years of the Date of their Letter, were employed as Iostruments of Vengeance against me. The Opinions of Counfei were taken in England, whether, upon the Informations of Nundcomar, a Prosecution could not be instituted against me for Money stated to be corruptly taken; and there was a Time when I was threatened with a Prosecution by Mahomed Reza Cawn, for a rigid Obedience to the Orders of my Superiors; — and I stand here now to answer to a Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors for having obeyed these Orders. I

I have not sufficient Time left to enter minutely into the Particular's of my Defence against the Charge intruded into this Article, of insolent and oppressive Treatment of the Nabob ul and

therefore borrow the Aid of Sir John who

02

was the Resident at the Durbar, and is charged with being the Instrument of my oppressive Acts to the Nabob, to recite, as he would do upon Oath, if required, all that he knows relative to these Transactions, and his Testimony is hereto annexed. It remains for me only to premise, in a few words, that I always regarded the Nabob Mobarek ul Doivlah as being under my Protection, and myself as his Guardian; that whenever he committed such Irregularities as tended to injure either his Interest or Reputation in an essential Manner, I admo-niffied him to avoid such Excesses in future; and by gentle Persuasions, for I never used any other, I tried, and generally with Success, to wean him from his bad Habits, as I became acquainted with them.

I prevailed upon him to remove discreditable People from his Society, and I gave him the Affi fiance of Sir John D’Oyley, under my own Instructions, to make a new Arrangement and Distribution of his Expences, because they had run out beyond all Bounds; and if I had not done this, he would have been involved in Debt, his Palace would have been surrounded by clamorous Creditors, and ultimately the Demand would have been defrayed from our Treasury. I hope nothing I-have laid will appear to reflect on the young Nabob, whose Disposition is gentle and pliant, and his general Behaviour such as merits every Instance of Kindness that can be shewn him by the East India Company.

" I was appointed Resident on the Resignation of Mr. Byam Martin, in the Month of Jatmary 1780, and took Charge about the Beginning of February of the same Year.

" The Substance of the Instructions I received was to endeavour, by every Means in my Power, to conciliate the good Opinion and Regard of the Nabob and his Family, that I might be able to persuade him to adopt effectual Measures for the better Regulation of his Expences, which were understood to have greatly exceeded his Income; that I might prevent his forming improper Connections, or taking any Steps derogatory to his Rank; and by every Means in my Power support his Credit and Dignity in the Eyes of the World; and with respect to the various Branches of his Family, I was instructed to endeavour to put a Stop to the Dissentions which had too frequently prevailed amongst them. The Nabob on his Part was recommended to pay the same Attention to my Advice as he would have done to that of the Governor General in Person.

" Some Time (I think) in the Month of February of the same Year, I received a Letter from Mr.

u When, on the Accession of the Nabob Niidjum " ul Dmiah, the Sum allotted for the Expences of " the Nizamut, the Subsistence of its Dependants, and " the Support of its Splendor, was fixed at upwards " of Fifty Lacks of Rupees, and that this Decrease " from what it had been in the Time of the Nabob " my Father, and his Predecessors, occasioned such " Ruin and Distress to Multitudes in Bengal, let the " Honourable Company judge how infinitely the Distress " must have been aggravated when the Stipend was reduced to the trifling Sum of Sixteen Lacks; and to " the former established Expences were added those " of supporting all the Women, Relations, Connections,

" and Dependants of my Father and the succeeding " Nazims (which in Hindostan amount to an incredible " Number, and inconceivable Expence) and they will " then be able to form some Judgment of the present " miserable State of the Nizamut. Those who are acquainted with the Manners and Customs of different " Countries, know that most of the Mussulmans of this " Country are totally detached from Trade and Manu-' faclures, particularly those who have been in the Service " of the King or Princes of the Country, who are accustomed to consider their Offices as for Life; this " being the Cafe, it must be evident to what a State " of Dittrels all under this Predicament, with their " Families, must be reduced, from having been so :‘J many Years out of Employ, through my Inability " to retain them in Pay.

" As the Almighty delegates his Power to Princes and Magistrates for the Purpose of supporting the Needy, and for the Ease and Happiness of Mankind, " a Multitude of People in Bengal derived their Subfiiteuce from the Bounty of the Nazims, the Fame of " which brought numerous Bodies, in Expectation of a " Livelihood, from the different Parts of Hindostan, from " Persia, &c. nor were they disappointed. Tiiere are " still Thousands of thele in the utmost Distress, who look forward with Hope to the Re-establishment of " the Ease and Splendor of Nizamut through the " Liberality of the Company. In fact, innumerable " Mussulmans and olhers depend on the Nizamut for a Subsistence.

" My Requests are,

" First, That as I have now attained my Twentyeighth Year, and am perfectly competent to the " Management of piy own Affairs in the properest " Manner, my undoubted Right to be Master in my " own Family, by the Appointment and Difiniffion of " my Minister (Naib) and Servants, be acknowledged. J‘ It can never be necessary that any Interference should take place in Matters of this Kind j such Interference " has already been highly detrimental to my Affairs; " and God is my Witness that, but for the Kindness and " friendly Attention of the Governor General, and the " Measures he has taken for the Regulation of my Affairs

A. 1786.

I should at this Time have been involved ih Tenfold Debt and Distress. By Means of his Kindness, and the Assiduity of Sir John D'Oyley, my Affairs have been put in such a Train as to enable me to expect your Determination. My Obligations to the Governor General are boundless: Were I to write Volumes on the Subject, I could never sufficiently express my Gratitude: The Virtues which adorn his Character are precious Gifts of the Almighty to the People of Hindostan, and ensure to them the Enjoyment of Comfort and Ease. — That God may preserv his Life and Power, and long continue him in the Government of this Country, is not my Wish alone, but that of the whole People.

" Although the great Respect shewn me by the Governor General on every Occasion calls for my warmest Gratitude, and God is my Witness that I am so perfectly content therewith, that had I a Thousand Tongues I should fail in the Praises justly due to his Virtues, yet, as such Qualities are rarely found, the Consideration of the future leads me to request you will direct that the Forms of Respect due to my Rank may be invariably observed."

Answer to the Twentieth Charge.

Maratta War, and Peace.

Tins and the following Charge I had no Opportunity of perusing until my Return last Night from this Honourable House; it will not, therefore, be expected that my Answer to each should be long; in Truth, the Subjects do not require a long Defence. — I affirm that I was not the Author of the Maratta War; and, if this Honourable House shall adopt the Charge, I will bring undoubted Proofs of the Truth of my Assertion. — I affirm, that every Step which I took in the Year 1778, from January to December, was regularly communicated to His Majesty's Minister, with whom I thought it my Duty to communicate on so momentous a Subject, enjoying, as I did, my Office under a Parliamentary Appointment. — I affirm that I bad not the most distant Idea of in* volving this Nation, or my Employers, the East India Company, in a War with France or the Mar alias; that every Measure I purlued had for its Object the Defence of the Company’s Possessions against the combined Attacks of the French and the The

Grounds which I had to expect these Attacks are such as I am sure this Honourable House will perceive to have been so strong as to justify me in every Measure I adopted: These I shall produce, if the Charge is entertained, unless their Production should be deemed dangerous to the National Interests. — I affirm, that the Court of Directors, with the Approbation of His Majesty’s Mini tiers, approved of my Conduct in forming a Detachment for the "Defence of our Possessions in the West of India. — I affirm, that when I proposed to change the Destination of this Detachment, and to form an Alliance with the Rajah of Bcrar, it was not to pursue Schemes of Conquest, but to defend the British Empire in India from the Dangers with which it was threatened by the War with France, of which we had then received Intelligence. — I affirm, that I bad received from Mr. Elliott a very particular Relation of the Steps which France meant to pursue at the Commencement of the War, and that Mr. Elliott's Information came-from the most respectable Authority in Europe; that it was confirmed to me beyond a Doubt by the Reception of a Dench Minister at the Court of Poona, and

Intelligence of the raoft exact Coincidence with his from Poona. — I affirm again, that I was not the Author of the MarattaWar; that the Truth of this Assertion has been proved again and again. — But I affirm, that the Merit of the Marat ta Peace is my own j that it was concluded under greater Difficulties than anyMinister, at any Period of Time, in any Nation, has had to contend with; tlmt every possible Obstruction was thrown in the Way of the Negociation for Peace, by the Advices which every Dispatch brought from England: These diminished my Authority, and announced my Difiniffion from the Service. Every Man in England, who spoke on the Subject of our desperate Situation in India, declared, as I have been informed, that Peace upon any Terms was desirable, and that no Peace could be a bad one. — I affirm, that under all these Disadvantages, the Peace concluded by Mr. David Anderson, under my Instructions, was honourable and advantageous in the highest Degree to this Nation and the East India Company; that it has now been ratified above Three Years; that it has never been infringed in a Angle Article by either Party; and that it promises to be lading. I have received the unanimous Thanks of the Directors, and the Thanks of the Proprietors, with One difienting V oice only amongst the latter, for effecting this important Service to my Country and the Company; nor did 1 believe, till I read it in the Charge, that a single Person in Europe, or in India, could have ltyled the Peace ignominious or dif-honourable. My whole Correspondence with Mr. Anderson, and his Letters to me, are at the India House; to those Letters I refer, and rest my Defence on the Evidence they contain.

Answer to the Twenty-first Charge.

Suppression of Correspondence.

This is a Charge for the Suppression of Correspondence with the Princes and Country Powers of India: I shall reserve my Reply till the Instances are stated in which I have suppressed Correspondence; denying for the present, as I solemnly do, that I had any improper or dangerous Practices of any Kind to cover or conceal from my Council, the Court of Directors, or the British Nation.

Bristol Bridge A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are

and Street*, thereunto fubl’cribed, on Behalf of themselves, and all other the Citizens and Inhabitants of, and Traders to, the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, an Act was passed for re-building, widening, and enlarging the Bridge over the River Avon, in the City of Bristol, and for erecting a Temporary Bridge adjoining, and for other Purposes therein expressed, and for appointing certain Trullees therein named for carrying the same into Execution, with Powers to collect certain Tolls, Rates, and Duties; and the Powers of such Act, as far as the Trustees thought necessary, have been by them carried into Execution, in Consequence whereof, the Petitioners are informed, they incurred a Debt of 49,000l. and upwards; and that the Petitioners are also informed, that the said Tolls, Rates, and Duties, together with certain Ground Rents arising from Overplus Ground in the Act mentioned, do amount, upon an Average, to about 3,400l. per Annum, which Income 'has continued and been collected for Twenty-five Years, or upwards, and, the Petitioners therefore conceive, that if the whole of the said Income of 3,400 /. per Annum had been judiciously and properly managed from Time to Time, as received, that the enormous Debt of 23,750 /. which now remains due, dould not, at this Time, have existed; and that the Petitioners urtderstand that the said Trustees have made Application to the House for another Act, as well to enlarge the Power# given them by the said above Act, as to open a hew Street or Streets, which by Computation, will incur a further Debt of 8,000l. or 10,000l. and that they are pursuing such Application, notwithstanding it meets the general Difepprobation of the Petitioners, and their Fellow Citizens; and Alledging, That the Tolls, Rates, and Duties above-mentioned fell very heavy upon the Trade and Commerce of the said City, and is detrimental to such Trade and Commerce, and the Petitioners are fully convinced that any Bill or Bills, nting the said Trustees Powers to create any further bt or Debts, will be materially injurious to them, and to the general Trade of the City, and that, instead of adding to the present subsisting enormous Debt, every Exertion ought to be made to discharge the same, that the Burthens complained of may be taken off: And therefore praying, That, for the Reasons above stated, the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against fudi Bill or Bills passing into a Law, or that the House will grant them such other Relief as to the House tliall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

of Aberdeen;

Were severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners are convinced, from well-founded Experience, of the Inefficacy of the late Tobacco Law enacted for the Purpose of curbing illicit Trade, protecting the fair Dealer, and securing his Majesty’s Revenue in that very valuable Branch of the Customs; and Representing to the House, That, so far as the Operation of those new Regulations has Come within the Sphere of the Petitioners Knowledge, it is their firm Opinion, that, so far from preventing the Evil for which the said Law was intended as a Remedy, it

has

26 Geo. Ill- 3° Mai 737

ha9 had a contrary Effect, and they are clearly of Opinion, that Three-fourths of the Confutnp-tion of Scotland at large (and more particularly of Aberdeen, and the Counties to the Northward thereof) is, at this Moment, supplied with Smuggled Tobacco, and at a Price not exceedingTeu Pence toThirteen Pence per Pound, thefairTrader therefore, whose Inclination leads him to contribute towards the Support and increase of His Majesty’s Revenue, is undersold in every Quarter, and Ruin itares him in the Face , and that, in the Petitioners Opinion, there is no Mode of Regulations, however strict, that cannot, and will not, be evaded by Men of desperate Fortunes, who, from the Magnitude of the Temptation, will risque every Penalty attending Detection, and they therefore request the House, that a considerable Reduction of Duty (which in many recent Instances has been attended with very salutary Effects) may likewise be put in Practice with respect to Tobacco, and, the Petitioners call upon the Wisdom, the Justice, and the Humanity of Parliament, not to suffer an Industrious and useful Body of Men to -be borne down by the Force of illicit Trade: And therefore praying. That the House will grant them such Relief as to the I louse shall seem proper.

Mr. Beaufoy reported from the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Encouragement and Extension, and to report the same from Time to Time, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House, That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred; and had come to several

Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read -, and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bounty which was granted by an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty, and which will expire at the End of the next Sessions of Parliament, should not be renewed; but that, in the Place thereof, there should be given on every Decked Vessel, of not leis than Fifteen Tons Burthen, employed in the Herring Fishery, and fitted out and navigated according to Law, a Bounty of Twenty Shillings per Ton; and that, on such Herrings as shall be landed from any such Vessel during any One Year, there should be paid a Bounty, after the Rate of Four Shillings for every Barrel of Herrings twice packed and completely cured; provided always, that if the Number of Barrels of Herrings imported in such Vessel shall, in any One Year, exceed the Proportion of Two Barrels and a Half of Herrings, lb packed and cured, for every Ton of the Vefiers Burthen, which, upon an Average of the last Twenty Years, is supposed to have been the Quantity of Herrings Annually caught, there shall be paid, on every Barrel so exceeding the said Proportion, a Bounty of no more than One Shilling, which Inland Bounties of Four Shillings and One Shilling, as the same may be, should be exclusive of the Bounty granted on all Herrings exported, so that, if the industry and Success of the Owner should not be leis than it has been upon an Average of the last Twenty Years, the Bounty he will receive will not be left than at present, and, should his industry and Success be greater than before, he will receive on additional Reward.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the more effectual Prevention of Frauds, the Quantity of Herrings, in any Cargo entitled to the Bounty, should be computed at the Time of their being unshipped, while they are in the State in which they are denominated Sea Sticks, or Herrings not re-packed: and that Four Barrels of Herrings in that State should be considered as equivalent to Three Barrels of Herrings packed a Second Time.

Resolved, That, for the Encouragement of the Deep Sea Fishery on the North and North Eall Coalts of the Island, it may, in the Opinion of the Committee, be expedient that Premiums, of which the Total Amount in any One Year shall not exceed the Sum of Two hundred Guineas, should, for a Time to be limited, be paid, at the End of each Season, to the Four Vessels that shall have taken, in the Course of that Season, in the aforesaid Fishery, the greatest Quantity of Herrings.

Resolved, That, in the Opinion of this Committee, it is highly expedient, as well for the Purpose of encouraging the Fisheries by an Extension of the Market, as for that of providing a cheap and wholesome Article of Food for the Support of the Poor, that all Duties at this Time payable by Law on such Herrings, Cod, Ling, and Salmon, or other Fish, caught and cured by British Subjects, as are removed for Home Consumption, should cease and determine.

Resolved, That, as it appears by Evidence, contained in a Report presented to the House on the 14th Day of July last, and referred to this Committee, that the Distinction between Haberdine Cod and Cod not Haberdine is useless, inasmuch as little less than the whole Quantity of Dried Cod exported during the last Thirty Years has been shipped as Haberdine; and, as it also appears, by Evidence contained in the said Report, that the Value of Cod, in feme of the

Foreign

i6 Geo. 111.

foreign Markets, is much diminHhed by that Degree of Dryness which is denominated Haberdine, and on which the highest Bounty is now payable by Law, it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Distinction of Haberdine and not Haberdine, in the Cure of Cod, ought to be abolished, and that the Bounty of Three Shillings per Hundred Weight, at present payable on British Haberdine Cod exported, should be paid on all British Cod exported, whether Haberdine or not.

Resolved, That, in the Opinion of this Committee, it is highly requisite, that, on all Barrels and Calks in which any Fish whatever (Frefli Fish excepted) shall be packed, either for Exportation or Home Consumption, the respective Names of the Curers should be marked in conspicuous and permanent Characters; and that the Staves of all Barrels, in which White Herrings shall be packed for Exportation, should not be of a less Thickness, at the Bulge, than Half an Inch; and that all such Barrels should be full Bound.

Resolved, That, as it appears to tins Committee, that, by an Act passed in the Twelfth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for allowing a Drawback upon the Exportation of Salt to be made use of " for the curing of Fish taken at the North Seas or at " Ireland and also by an Act passed in the Twenty-

fifth Year of llis present Majesty, intituled, "An Act " for the further Encouragement of the British Fifeeries," the Use of Salt Duty-free, for the Cure of such Cod, Ling, and Hake as are taken in the North Sea, is expressly allowed, whether such Fife shall be exported or fold for Home Consumption, which Privilege is accompanied by an express Declaration, that the Cod, Ling, and Hake, so cured, feall he entitled to a Bounty on Exportation: And as it also appears to this Committee, that, by an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for recovering the Credit of the British Fifeery in " Foreign Parts, and better securing the Duties on Salt," and also, by an Act, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for encouraging the Fifeeries in that " Part of Great Britain called Scotland," (which last

Acts, the Committee apprehend, relate to the Home Fifeeries alone) the Use of Salt Duty-free is allowed for the Cure of such Cod, Ling, or Hake only, as shall be cured for Exportation, a Restriction that is accompanied however by the Privilege of a Bounty on the Fife so exported: And as it further appears to this Committee, that Doubts have arisen how far the Seas between the North-East Parts of Great Britain and the opposite Coasts of the Continent of Europe are to be considered as included within the Limits of the North Sea, in consequence of which Doubts, Vessels failing for the same , Sea, and employed on the same Banks in taking the same Fife, are often fitted out under different Regulations, by which they are subjected to different Restrictions, and entitled to different Privileges, this Committee are of Opinion, that, for the Purpose of giving uniformity to the Law', and Relief from Doubt to the Subject, it is highly expedient, that the Boundary of the North Sea should be clearly ascertained, and expressly declared, by the Legislature.

Resolved, That the Committee are of Opinion, That, for the Encouragement of the Fifeeries, the Right of exercising any Trade, or Calling, in any City, Town, or Borough, in the Kingdom, should be extended to all such Persons as feall follow, for the Space of Seven successive Years, the Occupation of a Seaman, or Fifeerman, on Board of any Vessel, or Vessels, employed in any of the Fifeeries of Great Britain.

Resolved, That, as it appears by Evidence contained in the Report referred to this Committee, that the several Vo l. 41.

74*

Laws hich prohibit the Importation offrefe Fife taken by Foreigners, have proved ineffectual, it is, in the Opini^on of this Committee, highly expedient, that such furthe Regulations should be adopted, as may prevent the Continuance of an Abuse so injurious to the Fifeeries, and so obvioufiy detrimental to the Naval Interests of the K.ingd ora.

Received, That, in the Opinion of this Committee, it is higrJhly expedient, that Red Herrings, and all other Fish, on which, if cured in England, and exported from England, or if cured in Scotland, and exported from Scotland, a Bounty is payable by Law', should also be entitled to that Bounty if cured in England, and exported from Scotland or if cured in Scotland and exported from England.

Resolved, That, in the Opinion of this Committee, it is of the utmost Importance, that such Fish Curers as feall receive into their own Custody, for the Purpose of preserving Fish, Salt of British Manufacture, should not be required to give any other Security respecting the said Salt than their own Bonds, justly aiyl truly to account for the fame; and that Credit for such Quantities of the said Salt as feall have been used, and duly accounted for, should Annually be given by the proper Officer on the Back of the said Bond, and that such Bond should continue in Force till a proper Account -feall have been rendered of the Whole of the Salt specified therein, or the Duty shall be paid on the Deficiency.

Resolved, That, in the Opinion of this Committee, all Bonds, or other Securities, demandable from the Takers or Curers of Fife, or from the Matters or Owners of Boats employed in the Fisheries, or in the Exportation of Fife, or in the Conveyance of the same from onq British Port to another, should be written on unstamped Paper.

Resolved, That, as the Report referred to this Committee contains the strongest Evidence of the pernicious Effects which the Fees, or other Perquisites, of the Customhouse Officers, especially in Scotland, have produced on the Fifeeries of the Kingdom, and as the Requisition of such Fees, however lanftioned by long Usage, appears by the Orders of Parliament, in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King Charles the Second, to be contrary to the declared Intention of the Legislature, this Committee are of Opinion, that no Officer should be permitted to ask, or accept of any Fee, or other Perquisite, for or on Account of any Transaction relative to any Vessel, or Boat, employed in the Fifeeries, or in the Transportation, from one Place to another, of Fife, or of Salt for the Use of the Fifeeries, or for or on Account of the Payment of any Bounty or Debenture on Fife, on Pain of forfeiting, for every such Offence, treble the Value of the Sum received, together with Costs of Suit, and of being ipso facto, discharged, and rendered incapable of serving His Majesty in any Civil Office in future; the Committee at the same Time indulging an earnest Hope, that the Benevolence of the Legislature will induce them to make Compensation to the Officers for the Abolition of their Fees, especially as at present their Salaries are such, that the Fees they are accustomed to take, heavy and oppressive as they are to the Fifeer-men, are, in many Instances, absolutely requisite for the creditable Subsistence of the Officer.

Resolved, That, as the Value of the Privilege of Curing Fish with Salt of British Manufacture, Duty-free, is much diminifeed in Scotland, by the Provision of the Act of the Twenty-ninth of George the Second, that such Salt shall be taken from the Salt Works of that Part of the Island, it is the Opinion of this Committee, that the Fife Curers in every Part of Great Britain, so far as they are allowed by Law to employ in the Cure of Fish Home-manufactured Salt^ Duty-free, should be permitted

Resolved, That, as the opening a Communication between Lock Gilp and Lock by a Navigable Canal

across the Peninftila of Cantyre in would

prevent the Necessity of a Voyage of more than One hundred Miles in a very dangerous Sea, and greatly promote the Fisheries and Commerce of the North-Western Coasts of the I (land, and as it appears, by actual Survey, that the said Communication may be effefited at a moderate Expence, it is, in the Opinion of this Committee, extremely desirable that such Persons as are willing to perform, at their own Cost, a Work so useful to the Public, should receive all reasonable Encouragement.

Resolved, That, as the Business of the Fisheries can only be carried on to Advantage by the joint Labour of many Individuals, aided by the Skill of several distinct Classes of Manufacturers, and, as the Establishment of Villages, or Towns, in certain Situations on the Northern and Western ^Coasts of Scotland, would not only furnish the Means of that Co-operation and mutual Assistance, but would likewise afford a Market for (bme Part of the Produce of the Fisheries, and much facilitate the Conveyance of the Remainder, whether fold for Consumption in the Inland Country, or for Exportation to Foreign Parts, it is the Opinion of this Committee, that the liberal Disposition which appears in many public-spirited Proprietors of Land upon those Coasts, as well as in many respectable Individuals in the Southern Parts of the Kingdom, for the Establishment of such Villages and Towns, deserves the highest Encouragement.

Resolved, That, in order to encourage the forming by Subscription a Fund for the Establishment of such Villages and Towns, it is, in the Opinion of this Committee, highly expedient that the Subscribers should, by Act of Parliament, be declared to be a Joint Stock Company,

♦ that Power to appoint Agents for the Management of

their Business should be given them, and that the Members should be expressly exempted from a greater Extent of Responsibility than that of the original Sum w’hich each shall respectively subscribe; that the Fund should be declared to be applicable to no other Use but that of tenting or purchasing Lands, and that of erecting, by Contract, Houses and other necessary Buildings; that the Company should be impowered to let, or transfer in Perpetuity, such Parcels of their Land as Individuals, with a View of building at their own Expence, may be inclined to hire or to purchase; that the Company should be restrained from engaging as a Corporation in any Trade, as well as from issuing Notes payable to the Bearer, or other Species of circulating Security; and that, in order to prevent excessive and pernicious Fluctuations in the Value of their Stock, the Act should declare, that, during the Space of the first Five Years of the Company’s EllabiHhment, no Member shall dispose of his Stock in any other Way than that of Gift or Bequest.

Biitiih Resolved, That, for the Encouragement of such Fish-

Fisharie*. ermen, Manufacturers, and others, as shall become Householders in the said Villages and Towns, it may, in the Opinion of the Committee, be advisable to declare, that the Householders in each of the said Villages or Towns, as soon as their Number in such Town or Village shall amount to or exceed Fifty, shall have a Right Annually to choose from among their own Body certain Magistrates, who shall have the same Powers, for the Government of such Town or Village, as the Magistrates of Royal Burghs in North Britain are now, by Law, entitled to exercise; provided, however, that no separate or exclusive Corporation shall be erected within such Town or Village, nor Mqqey be exacted to entitle

any Person to his Freedom, or to the Privilege of exercising any Profession, or of carrying on any Trade, Business, or Employment in the said Village or Town; and provided also, that no private Rights or Jurisdictions, already subsisting, shall be infringed.

Resolved, That, for the further Encouragement of the said Villages and Towns, as well as for the more effectual Extension of Commerce, it may, in the Judgment of the Committee be expedient that, in every Village or Town of the Description aforesaid, in which the Householders, from their Number, shall be entitled to eleCfc Magistrates, a Poll Office and Custom House should, with all convenient Dispatch, be established.

Resolved, That, as Licences, imposing a heavy Tax on the Exercise of certain necessary Trades, are peculiarly unfavourable to the Establishment of Towns in the remote and unimproved DistriCfcs of the Kingdom, and as the Law, which declares that the different Branches of the Tannery shall not be carried on by one and the same Person, must be injurious to Infant Settlements, in which the Division of Labour that takes Place in more extended Societies is neither practised nor known, it may, in the Opinion of the Committee, be expedient that, in all such Villages or Towns as shall be erected in any Part of the Coast, from the Mull of Kyntire to the Murray Firth, the same Person should be allowed to carry on, at the same Time, the several Branches of the Tannery Business, and that the Inhabitants should, for the Space of Seven Years, have Periniffion to exercise the Trades of a Common Brewer, Maltster, Candle-maker, Tanner, Tawer, Dresser of Hides in Oil, or Currier, on Condition that every Person who shall fb carry on any of the said Trades, shall Annually pay, by Way of Licence, the Sum of One Shilling; provided always, that no Person should be entitled to that Indulgence who shall make, in any One Year, more than 1000 Barrels of Beer, or more than 200 Quarters of Malt.

Resolved, That as, by the Duty on Coal carried Coast-ways, the Inhabitants of many of the Districts of Scotland are deprived of the Benefit which the Abundance of this Article in the neighbouring Distri&s would otherwise afford, it would, in the Opinion of this Committee, be highly expedient that the Inhabitants of those Distri&s in Scotland, in which the said Duty is paid, should for

a Term of Years, be permitted Annually to raise, by Assessment or other Mode of Commutation, a Sum equal to that which, on an Average of the last Five Years, those Districts have Annually contributed to the said Duty, and should, on that Condition, be liberated from this burthensome Impost.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of African Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be pre- Company, fented to the House,

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House an Account of the Money granted in the Year 1784, examined and passed by the Cuditor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for " extending and improving the Trade to Africa," and that they have invested the Money, granted in 1785, for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and Settlements were delivered to the Petitioners in a very ruinous Condition by the Royal African Company, and the Sums Annually'granted by Parliament for their Support and Maintenance being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Establishments, and in the necessary contingent Charges, there remained little or nothing for the Jrurpole of Repairs; and that sundry Abuses having been alledged to exist in the Conduct of the Officers employed by the Petitioners on the Coast of Africa, and more particularly in the Management of the Public Money committed to their Care, the Petitioners thought proper, in the Year 1779, to suspend their Governor in Chief and the Council at Cape Coast Castle, and to appoint certain Commissioners to examine, in Africa, into the Conduct and Accounts of the Officers from the Beginning of the Year 1770; and the said Commissioners, or their Successors, having reported fully to the Petitioners, upon th^ different Objects referred to them, and in particular upon the Accounts of their Officers in Africa, and the Petitioners having carefully examined and confirmed the said Reports, it appears by the same that at the End of the Year 1776 the Petitioners were indebted to sundry of their said Officers, as specified in the said Reports, to the Amount of 24,694/. 14s. 11 f

Income so calculated, is not a Statement of the present exiltant Expenditure, or of that which must exist for some Years to come, but is formed upon the probable Reductions which it is alledged will have taken Place towards the End of the Year 1791, in the ProspeCfc of a permanent Peace;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the different Branches of Revenue, in the Period upon which the future is calculated, appear to have beeu Angularly productive, particularly in the Customs, and greatly to have exceeded the Amount of the preceding Year, with which alone it is contrafted;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That it does not appear that any Means were taken, nor Information called for, nor any Examination entered into by the said Committee, in order to ascertain whether such Increase of Revenue had arisen from Causes which were likely to have a permanent Operation, or otherwise;

It passed in the Negative,

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That such an Investigation is indispensably necessary before this House can, with Confidence calculate, by the Produce of One Year, the supposed future Amount of the public Income;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Uncertainty of estimating, by such a Criterion, the expected future produce of the Revenue, is (till more evident, upon a Comparison of the Quarter ending the 5th of Aprillaft, with the same Quarter in the preceding Year, upon which the future Income is calculated; by which Comparison it appears that the Amount of the latter Quarter is inferior by the Sum of 188,215/. 13$. 4 d.in the Branch of the Customs, to the former;

It passed hi the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That in the said Report there are certain Articles of Receipt erroneously stated, as proper to be added to the future Annual Income, and other Articles of Expence erroneously omitted to be added to the Expenditure;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Sums voted, and to be voted, for the Service of the Year 1786, including the Interest and Charges of the Public Debts, considerably exceeds that Sum.

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Means, by which the Deficiency is to be made good, arise from Aids and Debts which belong to the present Year only;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That there is no Surplus Income whatever applicable to the Reduction of the Public Debt now existing;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That a Surplus of Income in the ensuing Quarters can arise only by the Renewal of a Loan for an extraordinary Million, borrowed upon Exchequer Bills in the last, and charged upon the Supply of the present Year, and which Loan it would be unnecessary to make but for the Purpose of procuring the said Surplus; J

A. 1786.

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That any extraordinary Increase of Exchequer Bills, contrary to former Practice in Time of Peace, is an inexpedient Anticipation of that Assistance which the Government might receive in the same of any Circumstance rendering it necessary to strengthen the State of our National Preparation;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Saving to the Public upon the Interest of Money borrowed in this Way is rendered improbable or precarious by the Necessity which will arise for the more l'peedy issuing such Bills, in order that the Object for which the Loan is made may be punctually and effectually answered, nor even should such Saving accrue, will it compensate for the Disadvantage above stated;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That admitting that, by the foregoing Means, the expected Surplus will arise upon the Three Quarters next ensuing, and that thenceforward One Million Annually is to be applied to the Reduction of the Debt, it appears that there will then be an Interval of nearly Four Years before the Commencement of that permanent Peace Establishment, which is to furnish, in the Reduction of its Services, 900,000l. of the expected Million Surplus.

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That in this Period it appears from the Vouchers annexed to the said Report, and other Papers before this House, that a Sum amounting to 4,010,000l., besides Two Millions due to the Bank, making together the Sum of 6,010,000l. will be deficient and wanting, over and above the stated Annual Income;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That, for this Sum of 6,010,000l. there appears to be adequate Provision or Resource;

It passed in the Negative.

Rights of Fyzoola Khdn, under the Treaty of Lall-Dang.

I. That, notwithstanding the culpable and criminal Reluctance of the President Hastings, hereinbefore recited, a Treaty of Peace and Friendship between the Vizier Sujah ul Dowlahand the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn was finally signed and sealed, on the 7th October 1774, at a Place called Lall-Dang, in the Presence, and with the Attestation of the British Commander in Chief, Colonel Alexander Champion aforesaid; and that for the said Treaty the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn agreed to pay, and did actually pay, the valuable Consideration of Half his Treasure, to the Amount of 15 Lacks of Rupees, or 150,000l. Sterling, and upwards.

II. That by the said Treaty, the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn was established in the quiet Possession of Shawabad, and " some other Districts dependent thereon," subject to certain Conditions, of which the more important were as follow:

" That Fyzoola Khdn should retain in his Service " 5,000 Troops, and not a jfingle Mar\ more:

" That with whomsoever the Vizier should make " War, Fyzoola Khdn should fend Two or Three thousand Men, according to his Ability, to join the Forces " of the Vizier:

" And that, if the Vizier should march in Person, " Fyzoola Khdn should himself accompany him with his " Troops."

III. That from the Terms of the Treaty above recited it doth plainly, positively, and indisputably appear, that the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn, in case of War, was not bound to furnish more than Three thousand Men, under any Construction, unless the Vizier should march in Person.

IV. That the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn was not positively bound to furnish so many as 3,000 Men, but an indefinite N umber, not more than Three, and not left than Two thousand; that, of the precise Number within such Limitations, the Ability of Fyzoola Khdn, and not the Discretion of the Vizier, was to be the Standard; and that such Ability could only mean, that which was equitably consistent not only with the external Defence of his Jaghire, but with the internal good Management thereof, both as to its Police and Revenue.

V. That even in case the Vizier should march in Person, it might be reasonably doubted, whether the Personal Service of the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn " with his Troops" must be understood to be, with all his Troops, or only with the Number before stipulated, not more than Three, and not left than Two thousand Men; and that the latter is the Interpretation finally adopted by Warren Hastings aforesaid, and the Council of Bengal, who, in a Letter to the Court of Directors, dated April 5th, 1783, represent the Clause3 of the Treaty relative to the stipulated Aid as meaning Amply, that Fyzoola Khdn " should fend 2 or 3,000 Men to join the Vizier’s " Forces, or attend in Person, in case it should be " requisite."

VI. That from the aforesaid Terms of the Treaty, it doth not spedfically appear of what the stipulated Aid should consist, whether of Horse or Foot, or in what Proportion of both; but that it is the recorded Opi-

nion, maturely formed by the said Hastings and his Council, in January 1783, that even a Angle Horseman included in the Aid which Fyzoola Khdn might " furnish, would prove a literal Compliance with the " Stipulation."

VII. That, in the Event of any Doubt fairly arising from the Terms of the Treaty, the Nabob fyzoola , in Consideration of his Hereditary Right to the whole Country, and the Price by him actually paid for the said Treaty, was in Equity entitled to the most favourable Construction.

VIII. That, from the Attestation of Colonel Champion aforesaid, the Government of Calcutta acquired the same Right to interpose with the Vizier for the Protection of the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn, as they the said Government had before claimed, from a similar Attestation of Sir Robert Barker, to assist the Vizier in extirpating the whole N ation of the said Fyzoola Khdn; more especially, as in the same of Sir Robert Barker it was contrary to the Remonstrances of the then Administration, and the furthest from the Intentions of the said Barker himself, that his Attestation should involve the Company; but the Attestation of Colonel Champion was authorized by all the Powers of the Government, as a " Sanction " intended " to add Validity " to the Treaty: That they the said Government, and in particular the said Wart'en Hastings, as the first executive Member of the fame, were bound by the Ties of natural Justice duly to exercise the aforesaid Right, if Need were; and that their Duty so to interfere was more particularly enforced by the Spirit of the Censures past both by the Directors and Proprietors in the Rohilla War, and the Satisfaction expressed by the Directors, " in the honourable End put " to that War."

Guarantee of the Treaty of Lall-Dang.

I. That during the Life of the Vizier Sujah ul,

and for some Time after his Death, under his Son and Successor Asoph ul Dawla, the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn did remain without Disturbance or Molestation: That he did all the while imagine his Treaty to be under the Sandion of the Company, from Colonel Champions. affixing his Signature thereto as a Witness, " which " Signature, as he (Fyzoola Khdn) supposed," rendered the Company the Arbitrators between the Vizier and himself, in case of Disputes: And that, being " a Man " of Sense but extreme Pusillanimity, a good Farmer, " fond of Wealth, not possessed of the Passion of bition," he did peaceably apply himself to " improve " the State of his Country; and did, by his own Pru- denceand Attention, encrease the Revenues thereof

" beyond the Amount specified in Sujah ul Dawla,'s " Grant"

II. That in the Year 1777, and in the Beginning of the Year 1778, being " alarmed at the young Vizier’s " Resumption of a Number of Jaghires, granted by his " Father to different Persons, and the Injustice and Oppression of his Conduct in generaland_ having now learned (from whom does not appear, but probably from some Person supposed of competent Authority; that Colonel Champion formerly witnessed the Treaty as a private Person, the Nabob Fyzoola Khdn did make frequent and urgent Solicitations to Nathaniel Middleton, Esquire, then Resident at Chide, and to Warren Hastings aforesaid, then Governor General of Bengal, " for a " Renovation of his (the Nabob Fyzoola Khdna) Treaty " with the late Vizier, and the Guarantee of the Company," or for a " separate Agreement with the Company for his Defence;" considering them (the Company) as " the only Power in which he had Confidence, and " to which he could look up for Protection."

Demand of Five Thousand Horse.

I. That, notwithstanding his own private Honour, thus deeply engaged, notwithstanding the Public Justice and Generality of the Company and the Nation, thus solemnly committed, disregarding the plain Import and positive Terms of the guaranteed Treaty, the Governor General, Warren Hastings aforesaid, in November 1780 (while a Body of Fyzoola Kk&n's Cavalry, voluntarily granted, were still serving under a British Officer) did recommend to the Vizier " to require from Fyzoola " Kh&n the Quota of Troops stipulated by Treaty to " be furnished by the latter for his (the Vizier’s) Service,

He observes, it is " the Custom of the Honourable Company, when they deprive a Chief of his Country, to grant him some " Allowance. This he expects from Mr. Hastings's " Bounty; but if he should be disappointed, he will " certainly set off upon a Pilgrimage to Mecca and " Medina, and renounce the Cares of the World."

" He directs his Vakeel to ascertain whether the " English intend to deprive him of his Country; for if " they do, he is ready to surrender it, upon receiving an " Order from the Resident."

" He does not admit of the Improvements reported " to be made in his Jaghire, and even asserts, that " the Collefitions this Year will fall short of the original " Jurnma (or Estimate) by Reason of the long Drought.

" He denies having exceeded the limited Number " of Rohillas in his Service;

And having refuted the required Aid of Cavalry,

" made by Johnson, to afit with General Goddard.

A PETITION of the Shopkeepers and Traders Hawker* ud of the Town of Wellington, in the County of Ptdlars* Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Indulgences intended to be granted by a Bill now before the House, for repealing several Clauses of the Act, made last Session of Parliament, for-laying additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and regulating their Trade, will, if passed into a Law, prove highly detrimental to the resident Trader; and that the Petitioners, in common with other Traders who inhabit Market Towns, will be particularly injured by the Clause which disables Hawkers and Pedlars from vending, felling, or exposing to Sale, any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, in any City, Borough, or Corporate Town, in England, Wales, or Town of Berwick upon Tweed, or within the Suburbs thereof, except upon Market or Fair Days, but which Clause does not extend to Market Towns: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Petitioners same into Consideration, and, as they bear their Proportion of Taxes with Cities, Boroughs, and Corporate Towns, that they may enjoy the same Privileges, and be included in the Benefit of whatever Restrictions the House may fee meet to lay on Hawkers and Pedlars in the Bill now before them.

A Petition of the Shopkeepers, and other Inha- Ditto, bitants of the City of Ereter, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending to repeal so much of an Act, passed in the last Session, for granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their Trade, as restrains Hawkers and Pedlars from exposing to Sale Goods in Market Towns, and as enables Justices of the Peace to prohibit such Hawkers and Pedlars from vending their Goods within the same, and for further regulating their Trade; and that the Petitioners prefome, that the principal Object of the said Act was to make some Compensation to the resident Trader for the partial and oppressive Tax laid on Retail Shops, but, they apprehend, that if the Provisions contained in the said Act are repealed, as proposed by the present Bill, the good Intent of the Whole of the said Act will be entirely frustrated, and the resident Trader will receive as much Injury by Hawkers and Pedlars, felling'

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Inhabitants of the County of Montgomery, and Counties adjacent, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have, for many Years pall, found it convenient, and been accustomed, to deal with Licensed Hawkers and Pedlars, by whom they have been supplied with Linen, Cotton, and Silk Goods, of the Manufacture of this Kingdom, at as fair and reaion-able Prices as elsewhere, at their own Houses, without the Expence of travelling to Market Towns, and have always found them honest and upright in all their Dealings; and Representing to the House, That by the 9th and 1 ith Sections of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for laying an additional Duty on Hawkers and Pedlars, the Petitioners are deprived of the Benefit of dealing with Hawkers and Pedlars, and they are also not only limited so much in their Trade, as not to be able to carry it on to enable them to pay their Creditors, the Duty to Government, and maintain themselves and Families in any Degree of Comfort, but are liable to be fopprefied and prevented from carrying it on at all, without a Charge of Guilt, or being heard in their own Defence: And therefore praying the House to repeal the said Sections, and to regulate the said Trade in such Manner as they shall think lit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the following Bounties, under certain Conditions and Limitations, be allowed to Fifteen Ships of Great Britain, Ireland, or the Islands of Guernsey, Jersey, or Man, built, owned, and navigated according to Law, and employed in the Southern Whale Fishery, and which shall pals, for the Purpose of carrying on the said Fishery, to the Southward of the Seventh Degree of North Latitude, that is to say; to the Three Vessels which shall fb fail, between the First Day of May and the First Day of July, in each Year, and shall first return before the First Day of July in the following Year, to any Port of Great Britain, with the greatest Quantity of Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, not less than Tw enty Tons, being the Produce of One or more Whale or Whales, or other Creatures living in the Sea, taken or killed by the Crews of such Vessels, a Bounty of Five hundred Pounds each; to the Three Vessels that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of l'uch Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Four hundred Pounds each; to the Three Vessels that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Three hundred Pounds each; to the Three Vessels that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Two hundred Pounds each; and to the Three Vessels that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of One hundred Pounds each.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the following Bounties, under certain Conditions and Limitations, be allowed to Five Ships of Great Britain, Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey, or Man, built, owned, and navigated according to Law, and employed in the Southern Whale Fishery, and which shall pass to the Southward of Thirty-six Degrees of South Latitude; that is to say, to the Vessel which shall so fail between the First Day of May and the First Day of July, in each Year, and shall first arrive, in not less than Eighteen Months, and not more than Twenty-eight Months, from tire said First Day of May, in any Port of Great Britain, with the greatest Quantity of Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, not less than Twenty Tons, being the Produce of One or more Whale or Whales, or other Creatures living in the Sea, taken or killed by the Crew of such Vessel, a Bounty of Seven hundred Pounds; to the Vessel that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Six hundred Pounds; to the Vessel that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Five hundred Pounds; to the Vessel that shall fail and arrive, in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Vol. 41.

Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Four hundred Pounds; and to the Vessel that shall fail and arrive in like Manner, within the Periods before-mentioned, with the next greatest Quantity of such Oil, Blubber, or Head Matter, a Bounty of Three hundred Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Oil, Blubber, and Head Matter, being the Produce of any Whale or WT hales, or other Creatures living in the Sea, and all Whale Fins, and Seal Skins, taken or caught by any of His Majesty’s Subjects of Great Britain, Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey, or Man, in Ships built, owned, and navigated according to Law, be allowed to be imported Duty-free.

Mr. Mainwaring reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, in General Quarter Sessions assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Stirling being examined, laid, That the Grand Jury for the said County did, on the 24th Day of July, in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, present that the House of Correction for the said County was in a ruinous State, insecure, and by no Means large enough, or sufficiently airy, for the Confinement of the Number of Prisoners generally therein confined, or capable of answering the general Purposes of a House of Correction; in Proof of which he produced to your Committee the original Presentment of the said Grand Jury. And being further examined, he laid, That the Magistrates of the County have fixed upon a Piece of Ground, where a proper and commodious House of Correction may be built.

Sir Robert Taylor being then examined, said, That the Expence of purchasing the Ground, and building such House of Correction, and making proper Accommodations thereto, will amount to a very large Sum of Money, which, if raised according to the Mode prescribed by the present Laws for that Purpose, will be a much heavier Burthen upon the present Inhabitants of the said County, than if the same was to be raised by. the granting of Annuities for Lives, to be paid by a Rate to be made upon the said County.

Ordered, That Leave be giveu to bring in a Bill to enable the Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex to raise Money, in Manner therein mentioned, for erecting a House of Correction within the

A PETITION of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and other Inhabitants of the Counties of -

sex and Hertford, was pfefcnted to the- House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having had constant Dealings with Hawkers and Pedlars, have always found them honest and fair-dealing Trades-men, and have frequently experienced the Advantage of purchasing Goods from them, they having a great Variety of Fancy Articles, such as printed Callicoes, Mullins, and the various Manufactures of these Kingdoms, which, from their indefatigable Assiduity, they are enabled to fell on reasonable Terms; and that the Petitioners find, by the 9th and nth Sections of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, to lay an additional Duty on Hawkers and Pedlars, and to regulate their Trade, that they are not only deprived of the Liberty of trading to such Extent, as to difeble them from paying the just Demands of Government and their Creditors, and allb supporting their Families, but are subject to be expected from any County, without being beard in their Defence: And therefore the Petitioners beg Leave to recommend the perilous Situation of this useful Class of Traders to the Consideration of the House, and they have no Doubt but it will be found consistent with Justice, as well as conducive to the Advantage of Trade, to repeal the said 9th and 11 th SeClions.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Inhabitants of the County of was also pre-

iented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for many Years past, found it convenient, and been accustomed to deal with Li-cenled Hawkers and Pedlars, by whom they have been supplied with Linen, Cotton, and Silk Goods, of the Manufacture of this Kingdom, at as fair and rea-fonahlfl Prices as elsewhere, at their own Houses, without the Expence of travelling to Market Towns, and have always found them honest and upright in all their-Dealings; and Roprefeuting to the House, That, by the 9th and 11th SeClions of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for laying an additional Duty on Hawkers and Pedlars, the Petitioners are deprived of the Benefit of dealing with Hawkers and Pedlars, and they are also not only limited so much in their Trade as not to be able to cany it on to enable them to pay their Creditors, the Duty to Government, and maintain themselves and Families in any Degree of Comfort, but are liable to be foppressed and prevented from carrying it on at all, without a Charge of Guilt, or being heard in their own Defence: And therefore praying the House to repeal the said Sections, and to regulate the said Trade in such Manner as they shall think fit.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Inhabitants of the County of and Counties

t>7

adjacent, was allb presented to the House, and read; containing the same Allegations and Prayer as the last preceding Petition.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and other Inhabitants of the County of Oxford, and Parts adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,/ Thet the Petitioners have frequently had Dealings with Hawkers and Pedlars, and have always found them honest and fair-dealing Tradesmen; and that tISe Petitioners are informed, that, by the 9th and 11th Sections of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, they are not only reltricted from vend* ing their Goads, iu Market Towns, but are liable to be foppressed, and, the Petitioners have great Reason to fear that fitch Restrictions on One Branch of Trade

will give too great a Monopoly to another, and subject the Consumers to pay an extraordinary Profit for such Articles as are necessary for their Families: And therefore praying, That the House will take the said Restrictions into their serious Consideration, and they have no Doubt but it will be found necessary to repeal the said 9th and 11th SeClions.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the County of Norfolk, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that, by an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, the Hawkers and Pedlars are liable to be abolished, and the Petitioners having had constant Dealings with Hawkers and Pedlars for many Years, are enabled to inform the House, that they have found them regular and fair-dealing Tradesmen; and that the Petitioners have, for many Years, experienced the Advantage and Convenience of purchasing Goods from Hawkers and Pedlars, as they carry a Variety of useful and fafhioo-able Articles of the Manufactories of these Kingdoms, which, from their indefatigable Assiduity, they are enabled to fell on reasonable Terms; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the above Act was made at the Request of Tradesmen having a private Interest in the Suppression of those useful and industrious Traders, and not by the resident Inhabitants, who only can judge of their Usefulness: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same into Consideration, and repeal that Part of the late Act which tends, ta aholifo the Hawkers and Pedlars, and continue to the Petitioners the Liberty of dealing with them.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the Bill to repeal lb much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament intituled, "An Act for granting " to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for . " regelating their Trade," as refcrams Hawkers and Pedlars from exposing to Sale Goods in Market Towns, and as enables Justices of the Peace of any County, to prohibit such Hawkers and Pedlars from vending their Goods within the same, and for further regulating their Trade, be read a Second Time.

Sir Mattheio White Ridley seported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, and several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and the several other Persons, Holders of Land, and Parishioner* of and in the Parish or Parochial Chapetry of All Saints, in the Town and County of Newcastle upon was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered k m at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. David Stephenson, an Architect, being examined, said, That he has surveyed the Church or Chapel of the said Parish or Parochial Chapelry, and found it to be a very ancient Building, and by Length of Time is become so ruinous, that the Foundation of the greatest Part of the Pillars and Walls which fop port the Roof have lately shrunk, and the same are now io such a decayed State, and incline io far out of a perpendicular Line, that the said Church is become totally unsafe for the Celebration of Divine Service — That the said Church is ineapable of an effectual Repair, and it is therefore necessary that the same should be takeo dpwn and re-built. And the Wk-ness further said. That the said Parish being large and populous, the Church Yard is too confined and fnaall for the Burial of the Dead, and it is proposed to enlarge the fame, and make eommodiogs Avenues thereto: And he added. That the effecting the Purposes aforesaid, will contribute much to the Convenience of the said Parishioners, and be of public Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the pulling down and re-building the Church of All Saints, in the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne, and for enlarging the Church Yard, and making convenient Avenues and Passages thereto: And that Sir Matthew White Ridley and Mr. Brandling do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

The Memorial of Thomas Earl of Effingham, Master and Worker of His Majesty’s Mint,

Sheweth,

That in Consequence of a very large and extraordinary Coinage of Gold carried on by your Memorialist, during the Year 17S5, the Expence' incurred at the Mint within the said Time has amounted to the unusual Sum of Twenty-eight thousand Seven hundred Thirty-nine Pounds Five Shillings and One Farthing, the Particulars of which have already been laid before your I>ord(hhips.

That towards providing for the above Service, your Memorialist has received at different Times, within the said Year, in the common Course of Payment, and by Way of Imprest, from the Coinage Duties, Five thousand Two hundred Ninety-eight Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Eleven Pence, and is also to receive under your Lordships Warrant, pursuant to an Act lit G-.o. I. C. 43, the farther Sum of Eight thousand Five hundred and One Pound Four Shillings and One Penny.

But that after the above Receipt there will full remain due to your Memorialist the Sum of Fourteen You 41. . 9 N thousand

784 io" Mali. A. 1786.

thousand Nine hundred Thirty-nine Pounds Five Shillings and One Farthing; which it is presumed, can only he allowed to your Memorialist by special Vote of Parliament.

Your Memorialist therefore prays your Lordships to take the Premises into Consideration, and make the necessary Application to the Honourable House of Commons; or take such other Measures for paying the said Balance of 14,939/. 5$. o\d to your Memorialist, as to your Lordships shall feera meet

Mint Office,

10th March 1786. M' and Wr.

The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury are pleased to refer this Memorial, with the Account thereto annexed, to the Warden and Comptroller of His Majesty's Mint; who are to examine the fame, and report to their I<ordships their Opinion what is fit to be done therein.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

In Obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference Signified to us by Mr. , the 14th Instant, annexing the Aecount of the Earl of Effingham, as Matter and Worker of His Majesty’s Mint, for the Year 1785; — -we beg Leave to report.

That having carefully examined the said Account of the Earl of Effingham, as Matter and Worker of His Majesty’s Mint, for the Year 1785, we find the same to be truly Stated. That the Balance due at the Foot thereof amounts to 23,440/. 9#. 1 id;and that when his Lordship Shall have received 8,001/. 4s. 1 by virtue of your Lordships Warrant, as set forth in the Memorial referred, there will still remain due to the Skid Earl of Effingham the Sum of Fourteen thousand Nine hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Five Shillings and One Farthing; which we apprehend, with his Lordship, can only be paid under a special Vote of Parliament for that Purpose; but which we nevertheless humbly submit to your Lordships great Wisdom.
