To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

The humble Memorial of John Vernon, the Younger, Solicitor to His Majesty’s Mint.

Sheweth,

That your Memorialist, in the Month of March 1785, did present to your Lordships a Memorial; Setting forth, That in pursuance of Directions from Sir Robert Pigot, Baronet, Warden of His Majesty’s Mint, divers Prosecutions had been carried on against Offenders relating to the Gold arid Silver Coin, in the Years 1782, 1783, and 1784, and that the Expences of such Prosecutions in the said Periods had exceeded and was more than he had received out of the stipulated Allowance of 600l. per Annum, by the A of 15th and 16th George II. by the Sum of 916/. 5 s. 11 d.;which Memorial, together with the Account therewith sent, your Lordships were pleased to refer to the principal Officers of His Majesty’s Mint, who examined the fame, and made a Report thereupon to your Lordships, that the same was proper to be allowed. But no Order hath been issued by your Lordships for the Payment thereof.

And that your Memorialist had also been directed, by your Lordships Order, signified by Mr. Steele, the 26th June 1784, to pay the Sum of 801, to William Brook and William Clowes, of the County of Chester, Esquires, to be divided among Witnesses in Prosecutions against Persons convicted for coining, at Chester Spring Assizes 1784.

That your Memorialist, since the Close of his Account to 31st December 1784, presented to your Lordships with his said Memoral, has, in pursuance of Directions from the said Warden of His Majesty’s Mint, carried on divers Prosecutions relating to the Gold and Silver Coin, from the said 31st Day of December 1784 to die 31st Day of December 1785; and that the Expences incurred thereby, to 30th Day of September only, amount to the Sum of 599/. io$. an Account of which has been delivered into the Mint Office by your Memorialist: But that the Expences of Prosecutions for further Offences committed in the said Year 1785 amount to the Sum of 246/. 2 as will appear by the Account for the fame, hereunto annexed.

That your Memorialist has also been directed, by your Lordships Order, signified by Mr. Steele, the 12th July 1785, to pay to Benjamin Twigge, and Two other Persons, a Sum not exceeding 201, to each, and which your Memorialist thinks they justly merit, for apprehending Persons convicted of coining at Lincoln Summer Assizes 1783, and which Payments together make the Sum of 60 /.

That your Memorialist has also, in pursuance of Directions from the Right Honourable the Earl of Effingham, Master and Worker of His Majesty’s Mint, carried on divers Prosecutions against Offenders relating to the Copper Coin, from the lft Day of May 1784 to the 31st Day of December 1785; and that the Expence incurred by such Prosecutions amounts to the Sum of 380/.. 16$. gd. as will appear by the Accounts thereof, delivered into the Mint Office by your Memorialist.

That the several Particulars above-mentioned, exclusive of the said Sums of 80 /. and 60 /. fb ordered to be paid by your Lordships, amount together to the Sum of Two thousand One hundred and Forty-two Pounds and Fifteen Shillings, and the same still remains due to your Memorialist; which being added to the said Sums of 80/. and bo/, make in the Whole the Sum of Two thousand Two hundred and Eighty-two Pounds and Fifteen Shillings.

Your Memorialist therefore humbly prays your Lordships to take the Premises into your Consideration, and that your Lordships will please to give such Directions, in regard to the stating and auditing of your Memorialist’s Accounts, and for the Payment of what shall appear to remain due to your Memorialist, as to your Lordships shall seem meet.

And your Lordships Memorialist shall ever pray, &c.

3d March 1786. John Vernon, Junr.

I. of Wight A Petition of the Deputy Lieutenants, Freeholders, Militia. and others, Inhabitants of the Isle of Wight, whose Names are thereunto febscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Militia of the said Island has always heretofore been under the Order and Direction of the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Deputy Lieutenants thereof, totally independent of the Lord Lieutenant, or Deputy Lieutenants, of the County of Southampton; and that by an Act, passed in the Second Year of His present Majesty, the Powers of the said Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Deputy Lieutebants, were confirmed, and it was also enacted, that the Militia of the said Isle should remain within the said Island for the internal Defence thereof; and that the Militia of the Isle of Wight was first raised in the Year 1770, in Confidence that the same should, in Conformity to the said Act, constantly continue within the said Island for its internal Defence; and that the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill has been brought into the House, wherein is inserted a Clause to enact, that the Militia of the Isle of Wight shall, in future, be deemed and taken to be Part of the Militia of the County of Southampton, and shall form a Part of the Southern Battalion of the Militia of the said County, under the Order and Direction of the Lord Lieutenant and Deputy Lieutenants thereof, and, the Petitioners conceive the said Clause

06

(if passed into a Law) will be very injurious to the Inhabitants of the Isle of Wight, inso much as it will deprive them of an internal Defence, confirmed by the said Act of the Second of George the Third, and take away from the said Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Deputy Lieutenants, the Order and Direction of the Militia of that Island, in whom it has been, for salutary Purposes, hitherto veiled: And therefore praying, That the said Clause may not pals into a Law, and that the Militia of the Isle of Wight may remain in the same Situation as directed by the Act passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

habitants of the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, having had constant Dealings with Hawkers and Pedlars* have always found them honest and fair-dealing Trades-men, and having frequently experienced the Advantage of purchasing Goods from them, they having a great Variety of Fancy Articles, such as Printed Callicoes,

The MINUTES of what was offered by Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal, at the Bar of the House of Commons, upon the Matter of the Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors, presented against him on Friday last.

Answer -to the Twenty-second Charge.

Ftzooila Cawn.

This Charge was not delivered to me till late on the 8th Instant; and I was informed Yesterday Morning, that in Compliance with the Prayer of my Petition, to be heard in Reply to it, this Honourable House had been pleased to direct my Attendance on this Day. I moil respeQfully allude to the short Interval of Time allowed me for this Purpose, not as indicating the flightell Ground of Complaint; for I accept with equal Gratitude the Permission to appear in my own Defence, and the early Allowance of my Attendance, it being, next to my entire Acquittal, my First Wish to obtain a speedy Termination of the Enquiry. But it is proper to represent to this Honourable House the just Plea which I may have for any Deficiency of my Defence to this last Article of the Charge, arising from the Want of sufficient Time to examine every Part of it; every Part of it containing feme positive or insinuated, but not always a discoverable Charge; and the Whole comprising no less than 21 Folio Pages. These have furnished me with Employment for One Third of my allotted Portion of Time to read, to analyze, and to understand so much as I do understand of them, much of their Sense being dissipated by nice and subtle Distinctions, and obfeured by Allusions which I have not Leisure to trace to their Documents, and perplexed by forced Inferences, and the Introduction of other Charges, which are totally foreign from the Subject; such as, that I assumed " an illegal " Delegation of the whole Powers of the Governor General and Council in July 1781," " that I reflected " Discredit to the Crown of Great Britain, by a private " Conversation with Sir Elijah Impey," and many other lateral Accusations and Insinuations of the like extraneous Quality.

All such Matters, as of inferior Note, I shall pass without more Observation upon them, trusting to the Spirit of liberal Justice, which I have already experienced from this Honourable House, for my general Acquittal of these minuter Charges, if in the main Points I shall appear to have consulted the Interest, Honour, and Safety of my Employers; and that I could have had no View to my own Interest in the Proceedings which have a Relation to the Charge, as in Effect no such View is or could have been imputed to me in it.

The Charge consists of Eight titled Chapters or Divisions, and these subdivided altogether into Seventy-nine distinct and numbered Positions.

The First Chapter is intituled " Rights of Fyzoold " Khdn, 8cc. before the Treaty of

This I shall examine minutely, as it will serve to prove what I have asserted of the general Character of the whole Composition; and I will shew to this Honourable House, that in Twelve Positions or Affirmations, of which it consists, it contains as many Assertions, or Implications of Facts, which have no Foundation in Truth.

) ft'. The First Postion states, that Ally Mahmud, the Father of Fyzoolla Cazvn, was the Sovereign of Culteher or Rohilcund;and by aferibing to him a " Renown in

" the History of Hindostan," it must have been intended to convey the conclusive Opinion, that he inherited his Sovereignty from a Line of Ancestors who held it before him.

Both Points are false in Fad:. Ally Mahmud was not the Sovereign of Cutteher or llohilcund, but the Usurper of that Province, which he originally acquired as a Servant of the Crown, and converted into an Independency by repeated Acts of Rebellion against his lawful Master and Sovereign; and his Father Daood Cazvn (I think that was his Name) had no Authority or Footing in that Country.

2d. The Second Postion states in Terms the Province of Cutteher to be the " ancient Estates," and the " hereditary Rights," of Fyzoolla Cazvn, which I again assert to be false in Fact. These Words are indeed borrowed from Translations of Letters from Fyzoolla Cazvn to Colonel Champion; but I have Doubts, which I have a Right to express, of the Fidelity of the Translation; and even if it be genuine, it is but the Assertion of Fyzoolla Cazvn himself in Favour of his own Cause, which cannot be admitted in Evidence of it; and the Evidence against it abounds in the Records of the Company, which are before this Honourable House, and on undoubted Notoriety.

3d. In this Postion he is again, a Third Time, stated " the undoubted Heir of his Father’s Authority;" which, as the Chapter itself is intituled " Rights," and these can only mean Rights of which my Condufit was a Violation, is untrue in that Sense of it.

4th. This Postion states again (the 4th Time) the Country in Question to be " his ancient Possessions, the " Country of his Father;" and it states, by Implication, that he was innocent of the War; yet the 3d Postion has admitted, that " the Nabob Fyzoolla , with " feme of his People, was present at the deciGve s< Battle of St. George, but escaping from the Slaughter," " (a Word also of false Infmuation) made his Retreat " good towards the Mountains, with all his Treasure," and " these collected the scattered Remains of his " Countrymen;" that is, for so it was, dill continued the War against us in Chief. — Both Assertions cannot be true.

<)th. This states in Terms, that I rejected a specific Offer, by which, if accepted, an Annual Increase of near 400,000l. would have accrued to the Revenue of our Ally, and the immediate Acquisition of 300,000l. to the Company; which is not true; for no Consequences can be more remote from their Premises, than that the Performance of so extravagant an Offer would have followed the Acceptance of it, when it appears in Proof before this Honourable House, that a most sacred Engagement of the whole Rohilla Tribe, before the War, was insufficient to bind them to the Payment of little more than Half the Sum which Fyzoolla Cazvn offered to pay for the Possession of the Country after the War. In Effect, the Extravagance of the Offer was a clear Proof of the Insincerity of the Man who made it, and so I treated it.

6th. This seems to be a Charge of Deception; for it states, " that so great was the Confidence of the

" Nabob

6 Geo. Ill*

1 o° Mail.

789

Nabob FyzoollaCawn in the just, humane, and liberal

" Feelings of Englishmen, as to lull him into an -

These are Points which I claim to be allow ed me in the present Charge, because either they are already proved, or they rnuft operate to my Condemnation throughout the whole Course of the War, and cannot apply further than the general Charge itself to any Part of my Tran factions with Fyzoola Cazcn. The Commander in Chief was deflrous of concluding a Peace with Fyzoola Cawn, and leaving him in Possession of a Part of the Country for which we were contending. I was of a different Opinion, an Opinion not speculative, as it is described, but obligatory by the Principles of Conflftency, to which I have ever adhered as a primary Rule of Conduct, and by the Terms to which I myself had exacted the Compliance of the-Nabob Stya Doulah, before I would suffer the Company to be a Party to the War, namely, that if we were once engaged in it, we should not detift till we had accomplished the total Reduction of the Country — as will be seen by my Letter to the Nabob Suja Dowlah, entered in Confutation of the 2 2d November 1773, iQ the Appendix to the Fifth Report of the Secret Committee, N* 24. " These are my particular Objections to the several Propositions; but I have One general Objection to the Whole of them, which is, that they are diametrically opposite to the Principle on which the Rohilla Expedition was on our Part undertaken, which was not merely on Account of the pecuniary Acquisition of Forty Lacks of Rupees to the Company; for although this might be an accessory Argument, it was by no Means the Chief Object of the Undertaking.

H We engaged to assist the Vizier in reducing the Rohilla Country under his Dominion, that the Boundary of his Possessions might be compleated, by the Ganges forming a Barrier to cover them from the Attacks and Insults to which they were exposed by his Enemies, either possessing or having Access to the Rohilla Country; this our Alliance with him, and the Necessity of maintaining this Alliance, so long as he and his Successors shall deserve our Protection, rendered advantageous to the Company’s Interest, because the Security of his Pof-sessions from Invasions in that Quarter is in Fact the Security of ours. But if the Rohilla Country is delivered to Fyzoola Khan, the Advantages proposed from this Measure will be totally defeated; the same Objections from the Vizier will take place against him as against Hafez Rhamuthe will be actuated by the same Principles of Self-defence, and the same Impressions of Fear, to seek the Protection of other Powers against the Vizier, and of course will create the same Jealousies and Suspicions in the Mind of the Vizier, with the additional and strong Incentive to a mutual Animosity, of an enormous Debt, which probably Fyzoola Khan will find no - other Means to get clear of, but by engaging in Hol-tilkies against the Vizier.

" I cannot subscribe to your Opinion of the Vizier being unable to maintain Possession of the conquered Country; it is at leall certain that there is a much greater Probability of his maintaining Possession of it, supported by the Resources of his Hereditary Dominions, and the Credit of the English Protection, even without our actual Intervention, than that Fyzoola Khan should maintain the Possession of it; a Man of no Repute, without natural Power or Interest, and unprovided with every Means of Self-defence. The Board undertook the Rohilla Expedition on a firm Conviction, both that the Vizier would be able to maintain his Conquest of it, and that it would make his other Dominions more defensible for the Reason before assigned; and with respect to myself, I declare, that if I had not been morally certain of the Justness of this Reasoning, I would not have contented to enter upon the Enterprize at all.

" Upon the Whole, my Opinion is, that instead of soliciting the Vizier to relinquish his Conquest to Fyzoola Khan, every Argument should be used to dissuade him from such an Intention, and it is my Desire that you will discourage it as much as is in your Power. I make no Doubt but, from the Explanation I have given, you will be convinced both of the Propriety of adhering to the Principles laid down, and the Necessity of acting with Consistency. Excuse me for adding, that if we fuller our Attention to be drawn off from our grand and principal Design by every adventitious Allurement that may present itself, our Conduct must prove desultory, and we can adhere to no regular Plan, nor propose any certain End to our Pursuits.

" You mention the Necessity the Vizier will be under of constantly having a Brigade of our Troops with him, as an Argument against his retaining the 01

Rohilla Country, which you have repeated in several of your Letters, but I should be lorry to regard this Circumstance in that Light: It has always been

I shall now proceed to offer a connected Narrative of all my Proceedings, or to speak more properly the Proceedings of the Governor General and Council (for I had no exclusive Share in them) with the Nabob Cawn, from the Conclusion of the Treaty with him at Loll-Dong, on the 6th of October 1774, to the Close of my Administration.

From the Month of October 1774 to the latter End of February 1778, we had no Reference made to us relative to Fayzula Cawn; but on the 25th of February 1^78 we received a Letter from Mr. Middleton, in which he informed us, that Reports had prevailed at Lucknow, that Fayzula Cawn retained in his Service a greater Body of Troops than were specified in the Treaty of 1774, and that he bad given Protection and Encouragement to Zabitta Cawn’s defeated Army. Mr. Middleton in the same Letter told us, that he did not pay much Attention to these Reports; but added, that the Nabob’s oppressive and unjust Conduct, in various In-fiances, might induce Fayzula Cawn to form Connections, and to engage in Schemes incompatible with his Duty and Allegiance to the Vizier. Mr. Middleton also informed us, that Fayzula Cawn was very desirous to obtain the Guarantee of the Company to the Treaty which he had concluded with the late Vizier. Upon this Subject I bad had repealed Applications from him; but the Guarantee appeared to me unnecessary, except as it would afford great Satisfaction to Fayzula Cawn; for our Government must have interfered, if the Nabob Vizier had attempted to encroach upon the Rights which Fayzula Cawn enjoyed under his Treaty with the Vizier.

Mr. Middleton deputed Mr. IF Harwell to Rampore, the Residence of Fayzula Cawn. Mr. Harwell transmitted to Mr. Middleton a very particular Account of Fayzula Cawn’s Conduct, which appeared to have been in no Infiance contrary to his Engagements; and in the Month of April his Treaty with the Nabob Vizier was guaranteed by the Company, agreeably to his earned and reiterated Requests: By whole Suggefiions Doubts were infiilled into the Mind of FayzulaCawn, as to the Validity of the Treaty which Colonel Champion had witnessed, I know not; but I am equally at a Loft to discover in what Part of the Transaction which I have just detailed I am culpable.

On the 5th December 1778 Mr. Middleton informed us that Fayzula Cawn had offered a Body of Two thousand Horse to be employed in our Service. On the 19th of September 1781, I concluded an Agreement with the Nabob Vizier at At this Time the Rebellion of Benares was scarcely quelled, its Consequences uncertain, and the Province unsettled. Violent Commotions, excited by this Example, still prevailed in many Parts of the Vizier’s Dominions. A sincere and cordial Union betw’een his Government and ours, and even the most public Indication of it, were necessary to the Peace and Prosperity, and, as I believed, to the Existence of both: I was, therefore, more than ordinarily solicitous both to contribute to his Means of Power and Wealth, and to confirm his Confidence in my Attachment; nor was I without a Feeling of Gratitude for the recent Proofs which be had given me of his Attachment to me and to niy Government, in the precipitate Manner in which he had flown to offer me, and to afford me, if wanted, his Assistance. I was determined to gratify him in every Point which could be with Propriety and with Consistency granted. Here, too, I mull add, that I still retained die Impression of Fyzoolla Cawn's Refusal to furnish the Military Aid stipulated by his Treaty, and I maintain that I was warranted in considering it an Evasion, if not a Breach of his Treaty; since, though our Demand had exceeded the Letter of the Treaty, we had an undoubted Claim (I mean the Vizier under our Guarantee, for in this Instance we were One) to some Assistance, and he had eluded it altogether. Besides this, I had for fbme Time past received various and repeated Informations of trcache-

Vo L.41.

rous Intrigues, and other Acts imputed to him; to which, though I refused that degree of Credit which might have impelled me to any decided Act against him, yet I certainly yielded so far to the Belief as to seek to guard myself by every possible Means of Caution and Preparation against what might eventually happen. When therefore the Nabob presented to me the Paper of Re-quisition6, which, by my Assent to them afterwards, formed what has been styled the Engagement of Chunar, the Demand to be allowed to resume the Jagheer of Fyzoolla Cawn being One of them, I afiented to it, as I did to the rest; but in such a Manner as to reserve the Rights of further Examination, and of indefinite Suspen-fion, until the Grounds of proceeding to the Extremity portended in the Clause were sufficiently ascertained. In this Nicety of Discrimination, I desired the Nabob to insert the Words, " when Time shall suit," into the Requifi-tion, which was absolute in the First Draft of it; and with that Qualification of it I afiented to it. That this was my Intention, is demonstrated by the Declaration made of it to the Board, in the annexed Observations on the Engagement, when I transmitted to them immediately after the full Report of my Transactions with the Nabob Vizier, which terminated with it. My Words will better demonstrate this than any Realoning upon them.

After Hating the specific Instances of suspected Fidelity, which had appeared in the Behaviour of Fyzoolla Cawn, I concluded my Observation with the following Sentence: " But I am of Opinion, that neither the " Viziers nor the Company’s Interests would be promoted by depriving Fyzoola Khan of his Independency; and I have therefore reserved the Execution " of this Agreement to an indefinite Term, and our " Government may always interpole to prevent any " ill Effects from it.’’

Hence it is plain, that no Wrong, no substantial

Wrong, was either done or intended to Fyzoolla Cawn and that if I can be supposed to have been actuated by any secret Motive of Enmity to him, I had effectually precluded myself from gratifying it, by a Declaration so explicitly made, that it was contrary to the Interests both, of the Nabob and the Company (for such is the consequent Sense of it) to deprive FyzooUa Cawn of his Independency.

Had my Conduct in this Instance been arraigned at the Time, while the Senl’e of recent Provocation, the gathered Alarms around me, and the Consciousnel’s of internal Rectitude, had Post’eflion of my Mind, 1 w ould have justified the Act against the Judgment of all Mankind, if that had condemned it. In the calmer Reflection on Events, which have loft by Time their Hold on the Passions (though few, I hope, have been the Instances in which mine have prevailed over my Judgment) and to which subsequent Events have given a different Colour, I am not aihamed to acknowledge, that the Act itself was formally wrong, and yet more than formally, as it might become a Precedent for worse Purposes. — If this Honourable House shall judge that I deserve its Censure for an Error thus avowed, I shall respectfully submit to it.

After the Vizier had returned to Lucknow, in the Course of the Year 1782, I received repeated Complaints from the Nabob, and from the Resident, against Fyzulla Cawn; but I refifted every Application that was made to me for depriving him of his Jagheer; and when I appointed Mr. Bristow to the Residency of Oude, I gave him explicit Instructions on the Subject of Fyzulla Cozen, which will prove, beyond a World of Argument, how careful I was to avoid a Rupture with him. I desire to enter them entire, and to contract them with the garbled Quotation of them in the Charge.

I look back to the Length of this Defence, and to so long an Intrusion on the Time of this Honourable House, with a Regret aggravated by the Reflection, that after all I may have been employed in a Waste of Argument; for though the Production to which I have replied is intituled " an Article of Charge of High " Crimes and Misdemeanorsthough it consists of so long, laboured, and methodical an Arrangement, and I have studied it with all the Accuracy of Attention which I could give to it; yet am I still unable to draw from it any specific Charge. I know not whether it was intended to convey the Charge of Disobedience of Orders, of Opprefiion, of Corruption, of Embezzlement, of prohibited or unjust War, or of Breach of Treaty, for none of these Crimes are specified; and the Two last of these only seem to be implicated in it, and the First so remotely, that I scarce think myself warranted in supposing it. To these, however, I have directed my Defence, and with them, in the only Mode in which I could defend myself again!! all possible and unknown Imputations, by a plain Narrative of all the Transactions in which I have had any Participation with Fayzula Cawn, and which could serve either as the Ground of Accul'action, or the Refutation of it.

With respect to the Mode in which this Charge is drawn, 1 mean in the Subdivisions of it, I mull throw myself upon the Generality as well as Justice of this Honourable House, in full Confidence that they will acquit me of the Imputations with which these abound, on the Credit of my Refutation of those which stand in the First Division or Chapter, and to which alone I have applied a minute and appropriate Reply.

That in an intercourse of many Years I have committed Errors I will not deny; I have acknowledged it — and what mortal Being is exempt from the Corn-million of Error? But that I have ever committed intentional Wrong, I can truly and solemnly deny; and I appeal to the Judgment of this Honourable House for my complete Acquittal of such a Charge, if such a Charge does exist against me; for still I mull repeat that I have fought in vain to find it.

To sum up the Whole: Let the Charge, with my Defence, be taken together, and they will shew that I was vigilant in my Attention to Fayzula a Chief who

from his Situation might prove dangerous to the Interests of the Company, and the Ally of the Company; — that I protected him again!! any eventual Design of his Superior, in virtue of the Company’s Guarantee; — that I drew from the Connection a pecuniary Aid to the Company, at a Time when their Wants moll preflingly required it, and without any moral Objection made to it by the only Person who had a Right to object to it; — that I never

sent a Man in Arms, nor suffered one to be sent again!! Fayzula Cawn, during our Guarantee of the Treaty; — and I will add, with a Reference to the Records before this Honourable House, and to the Evidence of undoubted Notoriety, that though the Treaty with Fayzula Cawn has now subsisted above Eleven Years, his Country has enjoyed, through its Protection, a State of undillurbed Peace and improved Cultivation; and is at this Time in a more flourishing State, both in Population and Revenue, than it was known to possels before the Conclusion of his Treaty with the Nabob Shujah Dowlah.

Let it be remembered, that in all this Time I held the First Place in the Administration of the Government of Bengal, ou which the Subsistence of that Treaty depended; and from the Effects which I have detailed, let the Integrity of my Conduct be inferred, and its Influence allowed in their Production.

Attorniesand A Petition of the Attornies and Solicitors residing SoJici»o/r. within the several Counties of Anglesey, Carnarvon, and Merioneth, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Fees which Attornies and Solicitors are entitled to, having been settled at a very distant Period, are now become an inadequate Compensation for their Care and Trouble in conle-quenoe of the great Advance in the Price of all the Necessaries of Life, and the Duties which Attornies and Solicitors are made subject to by the late Act of Parliament: and that, for Want of a Law confining the Practice of Conveyancing to Persons regularly educated and brought up to the Profession, Country Schoolmasters, Parish Clerks, and other unqualified Persons, have intruded themselves into that Brand) of the Petitioners Profession, to the Ruin of many Families, and the great Detriment of the Public, and the said Act imposing a Tax on Attornies and Solicitors, does not afteft Persons acting as Con-

veyancers only; and that the Laws respecting Attornies and Solicitors are very defective, as many im«-proper Persons daily gain Admission on the Roll, and Bills of Fees and Disbursements for Law Proceedings are subject to Taxation without any Limitation as to Time, which is productive of great Hardships and Inconveniences to Attornies and Solicitors, and particularly to their Families after their Deaths: And therefore praying. The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Speirs and Committee, to whom the Petition of John Bowman, Bowman Archibald Speirs, George Buchanan, Andrew Buchanan, Sb, Ps-James Hopkirk, Peter Speirs, and William French, all Merchants in Glasgow, Owners of the Ships Speirs and Bowman, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Robert Burton being examined, said. That he is acquainted with the Petitioners, and with the Nature of the Trade earned on by them; and that previous to the American War, and at the Period when Hosti-Lrtiee commenced, they had, as he verily believes, a

Property

26 Geo. III. 11° Mail. 799

Properly in Virginia and ,to the Extent of

130,000l. Sterling at the least; which Money was chiefly vested in Debts due to them from Persons residing in those Provinces, in the Course of an extensive Trade, which they had carried on above Twenty-five Years.

That on the Return of Peace, the Petitioners not doubting but that they should experience every Facility in the Recovery of their Debts; and not having any Idea that there would be any legal Obstruction to the former Mode of carrying on Trade with ordered the Two Ships mentioned in the Petition to be built in the State of Maryland, for the Purpose of bringing home their Effects — That for the Purpose of building and completing the said Vessels, the Petitioners lent the necessary Iron-work, Sails, and Rigging, from Great Britain, composing fully One Half of the Value thereof.

That before it was known to the Petitioners, that it was the Intention of the British Government to exclude American Vessels, a very considerable Progress had been made in the Building of the said Ships.

That the Petitioners, not being able to recover any of their Property in Americ, were under the Necessity of paying in Great Britain for the Expence of building those Ships; and being thus disappointed in procuring Cargoes for the said Ships on their own Account, they were under the Necessity of taking in Tobacco, upon Freight, for Great Britain, where the Ships arrived in the Year 1784, and have ever since lain useless in the Harbour of Port Glasgow1.

That an humble Addrefe be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleated to direct, that such Captains in the Navy, who, notwithstanding their Seniority, have been set aside by any former Promotions of Flag Officers, as well as those who shall at any Time hereafter be set aside by future Promotions, and who are not entitled to a Pension equal to the Half Pay of a Rear Admiral, shall be esteemed as superannuated Captains, and placed for the rest of their Lives on the Ordinary Estimate of the Navy, with a Pension equal to their Half Pay as Senior Captains; and that the Captains now holding, or who may in future hold, any Civil Employment, shall not, during the Continuance of such Civil Employment, be counted amongst the Number of those entitled to receive Eight Shillings or Ten Shillings a Day on the Half Pay Lift:

Sir Adam Fergusscn, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of replacing to the Revenue the Sums granted towards the Augmentation of the Salaries of the Judges in Scotland, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of replacing to the Revenue arising out of that Part of Great Britain called Scotland the Sums granted towards the Augmentation of the Salaries of the Judges of the Courts of Session, Justiciary, Exchequer, Admiralty Courts in Scotland, and Commissary Court of Edinburgh, there be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed or written any Deposition or Depositions of a Witness or Witnesses, taken in any Caule or Suit before the Court of Session, or Commission of Tythes, or Court of Admiralty, or Commissary Court of Edinburgh (excepting such Causes or Suits as are insisted in, at the Instance of the Public Prosecutor, for the Public Interest, or w here the Party, at whose Instance such Deposition or Depositions is or are taken, is a Pauper, and on the Poors Roll) a Stamp Duty of One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the same Purpose, there shall be laid on every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed or written any Deposition or Depositions of a Witness or Witnesses, taken in any Civil Cause before any inferior Court in Scotland (except Revenue Causes, or any Causes or Suits where the Sum or Subject concluded for is under the Value of Five Pounds Sterling, or where such Deposition or Depositions is or are taken at the Instance of a Pauper upon the Poors Roll of such Court) a Stamp Duty of One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the same Purpose, there shall be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed or written any Affidavit or written Deposition produced Vol. 41.

in the Court of Exchequer iu Scotland, a Stamp Duty of One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That, for the same Purpose, there shall be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed or written any Extract or attested Copy of or from any Deed, Instrument, or Writing (except Protests upon Bills or Promissory Notes under Forty Shillings Sterling) given out from any Public Register, or from the Books or Record of any Court in a Stamp

Duty of One Shilling.

Mr. Gilbert, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One Million Five hundred thousand Pounds be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament, and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged with Interest thereupon on or before the 5th Day of April 1787, to be exchanged and received in Payment, in such Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the further Sum of One Million be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged upon the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament, and such Exchequer Bills, if not discharged with Interest thereupon on or before the 5th Day of April 1787, to be exchanged and received in Payment in l'uch Manner as Exchequer Bills have usually been exchanged and received in Payment.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-five thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account, towards carrying on the Buildings at Somerset House, for the Year 1786; and that the said Sum be issued and paid without any Deduction whatsoever.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Thirteen thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, to be employed in repairing, maintaining, and supporting the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Six hundred Eighty-one Pounds, Eighteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the extraordinary Expences attending the Prosecution of Offenders against the Laws relating to the Coin.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That a Sum, not exceeding Fourteen thousand Nine hundred Thirty-nine Pounds, Five Shillings and One Farthing, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the extraordinary Expences of His Majesty’s Mint in the Year 1785.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Farmers, and Hawkers and Inhabitants of the County of Worcester, and Counties Pedlars, adjacent, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for many Years past, found it convenient, and been accustomed, to deal with Licensed Hawkers and Pedlars, by whom they have been supplied with Linen, Cotton, and Silk Goods, of the Manufacture of this Kingdom, at as fair and reasonable Prices as elsewhere, at their own Houses, without the Expence of travelling to Market Towns, and have always found them honest and upright’in all their Dealings; and Representing to the House, That, by the 9th and 11th Sections of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for laying an additional Duty on Hawkers and Pedlars, the Petitioners are deprived of the Benefit of dealing with Hawkers and Pedlars, and they are also not only limited so much in their Trade as not to be able to carry it on to enable them to pay their Creditors, the Duty to Government, and maintain themselves and Families in any Degree of Comfort, but are liable to be suppressed and prevented from carrying it on at all, without a Charge of Guilt, or being heard in their own Defence: And therefore praying the House to repeal the said Sections, and to regulate the said Trade in such Manner as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to repeal so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for " granting to His Majesty additional Duties on Hawkers,

" Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen, and for regulating their " Trade," as restrains Hawkers and Pedlars from exposing to Sale Goods in Market Towns, and as enables Justices of the Peace, of any County, to prohibit such Hawkers and Pedlars from vending their Goods within the same, and for further regulating their Trade, be read a Second Time.

Bath, and great Part of Somersetshire; and that the Petitioners, from the general and known Characters of the Trustees, have not the least Suspicion that they have been guilty of Mismanageinent, and, from the Enquiry they have made, they cannot find they have been guilty ol any, but, if any Mismanagement had happened, the Petitioners hope, that the Mii'conduct of any Set of Men would not be flittered to operate to the Prevention of so great an Improvement of the said City: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pals into a Law.

A Petitition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and Common- Ditto, alty of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth.

That a Petition hath been presented, praying to be heard against the lame, and, although the said Petition is fiated to be on Behalf of all the Citizens and Inhabitants of, and Traders to, the said City of Bristol, it ought not to be considered as conveying their Sentiments in general, with regard to the said Bill, for that the Petitioners, and a very great Number of the Citizens and Inhabitants of the said City, are fully convinced that the making of a commodious Opening from Temple Street to the Bridge, as proposed to be done by the said Bill, will be a very great Accommodation and Convenience to the Inhabitants of Bristol, and to all Persons resorting thereto, from Places communicating with the same by the Temple Gate Road; and that the Petitioners have no Reason to suspect any Mismanagenient on the Part of the Trusteeo under the said Act of the Thirty-third Year of his late Majesty, and shall deem their Share of the Expence that may attend the making of the proposed Opening amply compensated by the Safety and Accommodation which will thereby be obtained for the Inhabitants of Bristol, and the Public: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pals into a Law.

A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Efiquire, Agent for Jamaica, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner hath received Instructions from the Committee of Correspondence, signifying, that it is the With of the Assembly that he should renew his Application to both Houses of Parliament, in respect to the Necessity of a partial Intercourse with the American States in American Bottoms, and atfo in respect to the high Duties upon Sugar and Rum, and the pre-' lent burthensome Mode of collecting the Duty on Sugar; and that the Petitioner hath it in Charge to represent, that the Condition of the Planters is now even more deplorable than it was in the last Year; they complain that, by Reason of the Restrictions laid upon their Trade with the American States, a Monopoly is carried on in Lumber and Flour, by a few Houses in the Island, who, having those Articles exclusively in their Hands, are enabled not only to fix what Prices they please upon them, but to regulate those Prices by their Calamities: Nor does the Measure of their Sufferings, under this restricted Trade, end here; the Prices paid for American Produce might, perhaps, be submitted to, if this Produce could be procured by the same Means which a more extended Trade with America, under proper Regulations, would undoubtedly furnish, that is, if they could, as they used to do, barter the Produce of one Country in Exchange for the Produce of the other, and thus fe-eure the old and uever-failing Market for their Rum; but, as the same now ltands, they have very little Vent for Rum in the Island, and, if shipped for Great Britain, R is sometimes sold at a depreciated Value, and sometimes at a Rate that leaves the Planter a Loler by his Importation; and, this Obstruction to the disposing of their Rum has been productive of another bad Consequence, which cannot have occurred to Government, but is very prejudicial to the Interests and Credit of the Island, for as the Planter has been used to trust to the Disposal of his Rum for the Payment of his Taxes,

and, indeed, to have it taken sometimes by the Collecting Constables in Payment of them,- the Loss of this easy Market for it has stopt the Resources of many Properties, and if it has not rendered the Collection of the Taxes impracticable, it has done what is next to doing lb, it has made it impossible for the Collecting Constables, in some Parishes, to col left them, without practising such Severities as must be fatal to the Planter; and that the Committee of Correspondence farther represents, that the Planters have been greatly alarmed at the Delay in carrying into Execution the Act of the Twenty-fourth of George the Third, Cap. 46. S. 33; and they attribute the low Price of their Rums at the British Market, in a great Measure, to the Apprehen-fions of the Dealers, left the great Quantities of seized and condemned Spirits should be brought to Market, instead of being staved and destroyed as directed by that Act; and that the Petitioner hath it further in Charge to pray for a farther Reduction of the Duties upon Rum, as it is impossible that Rum can meet the British Spirits at any Market, under the present Inequality of Duties, and, that the Discontinuance of the Duties upon Rum and Spirits from the West Indies, by the Act of the Twenty-fourth of George the Third, Cap. 46, may be re-enacted for a further limited Time. And that the Petitioner hath it further in Charge, to beseech the House to take into Consideration the heavy Duty on Sugar: It hath been suggested, that the Consumers pay all the Taxes, but it hath been found no eaiy Matter to persuade the Planter, that Fifty-six Shillings (more than used to lie) taken out of the Net Proceeds of every Hogshead of his Sugar, leaves the Net Proceeds neither more nor leis than they were before, and, even if he could be so perl'uaded, there remains not a Doubt of the Maxim, that high Duties upon any Commodity tend to lessen the Consumption, which the Revenue may one Day feel, as well as the Planter, who is at this Moment exerting, and with proper Encouragement will continue to exert, every Nerve to increase the Quantity; and that the Petitioner hath it further in Charge, to pray that Permission may be granted for the Bonding of the Duties on Sugar, in the same Manner that the Duties on Rum are now bonded, otherwise the Burthen of prompt Payment will, in the End, infallibly fall upon the Planter:

And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as to them shall seem meet, and that the Petitioner may be heard by his Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of John Christian, Esquire; and also, the Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being Freemen and Citizens of the City of Carlisle, in the County of Cumberland, and having a Right to vote in the Election of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, complaining of an uiylue Election and Return for the said City, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Forty-one Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on -both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And die Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Name of John Hunter, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Eight Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Mr. Alderman Townsend being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Five other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the C!><bMarine Committee, to whom the Petition of Alexander Brazen, Society. Dean of Guild, of the City of Glasgazc, and of James Dunlop, James Dermiston, Junior, Alexander Oszeald,

William French, James Sommerville, John Laurie, William Dunlop, John Douglas, John Paterson, Andrew Sym,

John Riddell, Robert Mackay, and Henry Ritchie, for themselves as Individuals, and also as Members, Managers, and Directors of a Society in Glasgow, known by the Name of The Glasgow Marine Society, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Mackay, Esquire, being examined, said. That in May 1758, a Society was instituted, under certain Regulations, for the Relief of decayed or disabled Seamen, their Widows and Children, belonging to the Ships of Glasgow; the Members of which Society not only subscribed considerable Sums, but also obliged themselves, that the Matters and Mariners of their Ships should pay to the Collector of the Society, Rates out of their Wages, for the Purposes of the Charity. — And being further examined, he said, That in February 1762 this Society was united with another of a similar Nature at Greenock, by certain Articles of Union, whereby the same Rates are payable from the Matters and Men employed in Ships belonging to the Port of Greenock, or Craze ford's Dyke as were chargeable, by the Articles of the Glasgow Society, on the Wages of Ship Matters and

Seamen of Glasgow. — And he further laid. That most of the considerable Merchants of Glasgow, Greenock, Port Glasgow, and Crazejord's Dyke, have now' become Mem-

bers of the Society with the Petitioners. — And being further examined, he said, That in consequence of this Institution, Pensions have been settled upon decayed or disabled Seamen, and their Widows and Children, and considerable Sums have likewise been paid for their Relief occasionally, when in Distress; and, on the Whole, very beneficial Consequences have resulted from this Institution; and that the Advantages would be much more considerable, if the Society was made a Body Corporate and Politic, under proper Regulations, respecting the Choice of Officers, and the Management of its Funds, and if Power was legally given to levy Irom the Owners of Ships belonging to the Ports of Port Glasgoze,

Greenock, and Craziford’s Dyke, certain small Rates upon the Wages of their ShipMasters and Seamen, to be applied not only for the Relief of disabled and decayed Ship Matters and Mariners, and their Widows and Children, but also for the fitting out and cloathing of Boys to be lent on board the Ships of those Ports, which would be a National Benefit, by in Time supplying the King’s and Merchants Ships with good Seamen, and would also assist the iuward Police of the Country, in providing for the idle, and consequently most dangerous Alembers of Society.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for incorporating the Members of a Society, to be called The Clyde Marine Society, for the better empowering and enabling them to carry on their charitable and useful Designs, and for levying certain Duties from Ship Matters and others for that Purpose: And that the Lord Advocate of Scotland and Sir Adam Fergusson do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Resolved, That, before any Petition is presented to standing this House, for erecting a Bridge, or for the Renewal Orders ie-or Alteration of any Act of Parliament passed for that Purpose, Notice of such intended Application to Par- n liament be given at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, which shall be held for every and each County, or District, to which such Bridge extends, or is intended to extend, at the Michaelmas immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

Resolved, That this Notice be given, by affixing to the Door of the Sessions House where such General Quarter Sessions are held, a printed or written Paper, describing the Parishes to which the said Bridge extends, or is intended to extend, and that such Notice be also printed in feme one Newspaper of the County, or, if there is no such Paper printed for that County, then in the Newspaper of feme near or adjoining County, Three Times at least, in the Months of August and September, or either of them, immediately preceding the Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be presented.

Resolved, That, when any Petition for a Bridge, or for renewing or altering any Act of Parliament passed for that Purpose, hath been presented to the House, the Committee, to whom the said Petition shall be referred, do examine, in the first Place, how far the Orders contained in the Two former Resolutions have been complied with; and the Chairman of such Committee shall report the Evidence upon such Examination to the House, on the Report of the Petition.

Ordered, That the said Refelu Uops be made Standing Orders of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Calk or Vessel of Pilchards containing Fifty Gallons, and so in Proportion for a greater or lesser Quantity thereof, which shall be exported from any Port or Place in Great Britain into Parts beyond the Seas, between the 25th Day of June 1786, and the 25th Day of June1791, upon which the Person or Persons exporting the same shall be entitled to the Bounty of Seven Shillings, by virtue of, or under, Two fevered former Acts, an additional Bounty of Two Shillings shall be paid.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolution: And that Sir William Lemon, Sir William Molesuorth, Mr. Rashleigh, and Mr. Young, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Owners of Estates and Inhabitant Householders within the Wards of Broad Street and Toner, in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Pay Office is situate within the Ward of Broad Street, and the Navy Office within the Ward of Touer, and the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers belonging thereto, have, ever since the Year 1693, been afi'efi'ed to the Land Tax for the said Wards respectively; and that the Petitioners have heard, that the said Offices are intended to be removed to, and held within, Somerset House, which is situatein the Parish of Saint Mary le Strand, within the liberty of the Duchy of Lancaster, and, if the said Commissioners, Clerks, and Officers, should not continue to be afieffed to the Land Tax for the said Wards of Broad Street and Tower, as heretofore, it will necessarily lay a very heavy and intolerable Burthen upon the Owners of Estates, and Inhabitant Householders within those Wards; and that the Petitioners were not informed, with sufficient Certainty, that the said Offices were intended to be removed to Somerset House so early as Midsummer next, until the Time limited by the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills was elapsed: And therefore praying. That, in Consideration of the above-mentioned Circumstances, and the extreme Hardship of the Cafe, they may now be permitted to present a Petition to the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for afieffing the said Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers to the Land Tax for the said Wards of Broad Street and Tower, as heretofore, notwithstanding the said Offices should be removed into any other Division or Place, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Owners of Estates and Inhabitant Householders, within the Wards of Broad Street and Tower, in the City of London.

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That since the Date of the Estimates presented to this House by the Directors of the said Company, in the Months of February and May 1784, many Circumstances have arisen to occasion material Variations therein, which could not at

03

that Time be foreseen; that, on the one Hand, the Sales of the Company have already greatly ex ceeded the Amount then calculated, and may probably be carried to a stili greater Extent; but, on the other Hand, this Extension of their Trade, and particularly of the Tea Trade, in Consequence of an Act, made in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled,

" An Act for repealing the several Duties on Tea, and " for granting to His Majesty other Duties in lieu thereof,

" and also several Duties on inhabited Houses, and upon " the Importation of Cocoa Nuts and Coffee, and for " repealing the Inland Duties of Excise thereon," has necessarily obliged the Petitioners to advance large additional Sums of Money, and, in order to carry into full Effect the salutary Objects of the said Act, and to secure to the Company the full Benefits which may be expected therefrom, an additional Capital must necessarily be employed to a large Amount; and that the Petitioners being also liable, in Consequence of the outstanding Expences of the War in India, to the Payment of additional Bills to a large Amount, beyond their former Estimates, will be unable to inveit so large a Capital as is necessary, from the Causes above mentioned, without the Aid of Parliament, to enable them to make Use of their Credit in providing such Sums of Money as may be necessary for this Purpose; and that the Petitioners were not able to present a Petition to the House so loon as the Day limited by the Resolution of the House for receiving Petitions for private Bills: And therefore praying for Leave to present a Petition to the House, praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make such Provision thereupon as to them shall seem meet.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " in Consideration " of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said " Petition."

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the Question

It wras resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put;

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies.

Then a Petition of the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, was presented to the House, and read; Containing the same Allegations as the last preceding Petition; and Praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to make such Provision thereupon as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

MnSpeaker’s The Speech of Mr. Speaker, this Day, upon pre-5pe*c ' fenting to His Majesty the Bill for veiling certain

Sums in Commissioners, at the End of every Quarter of a Year, to be by them applied to the Reduction of the National Debt; when it received the Royal Assent.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

Your faithful Commons have passed a Bill, intituled, "An Act for vesting certain Sums in Commissioners, at the End of every Quarter of a Year, to be by them applied to the Reduction of the National Debt;" by which they have manifested their Attention to Your Majesty’s Recommendation, at the Opening of this Session, for establishing a fixed Plan for the Reduction of the National Debt.

By the Unanimity which attended the lait and most important Stage of this Bill, they have given the most ^deciftve Proof, that they have but One Heart, and One ~Voice, in the Maintenance of the Public Credit, and ^rofperity of their Country.

The Public Credit of the Nation, which is the Result *of just and honourable Dealing, is now guarded by an additional Security — And the future Prosperity of this Country will effectually be provided for, when it is con--ftdered, that, for the Purpose of pleading the Cause of the Continuance of this Measure most powerfully with "Bofterity, Your faithful Commons have, to the Justice and good Policy of it, added the Authority of their own Example:

Qui Illejubet.

They have not been discouraged by the Burthens imposed during the lait Ten Years from submitting in the present Time, and in the Hour of Peace, to new, and the Possibility of other, Burthens; their Object being to attain a Situation for their Country more favourable to her Defence and Glory in the Event of future Emergencies.

A Plan lo honourable in its Principle, and so conducive to the future Happiness and Safety of the Kingdom, must be, in the highest Degree, acceptable to the Father of His People.

Under that Confidence, in the Name of all the Commons of Great Britain, I tender this Bill to Your Majesty; to which, with all Humility, Your faithful Commons desire Your Majesty’s Royal Assent.

Martis, 30° die Maii;

Anno 26* Georgii III*11 Regis, 1786.

Fi/her!e*. A Petition of the Merchants and Ship Owners concerned in the Fisheries on the Coasts of Iceland, Shetland, and in the Vicinity of the other Islands and Banks in the Northern Seas, from the Harbour of , was

Presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, 9fdently desirous to promote that laudable Spirit of Ad-vc/iture, in an Attempt to improve the Fisheries of Great Britain, which distinguishes the present Period, the Petitioners have fitted out, at a considerable Expence, Seven Vessels, which are to be employed solely in thoie Fisheries in the Northern Seas, and this, they are hopeful, may in Time be rendered profitable to the Adventurer, and contribute to the general Interests of the Nation, not only as an excellent Nursery for Seamen, But in drawing from the Ocean a Part of that Wealth which it is capable of furnishing to the Indus-tiio«s; but while the Petitioners are encouraged in their pjefent Undertaking by the Prospect of future Reward, they are fully aware of the Disadvantages they mull labour under, and the Hazards they must be exposed to, in their first Attempts to ascertain the Succels of a Scheme of which Experience alone can determine the Utility; and that, as the House has had it in Contemplation to provide Bounties for the Newfoundland, and other Brandies of the British Fisheries, the Petitioners hope that the same Indulgence may be extended to the Fisheries in the Northern Seas, and implore the filtering Protection of the House to their Infant Under-

Vol. 41.

taking: And therefore praying the House to take this Petition into Consideration, and to determine in tb? same as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee who are appointed to enquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Encouragement and Extension.

A Petition of the Importers of, and Dealers in, Wine, Duties 00 in the City of Glasgow, was presented to the House, and Wines, read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, a Bill is depending in the House, for putting Wines under the Laws of Excise; and that the Petitioners are sensible of the Frauds daily committed, to a considerable Extent, by smuggling and adulterating Wines, to the great Prejudice of His Majesty’s Revenue, and the Fair Trader, and while they feel an anxious Concern for every Measure which may have the most remote Tendency to endanger the Constitution and the Liberty of the Subject, they are convinced of the Necessity of applying feme effectual Remedy to prevent such gross Frauds, and will therefore chearfully submit to such Regulations as shall be judged necessary for those Purposes, trusting with fell Confidence in the Wisdom and Justice of the House, to devise such as may effectually secure His Majesty’s Revenue, and, at the same Time, preserve the Liberty of the People, with as little Inconvenieuce to the Fair Trader as the Necessity of the same will permit: And therefore praying the House to consider the Premises, and grant such Relief as to them shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for enforcing an Act, made in the tail Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for the better securing the Duties payable on Tobacco," and for altering the Discounts on the Prompt Payment of the Duties on Tobacco,

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the several Articles of Charge of High Crimes and Misdemeanors against Warren Hastings, Esquire, late Governor General of Bengal.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Gilbert reported from the Committee, That they had made a further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and that he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Articles.

Ordered, That the several Persons who were ordered to attend the said Committee this Day, do attend the said Committee Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

3i0 Mali. A. 1786.

upon the Report which mbs made from the Committee, who were appointed to examine into the Matter of the Complaint made to the House, That one of the Mem*: bers for the Town of Cambridge having offered a List of Commissioners for executing the Land Tax Act for the said Town, whilst the said Lift was in the Ingrossing Office of this House, in order to be ingrossed into the Bill, then depending, for appointing Commissioners for executing the said Act, the said Lift was altered, by several of the Names of the said Commissioners being changed, and falsely spelt, in order that the same might be Mifno-mers, and the Commissioners, whose Names were intended to be inserted, might be prevented from acting in the Execution of the said Act, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

The House was moved, That the said Report might be again read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Resolved, That it appears, by the said Report, That several material Alterations were made in the List of Commissioners of the Land Tax Act delivered in by General Adeane, One of the Members for the Town of Cambridge, after the said Lift had been delivered in by the said Member, and that the said Alterations were made without his Privity or Consent.

Resolved, That any Alteration made in any List of Commissioners for executing any Land Tax Act, delivered by a Member of this House, whereby the Persons whose Names were included in such Lift might be prevented from acting in the Execution of such Act, is highly criminal, and a Breach of the Privileges of this House.

Resolved, That; for the future, every List of Commissioners for executing any Land Tax Act shall be delivered in signed by the Member delivering in the fame, that the said Lift be carefully kept by the Officer to whom the same shall be intruded, and that no Person whatever do presume to make any Alteration in such Lift without the Order of this House, or of a Committee thereof.

Resolved, That every Member delivering in such Lift, shall, at the Time of the Delivery thereof, sign and deliver a Duplicate thereof, which Duplicate shall be kept upon a File, open to the Inspection of any Member of this House.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Graves:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Term and.Powers of Two Acts, passed in the Fifth and Sixth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from Tonbridge to Maidstone, and from Wat's Cross to Cowden, in the County of Kent, so far as the same relate to the Road from Tonbridge to Maidstone; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road leading from the Bottom of Church Lane, in the Town of Newcastle under Lyne, in the County of Stafford, to the Turnpike Road leading from Woor to Chester, near the Town of Namptwkh, in the County of Chester, and from Chesterton, through Audley and Balter ley, to Ghorsty; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and allotting the Open and Common Fields, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, in the Parish of Berwick Saint John, in the County of Wilts; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for paving, repairing, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and Places, within the Borough of Newport, in the Isle of Wight, and for the Removal of present, and Prevention of future, Encroachments, Nuisances, and Annoyances therein; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue and render more effectual an Act passed in the Twenty-first Year of His Majesty’s Reign, for the Encouragement of the Growth of Hemp and Flax in that Part of Great Britain called Englandwithout any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments made by this House to the Bill, intituled, An Act for enabling the Right honourable Charles Philip Lord Stourton, and the Right honourable Mary Lady Stourton, his Wife, the Right honourable Hugh Lord Clifford, and the Right honourable Appolonia Lady Clifford, his Wife, and Robert Butler, Esquire, and the Honourable Elizabeth Butler, his Wife, to charge their Estates at Holrhe, in the East Riding of the County of York, with a competent Sum of Money for the Purpose of improving the lame, and allb to grant Building and other Leases of the said Estates, and of their other Estates in the Counties of York and Stafford.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Resolved, That this House will, at the Rising of the House this Day, adjourn till Wednesday Morning next.

Mr. Rose, according to Order, reported from the Scotch Committee of die whole House, to whom it was referred Distillery. to consider of the Duties now payable upon fermented Wort or Walh, brewed or made from Malt, Corn, Grain, or Tilts, or any Mixture therewith, and also, upon Low Wines, and Spirits, and also, upon Licences taken out by Distillers, or Makers of Low Wines or Spirits from Corn or Malt, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Rates and Duties now payable upon fermented Wort, or Walh, brewed or made from any Malt, Corn, Grain, or Tilts, or from Cyder, Perry, or other Walh or Liquor made or brewed from any Sort of British Materials, or from Worts or Walh made from Melasses or Sugar, or from Foreign Refused Wine, or Foreign Cyder, or Walh prepared from Foreign Materials (except Melasses or Sugar) or any Mixture therewith; and also upon Low Wines and Spirits; and also upon Licences taken out by Distillers or Makers of Low Wines or Spirits from Corn or Malt, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, do cease, and be discontinued, for a Time to be limited.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Yearly Duty of One Pound Ten Shillings Sterling be charged for and upon every Gallon, English Wine Measure, of the Cubical Content of each and every Still, including the Head, which shall be ul’ed or employed for making Low Wines or Spirits from Corn,

Grain, Malt, Tilts, or Cyder or Perry, or other Walh or Liquor, made or brewed from any Sort of British Materials, or any Mixture therewith, or which shall be erected, kept, or used within the entered Warehouses of any Distiller, or Maker of Corn Spirits, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Yearly Duty of Two Pounds Ten Shillings Sterling be charged for and upon every Gallon, English Wine Measure, of the Cubical Content of each and every Still, including the Head, which shall be used or employed for making Low Wines or Spirits from Me-lasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith, or which shall be erefited, kept, or used within the entered Warehouses of any Distiller, or Maker of Spirits, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Yearly Duty of Three Pounds Sterling be charged for and upon every Gallon, English Wine Measure, of the Cubical Content of each and every Still, including the Head, which shall be used or employed for making Low Wines or Spirits from Foreign Refused Wine, or Foreign Cyder, or Walh prepared from Foreign Materials (except Melasses and Sugar) or any Mixture therewith, or which shall be erected, kept, or used within the entered Warehouses of any Distiller, or Maker of Spirits, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Duty of Two Shillings Sterling per Gallon be laid upon all Spirits brewed or made from Corn, Malt,

Grain, or Tilts, or from Cyder, Perry, or other Walh or Liquor made or brewed from any Sort of British Materials, or from Worts or Walh made from Melasses or Sugar, or from Foreign Refused Wine, or Foreign Cyder, or Walh prepared from Foreign Materials (except Melasses or Sugar) or any Mixture therewith, of the Strength of One to Ten over Hydrometer Proof, which shall be imported into England from that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.
