Mr. Phelips reported from the Committee, who were appointed to consider of the illicit Exportation of Wool, Live Sheep, Worsted, and Yarn, and to report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to report the same to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Gilbert Affleck, Esquire, being examined, said, That he was Resident at Boulogne last June and July, and has seen, at different Times, Five or Six of the Smugglers Boats laden entirely with Wool, and for the most Part unwashed; and that he has afterwards seen the same Wool carried out of the Town in Waggon Loads.

Your Committee then called John Anstie, Esquire, who has been Chairman of several Meetings of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Dealers in Wool, held for the Purpose of enquiring into the illicit Exportation of Wool, ever since September 178.4.

And being asked. What Proofs he had in his Possession of the Practice of smuggling British Wool, Yarn, and Live Sheep ? he said. He was possessed of the Informations communicated to him by several Persons examined at the above Meetings. — These Informations he delivered in to your Committee — they are annexed to this Report, in Appendix N* 1.

And being asked, Whether the Manufacturers conceived. that they were injured by the Exportation of such large Quantities of Wool? he said. They do conceive themselves to be essentially injured.

And being asked, What Sorts of British Wool the French covet most to be possessed of? he said, From the Information he had been able to get, he understood they most desire the Combing Wool of England', but he made, no Doubt that they are also desirous of considerable Quantifies of the Cloathing Wool of England.

And being asked. What induced Persons to fell Wool to the Smugglers in Preference to others? he said, The Temptation arises from the higher Price that the Smuggler gives for his Wool than what can be procured from the fair Dealer.

And being asked, What induces the French to give such an exorbitant Price for British Wool? he answered, That there may be various Reasons assigned for this — But, he did presume, from thelateft Observations he had been able to make from the Evidence communicated to him (of which before he confessed himself doubtful of) that it arises from the superior Quality of English Wool, and its being absolutely necessary to the French Manufacturers for producing particular Species of Goods; and that without such Wool (meaning the Combing Wool of England) he had Reason to believe that such Goods could not be produced.

And being asked, Whether he conceived that the Manufacturers of Great Britain were able to consume all the Wool Annually grown in the Kingdom ? he said. He did conceive that they are able to consume afi the Wool grown in general; and, from his own Experience, he was able to say, that they are capable of

Vol. 41.

of Wool, arising from the Introduction of a larger Breed of Sheep, and from the present Mode of Agriculture.

And being asked, Whether if a much greater Quantity of the finer Sort of Wool was grown in England, he apprehended there would be a Market for it, without felling any Part of it to Foreigners ? he said. He spoke with a Degree of Certainty that there would.

And being asked, What Steps had been taken by the Manufacturers to prevent the Exportation of Wool? he said, It was resolved, at the First Meeting, that the Practice did exist, from the Evidence he has produced; — That at the Second Meeting, in December 1784. a Memorial was agreed on to be presented to the Lords of the Treasury, stating the Grievances of the Manufacturers, and requesting that the present Laws might be duly enforced; — That in 1785, Abstracts of the present Laws were published by the Chairman of the Meeting, and distributed into various Parts of the Kingdom; Rewards were also held out to any Persons who would make Discovery of Offences against the Laws in being; — That they continued their Meetings, receiving various Informations, rill about February last, when the Gentlemen of Exeter, and also the Wool Dealers in Kent, requested a General Meeting might be held by the Manufacturers and others in London; at which Meeting it was unanimously determined to apply to Parliament for Relief, by obtaining a Repeal of all the present Laws, and that a more effectual Law might be enacted.

And being asked. What was the Price of the finer Sort of Wool be spoke of? he said, He spoke of Wool worth from Sixteen Pence to Two Shillings per lb.

And being asked. Whether that Wool was worth more now than it was before the American War? he said, That it was worth Three Pence per lb. more now, speaking within Compass; and that the finer Sort of the Combing Wool, that the French are most desirous of, has increased in Price Two Pence per lb.

And being asked, Whether he had received any Account from the Custom House of the Quantity of Wool seized ? he answered, That he requested to be favoured with an Account of all Wool that had been seized in the Years 1784 and 1785, specifying the particular Places where the Seizures were made, and distinguishing those Parcels that were actually condemned, from those that were either given up, or remained in a State of Suspence. — And he produced to Your Committee the original Account which he had received from the Custom House, together with an Abstract, which he had taken therefrom of the Quantity of Wool actually condemned: Which Abstract is hereunto annexed, in Appendix N° 2.

And the Witness added. That he had received within a Fortnight, from a Wool Dealer in Cornwall, who had been employed to communicate Intelligence respecting the Exportation of Wool, an Account of a Seizure of Worsted Yam of about 240 lbs. and about 15 C.wt. more had been rescued by the Smugglers.

He likewise produced Two Letters from France, containing Orders for Wool from; and point-

ing out the Method by which such Wool might be exported.

And he concluded with saying, That, exclusive of the foregoing Fa&s, which were chiefly collected during the Time he acted as Chairman of the Meetings in the Country of the Manufacturers and Dealers in Wool, and others intereffced therein; a great many strong and important Fads and Circumstances had come to his Knowledge since his Arrival in Town, where he had also acted as Chairman of the Meetings held by the Merchants, Manufacturers, and others interested in the Woollen Trade, for the express Purpose of enquiring into the illicit Exportation of Wool, and the several Frauds and Abuses above-mentioned; Which additional Evidence he should be ready to give whenever called upon so to do.

APPENDIX, N* 1.

Evidence and Information respecting the illicit Exportation of Wool — produced by Mr. Anstie.

Mr. Brown.

In the Beginning of August I bought Wool of a Fanner in the South Coast of Dorset. — After weighing, he tells me, Had not the Lugger been taken, Sir, the other Day, this would not have come to your Share. — For Years pall I have fold it to France.

Mr. George Oakley.

I was lately applied to by a Smuggler of Wool; he evidently was not a Judge of the Article — Without enquiring its Quality, he offered me 1 s. per Pound by the Hundred Weight. — I refused, presuming he meant to export it, from the high Price he offered to me; and hinting my Idea, he told me, that was no Business of mine; he would pay me for it immediately.

Mr. Hine.

I have been lately in London, where I met a particular Friend, a Merchant of Ostend. — He allured me, he had been often applied to in the strongest Terms, to buy jEnglish Wool for France — has often seen Quantities at Ostend', at Times 100 Bags together.

Mr. Richard Oakley Read a Letter from a Person at St. Makes, by the Hand of a Smuggler, with Orders for* any Quantity of Wool; at the same time quoting the different Sorts he would buy, and the Prices he would offer, which were considerably higher than the Current Prices; consequently, might be a Temptation to many to fell their Wool.

Mr. Samuel

In Conversation with Mr. Jones of Hastings, a Custom House Officer, Jams informed him, that he had lately seized 20 Packages of English Wool, which were sold by public Sale at Hastings — That One Package, in particular, being marked by him with a private Mark, was bought by a Woolstapler in that Neighbourhood, and mat such Package, so marked by Jones, was. a Second Time feised and brought again into the same Port.

In the Month of June lall, Mr. Reynolds, Draper in Dover, informed said Mr. Wathen, that, being at

Boulogne, in France, he saw Two Vessels come into that Port laden with English Wool.

Mr. Follett.

In July 1783, he saw in C a Ship unloading and that die principal Part of the Cargo, if not

the Whole, conftfted of English Wool; and that the Burthen of such Vessel was about *200 or 300 Tons.

Mr. Boughton Was some Time finee at Dunkirk, and saw a Cargo of English Wool landed.

Mr. William James Has been often applied to to purchase English Wool for France; but refused, knowing the Hazard of such Trade; was told by a Person, that same was a profitable Trade, and that he had lately received about 80 Packs that Way: That he has frequently seen large Quantities of English Wool in FranceThat die Quantity of Wool allowed for Guernsey, Jersey, 8cc. is more than is made ufie of in such Islands, and that the Overplus is usually lent to France.

Mr. Thomas Collins Was lately in Company with a Farmer in the Neighbourhood of Sherborn, who informed him that a Person who came to purchase his Sheep, in Discourse concerning the Price of them, informed him, that if he purchased such Sheep, they were intended to be sent to France.

Mr. Anstie,

The Chairman, having, in a Letter to Charles Baring, Esquire, intimated, that when he was at he was informed by a Person of Reputation, that an English Vessel belonging to a Port in Devonshire had lately been strandea near Cherburgh, loaden with English Wool, and that Ihe had made Two Trips that Season laden with the same Commodity — The following Answer was received.

Mr. Charles;

That the Chance, Captain John Ford, used the Coalting Trade occasionally, and sometimes smuggled: He is supposed to have bought the Wool from Combers, and not from Farmers.

Mr. John Simpson Deposed on Oath, That being in the County of Norfolk to buy Wool, he applied to a Wool Dealer to purchase his Wool: That the Price could not then be fixed, as he was informed another Person was to fee it the next Day: That be was at the Wool Grower's with the said Person the next Day, who purchased the Wool at an advanced Price of 1 6d. per Tod. — After

the Person was gone, Mr. Simpson hinted to the Grower that the Person was a Smuggler, and he confessed that he was — Being alarmed by Mr. Simpson’s informing him what Penalties he was subject to, he declined felling the Wool to the said Person, and Mr. Simpson afterwards bought the Wool at a left Price; and on examining the Wool, it was made up in small Quantities, tied round with Banda — Mr. Simpson was informed, that the said Person had bought Wool, in that Neighbourhood only, to the Amount of 1,000 L Sterling.

The Chairman has received repeated Accounts of Persons felling Wool in the County of Norfolk to Smugglers, though they are not particular enough to be given in.

In June 1784, an Officer of the Customs, on ad

information, seized in The Dawns, on Board The deaoour, Wilburn Elliott, for Dunkirk, 8 Bales, Weight 2,456 lbs. of English Wool — It appeared they were shipped as Slops, and so specified in the Cocket, and consigned to Dunkirk; the Ship was for some Time detained, but at Length permitted to proceed.

Information of Mr. Peter Maber.

That being at Dunkirk a few Years ago, he saw a Quantity of Wool, which, he would make Oath, was of the Growth of England; and that the Malter of the Vessel with whom he returned to England, offered to take any Quantity of Combing Wool from him he could procure, at a Price much superior to what it would yield at the English Market. — That he believes, from the Information he has obtained, that great Quantities of Wool are constantly smuggled to France.

An Officer of His Majesty’s Navy also informed the Chairman, that as he was walking on the Quay at Boulogne, he saw several Bags of English Wool landed from a small Vessel.

And a Lady, who has resided with her Father for many Years at Boulogne, being lately in England, declared, that never a week passed without Wool and Live Sheep being brought into that Port from England.

Mr. Anstie, The Chairman, is in Possession of several Facts that would lead to criminate several Persons; but he is not willing to involve them in Charges for what has been done some Time pad, and therefore he chuses to withhold such Accounts, conceiving that they are not necessary to establish the Truth of what is so fully proved from other Circumstances.

He has been informed, in Confidence, that One House in France has received Wool from England Annually, to the Amount of 50,0001. Sterling, and he can rely on the Veracity of the Information.

On examining at the Custom House, what Quantity of Wool was on Board a Vessel lately brought into Margate, he found that it amounted to above 3,000 Pounds Weight; and as there were Six other Vessels in Company, laden with the same Commodity, that made their Escape, it appears that full 100 Packs were sent off at One Time.

Translation of a Copy of Two Letters transmitted from Mons Del Porte, Merchant at Boulogne, to Mr. Decafour, Wool-comber at Canterbury.

Sir, Boulogne, 31st October 1775.

If you can furniffi me, in a Port of France, such as, Dunkirk, Calais, or this Place, with very fine White Wool of the finefr Quality, I will take One hundred Pounds Weight for Sample — It is for a Manufacture of Breeches Pieces which I have here — but I mult have the very First Quality, combed twice — Can you not easily fend it to Dunkirk or Calais by the Smugglers of your Parts, who go to those Places to fetch Brandy; or else fend it to London by Sea ? — Bales of Stuffs are never examined in England on Exportation — You may make the Tops of a Pound and Half or Two Pounds each; tie them tight, put them under a Press, then pack them as if they were Stuffs, and fend them to London to any Friend of yours who is a confidential Man; or otherwise to Folkstone or Rye — Let them be cleared out as Calimancoes or Stockings — I have at London a Captain of a Ship for this Place, a very l’afe and confidential Man, who would take them on Board after the Rate of Three Pence per Pound.

Answer — and the Price of these Sorts of Wool, delivered in France.

I have the Honour to be perfectly, Sir,

Your moll obedient Servant

Boulogne, 7th Nov. 1775. Since the Letter that I had the Honor of writing you, Sir, last Week, for White Wool, I have found out an Opportunity of getting it over to France. — It will be very easy for you to fend it to Dover; and you will run no Risque in doing it, as you do not export it to France. I will pay you punctually at the Time we shall agree upon, in Bills on London or Paris. — You may esquire my Character of my Friend, Mr. Claris, Silk-weaver at Canterbury. — If you are reasonable, I will take a great Deal of Wool from you in the Course of a Year; if not, I shall take it from others. — Inform me then the very lowest Price at which you will fell Wool by the Pound of France, of 16 Ounces, or the Pound of

A Petition of sundry Merchants and Ship Owners, in Behalf of themselves and others concerned in the Trade to Archangel in Russia, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed a Bill is brought into Parliament, for erectine Four Light Houses in Scotland, One at Kin-nurds Head, or the North Point of Aberdeenshire, the Second on the Island of North Roneldsha, in The neys, the Third on the Point of Scalpa, in the Island of Skerries, and the Fourth on the Mull of Kintire, and that every Ship passing any of those Outward or Homeward-bound, either on Foreign Voyage, or Sailing Coastwise, are to pay One renny per Ton, Vat. 41.

Foreign Ships Two Pence per [Ton, and Greenland Ships, and those on any Northern Whale Fishery, to be excepted; and that the Petitioners conceive, should the said Bill pass into a Law, as it now stands, that their same would be Angularly hard, by subjecting the Ships employed from the East Side of England to Archangel in Russia to pay for Lights manifestly erected for the Use of Fishing Boats and Coasting Vessels; the' Archangel Trade, being conduced in large Ships fel-dom come near that Coast, and consequently are not likely to receive Benefit therefrom: And therefore* praying, That the same Exemption may be granted to those Ships that go and return from the East Side of England to Archangel as to the Greenland Ships, and those on any Norihern Whale Fishery.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for erecting certain Light Houses in the Northern Parts of Great Britain, was committed.

Pawn- A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are

brokers. thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, Pawnbrokers within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceiving the Regulations contained in an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act made in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual Punishment " of Persons who shall attain, or attempt to attain, Possession of Goods or Money by false or untrue " Pretences; for preventing the unlawful Pawning of " Goods; for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned; " and for preventing Gaming in Public Houses, by " Journeymen, Labourers, Servants, and Apprentices," to far as the same relates to the preventing the unlawful Pawning of Goods, and for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned, were beneficial to the Public, they Applied to the House, in the present Session for a Bill to make that Act perpetual, and to consolidate the former Acts passed for regulating the Trade and Business of a Pawnbroker therewith, and to amend and render the same more effectual; and that the said Bill having been rejected in the House of Lords, the Petitioners beg Leave to represent, that the said Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, will expire at the End of this Session of Parliament, and thereby the Petitioners, and others carrying on the Trade and Business of a Pawnbroker, will be involved in all the Difficulties and Distresses respecting the Trade from which they were relieved by the Regulations contained in the said Act, and without which, they apprehend and believe, their Trade cannot be properly carried on; and that, as, from the latenels of the present Session, it may not be practicable to frame a new Act for the full and complete Alteration and Amendment of the Laws in being for regulating the Trade and Business of a Pawnbroker, the Petitioners apprehend, it may be expedient to continue the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for a limited Time: And therefore praying, That, as the Cause for their Application did not aril'e till after the Time fixed by the House for receiving Petitions for Private Bills was elapsed, they may be permitted to present a Petition, for Leave to bring in a Bill to Continue the said Act of the Twenty-fourth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said several Persons, Pawnbrokers within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality.

upon the 4th Day of May last, was made from the Committee appointed to inquire into the State of the British Fisheries, and into the most effectual Means for their Encouragement and Extension, the Resolurions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth j viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bounty which was granted by an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty, and which will expire at the End of the next Session of Parliament, should not be renewed; but that, in the Place thereof, there should be given, on every Decked Vessel of not less than Fifteen Tons Burthen, employed in the Herring Fishery, and fitted out and navigated according to Law, a Bounty of Twenty Shillings per Ton; and that, on. such Herrings as shall be landed from any such Vessel, after such Ju5g- during any One Year, there should be paid a Bounty be affirmed, or after the Rate of Four Shillings for every Barrel of Herrings Twice packed and completely cured; provided that; if the Number of Barrels of Herrings imported in such Vessel shall in any One Year exceed the Proportion of Two Barrels and a Half of Herrings, so packed and cured, for every Ton of the Vessel’s Burthen, there shall be paid, on every Barrel so exceeding the said Proportion, a Bounty of no more than One Shilling; which Inland Bounties of Four Shillings, and One Shilling, as the same may be, shall be exclusive of the Bounty granted on all Herring exported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the more effectual Prevention of Frauds, the Quantity of Herrings in any Cargo, entitled to the Bounty, shall be computed at the Time of their being un-shipped, while they are in the State in which they are denominated Sea Steeks, or Herrings not re-packed, and that Four Barrels of Herrings in that State shall be considered as equivalent to Three Barrels of Herrings packed a Second Time.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, on all such caught Herrings as (halt be

landed from any Boat, or Vessel, not entitled to a Tonnage Bounty, and shall afterwards be properly felted and cured, there shall be paid a Bounty after the Rate of One Shilling per Barrel; and that such Bounty shall be exclusive of that which is paid on Herrings exported.

Offencts in £. Indies.

93a 3° Junii. A. 1871?.

Selection of Men of high Rank, and liberal Education, to determine upon Charges supposed to involve a Variety of complicated Matter, and, had the Act provided such Persons to officiate in the Character only of Jurors, the Petitioners do not conceive any possible Objection that could have been made to them; but the new Judicature has nothing like that separate and distinct Character, which is performed by a Jury — The Tribunal is to consist of a certain Number of Commissioners, drawn by Ballot, from the Members of both Houses of Parliament, to which are to be added Three of the Judges of His Majesty’s Courts, the Whole amounting to Thirteen, of whom Seven (including One of the Judges) are to form a Quorum, and to meet and adjourn, from Time to Time, as they think fit; by this Means the Petitioners conceive the Court itself must be in a State of constant Fluctuation during every Trial, the same Commissioners will not be present at the Examination of all the Evidence, and, it may so happen, if the Trial be long, that the Majority of those present at the Time of passing Judgment may consist of Members that have attended but little, or perhaps not at all, during the Examination of the Evidence; a Court so constituted cannot, the Petitioners conceive, take in all the Circumstances of a Trial, so as to pass Judgment with a safe Conscience; an ordinary Juryman does not venture to pronounce upon the Truth of an Accusation unless he hears the whole Evidence himself; but in this new Court the Two distinct Offices of Judge and Jury (incompatible by the Constitution) are to be performed by the same Persons; the Fast too is to be found by Men who attend partially during the Examination of Evidence; the Judgment is pronounced according to the Effect of the Judgment of the Common Law, by a Court, the major Part of which cannot be supposed, from the Want of professional Knowledge, competent to such legal Decisions; and, the Petitioners observev with Concern too, that from this Court there lies no Appeal; and that the Petitioners submit, with the ereatelt Deference and Respect, that His Majesty’s Courts, before the Institution of this new Tribunal, were adequate to the Trial of all Offences committed in India, without touching, in the smallest Degree, upon the Constitutional Rights of the Subject; and, they further beg Leave to Shew, that, by the 80th Clause of the said Act, " All Writings transmitted " from the East Indies to the Court of Directors, by " their Officers or Servants, in the usual Course of " Correspondence, and Copies of all Writings which " shall have been transmitted by the Court of Directors, or any Committee of them, to their Officers " and Servants in the East , and which in any " Manner relate to the Subject Matter of the Charge <l to be contained in the Information, or the Defence " to be made, may be admitted as Evidence, and not u be deemed inadmissible or incompetent, unieis upon " Objections arising upon the Nature of the Contents of " such Writings, subject, nevertheless, to be impeached, 41 in Point of Credibility, by such Observations and 41 Objections as the Nature of such Evidence, or other " Circumstances, may fugged, any Rule of the Common " Law to the contrary notwithstanding and the Petitioners are apprehendve, that the above Clause admits of too great a Latitude in the Construction of written Evidence, by allowing a discretionary Power in the Court to admit all Writings, of whatever Nature, entered upon the Records and Confutations of the Company, and, among the rest, the Letters of Government, and of Individuals, containing Matters of Representation and Opinion; whereas the Petitioners conceive, that the Admission of public Writings ought strictly to be confined to Orders from the Court of Directors and Government, and Military Orders, proved to have been regularly

04

communicated to the Party at the Time, and those issued by him, if in Command, or in Station distant from the Presidency; with this strict Limitation, such Writings might be received in Evidence, subject to Impeachment in Point of Credibility, according to the Nature of such Evidence, but all other Writings lent from that Country, in the uiual ('ourse of Public Correspondence; ought, the Petitioners conceive, at once to be declared inadmissible; and that the great Distance at which the PeA titioners reside from the Seat of the British Empire, has induced them to Itate their Circumstances under this new Act more at large, and with a more pointed View to the Means of Redress, than they should otherwise have done; they trust, however, to the Candour of the House for their Excuse, and to the Wifdona and Justice of Parliament, and of their Most Gracious Sovereign, for Relief in the Object of their Petition, and they entertain a favourable, and even an auspicious, Hope of Success, from the lacred Motives which have guided them in this Pursuit, and the high Respect with which they have endeavoured to mark their Proceedings: And therefore praying, That the House will vote a Repeal of those Clauses in the said Act of Parliament, which have given such just Cause of Uneasiness and Alarm to the Petitioners, and that the House will grant such further and general Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sop« Manu- A Petition of the Manufacturers of Sope in London, facture. and elsewhere, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Petitioners, confiding in the Protection of the Laws, have erected Buildings, and purchased Utensils, at a great Expence, for carrying on the Maoufacture of Sope; and that the Petitioners, alarmed -at the Depredations which Smugglers and fraudulent Manufacturers have committed on their Trade, and consequently on that important Branch of the Revenue which depends upon it, are impelled by a Sense of public Duty, as well as of private Interest, to submit the following Fasts to the Consideration of Parliament, and beg Leave to inform the House, that those Frauds arise from Two Causes, First, That the Public, at present, finding themselves heavily burthened with the Tax on Sope, as it now (lands, seek to relieve

themselves by encouraging the Smuggling of Irish and other Foreign Sopes into this Kingdom, which they can and do purchase at much lower Prices than the Fair Trader can afford to fell Sope at; and Secondly, That the Duties on Sope cannot be fairly collected from the Country Sope Makers, who, lying dispersedly and at great Distances from each other, particularly in Scotland, . since the last additional Duty on Sope, the Excise Officers cannot visit them above Once a Day, for a few Minutes, and sometimes not so often, so that such Sope Makers can and do Daily commit very great Frauds on the Revenue, which cannot be detested, and pay, in Fast, only what Duty of Excise they please; and that the said Manufacturers of Sope did hope for Relief from an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth of His present Majesty, for the Purpose of enforcing the said Duty, which has not been carried into Effect generally: And therefore praying, That the Payment of the Duty of Excise on Sope in future may be fully and not partially enforced, or that the said Duty of Excise may be wholly discontinued, if it shall seem meet to the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Bicknell being examined, said, That the Petitioner has at a great Expence erected a Manufactory for making Geneva at Maidstone, in the County of Kent, and that he makes the same nearly upon the same Principles with that made in Holland.

Then an Act passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to discontioue for a limited Time the Payment of the " Duties upon Low Wines and Spirits for Home Con- fumption, and for granting and securing the due Payment of other Duties in lieu thereof, and for the better " Regulation of the making and vending British Spirits,

" as well for Home Confamption as for Exportation, and " for destroying all Home made and Foreign Spirits, after " the Condemnation thereof, and for vesting in His Majesty the Duties of Excise within the Lands of " tosh, io the County of Inverness, and for discontinuing " for a limited Time certain Imports and Duties upon " Rum and Spirits imported from the West was

read, whereby it appears that the Petitioner’s Manufactory was exempted from the Provisions and Restrictions of the said Act as therein mentioned, for the Term of Two Years from the First Day of November 1784. Then,

Mr. Biekneli being further examined, said, That llnce Mr. Bishop was again enabled to work by the said Act, he has made great Quantities of Geneva; and that from the ift of November 1784 to the ill of November 1785 he made 69,257 Gallons of Geneva One in Ten over Hydrometer Proof, for which he paid Duty amounting to the Sum of 9,261/. 14 8d. and from the ift of November 1785 to the 16th of March 1786 he made 40,888 Gallons, of the like Proof, for which he paid Duty, 5,220/. 17 s.3 id.; and that there is now in the Course of Payment for Duties from Mr. Bishop, for Geneva made by him since that Time, about the Sum of 2,000l.

And the Witness farther said, That he has fold for Mr. Bishop, at his Warehouse in from ill No-

vember 1784 to ift November 1785, 63,504 Gallons, at One in Seven under Hydrometer Proof, and from ill November 1785 to 24th June 1786, 78,190 Gallons, of the like Proof.

And being asked, Why are the Spirits sold as low as One in Seven under Hydrometer - Proof? he said, The Sale of this Geneva is very general throughout the Kingdom, and particularly in the Counties of Kent, Sussex, and Essex, and on the North Coast, where the People uled to be fapplied with finuggled Hollands Geneva, which is of a still lower Standard — That Mr. Bishop's Customers have therefore always been used to Geneva of nearly that Strength, and that is the Reason why it is lowered — -That Mr. Bishop's Is an increasing Trade, though the Geneva is still not equal to what it formerly 'was, because by the Operations of the Acts from Time to Time parted for regulating the Distillery, he has been prevented from working exactly in the same Way as he did when his Geneva was in its highest Esteem — That from the Nature of the Process, it is importable for him to work, unless the Duties to be paid upon his Spirit continue to be collected agreeable to the Regulations of the before-mentioned Act, but which Act, as far as respects him, is near expiring, and even under the Indulgence granted by that Act respecting the Mode of charg-

ing his Duty, lie still finds it importable to produce a Spirit that may effectually rival the heft Ge-

neva, unless his Exemption be continued, and the Proportion of Wash from which he shall’ be required to produce a given Quantity of Spirit be ftilli farther increased, without which he cannot use the same Quantity of Rye in manufacturing his Spirits, as is used in the Distilleries in Holland, and which is indispensably necessary in the making Geneva that will bear aqy Competition with the Foreign. A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Pepys and Mr.

Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Customs anJ Act for further continuing certain Acts therein men- Excise Law. tioned relating to the further Punishment of Persons going armed or disguised, in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise; and the preventing the committing of Frauds by Bankrupts; without any Amend-« ment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, so far as the same relates to the repairing and widening the Road leading from the River at Szoathling, through Botley, to the Turnpike Road at Sherrill Heath, in the County of Southampton; without any Amendment: And alfc,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing lb much of Two Acts, passed in the Fourteenth and Twenty-first Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, as prohibits the Exportation of Wool Cards of a limited Price; without any Amendment: And allb,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for assessing the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers of the Office for Victualling His Majesty’s Navy, for their Salaries, and the Profits of their respective Offices, to the Land Tax in the Manor of East Smithfield, in the Tower Division, in the County of Middlesex, notwithstanding the Removal of the said Office into any other Division or Place; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable the East India Company to raise Money by Sale of Annuities, and by increasing their Capital Stock; without any Amendment; And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for defraying the Charge of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-six; without any Amendment: And also,

Mr. Wilber force reported from the Committee, to Addrefc; whom the Petition of Doctor Cuthbert Gordon was re- ®^don’* ferred; That the Committee were proceeding to examine uye' the Matter of the said Petition, when a Member present informed them, That he had learned, upon Enquiry from several principal Manufacturers, that the Value and Importance of the Discoveries stated to have been made by Doctor Cuthbert Gordon depended on their being easily introduced into general Practice, which could only be ascertained by a long Course of Experience, and many repeated Trials; and that the Committee therefore did not find themselves at present competent to proceed in the Investigation of the Matter, so as to enable them to give the House any satisfactory Information on the Subject.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, That He will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that an Enquiry be made, under the Inspection and Control of the Committee of His Majesty’s Most Honourable Privy Costncil for the Affairs of Trade and Plantations, into the Faeis respecting certain valuable Discoveries in Dyeing, stated to have been made by Doctor Cuthbert Gordon; and humbly to beseech His Majesty to order such Reward to the said Doctor Cuthbert Gordon, as on due Investigation he shall appear to merit; and to allure His Majesty that this House will make good the fame.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty s Most Honourable Privy Council,

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being- returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission aforementioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills therein mentioned; and also impowering his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Lord President of the Council, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Earl Bathurst, the Lord Osborne, and the Lord Sydney, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act to discontinue, for a limited Time, the several Duties payable in Scotland upon Low Wines and Spirits and upon Worts, Wadi, and other Liquors there used in the Distillation of Spirits; and for granting to His Majesty other Duties in lieu thereof:

, An Act to enable the East India Company to raise Money by a Sale of Annuities, and by increasing their Capital Stock:

An Act for defraying the Charge of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, for One Year, beginning the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-six:

An Act for the further preventing Frauds and Abuses attending the Payment of Wages, Prize Money, and other Allowances due for the Service of Petty Officers and Seamen on Board any of His Majesty’s Ships:

An Act for repealing so much of Two Acts, passed in the Fourteenth and Twenty-first Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, as prohibits the Exportation of Wool Cards of a limited Price:

An Act for futther continuing certain Acts therein mentioned relating- to the further Punishment of Per-i’ons going armed or ditguised, in Defiance of the Laws of Custoni or Excise; and to the preventing the committing of Frauds by Bankrupts:

An Act to revive, continue, and amend so much of an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for allowing a Bounty on " the Exportation of made Cordage, and for

" diicontiriuing the Drawbacks upon Foreign rough " Hemp exported," as relates to allowing a Bounty on the Exportation of British-made Cordage:

have been lost or mislaid, and for allowing them Time to provide Admissions duly stamped; and to give further Time to such Persons as have omitted to make and file Affidavits of the Execution of Indentures of Clerks to Attornies and Solicitors:

An Act for appointing and enabling Commissioners further to examine, take, and state, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom:

An Act for assessing the Commissioners, Clerks, and other Officers of the Office for victualling His Majesty’s Navy, for their Salaries and the Profits of their respective Offices, to the Land Tax in the Manor of East Smithfield, in the Tower Division, in the County of Middlesex', notwithstanding the Removal of the said Office into any other Division or Place:

Adjourn-

ment.

Low Wine* and Spirits.

Ordered, That the said Plan do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Resolved, That this House will, at the Riling of the House this Day, adjourn till Morning next.

An in^rofied Bill to discontinue, for a Time to be limited, the Payment of the Duties upon Low Wines and Spirits for Home Consumption, and for granting and securing the due Payment of other Duties in lieu thereof and for the better Regulation of the making and vending British Spirits; and for discontinuing for a Time to be limited certain Imposts and Duties upon Hum and Spirits imported from The West Indies, was read the Third Time.

'The Amendment following was proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. si- 1. 24. After " together" to insert " except."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Bill, in Pr. 52. 1. 37, by leaving out the Words " including the Bran thereof."

And the Question being put. That those Words (land Part of the Bill;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

The Amendment following was likewise proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 61. 1. 33. To leave out " Four" and insert " Five " instead thereof.

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Fable accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act to discontinue, for a limited Time, the Payment of the Duties upon Low Wines and Spirits for Home Consumption, and for granting and securing

Vol. 41.

the due Payment of other Duties in lieu thereof, and for the better Regulation of the making and vending British Spirits; and for discontinuing, for a limited Time, certain Imposts and Duties upon Rum and Spirits imported from The ffrest Indies.

Ordered, That Mr. Gilbert do carty the Bill to th®

Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty; where his Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills and One Private Bill following; viz.

An Act for settling and securing a certain Annuity for the U fe of Lady Maria Carllon, Wife of Sir Guy Carlton, Knight of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath, and Guy Carlton and Thomas Carlton, Sons of the find Sir Guy Carlton, in Consideration of the eminent Services performed by him to His Majesty and this Country:

An Act to discontinue, for a limited Time the Payment of the Duties upon Low Wines and Spirits, for Home Consumption, and for granting and securing the due Payment of other Duties in lieu thereof, and for the better Regulation of the making and vending British Spirits, and for discontinuing, for a limited Time, certain Imposts and Duties upon Rum and Spirits imported from The West Indies.

An Act; to enable His Majesty to grant a certain Annuity to Brook Watson, Esquire, late CommiflTary General in 1Worth America, in Consideration of his diligent and meritorious Services in that Office:

An Act to limit a Time for the Re-payment of the Duties on Male Servants and Carriages by the Commissioners of Excise, and also on Horses, Waggons, Wains, and Carts, by the Commissioners of Stamps, and for the Amendment of several Laws relating, to the Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise:

An Act for appointing Commissioners to inquire into the State and Condition of the Woods, Forests, and "Land Revenues, belonging to the Crown, and to or alienate Fee Farm and other unimproveable Rents:

Vol. 41.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a King’s Most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses ^Peecb‘ of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I cannot close this Session of Parliament without expressing the particular Satisfaction with which I have observed your diligent Attention to the Public Business, and the Measures you have have adopted for improving the Resources of the Country.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you for the Supplies which you have granted for the Service of the current Year, and for the Provision you have made for discharging the Incumbrances on the Revenue applicable to the Uses of My Civil Government: The most lalutary Eflfefts are to be expected from the Plan adopted for the Reduction of the National Debt; an Object which I consider as inseparably connected with the eflfential Interests of the Public.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Assurances which I continue to receive from Abroad promise the Continuance of general Tranquillity.

The happy Eflfefts of Peace have already appeared in the Exlension of the National Commerce; and no Measures shall be wanting on My Part which can tend to confirm these Advantages, and to give additional Encouragement to the Manufactures and Industry of My People.

And afterwards the Earl Bathurst, by His Majesty’s Command, said.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the 14th Day of prorogued. September next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 14th Day of September next.
